### 206. Cypress Studio — Adding Tests to an Existing Spec Without Full Record Mode

Cypress 15.13.0 expanded Studio so you can add new tests to an existing spec file while focused on a single test — previously the recorder required "record all" mode. This enables targeted test authoring: open an existing spec, find the right `describe` block, and generate a new `it()` via Studio's point-and-click recorder.

```typescript
// Studio workflow — no TypeScript config required; Studio is a UI feature in Cypress open mode
//
// 1. npx cypress open
// 2. Click the spec containing the describe block you want to extend
// 3. Hover over the test name in the left panel → click the "+" icon
// 4. Studio opens a recorder focused on the NEW test in context of that describe block
// 5. Interact with your app — Studio generates typed Cypress commands
// 6. Click "Save Commands" → Studio appends the new it() to your spec file

// Example spec BEFORE Studio (manually written):
describe('Checkout flow', () => {
  it('adds item to cart', () => {
    cy.visit('/products/widget-pro');
    cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-cart"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="cart-count"]').should('have.text', '1');
  });
});

// Example spec AFTER Studio appends a new test (Studio-generated output):
describe('Checkout flow', () => {
  it('adds item to cart', () => {
    cy.visit('/products/widget-pro');
    cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-cart"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="cart-count"]').should('have.text', '1');
  });

  // Studio-generated — review selectors before committing:
  it('proceeds to checkout after adding item', () => {
    cy.visit('/products/widget-pro');
    cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-cart"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="checkout-btn"]').click();
    cy.url().should('include', '/checkout');
    cy.get('[data-cy="order-summary"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use Studio's per-test authoring for adding regression tests for recently reported bugs — you already have the right `describe` block, and Studio generates the selector scaffolding quickly. Review generated selectors before committing; Studio prefers positional selectors (`:nth-child`) when `data-cy` attributes are absent. When-NOT-to-use: complex interactions involving drag-and-drop, canvas elements, or iframes are not recorded correctly by Studio — write those manually.

**[official]** The per-test add capability in an existing spec was added in Cypress 15.13.0 as an expansion of Studio functionality.

---

### 207. `cy.intercept()` `res.setThrottle()` — Skeleton Loader and Loading State UX Testing

`res.setThrottle()` and `res.setDelay()` simulate slow or bandwidth-constrained API responses within an intercept handler. Unlike `cy.clock()`, these operate on actual network timing and combine naturally with `middleware: true` intercepts that apply globally across all requests.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts — reusable network throttle commands
declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      throttleApi(kbps: number): Chainable<null>;
      unthrottleApi(): Chainable<null>;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.add('throttleApi', (kbps: number) => {
  cy.intercept(
    { url: '/api/**', middleware: true },
    (req) => {
      req.continue((res) => {
        res.setThrottle(kbps); // 56 = modem, 256 = slow 3G, 1500 = fast 3G
      });
    }
  ).as('throttledApi');
});

Cypress.Commands.add('unthrottleApi', () => {
  // Re-register middleware intercept with no handler to effectively clear throttle
  cy.intercept({ url: '/api/**', middleware: true }).as('unthrottledApi');
});

// cypress/e2e/loading-states.cy.ts — test skeleton loaders under slow network
describe('Loading state UX', () => {
  it('shows skeleton loader during slow API response', () => {
    cy.throttleApi(50); // 50 kbps — very slow response

    cy.visit('/dashboard');

    // Skeleton loader should appear immediately — before data arrives
    cy.get('[data-cy="skeleton-loader"]').should('be.visible');

    // Wait for throttled data to arrive (generous timeout required)
    cy.wait('@throttledApi', { timeout: 30_000 });

    // After data loads, skeleton replaced by real content
    cy.get('[data-cy="skeleton-loader"]').should('not.exist');
    cy.get('[data-cy="dashboard-content"]').should('be.visible');

    cy.unthrottleApi();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `res.setThrottle()` to verify that loading states (skeletons, spinners, progress bars) render correctly under realistic network conditions. `middleware: true` ensures the throttle applies before any route-specific intercepts. When-NOT-to-use: do not combine `res.setDelay()` with `cy.clock()` / `cy.tick()` — `cy.clock()` controls JavaScript timers, not real network timing. `setDelay()` delays actual TCP stream delivery, which `cy.tick()` cannot accelerate.

**[community]** WHY: A common mistake is expecting `cy.tick(5000)` to skip past a `res.setDelay(5000)` — it does not. `cy.clock()` only controls `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `Date.now()`, and similar JS timer APIs. Network I/O delay is independent of the JS timer queue. Teams using this combination end up with tests that hang for the full delay duration even after calling `cy.tick()`, and cannot understand why the mock time advance has no effect.

---

### 208. TypeScript 6 `verbatimModuleSyntax` — Safe Import Patterns for Cypress Config and Plugins

Cypress 15.14.0 officially added TypeScript 6 support. TypeScript 6 introduces `verbatimModuleSyntax` as a recommended default, which requires type-only imports to use `import type` — otherwise the TypeScript compiler or `tsx` (used by Cypress) throws an error for imports that would be erased at runtime.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — TS6-safe config with verbatimModuleSyntax
// Use 'import type' for any import that is only used as a type

// WRONG (TS6 + verbatimModuleSyntax): value import that is only used as a type
import { defineConfig, ConfigOptions } from 'cypress'; // ConfigOptions is type-only

// CORRECT: separate type import
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import type { ConfigOptions } from 'cypress';

// 'satisfies' operator (TS4.9+) works well with TS6 for config objects
// It preserves the literal type while enforcing the target shape
const e2eConfig = {
  baseUrl:               'http://localhost:3000',
  specPattern:           'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts',
  viewportWidth:         1280,
  viewportHeight:        720,
  defaultCommandTimeout: 8_000,
  video:                 false,
} satisfies ConfigOptions['e2e'];

export default defineConfig({ e2e: e2eConfig });

// cypress/support/commands.ts — TS6-safe global namespace augmentation
// Must include 'export {}' to make this file a module, enabling global augmentation
export {};

declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      loginAs(role: 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'): Chainable<void>;
      throttleApi(kbps: number): Chainable<null>;
    }
  }
}

// cypress/tsconfig.json — TS6 recommended settings
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "target": "ES2022",
//     "module": "ESNext",
//     "moduleResolution": "bundler",
//     "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
//     "isolatedModules": true,
//     "strict": true,
//     "types": ["cypress"]
//   }
// }
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Upgrade to TS6 in Cypress when your project has adopted TS6 in application code — keeping Cypress on TS5 with TS6 app code creates mismatched type-checking contexts. The `satisfies` operator for config objects gives better IDE autocomplete than `as Cypress.ConfigOptions` casts. When-NOT-to-use: if you have third-party Cypress plugins that have not been updated for TS6, they may fail to compile — check plugin compatibility before upgrading.

**[official]** TypeScript 6 support was added in Cypress 15.14.0 alongside Vite 8 support.

**[community]** WHY: The `verbatimModuleSyntax` gotcha surfaces in plugin files that re-export Cypress types with plain `export { ... }` syntax. Under TS6, this produces `error TS1484: 'ConfigOptions' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import when 'verbatimModuleSyntax' is enabled`. The error appears during `cypress run` startup (via `tsx`) rather than during `tsc` if your project's `tsconfig.json` predates TS6 and doesn't have `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` — making it a CI-only failure that doesn't appear locally.

---

### 209. Cypress Cloud UI Coverage — Identifying Dead UI Regions

UI Coverage is a Cypress Cloud feature that maps E2E run interactions to UI elements, identifying which interactive elements have never been clicked or interacted with. It requires no code instrumentation — Cypress infers coverage from the Command Log of recorded runs.

```typescript
// No special code required to enable UI Coverage.
// Quality of coverage data depends on using stable, semantic selectors.

// cypress/e2e/coverage-maximal.cy.ts — patterns that maximise UI Coverage signal

describe('Product page — full CTA coverage', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.visit('/products/widget-pro');
  });

  it('exercises all primary CTAs', () => {
    // UI Coverage tracks which data-cy targets were interacted with.
    // Stable data-cy attributes give Coverage a reliable component identity.
    cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-cart"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-wishlist"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="share-product"]').click();
  });

  it('exercises all form controls', () => {
    // .type(), .select(), .check() and .uncheck() all register as interactions
    cy.get('[data-cy="quantity-input"]').clear().type('3');
    cy.get('[data-cy="size-selector"]').select('Large');
    cy.get('[data-cy="gift-wrap-checkbox"]').check();
  });

  it('exercises navigation tabs', () => {
    // Click every tab to register full tab coverage
    const tabs = ['description', 'specifications', 'reviews', 'shipping'];
    tabs.forEach((tab) => {
      cy.get(`[data-cy="tab-${tab}"]`).click();
      cy.get(`[data-cy="panel-${tab}"]`).should('be.visible');
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use UI Coverage to find dead UI — buttons, form fields, or navigation items never exercised by your E2E suite. Coverage reports are most useful when your E2E suite runs on every PR (recorded to Cloud), so coverage trends are visible over time. When-NOT-to-use: UI Coverage cannot track component-level coverage (only E2E); for per-component branch coverage, use Cypress CT with Istanbul/V8 instrumentation via `@cypress/code-coverage`.

**[official]** UI Coverage is computed from Cypress Cloud recorded runs with no code-level instrumentation required.

**[community]** WHY: Teams assume high E2E test count means high coverage. UI Coverage regularly reveals that 50+ tests exercise the same 20% of the UI surface (the happy path), while error states, confirmation dialogs, and edge-case flows added to the app never had tests written. The dashboard's "never interacted" list is the fastest way to find these gaps without reading every test file.

---

### 210. `cy.end()` Deprecation Migration — Chain-Breaking Anti-Pattern Removal

`cy.end()` was deprecated in Cypress 15.15.0. It was used to break a command chain and yield `null`, signalling "I'm done with this chain." The pattern created confusion because the next command then started from a `null` subject, which was semantically misleading.

```typescript
// DEPRECATED — cy.end() breaks the chain and yields null (Cypress 15.15.0+)
cy.get('[data-cy="items"]')
  .each(($el) => { cy.wrap($el).click(); })
  .end()                             // DEPRECATED: emits deprecation warning in Command Log
  .get('[data-cy="result"]')         // new chain from null — semantically confusing
  .should('be.visible');

// CORRECT PATTERN 1 — start a new chain from cy directly (preferred)
cy.get('[data-cy="items"]').each(($el) => {
  cy.wrap($el).click();
});
// Fresh chain — no ambiguity about the current subject
cy.get('[data-cy="result"]').should('be.visible');

// CORRECT PATTERN 2 — use .then() to sequence actions that must complete before continuing
cy.get('[data-cy="items"]')
  .each(($el) => { cy.wrap($el).click(); })
  .then(() => {
    // Everything here runs only after .each() has processed every element
    cy.get('[data-cy="result"]').should('be.visible');
  });

// MIGRATION SCRIPT — find all cy.end() usages in your project
// Run: grep -rn '\.end()' cypress/
// For each hit, apply CORRECT PATTERN 1 (start fresh from cy) or PATTERN 2 (.then())
// depending on whether the following command needs the previous chain's context
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Migrate away from `cy.end()` before the next Cypress major version removes it entirely. CORRECT PATTERN 1 (new `cy.` chain) is cleaner for independent assertions. CORRECT PATTERN 2 (`.then()`) is needed when the following commands must run after the chain's last command completes. When-NOT-to-use: there is no valid remaining use case for `cy.end()`.

**[official]** `cy.end()` was deprecated in Cypress 15.15.0 with guidance to start new chains from `cy` instead.

**[community]** WHY: The deprecation warning only appears in the Cypress Command Log at runtime — it does not cause a build or lint error. Teams running with `failOnConsoleError: false` (the default) silently accumulate deprecated `cy.end()` calls across their test suite. The first sign of a problem is a `cy.end is not a function` error in a future major version upgrade, at which point every occurrence must be tracked down and fixed. A `grep -rn '\.end()'` in CI prevents this.

---

## Additional Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 26) [community]

193. **`cy.intercept()` never fires for cached responses — browser HTTP cache silently bypasses Cypress's network proxy** [community] — If a resource is served from the browser's HTTP cache (ETag hit, `Cache-Control: max-age` not yet expired), the request never reaches Cypress's network proxy and the intercept handler is never invoked. The test continues, the alias is never matched, and `cy.wait('@alias')` times out. The symptom looks like a race condition. Fix: strip `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, and `Last-Modified` response headers via a middleware intercept in `beforeEach`, or set `cache: 'no-store'` globally on all fetch calls in `window:before:load`.

194. **`cy.prompt()` does not support `cy.request()` — natural-language steps cannot describe API interactions** [community] — Teams that write `cy.prompt('Call POST /api/orders and verify the 201 response')` get a test that tries to visit a URL instead of making an API call. `cy.prompt()` only understands UI interactions (clicks, types, DOM assertions). All API-layer steps must be written manually as `cy.request()` calls placed before or after `cy.prompt()` blocks.

195. **Svelte 5 CT alpha — `$effect` cleanup is not synchronous before the next `cy.mount()` call** [community] — When you re-mount a component (or mount in the next test), Svelte 5's `$effect` cleanup callbacks may run asynchronously. Resources registered in `$effect` (timers, ResizeObserver, WebSocket connections) can overlap between test setups. Add `cy.wait(0)` after `cy.mount()` to yield the JavaScript event loop and allow cleanup to complete before proceeding.

196. **`experimentalFastVisibility` point-sampling is fooled by translucent overlays** [community] — The fast visibility algorithm checks if the element's centre point is visible. A semi-transparent overlay (e.g., a cookie consent banner with `opacity: 0.01`) covering the viewport causes elements behind it to report as "not visible", even though users can click through. The legacy visibility algorithm checked computed opacity and `pointer-events` — the fast algorithm does not. Disable `experimentalFastVisibility` if your app uses loading overlays or cookie banners during test setup.

197. **Cypress Cloud MCP rate limit is shared across all AI tools in the organisation — 100 req/hour depletes fast with multiple engineers** [community] — If your team uses multiple AI coding assistants simultaneously (Cursor + Claude Desktop + Copilot Chat), all MCP tool calls draw from the same 100 requests/hour organisational bucket. A single AI debugging session that repeatedly calls `get_failed_tests` or `get_run_summary` can exhaust the entire hour's quota in minutes. Use targeted MCP queries (specific run IDs, specific spec files) rather than broad "show me all failures" queries, and coordinate usage across your team.

---

## Cycle 27 — 2026-05-14

### 211. `cy.press()` — Keyboard Navigation and Accessibility Testing

`cy.press()` was introduced in Cypress 15.x to dispatch real keyboard events for single keys (Tab, Escape, arrow keys, Enter). It is distinct from `cy.type()` which handles text input sequences. `cy.press()` uses `Cypress.Keyboard.Keys` constants and always yields `null`, requiring a fresh `cy.get()` or `cy.focused()` chain after it.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/accessibility/keyboard-nav.cy.ts
// Test that Tab key moves focus through form fields in correct order

describe('Form keyboard navigation', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.visit('/contact');
  });

  it('tabs through all fields in DOM order', () => {
    // Start focus on the first field
    cy.get('[data-cy="name-input"]').focus();

    // Tab to next focusable element — cy.press() yields null, start new chain
    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB);
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'email-input');

    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB);
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'message-textarea');

    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB);
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'submit-btn');
  });

  it('closes modal on Escape and returns focus to trigger', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="open-modal-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="modal"]').should('be.visible');

    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.ESCAPE);
    cy.get('[data-cy="modal"]').should('not.exist');

    // Focus should return to the trigger element — WCAG 2.1 requirement
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'open-modal-btn');
  });

  it('navigates listbox with arrow keys', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="country-listbox"]').focus();
    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.ARROW_DOWN);
    cy.get('[data-cy="listbox-option"]').first()
      .should('have.attr', 'aria-selected', 'true');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.press()` for accessibility-focused tests that verify keyboard operability — WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.1 requires all functionality be operable via keyboard. When-NOT-to-use: do not use `cy.press()` for text input — multiple characters are not supported and it will throw. Use `cy.type()` for any input involving characters. Also, `cy.press()` does not support modifier combos (Ctrl+A) — use `cy.type('{ctrl}a')` instead.

**[official]** `cy.press()` was added in Cypress 15.x with support for Tab, Escape, Enter, and arrow keys via `Cypress.Keyboard.Keys` constants. It dispatches real keyboard events rather than simulated ones.

**[community]** WHY: Teams initially try `cy.type('{tab}')` for focus management tests and discover it works on `<input>` elements but silently does nothing on non-input elements (divs with `tabindex`, custom ARIA widgets). `cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB)` dispatches the keyboard event at the document level and correctly moves focus regardless of element type — the semantically correct API for keyboard navigation tests.

---

### 212. `cy.prompt()` — AI-Powered Natural Language Test Steps (Beta)

`cy.prompt()` was promoted from experimental to beta in Cypress 15.0.0. It interprets plain-English instructions and generates Cypress commands at runtime, allowing test authors to describe steps in prose. It is strictly limited to UI interactions — it cannot make API calls, manipulate the database, or control timers.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/ai-authored/checkout.cy.ts
// Mix cy.prompt() prose steps with manual Cypress commands for hybrid tests

describe('Checkout flow (AI-assisted steps)', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Manual setup — cy.prompt() cannot call cy.request()
    cy.request('POST', '/api/test/seed', { scenario: 'cart-with-two-items' });
    cy.visit('/cart');
  });

  it('completes purchase as authenticated user', () => {
    // Manual login — cy.prompt() cannot handle auth state
    cy.loginAs('buyer');

    // AI prose steps for the UI flow
    cy.prompt('Click the Proceed to Checkout button');
    cy.prompt('Fill in the shipping address form with valid US address data');
    cy.prompt('Select Standard Shipping option');
    cy.prompt('Click Continue to Payment');

    // Manual assertion for a critical business invariant
    cy.url().should('include', '/checkout/payment');
    cy.get('[data-cy="order-total"]').should('be.visible');

    // AI step for card entry
    cy.prompt('Enter test Visa card number 4242424242424242, any future expiry, any CVV');

    // Manual wait + assertion — cy.prompt() cannot reason about network timing
    cy.intercept('POST', '/api/orders').as('placeOrder');
    cy.get('[data-cy="place-order-btn"]').click();
    cy.wait('@placeOrder').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 201);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.prompt()` for repetitive UI navigation steps where the DOM is predictable and selectors are stable (standard HTML form fields, semantic buttons). It accelerates test authoring for non-technical stakeholders writing BDD-style acceptance tests. When-NOT-to-use: avoid `cy.prompt()` for complex gestures (drag-and-drop, canvas), iframe interactions, and any step requiring `cy.request()`, `cy.intercept()`, or `cy.clock()`. Runtime LLM inference adds latency (~300–800 ms per step) — do not use in smoke suites where speed is critical.

**[official]** `cy.prompt()` moved to beta in Cypress 15.0.0 as part of foundational AI-assisted testing capabilities. It only understands UI interactions (clicks, types, DOM assertions).

**[community]** WHY: The most common `cy.prompt()` gotcha is assuming it can chain with Cypress commands. `cy.prompt('Click submit').should('not.exist')` throws because `cy.prompt()` yields `null`. Every assertion after a `cy.prompt()` step must begin with a fresh `cy.get()`. Teams discover this only after seeing confusing `Cannot read property 'should' of null` errors that look like framework bugs.

---

### 213. `Cypress.stop()` — Programmatic Test Halting for Guard Rails

`Cypress.stop()` immediately halts all pending test execution in the current spec, similar to pressing the Stop button in the Test Runner. It is useful in `before()` hooks where a prerequisite condition is unmet and continuing would produce misleading failures rather than a clear stop.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/feature-flags/premium-features.cy.ts
// Guard the entire spec behind a feature-flag check — stop cleanly if the flag is off

describe('Premium dashboard features', () => {
  before(() => {
    // Verify the feature flag is enabled before running any tests
    cy.request('/api/feature-flags').then((response) => {
      const flags = response.body as Record<string, boolean>;
      if (!flags['premium-dashboard']) {
        cy.log('WARNING: premium-dashboard flag is OFF — skipping entire spec');
        // Halt cleanly rather than failing 20 tests with misleading errors
        Cypress.stop();
      }
    });
  });

  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.loginAs('premium-user');
    cy.visit('/dashboard/premium');
  });

  it('shows analytics widgets', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="analytics-widget"]').should('have.length.gte', 3);
  });

  it('shows export button', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="export-btn"]').should('be.visible').and('be.enabled');
  });

  it('shows AI insights panel', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="ai-insights"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `Cypress.stop()` in `before()` hooks when an environment precondition (feature flag, third-party service availability, DB seed status) makes running subsequent tests meaningless. It produces a clean stop rather than N confusing failures. When-NOT-to-use: do not use `Cypress.stop()` as a substitute for proper test isolation — if individual tests can be skipped selectively, use `it.skip()` or `@cypress/grep` tag filtering instead. Important: `Cypress.stop()` does not run `afterEach` or `after` hooks — ensure test data cleanup is idempotent.

**[official]** `Cypress.stop()` was added in Cypress 15.x as part of programmatic test control improvements.

**[community]** WHY: Before `Cypress.stop()`, teams used `throw new Error('Precondition failed')` in `before()` hooks, which marks the hook itself as failed but still attempts to run all `it` blocks (they appear as "skipped due to hook failure"). The result is a test report showing a hook failure plus N skipped tests — which CI dashboards treat differently than a clean stop. `Cypress.stop()` gives a deterministic "stopped by design" outcome that is immediately distinguishable from genuine failures in Cloud run reports.

---

### 214. `Cypress.ElementSelector` API — Replacing `SelectorPlayground` for Custom Selector Logic

The `Cypress.ElementSelector` API (formerly `Cypress.SelectorPlayground`) was redesigned in Cypress 15.x with expanded capabilities. It lets you define custom selector priority rules and add new selector strategies, controlling what Cypress Studio and the DevTools picker suggest.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts — configure ElementSelector to prefer data-testid over data-cy

// Priority order for generated selectors — first match wins
Cypress.ElementSelector.defaults({
  selectorPriority: [
    'data-testid',   // prefer React Testing Library convention (highest priority)
    'data-cy',       // Cypress project convention fallback
    'id',            // stable HTML IDs
    'name',          // form field names
    'aria-label',    // accessibility label
    'tag,type',      // type-qualified tag (e.g. input[type="submit"])
    'nth-child',     // positional — last resort
  ],
});

// Custom strategy: prefer ARIA role + accessible name for interactive elements
Cypress.ElementSelector.add('aria-role', ($el: JQuery<HTMLElement>): string | null => {
  const role = $el.attr('role');
  const label =
    $el.attr('aria-label') ??
    $el.attr('aria-labelledby') ??
    $el.text().trim().slice(0, 40);
  if (role && label) {
    return `[role="${role}"][aria-label="${label}"]`;
  }
  return null; // return null to fall through to the next strategy
});

// Verify the custom strategy generates the expected selector
it('ElementSelector uses data-testid first', () => {
  cy.visit('/components/button');
  cy.get('[data-testid="primary-cta"]').then(($el) => {
    const generatedSelector = Cypress.ElementSelector.getSelector($el);
    expect(generatedSelector).to.equal('[data-testid="primary-cta"]');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Configure `Cypress.ElementSelector` when your design system uses a non-standard attribute (like `data-testid` from RTL conventions) and you want Studio-generated selectors to be immediately usable without manual editing. When-NOT-to-use: if your codebase consistently uses `data-cy` and the team is disciplined, default priority is fine. Custom strategies add configuration complexity that new contributors must understand.

**[official]** `Cypress.ElementSelector` replaces the deprecated `Cypress.SelectorPlayground` API in Cypress 15.x with an expanded, documented plugin interface for selector strategies.

**[community]** WHY: Teams using both Cypress and React Testing Library end up with split conventions — RTL tests use `getByRole`/`data-testid`, Cypress tests use `data-cy`. When `Cypress.SelectorPlayground` was the API, configuring it to prefer `data-testid` was underdocumented and broke Studio-generated selectors. The redesigned `Cypress.ElementSelector` has a documented plugin API that makes shared selector strategies between RTL and Cypress maintainable across the full team.

---

### 215. `cy.env()` Async Command — Secure Runtime Environment Variable Access

`cy.env()` (async command) was added in Cypress 15.x alongside the existing synchronous `Cypress.env()` getter. The async version is needed when environment variables are resolved lazily at test runtime (from a remote secrets manager or CI vault) rather than baked into the config at startup.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/auth/sso-login.cy.ts
// Use async cy.env() for secrets fetched from CI vault at runtime

describe('SSO login with dynamic credentials', () => {
  it('authenticates with vault-resolved OIDC credentials', () => {
    // Synchronous Cypress.env() — only for values set in cypress.config.ts or --env flag
    const staticApiUrl = Cypress.env('API_URL') as string;

    // Async cy.env() — for values resolved lazily by a setupNodeEvents plugin
    cy.env('OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET').then((secret: string) => {
      expect(secret).to.be.a('string').and.have.length.above(0);

      cy.request({
        method: 'POST',
        url: `${staticApiUrl}/oauth/token`,
        body: {
          grant_type:    'client_credentials',
          client_id:     Cypress.env('OIDC_CLIENT_ID') as string,
          client_secret: secret,
        },
      }).then((tokenResponse) => {
        const { access_token } = tokenResponse.body as { access_token: string };
        cy.setCookie('auth_token', access_token, { httpOnly: false });
        cy.visit('/dashboard');
        cy.get('[data-cy="user-greeting"]').should('be.visible');
      });
    });
  });
});

// cypress.config.ts — plugin that resolves OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET via cy.env()
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      on('task', {
        async resolveEnvSecret(key: string): Promise<string> {
          // Fetch from HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, etc.
          return fetchFromVault(key);
        },
      });
      return config;
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.env()` (async) when secrets are resolved at runtime via `setupNodeEvents` tasks or a CI secrets plugin. When-NOT-to-use: for values known at config load time (static `baseUrl`, viewport dimensions, feature flags), use `Cypress.env()` (synchronous) — it is simpler and does not introduce command queue entries. Never store actual secrets in `cypress.config.ts` or committed `.cypress.env.json` files.

**[official]** `cy.env()` async command was added in Cypress 15.x for runtime-resolved environment variable access from the test side of the command queue.

**[community]** WHY: Teams confuse `Cypress.env('KEY')` (synchronous, returns the value immediately) with `cy.env('KEY')` (async, enqueues and yields via `.then()`). Using `const val = cy.env('KEY')` assigns a Cypress Chainable, not the value — using it synchronously gives `[object Object]` with no error. The only correct usage is `cy.env('KEY').then((val) => { ... })`. This trips up experienced JavaScript developers who expect a getter that looks synchronous to be synchronous.

---

### 216. React 19 Component Testing — Server Component Boundary Stubs

Cypress Component Testing supports React 19 as of Cypress 15.0.0. React Server Components cannot be mounted directly in a browser CT environment — they must be stubbed at the import boundary, similar to how you mock Node.js-only modules.

```typescript
// cypress/component/ProductCard.cy.tsx
// ProductCard imports ProductDetails.server.tsx which uses Node.js APIs

import React from 'react';
import { mount } from 'cypress/react';

// Stub the server component BEFORE importing the client component
// This intercepts the import and replaces with a browser-safe stub
import './stubs/server-component-stub'; // sets up mock via cy.stub() or import map

import { ProductCard } from '../../src/components/ProductCard';

const mockProduct = {
  id:       '123',
  name:     'Widget Pro',
  price:    49.99,
  imageUrl: '/images/widget-pro.jpg',
  inStock:  true,
};

describe('ProductCard (React 19 CT)', () => {
  it('renders product details from props', () => {
    mount(
      <ProductCard
        product={mockProduct}
        onAddToCart={cy.stub().as('addToCart')}
      />
    );

    cy.get('[data-cy="product-name"]').should('have.text', 'Widget Pro');
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-price"]').should('have.text', '$49.99');
    cy.get('[data-cy="stock-badge"]').should('have.text', 'In Stock');
  });

  it('calls onAddToCart with product id on button click', () => {
    mount(
      <ProductCard
        product={mockProduct}
        onAddToCart={cy.stub().as('addToCart')}
      />
    );

    cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-cart-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('@addToCart').should('have.been.calledOnceWith', '123');
  });

  it('shows out-of-stock state correctly', () => {
    mount(
      <ProductCard
        product={{ ...mockProduct, inStock: false }}
        onAddToCart={cy.stub().as('addToCart')}
      />
    );

    cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-cart-btn"]').should('be.disabled');
    cy.get('[data-cy="stock-badge"]').should('have.text', 'Out of Stock');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use RSC boundary stubs in CT when your React 19 component tree mixes server and client components. This lets you test the client component in isolation without needing a Next.js or Remix dev server. When-NOT-to-use: if you need to test RSC data-fetching behavior end-to-end, use E2E tests against the running framework server — CT cannot simulate the RSC rendering pipeline.

**[official]** React 19 support was added in Cypress 15.0.0 alongside support for Angular 21, Next.js 16, Svelte 5, and Vite 6–8.

**[community]** WHY: The most common React 19 CT failure mode is an import chain from a client component to a server component that uses `fs` or `path` (Node.js APIs). The CT environment runs in the browser — any `import` of a `.server.tsx` that touches Node APIs throws `ReferenceError: process is not defined`. Teams waste hours thinking Cypress CT broke their app when the real fix is a module boundary stub. The error message does not mention "server component" — it just shows the Node.js API that failed.

---

### 217. Angular 21 Zoneless Component Testing

Cypress 15.0.0 adds support for Angular 21, including its zoneless change detection mode (`provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()`). Zoneless Angular requires explicit change detection triggers in tests rather than relying on Zone.js to auto-detect async operations.

```typescript
// cypress/component/CounterComponent.cy.ts — Angular 21 zoneless CT

import { mount } from 'cypress/angular';
import { provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection } from '@angular/core';
import { CounterComponent } from '../../src/app/counter/counter.component';

describe('CounterComponent (Angular 21 zoneless)', () => {
  const mountZoneless = (props?: Partial<typeof CounterComponent.prototype>) =>
    mount(CounterComponent, {
      providers: [
        // Must match the production app.config.ts provider — zoneless CT requires this
        provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection(),
      ],
      componentProperties: props,
    });

  it('starts at 0 and increments on click', () => {
    mountZoneless();

    cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '0');
    cy.get('[data-cy="increment-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '1');
    cy.get('[data-cy="increment-btn"]').click().click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '3');
  });

  it('accepts an initialCount input', () => {
    mountZoneless({ initialCount: 5 });

    cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '5');
    cy.get('[data-cy="reset-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '0');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()` in CT fixtures when your Angular 21 app is migrating away from Zone.js. Testing zoneless components in CT confirms they correctly use signals or `markForCheck()`. When-NOT-to-use: do not mix zone and zoneless providers in the same test suite — `zone.js` and `provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()` conflict and produce unpredictable change detection behavior.

**[official]** Angular 21 with zoneless change detection support was added in Cypress 15.0.0.

**[community]** WHY: Teams migrating Angular apps to zoneless mode discover their CT tests hang after interactions — `cy.get('[data-cy="x"]').should('have.text', '1')` never resolves. The problem is that the CT harness was created with Zone.js providers but the component is now zoneless — change detection never runs after the click. Adding `provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()` to the `mount()` providers is the one-line fix, but it only appears in a deprecation log rather than a clear error message, so it is easy to miss.

---

### 218. `cy.intercept()` with `times` Option — Precise Request Limiting for Sequential State Machines

The `times` option on `cy.intercept()` limits how many requests a given intercept handles before the route falls through to the real network. This is essential for testing UI state machines where the same endpoint returns different payloads on successive calls (loading → loaded → refreshed).

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/dashboard/status-progression.cy.ts
// Simulate a job-status endpoint that progresses through pending → completed

describe('Job status polling UI', () => {
  it('shows pending, then completed, then refreshed state', () => {
    // IMPORTANT: Cypress intercepts are matched LIFO (last registered = first matched).
    // Register in REVERSE order so the first real request hits the first stub.

    // Third and subsequent requests → refreshed
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/job/status', {
      statusCode: 200,
      body: { state: 'completed', refreshedAt: '2026-05-14T10:00:00Z' },
    }).as('statusRefreshed');

    // Second request → completed (times: 1 → handled once, then falls through above)
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/job/status', {
      statusCode: 200,
      body: { state: 'completed', progress: 100 },
      times: 1,
    }).as('statusCompleted');

    // First request → pending (registered last = matched first)
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/job/status', {
      statusCode: 200,
      body: { state: 'pending', progress: 0 },
      times: 1,
    }).as('statusPending');

    cy.visit('/jobs/42');
    cy.wait('@statusPending');
    cy.get('[data-cy="status-badge"]').should('have.text', 'Processing');

    cy.wait('@statusCompleted');
    cy.get('[data-cy="status-badge"]').should('have.text', 'Completed');

    cy.get('[data-cy="refresh-btn"]').click();
    cy.wait('@statusRefreshed');
    cy.get('[data-cy="refreshed-at"]').should('contain', '10:00');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `times: N` to model sequential API states without needing a stateful reply handler. It is the correct approach for 2–3 state progressions. When-NOT-to-use: for 4+ sequential states, `times`-chaining requires registering in reverse order (counterintuitive) — use the stateful array pattern from pattern 219 instead.

**[official]** The `times` option is part of the `cy.intercept()` `StaticResponse` interface and has been available since Cypress 7.0.

**[community]** WHY: The classic gotcha with `times` is intercept ordering — Cypress matches intercepts LIFO (last registered wins). When registering state-1, state-2, state-3 in natural order, state-3 is always matched first, making all three stubs behave identically to state-3. The correct pattern is to register in reverse order (state-3, state-2, state-1), which feels unnatural to read. This is the single most reported `cy.intercept()` confusion in the Cypress GitHub Discussions.

---

### 219. `cy.intercept()` Stateful Reply Handler — Response Array Pattern

Instead of chaining `times`-limited intercepts (which have LIFO ordering issues per pattern 218), use a single intercept with a stateful reply handler that shifts responses from a pre-defined array. This eliminates LIFO confusion and is more readable for 3+ sequential states.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts — reusable sequential intercept helper

export {};  // make this file a module for global augmentation

declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      interceptSequence<T>(
        method: string,
        url: string,
        responses: T[],
        alias: string
      ): Chainable<null>;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.add(
  'interceptSequence',
  <T>(method: string, url: string, responses: T[], alias: string) => {
    const queue = [...responses]; // copy to avoid mutating caller's array

    cy.intercept({ method, url }, (req) => {
      // Shift until one item remains — last item is the "steady state" stub
      const body = queue.length > 1 ? (queue.shift() as T) : queue[0];
      req.reply({ statusCode: 200, body });
    }).as(alias);
  }
);

// cypress/e2e/pipeline/build-progression.cy.ts — 4-state pipeline UI test
describe('Build pipeline status', () => {
  it('progresses through all four pipeline stages', () => {
    cy.interceptSequence(
      'GET',
      '/api/pipeline/current',
      [
        { stage: 'queued',   pct:  0 },
        { stage: 'building', pct: 35 },
        { stage: 'testing',  pct: 72 },
        { stage: 'deployed', pct: 100 },
      ],
      'pipelineStatus'
    );

    cy.visit('/pipeline');

    const stages = ['Queued', 'Building', 'Testing', 'Deployed'] as const;
    stages.forEach((label) => {
      cy.wait('@pipelineStatus');
      cy.get('[data-cy="stage-label"]').should('have.text', label);
      if (label !== 'Deployed') {
        cy.get('[data-cy="refresh-btn"]').click();
      }
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the response-array pattern over `times`-chaining whenever you have 3+ sequential states. States are registered in natural reading order (first first), eliminating LIFO confusion. When-NOT-to-use: when each state also requires different status codes, headers, or network delays (not just body), extend the helper to accept full `Cypress.StaticResponse` objects instead of plain body values.

**[community]** WHY: The LIFO ordering gotcha (described in pattern 218) is the most commonly reported `cy.intercept()` confusion. Developers register stubs in natural order and then spend hours debugging why the third stub always fires. The stateful array pattern eliminates the LIFO issue entirely — there is only one intercept registered, and it manages its own state. Teams that adopt this helper almost never file "my intercept fired in wrong order" bugs.

---

### 220. `cy.origin()` Cross-Origin Navigation — Third-Party OAuth and SSO Flows

`cy.origin()` allows Cypress commands to run in the context of a different origin within a single test. This is essential for OAuth, SSO (SAML/OIDC), and any flow where the browser navigates to a third-party login page and redirects back.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/auth/github-oauth.cy.ts
// Test a GitHub OAuth flow — real redirect, real third-party login page

describe('GitHub OAuth login', () => {
  it('authenticates via GitHub and lands on the dashboard', () => {
    cy.visit('/login');
    cy.get('[data-cy="login-with-github"]').click();

    // Browser navigates to github.com — must use cy.origin() for all commands there
    cy.origin(
      'https://github.com',
      // Pass outer-scope data via args — closures do NOT work across origin boundary
      { args: {
          user: Cypress.env('GITHUB_TEST_USER') as string,
          pass: Cypress.env('GITHUB_TEST_PASSWORD') as string,
        },
      },
      ({ user, pass }) => {
        cy.get('#login_field').type(user);
        cy.get('#password').type(pass, { log: false }); // suppress from Command Log
        cy.get('[type="submit"]').click();
      }
    );

    // Back in the app origin after redirect
    cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
    cy.get('[data-cy="user-avatar"]').should('be.visible');

    // Verify the session cookie was set with correct flags
    cy.getCookie('session_id')
      .should('exist')
      .and('have.property', 'httpOnly', true);
  });
});

// cypress.config.ts — required for cy.origin() with GitHub/Google
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    // Required for providers that inject obstructive third-party scripts
    experimentalModifyObstructiveThirdPartyCode: true,
    baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
    chromeWebSecurity: false,
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.origin()` in staging environments with real OAuth test accounts to verify the complete redirect chain. This catches provider-side changes (new 2FA prompts, changed consent screens) that mock-based tests miss. When-NOT-to-use: do not use real OAuth flows in high-frequency CI — provider rate limits apply, and test account credentials in env vars are a security risk. For most CI pipelines, stub the OAuth exchange with `cy.intercept()` + a fixture token.

**[official]** `cy.origin()` requires `chromeWebSecurity: false` and is only available in Chrome-family browsers. `experimentalModifyObstructiveThirdPartyCode: true` is needed for providers that inject frame-busting scripts.

**[community]** WHY: The most common `cy.origin()` mistake is trying to reference outer-scope variables inside the callback. The callback is serialized as a string and re-executed in a separate JavaScript context — all outer `const`/`let` bindings are silently `undefined`. Data must be passed via the `args` option (as shown above). This is not obvious from the error message, which just says the variable is `undefined`, not "closure is serialized".

---

### 221. CI Parallelization with `--parallel` — Optimal GitHub Actions Configuration

Cypress Cloud's Smart Orchestration distributes spec files across parallel machines by historical duration. Configuring `--parallel` incorrectly — wrong `--ci-build-id`, mismatched machine counts, missing `fail-fast: false` — is a common source of test fragmentation and wasted CI minutes.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/cypress.yml — production-grade parallel Cypress CI

name: Cypress E2E Tests
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  cypress-run:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false          # do NOT cancel remaining machines on first failure
      matrix:
        containers: [1, 2, 3, 4]  # 4 parallel machines

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Cache Cypress binary
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/Cypress
          key: cypress-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}

      - name: Run Cypress
        uses: cypress-io/github-action@v6
        with:
          record: true
          parallel: true
          # Append run_attempt — see community note below
          ci-build-id: '${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}'
          group: 'e2e-chrome'
          browser: chrome
          start: npm run dev
          wait-on: 'http://localhost:3000'
          wait-on-timeout: 60
        env:
          CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY: ${{ secrets.CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY }}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `--parallel` when your E2E suite exceeds 3 minutes on a single machine. Four machines is the sweet spot for most medium suites (100–300 tests). Beyond 8 machines, diminishing returns emerge because spec-level granularity limits load balancing. When-NOT-to-use: do not use `--parallel` without `--record` — Smart Orchestration only works when specs are coordinated through Cypress Cloud.

**[official]** Cypress recommends minimum 4 vCPUs / 8 GB RAM per machine and caching `~/.cache/Cypress` to avoid re-downloading the binary on every run.

**[community]** WHY: The most common parallel CI gotcha is setting `ci-build-id` to `${{ github.run_id }}` without `${{ github.run_attempt }}`. When a workflow is re-triggered ("Re-run all jobs"), all new machines join the original run's group in Cypress Cloud — the orchestrator thinks specs are already distributed and stalls new machines with "No specs to run". Appending `run_attempt` ensures each re-run creates a fresh orchestration group. Every team running Cypress in parallel on GitHub Actions hits this eventually.

---

### 222. `@cypress/grep` Tag-Based Selective Test Execution — Smoke, Regression, and Feature Tags

`@cypress/grep` enables tagging `describe`/`it` blocks and running subsets by tag at CI time. It integrates with Cypress 15's Studio and supports simultaneous title and tag grep.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/checkout/complete-flow.cy.ts — tagged test hierarchy

describe('Checkout — complete flow', { tags: '@regression' }, () => {
  it('smoke: adds item and sees cart count', { tags: ['@smoke', '@cart'] }, () => {
    cy.visit('/products');
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-card"]').first()
      .find('[data-cy="add-to-cart"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="cart-count"]').should('have.text', '1');
  });

  it('enters valid shipping details', { tags: '@regression' }, () => {
    cy.visit('/checkout/shipping');
    cy.get('[data-cy="first-name"]').type('Jane');
    cy.get('[data-cy="last-name"]').type('Doe');
    cy.get('[data-cy="address"]').type('123 Test Street');
    cy.get('[data-cy="city"]').type('Austin');
    cy.get('[data-cy="zip"]').type('78701');
    cy.get('[data-cy="continue-btn"]').click();
    cy.url().should('include', '/checkout/payment');
  });
});

// cypress.config.ts — register grep plugin
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import registerGrepPlugin from '@cypress/grep/src/plugin';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      registerGrepPlugin(config);
      return config;
    },
  },
});

// cypress/support/e2e.ts — register grep support
import registerGrepSupport from '@cypress/grep/src/support';
registerGrepSupport();
```

```bash
# Run only smoke tests in CI pre-deploy gate
npx cypress run --env grep=@smoke

# Run tests tagged both @smoke AND @cart
npx cypress run --env grep='@smoke+@cart'

# Run @regression but exclude @slow — comma-separated single --env flag
npx cypress run --env "grep=@regression,grepTags=~@slow"
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `@cypress/grep` to gate CI on test subsets — smoke on every commit, full regression on PR merge, feature tags for canary deployments. When-NOT-to-use: do not use grep tags as the only mechanism to exclude flaky tests — fix the flaky test or use `it.skip()` with a ticket reference. Tag-filtering without a naming convention quickly becomes an unmaintainable folksonomy.

**[community]** WHY: Teams that discover grep tags start retroactively tagging tests and end up with 12 variants of "smoke" (`@smoke`, `@critical`, `@p0`, `@fast`, `@sanity`). Without a canonical tag list committed to `CONTRIBUTING.md`, new tests get inconsistent tags and the smoke suite silently shrinks or grows. Establish a tag registry and enforce it with a custom ESLint rule or CI check that fails if unknown tags appear in spec files.

---

### 223. `cy.task()` Bridge Pattern — TypeScript-Safe Node.js Operations from Tests

`cy.task()` runs arbitrary Node.js code in the Cypress process (not the browser), bridging the test and server environments for database seeding, file operations, and email inspection. Type-safe task definitions prevent silent mismatches between task names and payloads.

```typescript
// cypress/plugins/tasks.ts — typed task registry

import type { PluginEvents } from 'cypress';

export function registerTasks(on: PluginEvents): void {
  on('task', {
    async seedUser(data: { email: string; role: 'admin' | 'viewer' }) {
      const db = await getTestDb();
      const user = await db.users.create({
        email:    data.email,
        role:     data.role,
        password: 'TestPass1!',
      });
      return { id: user.id }; // cy.task() MUST return a non-undefined value
    },

    async cleanupUser(email: string) {
      const db = await getTestDb();
      await db.users.deleteByEmail(email);
      return null; // void tasks must explicitly return null
    },

    async getLastEmail(recipient: string) {
      const email = await mailhogClient.getLastEmail(recipient);
      return email ?? null; // never return undefined
    },
  });
}

// cypress/e2e/auth/registration.cy.ts — type-safe task invocation
describe('User registration', () => {
  const testEmail = `test-${Date.now()}@example.com`;

  afterEach(() => {
    // Cleanup runs even if the test fails
    cy.task('cleanupUser', testEmail);
  });

  it('registers a new user and receives a welcome email', () => {
    cy.visit('/register');
    cy.get('[data-cy="email-input"]').type(testEmail);
    cy.get('[data-cy="password-input"]').type('SecurePass1!');
    cy.get('[data-cy="submit-btn"]').click();

    cy.url().should('include', '/welcome');

    // Type the return value — cy.task() generic parameter for TypeScript safety
    cy.task<{ subject: string; body: string } | null>('getLastEmail', testEmail)
      .then((email) => {
        expect(email).to.not.be.null;
        expect(email!.subject).to.equal('Welcome to the platform!');
        expect(email!.body).to.include(testEmail);
      });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.task()` for any operation requiring Node.js (file system, database, child processes, email inspection). Always return a value — `cy.task()` throws `Task must return a value` if the handler returns `undefined`. When-NOT-to-use: do not use `cy.task()` for operations achievable via `cy.request()` (calling your app's API) — `cy.request()` is simpler and tests the real API contract.

**[official]** `cy.task()` communicates between the browser test and the Node.js process via the `setupNodeEvents` `task` event handler.

**[community]** WHY: The `null` return requirement catches every new Cypress developer. A `cleanupUser` task that does `await db.delete(email)` and returns nothing silently compiles in TypeScript (because `void` is assignable in many contexts) but throws `CypressError: cy.task('cleanupUser') failed with: Task must return a value` at runtime. The team convention of explicitly returning `null` for all void tasks (as shown above) prevents this class of runtime error entirely.

---

## Additional Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 27) [community]

198. **`cy.origin()` callback cannot close over outer-scope variables — serialization boundary is invisible** [community] — The `cy.origin()` callback is serialized as a string and re-evaluated in a separate JavaScript context. Any variable from the outer closure (including `const`/`let` bindings, imported functions) is silently `undefined` inside the callback. Teams spend hours thinking a variable is being mutated when the real cause is the entire closure scope being lost at serialization. Fix: pass all required data via the `args` option: `cy.origin(url, { args: { user } }, ({ user }) => { ... })`.

199. **`cy.press()` yields `null` — chaining `.should()` directly throws a runtime error** [community] — Unlike `cy.type()` which yields the typed element, `cy.press()` always yields `null` because it operates at the document level rather than on a specific element. `cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB).should('be.visible')` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`. Always follow `cy.press()` with a fresh `cy.get()` or `cy.focused()` chain to make assertions.

200. **React 19 `use()` hook triggers Suspense — CT assertions fire against fallback content** [community] — React 19's `use(promise)` hook triggers Suspense boundaries synchronously during mounting. When a component using `use()` is mounted in CT, Cypress may see the Suspense fallback (skeleton/spinner) briefly before the resolved content appears. Assertions placed immediately after `mount()` can match the fallback instead of real content. Use `cy.get('[data-cy="real-content"]').should('be.visible')` with the default timeout rather than asserting on the mount return value.

201. **`Cypress.stop()` skips `afterEach` and `after` hooks — test data cleanup never runs** [community] — When `Cypress.stop()` halts execution inside a `before()` hook, Cypress does not run `afterEach` or `after` cleanup hooks. Any database state or seeded data created before the `stop()` call persists across test runs, causing pollution. Design cleanup to be idempotent and run at the start of `before()` (clean-then-seed pattern) rather than trusting `after()` to clean up after a stop.

202. **Next.js 16 Turbopack dev server injects CSP headers that block Cypress CT script injection** [community] — Next.js 16's built-in Turbopack-based dev server serves scripts with `Content-Security-Policy` headers that block Cypress's injected test script in CT mode. Without `experimentalModifyObstructiveThirdPartyCode: true` in `cypress.config.ts`, CT tests hang at "Cypress could not inject its script" with no actionable error message. Adding the config option causes Cypress to rewrite obstructive CSP headers before they reach the browser.

203. **`@cypress/grep` multiple `--env` flags overwrite rather than merge — `grep` is silently lost** [community] — Running `npx cypress run --env grep=@smoke --env grepTags=@regression` causes the second `--env` flag to overwrite the first entirely (Cypress does not merge multiple `--env` flags). The result is that `grep` is `undefined` and only `grepTags=@regression` is applied, causing the smoke filter to be silently ignored. The correct pattern is a single comma-separated `--env` flag: `--env "grep=@smoke,grepTags=@regression"`.

### 183. IndexedDB Testing via cy.window() and Cypress.Promise  [community]

Applications using IndexedDB for offline storage, draft saving, or large dataset caching require dedicated testing patterns. Cypress runs inside the browser and has direct access to the IndexedDB API via `cy.window()`.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts — typed IndexedDB helpers
declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      clearIndexedDB(dbName: string): Chainable<void>;
      readIndexedDB<T>(
        dbName: string,
        storeName: string,
        key: IDBValidKey
      ): Chainable<T | undefined>;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.add('clearIndexedDB', (dbName: string) => {
  cy.window().then((win) => {
    return new Cypress.Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => {
      const req = win.indexedDB.deleteDatabase(dbName);
      req.onsuccess = () => resolve();
      req.onerror = () => reject(req.error);
    });
  });
});

Cypress.Commands.add(
  'readIndexedDB',
  <T>(dbName: string, storeName: string, key: IDBValidKey) => {
    cy.window().then((win) => {
      return new Cypress.Promise<T | undefined>((resolve, reject) => {
        const openReq = win.indexedDB.open(dbName);
        openReq.onsuccess = () => {
          const db = openReq.result;
          const tx = db.transaction(storeName, 'readonly');
          const getReq = tx.objectStore(storeName).get(key);
          getReq.onsuccess = () => resolve(getReq.result as T | undefined);
          getReq.onerror = () => reject(getReq.error);
        };
        openReq.onerror = () => reject(openReq.error);
      });
    });
  }
);

// In a spec — verify that the editor auto-saves to IndexedDB
it('auto-saves draft to IndexedDB within 3 seconds', () => {
  cy.clearIndexedDB('app-drafts');
  cy.clock();
  cy.visit('/editor');
  cy.get('[data-cy="editor-content"]').type('Draft content for test');
  cy.tick(3000); // advance the auto-save debounce timer
  cy.readIndexedDB<{ content: string }>('app-drafts', 'drafts', 'current')
    .should('have.property', 'content', 'Draft content for test');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use when the app stores non-trivial state in IndexedDB (offline-capable PWAs, rich text editors, large local datasets). When NOT to use: prefer `cy.getAllLocalStorage()` for simple key-value persistence — IndexedDB helpers add async complexity that is not justified for `localStorage` scenarios. Named alternative: `cy.task()` with a Node.js `better-sqlite3` driver for SQLite-backed IndexedDB inspection in Electron apps.

**[community]** WHY: Many teams test IndexedDB features by clicking through the UI and asserting on displayed content, never verifying that the data was actually persisted. The `readIndexedDB` helper lets you assert on the stored value directly, catching bugs where the UI appears to save but the write never commits (e.g., a transaction error swallowed silently by a catch block).

### 184. Service Worker Lifecycle Testing  [community]

Progressive Web Apps register Service Workers for offline caching and background sync. Testing SW installation, activation, and cache serving requires explicit lifecycle control.

```typescript
// cypress/support/sw-helpers.ts
export function waitForServiceWorkerActive(): void {
  cy.window().then((win) => {
    if (!win.navigator.serviceWorker) {
      throw new Error('ServiceWorker API not available — run in Chrome/Firefox, not Electron');
    }
    return new Cypress.Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      win.navigator.serviceWorker.ready.then(() => resolve());
    });
  });
}

export function unregisterAllServiceWorkers(): void {
  cy.window().then((win) => {
    return new Cypress.Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      win.navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistrations().then((regs) => {
        Promise.all(regs.map((r) => r.unregister())).then(() => resolve());
      });
    });
  });
}

// In a spec — test offline fallback served by the Service Worker
it('serves cached page when the network is offline', () => {
  // Visit once to warm the SW cache with real network requests
  cy.visit('/');
  waitForServiceWorkerActive();

  // Simulate offline — all subsequent requests fail at the network level
  cy.intercept('**', { forceNetworkError: true });

  // Navigate to the cached page — SW should intercept and serve from cache
  cy.visit('/about', { failOnStatusCode: false });
  cy.get('[data-cy="offline-banner"]').should('not.exist');
  cy.get('[data-cy="about-heading"]').should('be.visible');
});

// Test that the update banner appears when the SW detects a new version
it('shows update banner when Service Worker has a new version', () => {
  cy.visit('/');
  waitForServiceWorkerActive();
  cy.window().then((win) => {
    win.dispatchEvent(new win.CustomEvent('sw:updateAvailable'));
  });
  cy.get('[data-cy="update-banner"]').should('be.visible');
  cy.get('[data-cy="reload-btn"]').should('not.be.disabled');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use when the app has a registered Service Worker (any PWA). When NOT to use: don't run SW tests against a fully stubbed network — the whole value of the SW is intercepting real network calls; removing the real network defeats the test. Avoid running SW tests in parallel CI workers sharing the same origin, as SW registration is per-origin and workers can interfere. Named alternative: Playwright has a `page.serviceWorkers()` API for more direct SW introspection.

**[official]** Cypress Service Worker tests must run in Chrome or Firefox. The default Electron browser does not fully implement the SW lifecycle.

### 185. Web Worker Communication Stubbing  [community]

Applications that offload computation to Web Workers require testing the message round-trip. Expose the Worker instance on `window` in test builds and spy on its `postMessage`.

```typescript
// In the app (test build only) — expose the worker for Cypress to access
if (import.meta.env.VITE_CYPRESS === 'true') {
  const worker = new Worker(new URL('./data-worker.ts', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });
  (window as Window & { __dataWorker: Worker }).__dataWorker = worker;
}

// In a spec — spy on and assert the message sent to the worker
it('sends correct payload to the Web Worker for analysis', () => {
  cy.visit('/data-processor');

  cy.window().then((win) => {
    type AppWindow = typeof win & { __dataWorker: Worker };
    const worker = (win as AppWindow).__dataWorker;
    cy.spy(worker, 'postMessage').as('workerPost');
  });

  cy.get('[data-cy="dataset-select"]').select('Q1 Sales');
  cy.get('[data-cy="run-analysis"]').click();

  cy.get('@workerPost').should('have.been.calledWithMatch',
    sinon.match({ type: 'ANALYZE', payload: sinon.match.array })
  );

  cy.get('[data-cy="analysis-result"]').should('be.visible').and('contain.text', 'complete');
});

// Test the UI error state when the Worker throws
it('shows error UI when the Web Worker posts an error message', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '**/data-worker.js', (req) => {
    req.reply({
      statusCode: 200,
      body: `self.onmessage = () => self.postMessage({ type: 'ERROR', message: 'Worker crash' });`,
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/javascript' },
    });
  });
  cy.visit('/data-processor');
  cy.get('[data-cy="run-analysis"]').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="worker-error-banner"]').should('be.visible');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use when the app exposes a testable interface to Web Workers in test builds (gated by an env var). When NOT to use: if the worker is a pure implementation detail, test the end-to-end rendered result instead of the internal message protocol. Named alternative: Unit-test the Worker script in isolation with Vitest `experimentalVmWorkers` — faster than a Cypress round-trip for pure computation logic.

**[community]** WHY: Web Worker crashes produce uncaught exceptions off-thread, which bypass React/Angular error boundaries (those run on the main thread only). Without an explicit test of the Worker error path, a crashed worker produces a frozen UI with no visible error message — a silent failure mode that standard error boundary tests never catch.

### 186. CTRF Test Reporter — Full Setup and GitHub Actions Integration  [community]

CTRF (Common Test Results Format) is an open standard JSON format for test results. It integrates with GitHub Actions job summaries, Slack bots, and custom dashboards without the JUnit XML fragility.

```typescript
// Install: npm install --save-dev cypress-ctrf-json-reporter cypress-multi-reporters
// cypress.config.ts — use multi-reporter to run spec and CTRF reporters together
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: 'cypress-multi-reporters',
  reporterOptions: {
    configFile: 'reporter-config.json',
  },
  e2e: {
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      return config;
    },
  },
});
```

```json
// reporter-config.json — BOTH reporters must be listed here
{
  "reporterEnabled": "spec, cypress-ctrf-json-reporter",
  "cypressCtrfJsonReporterReporterOptions": {
    "outputDir": "ctrf",
    "outputFile": "ctrf-report.json",
    "appName": "my-app",
    "appVersion": "1.0.0"
  }
}
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml — publish CTRF as GitHub job summary
- name: Run E2E tests
  run: npx cypress run
  continue-on-error: true

- name: Publish CTRF summary
  uses: ctrf-io/github-test-reporter@v1
  with:
    report-path: ctrf/ctrf-report.json
  if: always()

- name: Upload CTRF artifact
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  if: always()
  with:
    name: ctrf-report
    path: ctrf/ctrf-report.json
    retention-days: 30
    if-no-files-found: warn
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use CTRF when your team needs structured, machine-readable test results beyond Cypress Cloud (e.g., feeding results into an internal BI tool, Slack bot, or cross-project test health dashboard). When NOT to use: if Cypress Cloud already satisfies your reporting needs, CTRF adds configuration complexity for marginal gain. Named alternative: `mocha-junit-reporter` (JUnit XML) is more widely supported by legacy CI systems but is less structured and harder to parse than CTRF.

**[community]** WHY: The `reporter-config.json` must list ALL reporters — putting one reporter in `cypress.config.ts` (`reporter: 'spec'`) and listing only CTRF in `reporter-config.json` causes CTRF to be silently ignored because Cypress uses whichever `reporter` key is set in `cypress.config.ts` and ignores the file. Teams discover this only after a full CI run produces no CTRF output file.

### 187. Angular Signals Component Testing  [official]

Angular 17+ Signals components are synchronously reactive — the DOM updates immediately when a signal changes, making them straightforward to test in Cypress CT without `zone.js` ticking.

```typescript
// src/components/counter/counter.component.ts
import { Component, signal, computed } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-counter',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <span data-cy="count">{{ count() }}</span>
    <span data-cy="double">{{ doubleCount() }}</span>
    <button data-cy="increment" (click)="increment()">+</button>
    <button data-cy="reset" (click)="count.set(0)">Reset</button>
  `,
})
export class CounterComponent {
  readonly count = signal(0);
  readonly doubleCount = computed(() => this.count() * 2);
  increment(): void { this.count.update((n) => n + 1); }
}

// counter.component.cy.ts — Signals CT spec
import { CounterComponent } from './counter.component';
import { NoopAnimationsModule } from '@angular/platform-browser/animations';

describe('CounterComponent (Angular Signals)', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.mount(CounterComponent, { imports: [NoopAnimationsModule] });
  });

  it('renders initial signal values', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="count"]').should('have.text', '0');
    cy.get('[data-cy="double"]').should('have.text', '0');
  });

  it('computed signal updates synchronously when source signal changes', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="increment"]').click().click().click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="count"]').should('have.text', '3');
    cy.get('[data-cy="double"]').should('have.text', '6');
  });

  it('reset signal restores to initial value', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="increment"]').click().click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="reset"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="count"]').should('have.text', '0');
    cy.get('[data-cy="double"]').should('have.text', '0');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use for Angular 17+ standalone Signals-based components. Synchronous Signal updates mean no need for `fixture.detectChanges()` ticks — assertions are immediately consistent after a click. When NOT to use: for Signal `effect()` that triggers async HTTP calls, pair with `cy.intercept()` and `cy.clock()` as with any async test. Named alternative: Angular Testing Library (`@testing-library/angular`) with `render()` is excellent for behaviour-focused Signals tests but lacks Cypress's visual time-travel debugger.

**[official]** Cypress Component Testing for Angular requires `@angular/core` 17+ and `framework: 'angular'` in the `devServer` config.

### 188. Intercepting multipart/form-data Request Bodies  [community]

File upload endpoints use `multipart/form-data`. Asserting on uploaded file contents and accompanying form fields requires parsing the boundary-delimited request body inside the intercept handler.

```typescript
// cypress/support/multipart.ts — lightweight boundary parser
export function parseMultipartBody(
  body: string,
  boundary: string
): Record<string, { filename?: string; content: string }> {
  const parts: Record<string, { filename?: string; content: string }> = {};
  body.split(`--${boundary}`).slice(1).forEach((chunk) => {
    const sep = chunk.indexOf('\r\n\r\n');
    if (sep === -1) return;
    const headers = chunk.slice(0, sep);
    const content = chunk.slice(sep + 4).replace(/\r?\n--$/, '').replace(/\r?\n$/, '');
    const nameMatch = headers.match(/name="([^"]+)"/);
    const filenameMatch = headers.match(/filename="([^"]+)"/);
    if (nameMatch) {
      parts[nameMatch[1]] = { filename: filenameMatch?.[1], content };
    }
  });
  return parts;
}

// In a spec — assert on uploaded file contents and a companion form field
it('uploads CSV with correct filename and row data', () => {
  cy.intercept('POST', '/api/import', (req) => {
    const contentType = req.headers['content-type'] as string;
    const boundaryMatch = contentType.match(/boundary=([^\s;]+)/);
    expect(boundaryMatch, 'content-type must include boundary').to.not.be.null;

    const parts = parseMultipartBody(req.body as string, boundaryMatch![1]);
    expect(parts['file'].filename).to.eq('users.csv');
    expect(parts['file'].content).to.include('id,name');
    expect(parts['uploadType'].content).to.eq('bulk-import');

    req.reply({ statusCode: 200, body: { importedRows: 3 } });
  }).as('importUpload');

  cy.visit('/import');
  cy.get('[data-cy="file-input"]').selectFile({
    contents: Cypress.Buffer.from('id,name\n1,Alice\n2,Bob\n3,Carol'),
    fileName: 'users.csv',
    mimeType: 'text/csv',
  });
  cy.get('[data-cy="upload-type-select"]').select('bulk-import');
  cy.get('[data-cy="submit-import"]').click();
  cy.wait('@importUpload');
  cy.get('[data-cy="import-success"]').should('contain', '3 rows imported');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use when you need to assert on individual multipart parts (filename, per-field values, MIME types) rather than just the response. When NOT to use: if you only need to verify the server's response, use a static stub without parsing the request body. Named alternative: intercept and forward to the real server, then assert on the resulting database state via `cy.task()`.

**[community]** WHY: A server can silently accept a malformed multipart body (missing filename, wrong boundary, incorrect MIME type) without returning an error — the imported data is simply wrong or null. Asserting on the request body in the intercept handler is the only way to catch multipart encoding bugs that the server swallows.

### 189. Cypress Studio AI Assertion Review Workflow  [official]

Cypress Studio AI records browser interactions and suggests assertions based on the observed DOM state. This pattern describes the correct review workflow to prevent low-quality assertions reaching the test suite.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — enable Studio (requires Cypress Cloud project key)
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  projectId: 'your-project-id', // required for Studio AI features
  e2e: {
    experimentalStudio: true,
    baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Workflow: Studio AI generates assertions from recorded interactions
// 1. npx cypress open
// 2. Click the magic wand icon next to a test
// 3. Interact with the app — Studio records cy.get().click() commands
// 4. Studio AI suggests .should() assertions based on visible DOM changes
// 5. Accept, reject, or edit each suggestion before saving

// Quality checklist for reviewing Studio AI assertions:
// ✓ Selector uses data-cy (not auto-generated CSS class)?
// ✓ Assertion checks behaviour (not implementation detail)?
// ✓ Uses .should() — not .then() — for retry-ability?
// ✓ Text assertions use regex for dynamic values?

// Example: Studio AI generated this — reviewed and accepted with one edit
it('adds a product to the cart', () => {
  cy.visit('/products/widget-pro');
  cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-cart"]').click();

  // Studio suggestion (accepted): cart count incremented
  cy.get('[data-cy="cart-count"]').should('have.text', '1');

  // Studio suggestion (edited): was .should('contain', '$29.99') — changed to regex
  cy.get('[data-cy="total-price"]').should('match', /\$\d+\.\d{2}/);

  // Studio suggestion (rejected): asserted on implementation class .cart-item--active
  // Replaced manually with:
  cy.get('[data-cy="cart-preview"]').should('contain', 'Widget Pro');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use Studio AI to bootstrap tests for existing flows quickly, especially when onboarding a large legacy app to Cypress. The recording removes the blank-page friction of test authoring. When NOT to use: don't use Studio AI for security-sensitive flows (auth, payment, data integrity) — always hand-author assertions for these paths where assertion correctness is critical. Named alternative: Playwright `codegen` offers similar recording without a cloud subscription.

**[official]** Studio AI requires a Cypress Cloud subscription and a `projectId` in `cypress.config.ts`. It is not available in offline or air-gapped environments.

### 190. UI Coverage Workflow for Identifying Untested Elements  [official]

Cypress UI Coverage (2024) provides a visual heat map of which pages and interactive elements have test coverage. Use it to prioritise new test authoring.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — UI Coverage is enabled automatically with --record
// No additional config required beyond a projectId
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  projectId: 'your-project-id',
  e2e: {
    baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
    specPattern: 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.{ts,tsx}',
  },
});
```

```bash
# Run with recording to collect UI Coverage data
npx cypress run --record --key $CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY
# View: Cypress Cloud → your project → UI Coverage tab
```

```typescript
// Pattern: after reviewing UI Coverage report, add targeted tests for gaps
// UI Coverage showed [data-cy="language-selector"] had zero test interactions

it('settings page language selector changes the UI language', () => {
  // Previously uncovered element — identified via UI Coverage heat map
  loginAsRole('user');
  cy.visit('/settings');

  cy.get('[data-cy="language-selector"]').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="language-option"]').contains('Français').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="language-selector"]').should('contain', 'Français');

  cy.get('[data-cy="save-settings"]').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="settings-saved-toast"]').should('be.visible');

  // Verify the language persists after reload
  cy.reload();
  cy.get('[data-cy="language-selector"]').should('contain', 'Français');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use UI Coverage for applications with 50+ distinct pages where maintaining a manual test inventory is impractical. Most valuable when combined with weekly coverage reviews to ensure new UI features are tested. When NOT to use: UI Coverage measures which elements are interacted with — not assertion quality or business logic coverage. It is a diagnostic tool, not a quality gate. Named alternative: Istanbul/V8 code coverage (`@cypress/code-coverage`) measures executed JavaScript lines — complementary to UI Coverage, not a substitute.

**[official]** UI Coverage requires `--record` to a Cypress Cloud project. AI-generated test suggestions from UI Coverage are rate-limited on suites with more than 500 uncovered elements.
