## Additional Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 30) [community]

216. **`cy.press(['Shift', 'Tab'])` fires the keys sequentially, not simultaneously — use `cypress-real-events` for true chord behaviour** [community] — `cy.press()` with an array argument dispatches keyboard events for each key in order, not in a true simultaneous chord. For Shift+Tab, this means `keydown(Shift)` → `keydown(Tab)` → `keyup(Tab)` → `keyup(Shift)`, which matches browser native behaviour in most cases. However, some focus-trap polyfills check for `event.shiftKey` being `true` on the `Tab` keydown event specifically, and `cy.press(['Shift', 'Tab'])` may not set `shiftKey: true` on the Tab event in all Cypress versions prior to 15.12.0. WHY: The internal keyboard event dispatch in older Cypress builds constructed each key event independently without carrying modifier state from the preceding key in the array. Always test Shift+Tab focus reversal in a patched Cypress 15.12+ build and verify with `cypress-real-events` if the focus trap library uses `event.shiftKey` checks.

217. **`cy.intercept()` with `forceNetworkError: true` does not trigger `cy.wait('@alias')` reliably in all browser contexts** [community] — When a request is killed at the TCP level by `forceNetworkError`, the request is registered in Cypress's intercept log but the response never arrives. In Chrome 124+, `cy.wait('@alias')` resolves after the connection drop, but in Firefox and WebKit the wait may time out waiting for a response event that never fires. WHY: The Cypress proxy uses different connection-close signalling paths per browser; only Chrome reliably emits a `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` event that Cypress maps to the alias resolution. In Firefox, use `req.reply({ statusCode: 503 })` as a substitute for `forceNetworkError` when you need alias wait reliability.

218. **Zod `safeParse` in a `cy.request().then()` callback does NOT trigger Cypress retry-ability — schema failures appear as unhandled errors, not assertion failures** [community] — When you call `ProductListSchema.safeParse(body)` inside a `.then()` callback and `throw new Error(...)` on failure, the error propagates as an unhandled exception rather than a Cypress assertion failure. This means the Cypress Command Log shows a generic "unhandled error" entry rather than a clear assertion diff. WHY: `.then()` callbacks execute outside Cypress's assertion retry loop — any `throw` inside them is treated as a spec-level error, not an assertion retry trigger. Wrap the schema check in `cy.wrap(body).should((b) => { const r = ProductListSchema.safeParse(b); expect(r.success, r.error?.message).to.be.true; })` to get retry-able, diff-friendly failure output.

219. **`cy.session()` `idleTimeout` is measured from the last time the session was *created or restored*, not from the last test that used it** [community] — The `idleTimeout` clock resets when a session is created (setup function runs) or when it is restored from cache (setup is skipped). It does NOT reset each time `cy.session()` is called in `beforeEach`. If 5 consecutive tests each call `cy.session()` but the session is restored from cache (no setup), the idle clock advances. A 30-minute `idleTimeout` set for a suite that has tests running every 2 minutes will never expire mid-suite, but if a CI machine is paused by a queue and resumes 31 minutes later, the session will be invalidated — triggering an unexpected cold re-login in the middle of the run. WHY: This behaviour is designed to match real-world token TTLs but surprises teams who expect `idleTimeout` to behave like an activity-based keepalive.

220. **Angular CT `fixture.detectChanges()` in a `.then()` callback does NOT schedule an Angular zone tick — changes may not be reflected in the DOM** [community] — When you chain `.then(({ fixture }) => { fixture.componentInstance.user = newUser; fixture.detectChanges(); })` in a Cypress CT spec, `detectChanges()` runs outside Angular's NgZone. For components that use `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`, this means the change detection cycle never runs for the mutated input and the DOM remains stale. WHY: Cypress CT mounts the component inside a Cypress-managed iframe; Angular's zone is patched but Cypress's `.then()` callback executes in the outer Cypress command queue context, not inside the Angular zone. Fix: use `cy.wrap(null).then(() => fixture.ngZone!.run(() => { fixture.componentInstance.user = newUser; fixture.detectChanges(); }))` to execute the mutation inside the zone.

221. **`cy.request()` with Zod schema validation does not catch extra undocumented fields returned by the backend** [community] — Zod's default parsing mode is `strip` (extra keys are silently removed). When you call `ProductSchema.safeParse(body)`, extra fields like `internalId` or `debugMeta` from the backend pass validation without error. This means a breaking addition of a required field that renames an existing one goes undetected — the old field is stripped and the new one fails later. WHY: Zod strips unknown keys by design to be forward-compatible. To enforce strict API contracts, use `ProductSchema.strict().safeParse(body)` (throws on extra keys) or `ProductSchema.passthrough().safeParse(body)` (retains extra keys for manual logging). Use `.strict()` in contract test suites and `.strip()` (default) in UI integration tests where backend additive changes are acceptable.

## Cycle 31 — 2026-05-14

### 231. GraphQL Operation-Name Aliasing via `cy.intercept()` Dynamic `req.alias`  [official]

When a page fires multiple GraphQL requests to the same endpoint, static `cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql').as('gql')` aliases all of them under one name, making `cy.wait('@gql')` ambiguous. Instead, inspect `req.body.operationName` inside the handler and set `req.alias` dynamically so each mutation or query gets its own wait handle.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts
Cypress.Commands.add('interceptGql', (operationName: string) => {
  cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql', (req) => {
    if (req.body?.operationName === operationName) {
      req.alias = operationName;
    }
  });
});

// cypress/e2e/cart.cy.ts
describe('Shopping cart mutations', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.interceptGql('AddToCart');
    cy.interceptGql('RemoveFromCart');
    cy.interceptGql('GetCartTotals');
    cy.visit('/shop');
  });

  it('adds an item and refreshes totals', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-0-add"]').click();
    cy.wait('@AddToCart').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 200);
    cy.wait('@GetCartTotals').its('response.body.data.cart.itemCount').should('eq', 1);
    cy.get('[data-cy="cart-badge"]').should('have.text', '1');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use whenever a page or component fires multiple GraphQL operations to the same endpoint — this is the canonical Cypress pattern for distinguishing queries. When NOT to use: if the same operation fires more than once in a test (e.g., a poll), dynamic aliasing only resolves the *first* match; subsequent requests with the same `operationName` do not re-trigger the alias. Use `cy.intercept()` with a `times` counter and multiple explicit waits instead. Named alternative: `msw` (Mock Service Worker) with the `msw/browser` handler provides operation-level mocking at the service worker layer and does not require Cypress-specific instrumentation.

---

### 232. Svelte 5 Component Testing with Runes (`$state`, `$props`, `$effect`)  [official]

Svelte 5's runes compiler model changes how component state flows. In Cypress CT, mount the component normally but pass reactive `$props` through `cy.mount()`'s `props` option. Use `.rerender()` on the mount result to simulate prop changes and verify derived `$state` re-renders.

```typescript
// cypress/component/Counter.cy.ts
import Counter from '../../src/Counter.svelte';

it('increments $state counter on click', () => {
  cy.mount(Counter, { props: { initialCount: 5 } });

  cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '5');
  cy.get('[data-cy="increment"]').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '6');
});

it('reacts to external $props change via rerender', () => {
  cy.mount(Counter, { props: { initialCount: 0 } }).then(({ rerender }) => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '0');
    // Simulate parent updating props
    cy.wrap(rerender({ initialCount: 10 }));
    cy.get('[data-cy="count-display"]').should('have.text', '10');
  });
});

it('$effect side-effects are observable after DOM update', () => {
  cy.mount(Counter, { props: { initialCount: 0 } });
  cy.get('[data-cy="increment"]').click().click().click();
  // $effect that sets document.title is observable
  cy.title().should('include', 'Count: 3');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use for Svelte 5 projects that have migrated to runes — rune-based components require Svelte 5.x peer dep in Cypress CT configuration (`@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte` ≥ 5.0). When NOT to use: do not test Svelte 5 `.svelte.ts` rune stores in isolation via `cy.mount()` — rune stores run at module level and are not React-like contexts; use `cy.task()` + Node.js import to validate store logic. Named alternative: Vitest + `@testing-library/svelte` is faster for pure unit/rune logic; reserve Cypress CT for DOM interaction and visual rendering assertions.

---

### 233. `cy.intercept()` `before:response` Event for Non-Blocking Response Header Injection  [official]

The `before:response` event fires after the real server responds but before the browser receives it. Use it to inject or modify response headers (e.g., `Content-Security-Policy`, `Feature-Policy`) without changing the response body, and without blocking the request with `req.continue((res) => { ... })`.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts — globally inject a relaxed CSP for all tests
beforeEach(() => {
  cy.intercept({ middleware: true }, '*', (req) => {
    req.on('before:response', (res) => {
      // Strip strict CSP that would block inline test instrumentation
      delete res.headers['content-security-policy'];
      delete res.headers['content-security-policy-report-only'];
      // Inject permissive CORS for localhost API calls during tests
      res.headers['access-control-allow-origin'] = '*';
    });
  });
});

// Per-test: verify that the app correctly handles a specific security header
it('renders without error when Permissions-Policy blocks camera', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/', (req) => {
    req.on('before:response', (res) => {
      res.headers['permissions-policy'] = 'camera=()';
    });
  }).as('homePage');

  cy.visit('/');
  cy.wait('@homePage');
  cy.get('[data-cy="camera-prompt"]').should('not.exist');
  cy.get('[data-cy="app-shell"]').should('be.visible');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `before:response` when you need to modify headers on real server responses without touching the body — it is non-blocking and runs on every response. When NOT to use: do not use `before:response` to modify the response *body* — it is read-only at this stage; use `req.continue((res) => { res.body = ...; })` instead (which *is* blocking). Named alternative: `experimentalCspAllowList` in `cypress.config.ts` is the official way to whitelist specific CSP directives without removing them wholesale — prefer it for production-like CSP testing.

---

### 234. Cypress Accessibility Testing with `cypress-axe` — WCAG Violation Reporting  [community]

Integrate `cypress-axe` to run automated WCAG 2.1 AA checks on every page and component. Configure `checkA11y()` with a custom violation handler to surface actionable failure messages in the Cypress Command Log and CI output.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts
import 'cypress-axe';

// cypress/support/a11y-helpers.ts
export function checkPageA11y(context?: string): void {
  const violationCallback = (violations: Axe.Result[]) => {
    violations.forEach((v) => {
      Cypress.log({
        name: 'a11y violation',
        message: `[${v.impact?.toUpperCase()}] ${v.id}: ${v.description}`,
        consoleProps: () => ({
          id: v.id,
          impact: v.impact,
          nodes: v.nodes.map((n) => n.html),
          helpUrl: v.helpUrl,
        }),
      });
    });
    expect(violations).to.have.length(0, `${violations.length} WCAG violation(s) found`);
  };

  cy.checkA11y(context, {
    runOnly: { type: 'tag', values: ['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa'] },
    rules: {
      'color-contrast': { enabled: true },
      'label': { enabled: true },
    },
  }, violationCallback, true);
}

// cypress/e2e/checkout.cy.ts
import { checkPageA11y } from '../support/a11y-helpers';

it('checkout flow meets WCAG 2.1 AA', () => {
  cy.visit('/checkout');
  cy.injectAxe();
  checkPageA11y();

  cy.get('[data-cy="step-payment"]').click();
  checkPageA11y('[data-cy="payment-form"]'); // scope to form only
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cypress-axe` as a first-pass automated accessibility gate — it catches ~30-40% of WCAG violations automatically (color contrast, label associations, ARIA roles). When NOT to use: do not treat a passing axe scan as a complete accessibility audit — screen reader testing, keyboard navigation verification, and cognitive load review require manual QA. Named alternative: `@axe-core/playwright` provides the same axe scanning if you are migrating to Playwright; for Cypress-specific reporting, `cypress-axe` with a custom `violationCallback` is more CI-friendly.

---

### 235. `cy.session()` with `idleTimeout` — Token Expiry Sentinel via `localStorage`  [official]

Set `idleTimeout` on `cy.session()` to match your app's JWT or cookie TTL. Pair it with a `localStorage` sentinel key written during setup — `validate()` reads the sentinel instead of making an API call, reducing network overhead in suites with hundreds of tests.

```typescript
// cypress/support/auth.ts
const SESSION_EXPIRY_KEY = '__cy_session_expires_at__';

export function loginWithSentinel(email: string, password: string): void {
  cy.session(
    [email, 'v2'],  // bump cache key version when session shape changes
    () => {
      cy.visit('/login');
      cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(email);
      cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type(password);
      cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
      cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');

      // Write expiry sentinel — 55 minutes (5-minute buffer before 60-min JWT TTL)
      const expiresAt = Date.now() + 55 * 60 * 1000;
      cy.window().then((win) =>
        win.localStorage.setItem(SESSION_EXPIRY_KEY, String(expiresAt))
      );
    },
    {
      validate() {
        cy.window().its(`localStorage.${SESSION_EXPIRY_KEY}`)
          .should('exist')
          .then((val) => {
            expect(Number(val)).to.be.greaterThan(Date.now());
          });
      },
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
      idleTimeout: 55 * 60 * 1000,  // evict after 55 min idle
    }
  );
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the sentinel pattern when your `validate()` function makes a network call (e.g., `GET /api/me`) and the suite has >50 tests — the sentinel avoids one HTTP round-trip per test restore. When NOT to use: do not use a sentinel if your app rotates JWT tokens on each request (sliding expiry) — the sentinel will expire even though the real session is still valid. In that case, keep `validate()` as a `cy.request()` call. Named alternative: `cy.getCookie('auth_token').should('exist')` is a simpler validate approach that works for cookie-based sessions without a localStorage write step.

---

### 236. Cypress Module API — Programmatic Spec Runner with `result.exitCode`  [official]

Use the Cypress Node.js Module API to run specs programmatically from a custom CI script, seed databases before the run, and capture structured results. Note: Cypress 15.x changed `result.code` to `result.exitCode` — older scripts break silently.

```typescript
// scripts/ci-run.ts
import cypress from 'cypress';
import { seedTestDatabase, teardownTestDatabase } from './db-utils';

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  console.log('[ci] Seeding test database...');
  await seedTestDatabase();

  let exitCode = 1;
  try {
    const result = await cypress.run({
      spec: 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts',
      browser: 'chrome',
      headless: true,
      config: { baseUrl: process.env.APP_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000' },
    });

    // Cypress 15+: result.exitCode (was result.code in Cypress <15)
    exitCode = result.exitCode ?? 0;

    console.log(`[ci] Runs: ${result.totalTests}, Failed: ${result.totalFailed}`);
    if (result.totalFailed > 0) {
      console.error(
        '[ci] Failed specs:',
        result.runs.filter((r) => r.stats.failures > 0).map((r) => r.spec.relative)
      );
    }
  } finally {
    console.log('[ci] Tearing down test database...');
    await teardownTestDatabase();
    process.exit(exitCode);
  }
}

main();
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the Module API when you need to orchestrate database seeding, third-party service mocking, or artifact collection *around* a Cypress run from a single Node.js process. When NOT to use: do not use the Module API for parallel CI runs managed by Cypress Cloud — it bypasses Smart Orchestration load balancing. Let `cypress run --record` handle parallelization and use the Module API only for single-machine custom orchestration. Named alternative: `cypress-io/github-action` handles setup/teardown via `start` and `wait-on` options and is simpler for standard CI pipelines without custom seeding needs.

---

### 237. `cy.intercept()` `times` Option — Deterministic One-Shot Stubs  [official]

The `times` option on `cy.intercept()` limits how many requests a stub handles before falling through to the real server. This enables a "first call returns error, subsequent calls succeed" pattern that simulates transient backend failures without permanently stubbing the endpoint.

```typescript
describe('Retry on 503 — transient failure recovery', () => {
  it('retries the request after a transient 503 and succeeds', () => {
    // First request → 503
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/dashboard', { statusCode: 503, times: 1 }).as('failedLoad');
    // All subsequent requests → real server (or a success stub)
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/dashboard', { fixture: 'dashboard.json' }).as('successLoad');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.wait('@failedLoad');

    // App should auto-retry within 3 seconds (retry logic is in the SUT)
    cy.wait('@successLoad', { timeout: 10_000 });
    cy.get('[data-cy="dashboard-content"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="error-banner"]').should('not.exist');
  });

  it('shows persistent error after 3 consecutive 503s', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/dashboard', { statusCode: 503, times: 3 }).as('failedLoad');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    // Wait for all 3 retries to exhaust
    cy.wait('@failedLoad');
    cy.wait('@failedLoad');
    cy.wait('@failedLoad');

    cy.get('[data-cy="error-banner"]').should('be.visible').and('contain.text', 'Service unavailable');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `times: N` when testing retry logic, circuit breakers, or progressive backoff — it is the cleanest way to simulate N failures followed by recovery without manually toggling stubs. When NOT to use: do not rely on `times` ordering when multiple `cy.intercept()` calls match the same URL — Cypress matches in reverse-declaration order (last declared wins). Declare the "success" stub first and the "failure" stub second so the failure handler takes precedence for the first N calls. Named alternative: A stateful `cy.task()` counter in the Node.js process lets you control stub responses with arbitrary server-side logic, which is more flexible but more verbose.

---

### 238. Component Testing with React 19 `use()` Hook and Suspense Boundaries  [official]

React 19's `use()` hook reads from Promises and Context inside render. In Cypress CT, wrap the component in a `Suspense` boundary in the `cy.mount()` call, and stub the data Promise using a resolved/pending Promise passed through a Provider to avoid real network calls in component tests.

```typescript
// cypress/component/UserProfile.cy.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import UserProfile from '../../src/UserProfile';
import { UserDataContext } from '../../src/UserDataContext';

const mockUser = { id: '1', name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' };

it('renders user data from use() hook', () => {
  // Provide a resolved Promise so use() returns immediately
  const resolvedPromise = Promise.resolve(mockUser);

  cy.mount(
    <UserDataContext.Provider value={resolvedPromise}>
      <Suspense fallback={<div data-cy="loading">Loading…</div>}>
        <UserProfile />
      </Suspense>
    </UserDataContext.Provider>
  );

  cy.get('[data-cy="user-name"]').should('have.text', 'Alice');
  cy.get('[data-cy="user-role"]').should('have.text', 'admin');
  cy.get('[data-cy="loading"]').should('not.exist');
});

it('shows Suspense fallback while Promise is pending', () => {
  let resolveUser!: (u: typeof mockUser) => void;
  const pendingPromise = new Promise<typeof mockUser>((res) => { resolveUser = res; });

  cy.mount(
    <UserDataContext.Provider value={pendingPromise}>
      <Suspense fallback={<div data-cy="loading">Loading…</div>}>
        <UserProfile />
      </Suspense>
    </UserDataContext.Provider>
  );

  cy.get('[data-cy="loading"]').should('be.visible');
  cy.wrap(null).then(() => resolveUser(mockUser));
  cy.get('[data-cy="user-name"]').should('have.text', 'Alice');
  cy.get('[data-cy="loading"]').should('not.exist');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use this pattern to test loading/error/success states of React 19 `use()`-based components without mocking network requests at the HTTP layer. When NOT to use: do not use a real `fetch()` call inside the mounted component in CT — it will hit the real backend or fail with a CORS error. Always provide the data Promise through a Context or prop. Named alternative: `cy.intercept()` at the HTTP level is simpler for integration tests where you want to test the full data-fetching path; the Context/Promise pattern above is for pure component-level unit tests.

---

### 239. `cy.task()` Typed Task Map — Null Return Enforcement  [official]

Define a `TaskMap` interface in a shared types file to get TypeScript autocomplete and type safety for `cy.task<T>()` calls. Enforce the Cypress rule that tasks must return `null` (not `undefined`) by adding a typed wrapper in `cypress.config.ts`.

```typescript
// cypress/support/task-types.ts
export interface TaskMap {
  'db:seed': (scenario: string) => null;
  'db:reset': () => null;
  'file:read': (path: string) => string;
  'email:get': (address: string) => { subject: string; html: string } | null;
  'redis:flush': () => null;
}

// cypress/support/commands.ts — typed cy.task wrapper
declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      task<K extends keyof TaskMap>(
        event: K,
        arg?: Parameters<TaskMap[K]>[0],
        options?: Partial<Timeoutable>
      ): Chainable<ReturnType<TaskMap[K]>>;
    }
  }
}

// cypress.config.ts — every task implementation must return null, NOT undefined
import type { TaskMap } from './cypress/support/task-types';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    setupNodeEvents(on) {
      on('task', {
        'db:seed': async (scenario: string) => { await seedDb(scenario); return null; },
        'db:reset': async () => { await resetDb(); return null; },
        'file:read': (path: string) => fs.readFileSync(path, 'utf-8'),
        'email:get': async (address: string) => fetchLatestEmail(address),
        'redis:flush': async () => { await redis.flushAll(); return null; },
      } satisfies { [K in keyof TaskMap]: (arg: Parameters<TaskMap[K]>[0]) => ReturnType<TaskMap[K]> | Promise<ReturnType<TaskMap[K]>> });
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the typed `TaskMap` pattern in TypeScript projects with >5 tasks — it eliminates `cy.task('db:seed', undefined)` typos and provides IDE autocomplete. When NOT to use: do not add the typed `task` override to `Chainable` if your project uses `@cypress/grep` or other plugins that extend `cy.task` — the interface extension may conflict with the plugin's typings. Named alternative: a plain `cy.wrap(callApi(...)).as('data')` pattern avoids `cy.task()` entirely for tasks that can be expressed as HTTP calls in tests.

---

### 240. `cy.clock()` + `cy.tick()` — Deterministic Debounce and Token Expiry Testing  [official]

Control the JavaScript clock with `cy.clock()` to test debounced inputs, timer-based UI updates, and JWT expiry flows without real `setTimeout` delays. Always call `cy.clock()` before `cy.visit()` to ensure the app's timers are patched from startup.

```typescript
describe('Search debounce — 300ms delay', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.clock();  // freeze time at current timestamp
    cy.visit('/search');
  });

  it('does NOT fire search API until 300ms after last keystroke', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/search*').as('search');
    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('cyp');

    // Advance 200ms — debounce should NOT have fired yet
    cy.tick(200);
    cy.get('@search.all').should('have.length', 0);

    // Advance another 150ms — total 350ms past last keystroke
    cy.tick(150);
    cy.wait('@search').its('request.url').should('include', 'q=cyp');
  });

  it('resets debounce timer on additional keystrokes', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/search*').as('search');
    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('c');
    cy.tick(200);
    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('y');  // resets timer
    cy.tick(200);
    cy.get('@search.all').should('have.length', 0);  // still no call
    cy.tick(150);
    cy.wait('@search').its('request.url').should('include', 'q=cy');
  });
});

describe('Session expiry banner — JWT TTL simulation', () => {
  it('shows expiry warning 5 minutes before session ends', () => {
    const nowMs = Date.now();
    cy.clock(nowMs);
    cy.visit('/dashboard');

    // Jump to 55 minutes in — 5 minutes before 60-min JWT expiry
    cy.tick(55 * 60 * 1000);
    cy.get('[data-cy="session-warning"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="session-warning"]').should('contain.text', '5 minutes');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.clock()` + `cy.tick()` for any timer-dependent behaviour — it converts non-deterministic waits into instant assertions. When NOT to use: `cy.clock()` does not control `performance.now()` (used by some animation frameworks and Web Animations API) — animations timed with `requestAnimationFrame` based on `performance.now()` will not be controlled. Named alternative: for `setInterval`-heavy polling, consider stubbing the polling mechanism itself with `cy.stub()` and triggering it manually rather than ticking through each interval.

---

### 241. `cy.intercept()` Middleware Pattern — Global Request Header Injection  [official]

Declare a `{ middleware: true }` intercept in `beforeEach` to inject headers into every outgoing request (e.g., feature flags, test correlation IDs, `X-Cypress-Test` headers) without touching individual test intercepts.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts
beforeEach(() => {
  const correlationId = Cypress.currentTest.titlePath.join(' > ');

  cy.intercept({ middleware: true }, /^(?!.*__cypress).*$/, (req) => {
    req.headers['x-cypress-test-id'] = Cypress.currentTest.title;
    req.headers['x-correlation-id'] = correlationId;
    req.headers['x-cypress-run'] = Cypress.env('CI_RUN_ID') ?? 'local';
  });
});

// cypress/e2e/feature-flag.cy.ts
describe('Feature flag: new checkout', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Layer a feature-flag header on top of the middleware injector
    cy.intercept({ middleware: true }, '/api/**', (req) => {
      req.headers['x-feature-flags'] = JSON.stringify({ newCheckout: true });
    });
    cy.visit('/checkout');
  });

  it('renders new checkout UI when flag is enabled', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="new-checkout-form"]').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('falls back to old checkout when flag is disabled', () => {
    cy.intercept({ middleware: true }, '/api/**', (req) => {
      req.headers['x-feature-flags'] = JSON.stringify({ newCheckout: false });
    });
    cy.reload();
    cy.get('[data-cy="legacy-checkout-form"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use middleware intercepts for cross-cutting concerns that apply to every test (correlation IDs, auth tokens injected via header, feature-flag headers) — they compose cleanly with specific per-test intercepts without override conflicts. When NOT to use: do not use `middleware: true` with a broad `'**'` URL pattern when also modifying request bodies — middleware intercepts run for all requests including Cypress internal paths. Always use a negative regex to exclude `/__cypress/` paths. Named alternative: per-test `cy.intercept()` declarations are more explicit but create duplication; middleware intercepts are the idiomatic DRY approach for global header injection.

---

### 242. Cypress Cloud `autoCancelAfterFailures` — Fail-Fast Smart Orchestration  [official]

Configure `autoCancelAfterFailures` in `cypress.config.ts` to cancel a Cloud run after N sequential test failures. This reduces CI cost on catastrophically broken builds (e.g., app fails to start) that would otherwise run thousands of tests before timing out.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  projectId: 'abc123',  // Cypress Cloud project ID
  e2e: {
    autoCancelAfterFailures: 5,  // cancel after 5 consecutive failures
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      // In interactive open mode, disable auto-cancel for debugging
      if (!config.isTextTerminal) {
        return { ...config, autoCancelAfterFailures: false };
      }
      // Allow per-job override from CI environment
      const threshold = Number(config.env['CANCEL_AFTER'] ?? 5);
      return { ...config, autoCancelAfterFailures: threshold };
    },
  },
});

// GitHub Actions — vary cancel threshold by suite type
// jobs:
//   smoke:
//     env:
//       CYPRESS_CANCEL_AFTER: 2   # cancel immediately on 2 failures in smoke
//   regression:
//     env:
//       CYPRESS_CANCEL_AFTER: 20  # tolerate more failures in nightly regression
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `autoCancelAfterFailures` on projects where a broken build causes cascade failures (e.g., authentication is broken and every test that calls `loginAsUser()` fails). It prevents paying for 500 test failures when 1 root cause exists. When NOT to use: do not use auto-cancel for acceptance/regression suites where failures are expected to be isolated — a single flaky test should not cancel a 2-hour regression run. Set the threshold proportional to your expected flake rate. Named alternative: Cypress Cloud "Spec Prioritization" reorders specs to run the most-likely-to-fail specs first; combine both features for the fastest fail-fast CI feedback loop.

---

### 243. `cy.origin()` Cookie Bridge for Subdomain SSO Flows  [official]

When an app uses SSO that sets cookies on a parent domain (e.g., `.example.com`) before redirecting to `app.example.com`, use `cy.origin()` to navigate to the auth domain, perform login, and then verify cookies propagate to the app subdomain. Pass credentials through `cy.origin()` `args` (plain serializable objects only).

```typescript
// cypress/support/sso-auth.ts
export function loginViaSso(username: string, password: string): void {
  const authDomain = Cypress.env('SSO_DOMAIN') as string;
  const appDomain = Cypress.env('APP_BASE_URL') as string;

  cy.session([username, 'sso-v1'], () => {
    cy.visit(`${appDomain}/login`);
    // App redirects to SSO domain
    cy.origin(authDomain, { args: { username, password } }, ({ username, password }) => {
      cy.get('[name="username"]').type(username);
      cy.get('[name="password"]').type(password);
      cy.get('[type="submit"]').click();
    });
    // After SSO redirect we are back on app domain
    cy.url().should('include', appDomain);
    cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
  }, {
    validate() {
      cy.getCookie('sso_token').should('exist');
    },
    cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
  });
}

// cypress/e2e/sso-login.cy.ts
it('authenticates via SSO and lands on dashboard', () => {
  loginViaSso('testuser', Cypress.env('SSO_PASS'));
  cy.visit('/dashboard');
  cy.get('[data-cy="welcome-banner"]').should('contain.text', 'testuser');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the `cy.origin()` + `cy.session()` combination for SSO flows — it is the only supported Cypress approach since Chrome deprecated `document.domain` in Cypress 14+. When NOT to use: do not pass functions, class instances, or non-serializable objects through `cy.origin()` `args` — they are silently stripped because args are serialized via structured clone. Serialize to plain objects before passing. Named alternative: if the SSO provider has a test API endpoint (e.g., Okta sandbox), use `cy.request()` to obtain a session cookie directly without browser-based login — this is faster and avoids cross-origin complexity entirely.

---

### 244. `cy.selectFile()` for Drag-and-Drop File Upload with `Cypress.Buffer`  [official]

`cy.selectFile()` with `action: 'drag-drop'` simulates drag-and-drop file uploads onto a dropzone. Use `Cypress.Buffer.from()` to create file content programmatically for deterministic tests that do not depend on fixture files on disk.

```typescript
describe('File upload dropzone', () => {
  it('accepts a CSV file via drag and drop', () => {
    cy.visit('/import');

    const csvContent = 'name,email\nAlice,alice@example.com\nBob,bob@example.com';
    cy.get('[data-cy="dropzone"]').selectFile(
      {
        contents: Cypress.Buffer.from(csvContent),
        fileName: 'users.csv',
        mimeType: 'text/csv',
        lastModified: Date.now(),
      },
      { action: 'drag-drop' }
    );

    cy.get('[data-cy="upload-preview"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="row-count"]').should('have.text', '2 rows');
  });

  it('rejects files larger than 5 MB', () => {
    const largeBuffer = Cypress.Buffer.alloc(6 * 1024 * 1024, 'x');
    cy.get('[data-cy="dropzone"]').selectFile(
      { contents: largeBuffer, fileName: 'large.csv', mimeType: 'text/csv' },
      { action: 'drag-drop' }
    );

    cy.get('[data-cy="upload-error"]').should('contain.text', 'File too large');
    cy.get('[data-cy="upload-preview"]').should('not.exist');
  });

  it('accepts multiple files at once', () => {
    const files = ['report-q1.pdf', 'report-q2.pdf'].map((fileName) => ({
      contents: Cypress.Buffer.from(`%PDF-1.4 mock content for ${fileName}`),
      fileName,
      mimeType: 'application/pdf',
    }));

    cy.get('[data-cy="multi-upload-zone"]').selectFile(files, { action: 'drag-drop' });
    cy.get('[data-cy="queued-file"]').should('have.length', 2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `Cypress.Buffer.from()` for text-based files (CSV, JSON, XML) and `Cypress.Buffer.alloc()` for size-limit testing — no fixture files needed, tests are self-contained. When NOT to use: `cy.selectFile()` with `action: 'drag-drop'` does NOT fire `dragstart` or `dragend` events — only `dragenter`, `dragover`, `drop`, and `dragleave`. If your dropzone logic depends on `dragstart` data, use `cypress-real-events` instead. Named alternative: `cy.selectFile(path, { action: 'input' })` is simpler for file `<input>` elements and covers the majority of upload UIs without needing drag-and-drop simulation.

---

### 245. `cy.env()` Async Command vs. `Cypress.env()` Sync API — Security-Conscious Config Access  [official]

`cy.env()` (Cypress 15.10+) runs in the Node.js process and accesses secrets from `process.env` that are never serialized to the browser. Use it for credentials, API keys, and tokens. `Cypress.env()` (synchronous, browser-side) is for non-sensitive public config only.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/payment.cy.ts

// CORRECT: use cy.env() for secrets — value stays in Node.js context
it('creates a payment intent with real Stripe key', () => {
  cy.env('STRIPE_TEST_API_KEY').then((apiKey: string) => {
    cy.request({
      method: 'POST',
      url: 'https://api.stripe.com/v1/payment_intents',
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
      },
      body: { amount: 1000, currency: 'usd' },
      log: false,  // never log the Authorization header value
    }).its('status').should('eq', 200);
  });
});

// CORRECT: Cypress.env() for non-sensitive public config values
const baseUrl: string = Cypress.env('APP_BASE_URL');

// cypress/support/auth.ts
export function getAdminToken(): Cypress.Chainable<string> {
  // cy.env() chains like any other Cypress command
  return cy.env('ADMIN_API_TOKEN');
}

// Usage:
// getAdminToken().then((token) => {
//   cy.request({ headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` }, ... });
// });

// INCORRECT: never use Cypress.env() for secrets in CI
// const apiKey = Cypress.env('STRIPE_TEST_API_KEY');  // ← exposed in browser context + Command Log
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.env()` for any `CYPRESS_`-prefixed CI environment variable that contains a credential or token — it ensures the value is never sent to the browser. When NOT to use: do not use `cy.env()` for config values that need to be read synchronously (e.g., in a `Cypress.Commands.add()` definition body outside a command chain) — `cy.env()` is asynchronous and cannot be awaited outside a Cypress command. Named alternative: `cy.task('getSecret', 'STRIPE_KEY')` achieves the same Node.js-side isolation and was the recommended pattern before `cy.env()` existed in Cypress 15.10+.

---

## Additional Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 31) [community]

222. **`cy.origin()` does NOT inherit `cy.intercept()` routes defined in the outer test context — you must re-declare intercepts inside the `cy.origin()` callback** [community] — When a test defines `cy.intercept('POST', '/api/track')` before calling `cy.origin()`, the intercept is registered in the primary origin's network context. Requests made by pages loaded within `cy.origin()` run in a separate browsing context and do NOT match the outer intercept. WHY: Cypress's proxy intercept routing is scoped per-origin; `cy.origin()` creates an isolated execution context with its own intercept registry. If you need to intercept requests from within a cross-origin page, call `cy.intercept()` again inside the `cy.origin()` callback. This is one of the most common sources of "intercept never matched" bugs in OAuth + SSO test suites.

223. **`cy.selectFile()` with `action: 'drag-drop'` silently succeeds on elements that are NOT real dropzones — no error is thrown if the `drop` event is ignored by the app** [community] — `cy.selectFile({ contents, fileName }, { action: 'drag-drop' })` fires a synthetic `drop` event on the target element. If the target element does not have a `drop` event listener, the command still resolves successfully — Cypress does not check whether the app handled the event. WHY: `cy.selectFile()` is a DOM event dispatcher, not a file upload validator. The test will pass but no upload will occur, leading to false-positive tests. Always assert on a visible upload confirmation element (preview, row count, progress bar) after `selectFile()` to confirm the app processed the file.

224. **`cy.clock()` freezes `Date.now()` in the main thread but does NOT freeze `Date.now()` inside Web Workers** [community] — When `cy.clock()` is active, `Date.now()` in the page's main execution context returns the frozen timestamp. Web Workers have their own global scope and are not patched by Cypress's clock override — they return the real system time. WHY: Cypress injects clock patching via `window` manipulation in the page's main execution context; Web Workers load in separate global scopes (`self` not `window`) that Cypress's injected script does not reach. For Worker-aware timer testing, stub the worker's communication channel (e.g., `postMessage`) instead of relying on `cy.clock()`.

225. **Middleware `cy.intercept()` with the pattern `'**'` in `support/e2e.ts` intercepts Cypress's own internal socket.io polling — mutating certain headers corrupts the Cypress runner protocol** [community] — Using `cy.intercept({ middleware: true }, '**', handler)` in a global `beforeEach` will intercept all requests, including the WebSocket upgrade requests Cypress makes to its own runner at `/__cypress/...` paths. Mutating headers like `origin`, `upgrade`, or `sec-websocket-key` on these requests breaks the Cypress/AUT bridge, causing "lost connection to the running browser" errors. WHY: Cypress's internal communication uses XHR/WebSocket requests in the same browser context. Always exclude Cypress-internal paths: `cy.intercept({ middleware: true }, /^(?!.*__cypress).*$/, handler)`.

226. **`cy.wait('@alias')` called more times than the `times: N` limit on a `cy.intercept()` resolves from the cached queue rather than throwing — you can get false-positive assertions on stale requests** [community] — If you set `times: 2` on an intercept alias and then call `cy.wait('@alias')` three times in a test, the third `wait` does not throw. Instead it resolves immediately with the last matched request object from Cypress's internal alias queue. WHY: Cypress caches matched requests in the alias queue; once `times` is exhausted, new requests fall through to the real network, but the cached responses are still dequeue-able. The third `cy.wait('@alias')` dequeues a stale cached response, making it appear a third request was intercepted when it was not. Always follow up with `cy.get('@alias.all').should('have.length', N)` to assert the exact request count.

227. **`cy.task()` that returns `undefined` (not `null`) throws `Error: Task must return a value` in Cypress 14+, and the error message does not identify which task failed** [community] — Node.js functions that call `return;` or fall off the end return `undefined`. Cypress tasks require an explicit return value; `undefined` is treated as a missing return and throws an uncaught error that crashes the test with a generic message that does not name the task. WHY: Cypress's task protocol serializes the return value for transmission to the browser context via JSON; `undefined` cannot be JSON-serialized and is rejected at the IPC boundary. Always return `null` (not `undefined`) from tasks that have no meaningful return value — this is especially easy to miss in `async` functions that `await` a void database call and then fall off the end without an explicit `return null;`.

### 246. `cy.intercept()` Browser Cache Bypass via Middleware Header Stripping  [official]

Browser caching silently prevents `cy.intercept()` from firing — cached responses never reach the network layer. Use a middleware intercept to strip cache-control headers from requests, forcing every request through the Cypress proxy.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts — register globally before every test
beforeEach(() => {
  // Middleware strips cache headers so cy.intercept() always fires for /api/* routes
  cy.intercept({ url: '/api/**', middleware: true }, (req) => {
    // Remove conditional-request headers that would trigger 304 Not Modified
    delete req.headers['if-none-match'];
    delete req.headers['if-modified-since'];
    // Force no-cache so the browser always re-fetches from the server
    req.headers['cache-control'] = 'no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate';
    req.headers['pragma'] = 'no-cache';
    // Continue to the real server or the next matching intercept — no req.reply() needed
  });
});

// Now downstream intercepts always fire — no silent cache misses
it('always intercepts the products API even after prior spec cached it', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products', { fixture: 'products.json' }).as('getProducts');
  cy.visit('/products');
  cy.wait('@getProducts'); // guaranteed to fire — no 304 bypass possible
  cy.get('[data-cy="product-card"]').should('have.length', 3);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use this middleware pattern in any suite where `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` on `cy.session()` or aggressive HTTP cache headers cause intermittent "intercept never matched" failures. Essential when testing pages backed by CDN-served APIs that set `Cache-Control: max-age=3600`. When NOT to use: do not apply globally if you have tests that specifically verify caching behavior (e.g., testing that a second page load hits the browser cache and does not re-fetch). Scope the middleware to a specific `describe` block using a local `beforeEach`. Named alternative: `Cypress.automation('remote:debugger:protocol', { command: 'Network.setCacheDisabled', params: { cacheDisabled: true } })` achieves the same result via CDP but is Chromium-only and applies to all traffic, not just `/api/**`.

---

### 247. `cy.spy()` on `window.fetch` for Request Assertion Without Stubbing  [official]

`cy.spy()` wraps a function and records calls without altering behavior. Use it on `window.fetch` when you need to assert that a specific fetch was made (URL, method, body) without intercepting or stubbing the response — the real response still flows through.

```typescript
it('dashboard sends a telemetry ping on first load', () => {
  cy.visit('/dashboard', {
    onBeforeLoad(win) {
      // Spy on fetch — records calls without changing responses
      cy.spy(win, 'fetch').as('fetchSpy');
    },
  });

  cy.get('[data-cy="dashboard-content"]').should('be.visible');

  // Assert the telemetry call was made with the correct URL
  cy.get('@fetchSpy').should('have.been.calledWithMatch',
    Cypress.sinon.match('/api/telemetry'),
    Cypress.sinon.match({
      method: 'POST',
      body: Cypress.sinon.match(/"event":"dashboard_view"/),
    })
  );
});

it('does NOT send telemetry when analytics opt-out is set', () => {
  cy.visit('/dashboard', {
    onBeforeLoad(win) {
      win.localStorage.setItem('analytics_opt_out', 'true');
      cy.spy(win, 'fetch').as('fetchSpy');
    },
  });

  cy.get('[data-cy="dashboard-content"]').should('be.visible');

  // Verify telemetry endpoint was never called
  cy.get('@fetchSpy').should('not.have.been.calledWithMatch',
    Cypress.sinon.match('/api/telemetry')
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.spy()` on `window.fetch` when you need to assert on request parameters while still exercising the real API — no mock response needed. Ideal for analytics events, feature-flag reporting, and telemetry calls where only the request matters. When NOT to use: do not spy on `window.fetch` when `cy.intercept()` is available for the same purpose — `cy.intercept()` provides richer assertion API (`.its('request.body')`, typed response stubs, `times` counters) and produces better Command Log output. Spying on `fetch` also breaks down when the app uses `XMLHttpRequest` or an `axios` adapter. Named alternative: `cy.intercept('POST', '/api/telemetry').as('tel')` followed by `cy.wait('@tel').its('request.body')`.

### 248. Angular Zoneless Component Testing with `angular-zoneless` Mount  [official]

Angular 18+ supports zone-free change detection via Angular Signals. The standard `cy.mount()` wrapper assumes Zone.js — use the `angular-zoneless` harness for components built with `signal()` / `computed()` and `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush` without Zone.js.

```typescript
// cypress/support/component.ts — register zoneless mount for Angular signals
import { mount } from 'cypress/angular-zoneless';

Cypress.Commands.overwrite('mount', mount);

// cypress/component/counter.cy.ts
import { Component, signal, computed } from '@angular/core';
import { mount } from 'cypress/angular-zoneless';

@Component({
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <button data-cy="dec" (click)="decrement()">-</button>
    <span data-cy="count">{{ count() }}</span>
    <button data-cy="inc" (click)="increment()">+</button>
    <span data-cy="double">{{ double() }}</span>
  `,
})
class CounterComponent {
  count  = signal(0);
  double = computed(() => this.count() * 2);
  increment() { this.count.update((n) => n + 1); }
  decrement() { this.count.update((n) => n - 1); }
}

it('signal-based counter increments and computes double correctly', () => {
  mount(CounterComponent);

  cy.get('[data-cy="count"]').should('have.text', '0');
  cy.get('[data-cy="double"]').should('have.text', '0');

  cy.get('[data-cy="inc"]').click().click().click();

  cy.get('[data-cy="count"]').should('have.text', '3');
  cy.get('[data-cy="double"]').should('have.text', '6');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `angular-zoneless` mount for Angular components that use Signals and do not import `BrowserModule`/`CommonModule` — Zone.js-based mount causes change detection to fire at incorrect times, leading to timing-sensitive assertion failures. When NOT to use: if your app still uses Zone.js globally (most Angular 17 and earlier projects do), use the standard `cypress/angular` mount — the zoneless harness will break Zone.js-dependent components. Named alternative: `TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()] })` in Jest/Vitest achieves the same for non-browser unit tests.

### 249. `cy.stub()` for Browser Dialog Interception (alert / confirm / prompt)  [official]

Native browser dialogs (`window.alert`, `window.confirm`, `window.prompt`) block test execution in Cypress unless handled. Use `cy.stub()` to replace them with recorded fakes before the action that triggers them.

```typescript
it('delete confirmation dialog: cancel keeps the item', () => {
  cy.visit('/items');

  cy.window().then((win) => {
    // Stub confirm to return false (user clicks "Cancel")
    cy.stub(win, 'confirm').returns(false).as('confirmDialog');
  });

  cy.get('[data-cy="delete-btn"]').first().click();

  // Verify dialog was shown with correct message
  cy.get('@confirmDialog').should('have.been.calledOnceWith',
    'Are you sure you want to delete this item?'
  );

  // Item still exists — cancel was effective
  cy.get('[data-cy="item-row"]').should('have.length.greaterThan', 0);
});

it('delete confirmation dialog: confirm removes the item', () => {
  cy.visit('/items');
  cy.intercept('DELETE', '/api/items/*', { statusCode: 204 }).as('deleteItem');

  cy.window().then((win) => {
    cy.stub(win, 'confirm').returns(true).as('confirmDialog');
  });

  cy.get('[data-cy="delete-btn"]').first().click();

  cy.wait('@deleteItem');
  cy.get('@confirmDialog').should('have.been.calledOnce');
  cy.get('[data-cy="success-toast"]').should('be.visible');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Always stub browser dialogs before clicking anything that triggers them — Cypress's default handler auto-dismisses `alert` and `confirm` (returns `true`) without asserting call arguments. Use explicit `cy.stub()` when you need to verify the message shown or test both cancel and confirm paths. When NOT to use: do not stub `window.confirm` when the component uses a custom modal (not a native browser dialog) — use `cy.get('[data-cy="modal"]')` assertions instead. Named alternative: `cy.on('window:confirm', (msg) => { /* return true/false */ })` handles dialogs via the Cypress event system — simpler for one-off interception but cannot use `.should('have.been.calledWith')` assertion syntax.
