### 250. React Context + Custom `mountWithProviders` Command for CT  [official]

Components that consume React Context (`useContext`) fail in CT when mounted without a Provider ancestor. Build a typed `mountWithProviders` command that wraps any component with all required providers.

```typescript
// cypress/support/mount-with-providers.tsx
import React, { ReactNode } from 'react';
import { mount } from 'cypress/react';
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { ThemeProvider } from '../../src/contexts/ThemeContext';
import { AuthProvider } from '../../src/contexts/AuthContext';

interface MountOptions {
  initialTheme?: 'light' | 'dark';
  initialUser?: { id: string; name: string; role: string } | null;
}

function AllProviders({ children, options }: { children: ReactNode; options: MountOptions }) {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient({
    defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false, staleTime: 0 } },
  });
  return (
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <ThemeProvider initialTheme={options.initialTheme ?? 'light'}>
        <AuthProvider initialUser={options.initialUser ?? null}>
          {children}
        </AuthProvider>
      </ThemeProvider>
    </QueryClientProvider>
  );
}

Cypress.Commands.add(
  'mountWithProviders',
  (component: React.ReactElement, options: MountOptions = {}) =>
    mount(<AllProviders options={options}>{component}</AllProviders>)
);

declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      mountWithProviders(component: React.ReactElement, options?: MountOptions): Chainable<void>;
    }
  }
}

// Usage in a spec:
it('UserMenu shows admin controls for admin role', () => {
  cy.mountWithProviders(<UserMenu />, {
    initialUser: { id: '1', name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' },
    initialTheme: 'dark',
  });

  cy.get('[data-cy="admin-panel-link"]').should('be.visible');
  cy.get('[data-cy="user-avatar"]').should('have.attr', 'data-theme', 'dark');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `mountWithProviders` as the single CT mount entry point so provider configuration is DRY and per-test overrides require only a small options object. When NOT to use: do not wrap ALL providers unconditionally if a component is intentionally provider-free — a monolithic wrapper hides bugs where a pure UI component accidentally depends on a context it should not need. Named alternative: MSW (Mock Service Worker) paired with raw `cy.mount()` is an alternative to `QueryClientProvider` wrapping — MSW intercepts `fetch` at the Service Worker level and works in both CT and E2E.

---

### 251. `cy.clock()` + `cy.tick()` for Deterministic Polling Assertion  [official]

Components that poll an API on a `setInterval` produce non-deterministic tests when real time is used. Freeze time with `cy.clock()` and advance it with `cy.tick()` to trigger polls exactly at the desired intervals.

```typescript
it('status badge auto-refreshes every 30 seconds via setInterval polling', () => {
  let callCount = 0;

  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/job/status', (req) => {
    callCount += 1;
    req.reply({
      statusCode: 200,
      body: { status: callCount < 3 ? 'running' : 'complete' },
    });
  }).as('pollStatus');

  cy.clock(); // freeze time before visit
  cy.visit('/job/42');

  // First poll fires immediately on component mount
  cy.wait('@pollStatus');
  cy.get('[data-cy="job-status"]').should('have.text', 'running');

  // Advance 30 seconds — triggers second poll
  cy.tick(30_000);
  cy.wait('@pollStatus');
  cy.get('[data-cy="job-status"]').should('have.text', 'running');

  // Advance another 30 seconds — triggers third poll, status becomes complete
  cy.tick(30_000);
  cy.wait('@pollStatus');
  cy.get('[data-cy="job-status"]').should('have.text', 'complete');

  // Verify polling stops after completion (no 4th request after another 30s)
  cy.tick(30_000);
  cy.get('@pollStatus.all').should('have.length', 3);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.clock()` + `cy.tick()` for any component using `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, or `Date.now()` in polling, debounce, or session-expiry logic. This eliminates `cy.wait(30000)` calls that bloat wall-clock time. When NOT to use: `cy.clock()` does NOT affect Web Workers or Service Workers (separate global scopes). It also does NOT affect `performance.now()` — stub that separately if your app uses it for timing. Named alternative: `vi.useFakeTimers()` in Vitest component tests achieves the same outside a real browser; use `cy.clock()` for real-browser CT or E2E scenarios.

---

### 252. `cy.task()` for Database Seeding with Typed Task Map  [official]

`cy.task()` delegates to Node.js for operations the browser sandbox cannot perform: database writes, file system access, secret retrieval. A typed task map gives compile-time safety on task names and argument shapes.

```typescript
// cypress/plugins/tasks.ts — typed task registry
import { Pool } from 'pg';

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

export interface CypressTasks {
  'db:seed:user': (args: { email: string; role: string }) => Promise<{ id: string }>;
  'db:clean':     (args: { table: string }) => Promise<null>;
  'db:query':     (args: { sql: string; params: unknown[] }) => Promise<unknown[]>;
}

export const tasks: CypressTasks = {
  'db:seed:user': async ({ email, role }) => {
    const result = await pool.query(
      'INSERT INTO users (email, role) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id',
      [email, role]
    );
    return { id: result.rows[0].id as string };
  },
  'db:clean': async ({ table }) => {
    await pool.query(`DELETE FROM ${table} WHERE test_data = TRUE`);
    return null; // cy.task() requires non-undefined return
  },
  'db:query': async ({ sql, params }) => {
    const result = await pool.query(sql, params);
    return result.rows as unknown[];
  },
};

// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import { tasks } from './cypress/plugins/tasks';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: { setupNodeEvents(on) { on('task', tasks); } },
});

// cypress/e2e/user-profile.cy.ts — type-safe usage
it('displays the seeded user profile', () => {
  cy.task('db:seed:user', { email: 'seed@example.com', role: 'admin' }).then(({ id }) => {
    cy.visit(`/users/${id}`);
    cy.get('[data-cy="user-email"]').should('have.text', 'seed@example.com');
    cy.get('[data-cy="user-role-badge"]').should('have.text', 'Admin');
  });
});

afterEach(() => { cy.task('db:clean', { table: 'users' }); });
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.task()` for pre-test data setup requiring database access or file system writes that the browser sandbox cannot perform. The typed task map prevents typos in task names and mismatched argument types at build time. When NOT to use: do not use `cy.task()` for test-time assertions — prefer `cy.request()` to query an API endpoint, which stays in the browser context and produces Command Log output. Named alternative: `cy.request('POST', '/api/test/seed', payload)` using a test-only API endpoint is simpler when the backend exposes one; `cy.task()` is the fallback when it does not.

---

### 253. `cy.intercept()` `times` Counter for Request-Sequence Assertions  [official]

The `times` option on `cy.intercept()` limits how many requests the intercept matches. Chain multiple intercepts for the same route with different `times` values to simulate a response-state progression (first call fails, subsequent calls succeed).

```typescript
describe('Auto-retry on transient error', () => {
  it('retries after a 503 and displays data on success', () => {
    // First request only: 503 Service Unavailable
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/inventory', {
      statusCode: 503,
      body: { message: 'Service temporarily unavailable' },
      times: 1,
    }).as('inventoryFail');

    // All subsequent requests (times omitted = unlimited): 200 OK
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/inventory', { fixture: 'inventory.json' }).as('inventoryOk');

    cy.clock();
    cy.visit('/inventory');

    cy.wait('@inventoryFail');
    cy.get('[data-cy="retry-banner"]').should('be.visible');

    // App auto-retries after 2s delay
    cy.tick(2000);

    cy.wait('@inventoryOk');
    cy.get('[data-cy="inventory-table"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="retry-banner"]').should('not.exist');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `times: N` when testing multi-step request sequences (loading states, retry logic, progressive loading) without stateful server-side setup. It eliminates the need for a closure counter variable. When NOT to use: Cypress processes intercepts in reverse-registration order — register the "later state" intercept FIRST and the "first call" intercept LAST so the first-call rule takes precedence. If this ordering is non-obvious to readers, a handler function with a closure counter is more explicit. Named alternative: a stateful handler `let count = 0; cy.intercept(..., (req) => { count++; req.reply(count === 1 ? err : ok); })` gives more control but is less declarative.

---

### 254. `cy.session()` with `localStorage` Expiry Sentinel for Short-TTL JWTs  [official]

`cy.session()` restores `localStorage` but does not restore session expiry timers. If your app stores a JWT with a short TTL, a session cached by `cy.session()` may arrive pre-expired. A `localStorage` expiry sentinel in `validate()` detects and rejects stale sessions before they cause mid-test auth failures.

```typescript
// cypress/support/auth.ts
export function loginWithJwt(email: string, password: string): void {
  cy.session(
    [email, 'jwt-v2'],
    () => {
      cy.request('POST', '/api/auth/login', { email, password }).then((res) => {
        window.localStorage.setItem('auth_token', res.body.token as string);
        const expiresAt = Date.now() + (res.body.expires_in as number) * 1000;
        window.localStorage.setItem('auth_expires_at', String(expiresAt));
      });
    },
    {
      validate() {
        const expiresAt = Number(window.localStorage.getItem('auth_expires_at') ?? '0');
        const bufferMs  = 60_000; // reject if within 60s of expiry
        if (Date.now() + bufferMs > expiresAt) {
          throw new Error('JWT session nearing expiry — re-authenticating');
        }
        cy.request({ url: '/api/me', failOnStatusCode: false })
          .its('status').should('eq', 200);
      },
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
    }
  );
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the expiry sentinel when your app stores short-lived JWTs (TTL under 30 minutes) and your suite runs for longer than that across many specs with `cacheAcrossSpecs: true`. Without the sentinel, `validate()` may pass the `/api/me` check on a fast machine but the JWT expires mid-test. When NOT to use: if your app uses `httpOnly` cookies for auth (server-set, not readable from `localStorage`), this pattern does not apply — rely solely on `cy.request('/api/me')` in `validate()`. Named alternative: `cy.session()` `idleTimeout` option (Cypress 15.8+) expires the cache after a period of test inactivity and complements the sentinel — combine both for maximum session freshness.

---

### 255. `cy.intercept()` `req.on('before:response')` for Non-Blocking Response Inspection  [official]

The `req.on('before:response', handler)` event fires after the real server responds but before Cypress delivers the response to the browser. Use it to assert on real response bodies or lightly inject response headers without replacing the response.

```typescript
it('real API returns correctly shaped paginated response', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/orders*', (req) => {
    req.on('before:response', (res) => {
      // Assert on real response body — does NOT alter delivery to the browser
      expect(res.statusCode).to.eq(200);
      expect(res.body).to.have.property('data').that.is.an('array');
      expect(res.body).to.have.nested.property('pagination.perPage', 20);
    });
  }).as('getOrders');

  cy.visit('/orders');
  cy.wait('@getOrders');
  cy.get('[data-cy="order-row"]').should('have.length', 20);
});

it('rate-limit header triggers a user-visible warning', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/data', (req) => {
    req.on('before:response', (res) => {
      // Inject response headers while keeping the real body
      res.headers['x-rate-limit-remaining'] = '0';
      res.headers['retry-after'] = '60';
    });
  }).as('dataWithRateLimit');

  cy.visit('/data');
  cy.wait('@dataWithRateLimit');
  cy.get('[data-cy="rate-limit-warning"]').should('be.visible');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `req.on('before:response')` for contract testing in integration environments where full stubs would hide API regressions — it asserts on the real shape without losing real data flow. When NOT to use: for simple response assertions after the fact, `cy.wait('@alias').its('response.body')` is simpler. Named alternative: `req.continue((res) => { ... })` is functionally equivalent and also delivers the (optionally modified) response — use `req.on('before:response')` for read-only inspection and `req.continue()` when you need to modify the response body.

---

### 256. Svelte 5 Runes Component Testing — `$state` + `$derived` Verification  [community]

Svelte 5 replaces opt-in reactivity with explicit runes (`$state`, `$derived`, `$effect`). Use the Cypress Svelte 5 CT adapter to mount rune-based components and assert on their rendered output after reactive state changes.

```typescript
// src/components/ShoppingCart.svelte (Svelte 5 runes)
// <script lang="ts">
//   let items  = $state<Array<{ name: string; price: number }>>([]);
//   let total  = $derived(items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0));
//   function addItem(item: { name: string; price: number }) { items = [...items, item]; }
// </script>
// <ul>{#each items as item}<li data-cy="item">{item.name} — ${item.price}</li>{/each}</ul>
// <p data-cy="total">${total.toFixed(2)}</p>
// <button data-cy="add-widget" onclick={() => addItem({ name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 })}>+</button>

import { mount } from 'cypress/svelte';
import ShoppingCart from '../../src/components/ShoppingCart.svelte';

describe('ShoppingCart — Svelte 5 runes', () => {
  it('$derived total updates reactively when $state items array changes', () => {
    mount(ShoppingCart);

    cy.get('[data-cy="total"]').should('have.text', '$0.00');
    cy.get('[data-cy="add-widget"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="item"]').should('have.length', 1).and('contain.text', 'Widget');
    cy.get('[data-cy="total"]').should('have.text', '$9.99');

    cy.get('[data-cy="add-widget"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="item"]').should('have.length', 2);
    cy.get('[data-cy="total"]').should('have.text', '$19.98');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use Cypress CT for Svelte 5 rune components when you need real browser DOM interaction (hover, keyboard, drag). When NOT to use: Svelte 5 CT adapter is still alpha in Cypress 15.x — expect potential breaking changes on major Svelte updates. For pure logic testing of `$derived` values without DOM, use Svelte's `$inspect` + Vitest. Named alternative: Playwright CT has more stable Svelte 5 support as of 2026 for teams that encounter persistent Cypress adapter issues.

**[community]** WHY: Svelte 5 runes compile differently from Svelte 4. Using the Svelte 4 Cypress adapter with Svelte 5 components causes a silent render failure — the component mounts but reactivity is broken, all `$state` variables appear frozen at their initial values, and `cy.get()` assertions on updated values time out with no helpful error message.

---

### 257. `cy.intercept()` GraphQL Operation Matching via `body.operationName`  [community]

GraphQL sends all operations to the same endpoint (`/graphql`). Use a `RouteHandler` function that inspects `req.body.operationName` to match only the specific operation under test without accidentally stubbing unrelated queries.

```typescript
// cypress/support/graphql.ts — reusable typed GraphQL intercept helper
type GqlBody = { operationName: string; variables?: Record<string, unknown> };

export function interceptGql<T>(
  operationName: string,
  stub: T | ((req: Cypress.Request<GqlBody>) => void)
): Cypress.Chainable {
  return cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql', (req: Cypress.Request<GqlBody>) => {
    if (req.body.operationName !== operationName) return; // pass through other operations
    if (typeof stub === 'function') {
      (stub as (req: Cypress.Request<GqlBody>) => void)(req);
    } else {
      req.reply({ data: stub });
    }
  }).as(operationName);
}

// cypress/e2e/products.cy.ts
it('renders stubbed GetProducts query result', () => {
  interceptGql('GetProducts', {
    products: [
      { id: '1', name: 'Widget Pro', price: 29.99 },
      { id: '2', name: 'Gadget Plus', price: 49.99 },
    ],
  });

  cy.visit('/products');
  cy.wait('@GetProducts');
  cy.get('[data-cy="product-card"]').should('have.length', 2);
});

it('shows error state when GetProducts returns a GraphQL error', () => {
  interceptGql('GetProducts', (req) => {
    req.reply({ errors: [{ message: 'Product service unavailable' }] });
  });

  cy.visit('/products');
  cy.wait('@GetProducts');
  cy.get('[data-cy="error-banner"]').should('contain.text', 'Product service unavailable');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `operationName`-based matching for all GraphQL testing — it is the only reliable way to isolate individual operations when multiple queries fire on page load. When NOT to use: if your client sends anonymous GraphQL operations (no `operationName` field), match on `req.body.query` content with a regex instead. Also guard against batched requests — add `if (Array.isArray(req.body)) return;` at the top since batching sends an array body where `req.body.operationName` would be `undefined`. Named alternative: MSW (`@mswjs/msw`) with `graphql.query('GetProducts', ...)` provides a typed GraphQL mock layer that also works in Jest, Storybook, and browser dev mode.

**[community]** WHY: A single `cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql')` stub with a static fixture body stubs ALL GraphQL operations to the same response — unrelated queries (pagination, auth refresh) that fire concurrently on load all get the products stub, causing cascading failures that appear unrelated to the test under development.

---

### 258. `Cypress.Commands.overwrite` for Structured Request Logging in Debug Mode  [community]

`Commands.overwrite('request', ...)` wraps every `cy.request()` call with structured logging — useful when debugging CI failures caused by flaky API responses. Gate it on a `DEBUG_REQUESTS` environment variable to avoid overhead in normal runs.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts — gated debug instrumentation
if (Cypress.env('DEBUG_REQUESTS') === 'true') {
  Cypress.Commands.overwrite(
    'request',
    (
      originalFn: Cypress.CommandOriginalFn<'request'>,
      ...args: Parameters<Cypress.Chainable['request']>
    ) => {
      const start = Date.now();
      return originalFn(...args).then((response: Cypress.Response<unknown>) => {
        const duration = Date.now() - start;
        cy.task('log:request', {
          url:      response.allRequestResponses?.[0]?.['Request URL'] ?? 'unknown',
          status:   response.status,
          duration,
          bodySnip: JSON.stringify(response.body).slice(0, 200),
        }, { log: false });
        return response;
      });
    }
  );
}

// cypress/plugins/log-task.ts
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';

const LOG_FILE = path.join(process.cwd(), 'cypress/logs/requests.ndjson');

export const logRequestTask = {
  'log:request': (entry: Record<string, unknown>) => {
    const line = JSON.stringify({ ...entry, ts: new Date().toISOString() }) + '\n';
    fs.appendFileSync(LOG_FILE, line);
    return null;
  },
};
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Enable `DEBUG_REQUESTS=true` on CI when investigating intermittent 401/502 failures — the NDJSON log gives exact timing and status codes for every `cy.request()` call in the failing run. When NOT to use: do not enable globally in all runs — the `cy.task()` Node.js IPC round-trip per request adds measurable overhead in high-traffic suites. Named alternative: Cypress Cloud Test Replay records the full network activity with timestamps — use that instead if your project already records to Cypress Cloud.

**[community]** WHY: CI-only failures from transient API latency or expired tokens are invisible in the standard Cypress output — you only see "Timed out waiting for `@alias`" with no HTTP status or timing data. The overwrite pattern surfaces the exact status and response time for every `cy.request()` call, immediately distinguishing a 504 timeout from a 401 token expiry from a 503 backend deploy in progress.

---

### 259. `cy.intercept()` `res.setDelay()` + `res.setThrottle()` for Loading State UX Testing  [official]

Use `res.setDelay()` and `res.setThrottle()` in a `req.continue()` handler to simulate slow 3G or high-latency API responses. This verifies skeleton loaders, progress bars, and timeout error UX without real network degradation.

```typescript
describe('Loading state UX under slow network conditions', () => {
  it('shows skeleton loader during a slow API response', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/dashboard/summary', (req) => {
      req.continue((res) => {
        res.setDelay(2500);    // 2.5-second artificial delay
        res.setThrottle(50);   // 50 kbps bandwidth cap for realism
      });
    }).as('slowSummary');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');

    // Skeleton visible immediately before the response arrives
    cy.get('[data-cy="summary-skeleton"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="summary-content"]').should('not.exist');

    cy.wait('@slowSummary');

    cy.get('[data-cy="summary-skeleton"]').should('not.exist');
    cy.get('[data-cy="summary-content"]').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('shows timeout error after exceeding the 5-second client timeout', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/critical-data', (req) => {
      req.continue((res) => {
        res.setDelay(6000); // exceeds the app's 5s timeout
      });
    }).as('timeoutData');

    cy.clock();
    cy.visit('/critical-view');

    cy.tick(5100); // advance past the app's client-side timeout threshold

    cy.get('[data-cy="timeout-error"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="retry-btn"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `setDelay()` + `setThrottle()` to regression-test loading state UI without needing DevTools network throttling. Essential for verifying skeleton loaders and spinners actually render before data arrives — easy to miss in fast local dev environments where responses arrive in milliseconds. When NOT to use: do not use very long delays (>10s) without `cy.clock()` + `cy.tick()` — real time passes and the test will be genuinely slow. Named alternative: `Cypress.automation('remote:debugger:protocol', { command: 'Network.emulateNetworkConditions', ... })` applies throttling at the TCP level (more realistic) but is Chromium-only and applies to all requests globally, not just specific routes.

---

### 260. `cy.window().its('__APP_STATE__')` for Internal State Verification  [community]

Some apps expose a debug state object on `window` in test/development mode. Use `cy.window().its()` to read this state and assert on complex state transitions that are difficult to verify purely through DOM inspection.

```typescript
// Assumes the app exposes: window.__APP_STATE__ = () => store.getState()
// in non-production builds (e.g., process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production')

it('cart state reflects items added via the UI', () => {
  cy.visit('/products/widget-pro');
  cy.get('[data-cy="add-to-cart"]').click();

  // Read internal store state — no need to parse DOM text or intercept APIs
  cy.window()
    .its('__APP_STATE__')
    .invoke('call', null)
    .its('cart.items')
    .should('have.length', 1)
    .its('0')
    .should('deep.include', { productId: 'widget-pro', quantity: 1 });
});

it('cart is empty after checkout completes', () => {
  cy.visit('/checkout');
  cy.get('[data-cy="confirm-purchase"]').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="order-confirmation"]').should('be.visible');

  cy.window()
    .its('__APP_STATE__')
    .invoke('call', null)
    .its('cart.items')
    .should('have.length', 0);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `window.__APP_STATE__` assertions for complex state transitions that are hard to verify through DOM inspection alone — multi-step wizards, undo/redo stacks, async state machines with intermediate states that produce no visible DOM change. When NOT to use: do not write tests that ONLY assert on `window.__APP_STATE__` without any DOM assertions — this tests the store, not the UI. Always pair store assertions with at least one DOM assertion. Named alternative: `cy.get('[data-testid="debug-state"]').invoke('text').then(JSON.parse)` reads a hidden DOM element rendering state as JSON — lower coupling than `window` exposure but requires a test-only DOM element to maintain.

**[community]** WHY: Redux DevTools and Zustand's `devtools()` middleware expose store state on window globals in dev builds. Teams that discover this pattern start writing tests that exclusively assert on store state and skip DOM assertions — this creates a suite that passes even when the UI breaks its connection to the store (e.g., a broken `connect()` call). DOM assertions must remain the primary signal; store state is supplementary.

---

## Additional Real-World Gotchas (Cycle 32) [community]

228. **`cy.spy()` on `window.fetch` misses requests fired during JavaScript module initialization — module-level `fetch` calls run before `onBeforeLoad` installs the spy** [community] — `onBeforeLoad` runs after HTML parsing but before the page's JavaScript initializes. Module-level `fetch` calls (e.g., `const config = await fetch('/api/config')` at module top-level) fire during module evaluation, which can precede `onBeforeLoad` in some bundler configurations. WHY: JavaScript module initialization is synchronous and executes before Cypress's `onBeforeLoad` callback for eagerly evaluated modules. To intercept initialization-phase fetches, use `cy.intercept()` instead — it hooks at the Cypress proxy level before the browser processes the response, regardless of when the request fires.

229. **`cy.stub(win, 'confirm')` must be called via `cy.window().then(...)` — calling it on the `win` reference from `onBeforeLoad` throws `TypeError: Cannot stub non-configurable property`** [community] — `window.confirm` is non-writable and may not be configurable on the `win` object captured early in `onBeforeLoad`. Cypress's `cy.stub()` uses `Object.defineProperty` which requires the property to be configurable. WHY: The `win` object accessed via `cy.window()` returns Cypress's fully instrumented `window` reference where property descriptors are set up correctly. The raw `win` parameter in `onBeforeLoad` is the pre-instrumentation window and `confirm` may not yet be configurable. Always prefer `cy.window().then((win) => cy.stub(win, 'confirm'))` over `onBeforeLoad` for stubs.

230. **`interceptGql` (operationName matching) breaks silently when Apollo Client batching is enabled — batched requests send an array body where `req.body.operationName` is `undefined`** [community] — Apollo Client's `BatchHttpLink` and urql's batch exchange send an array of operation objects in a single `POST /graphql` request. A handler checking `req.body.operationName !== operationName` on an array body evaluates `undefined !== operationName`, passes the guard, and does nothing — the batch is not matched. WHY: The body shape changes from `{ operationName, variables, query }` to `[{ operationName, variables, query }, ...]` when batching is active. Always add `if (Array.isArray(req.body)) return;` at the top of GraphQL intercept handlers and disable GQL batching via a test-environment feature flag (`CYPRESS_DISABLE_GQL_BATCH=true`).

231. **`cy.clock()` applied before `cy.visit()` does NOT freeze time for code running during JavaScript module initialization — module-level `Date.now()` calls capture the real timestamp** [community] — When `cy.clock()` is called before `cy.visit()`, Cypress installs `sinon.useFakeTimers()` on the current browser window. Navigation triggers a full page reload, resetting `window` — Cypress re-installs the fake clock after the new page's JavaScript initializes. Module-level code that calls `Date.now()` during initial evaluation runs with the real clock before re-installation. WHY: Module evaluation order means some `Date.now()` calls in app code fire before Cypress can patch the new window's clock. Workaround: use `cy.clock(new Date('2026-01-01'))` and write tests against date-relative behavior (e.g., "2 days ago") rather than exact timestamp values.

232. **`cy.intercept()` with `times: 1` followed by `cy.get('@alias.all').should('have.length', 1)` does NOT verify the server received only one request — it only confirms Cypress matched one request via the now-exhausted rule** [community] — After `times: 1` exhausts the intercept rule, subsequent requests to the same URL bypass Cypress's intercept entirely and hit the real server unrecorded. `cy.get('@alias.all')` only shows Cypress-matched requests. WHY: Cypress intercept recording is tied to the rule's lifetime — once `times` is consumed, the rule is removed and overflow requests are invisible to the alias queue. To assert "exactly one request was sent in total," register a second intercept with no `times` restriction to catch overflows, then assert `cy.get('@overflowAlias.all').should('have.length', 0)`.

233. **`Cypress.Commands.overwrite('request', ...)` wraps ALL `cy.request()` calls including those made internally by `cy.session()` validate callbacks — overwriting request in a debug wrapper can cause validate() to emit unexpected log output or task calls** [community] — `cy.session()`'s `validate()` callback calls `cy.request('/api/me')` to check session freshness. If `request` is overwritten with a debug logger that calls `cy.task('log:request', ...)`, every session validation triggers a task call — adding overhead and log noise that makes the output harder to parse. WHY: `Commands.overwrite()` is global; there is no "internal only" call path. Guard the overwrite with a test-name or context check, or use `cy.task(..., { log: false })` with a path filter that skips `/api/me` and other health-check endpoints: `if (entry.url.includes('/api/me')) return null;`.

---

## Cycle 33 — 2026-05-14

### 261. `cy.env()` — Secure Async Environment Variable Access (v15.10+)  [official]

Cypress 15.10 introduced `cy.env()` as an asynchronous replacement for the now-deprecated `Cypress.env()`. The new command returns a chainable Cypress promise rather than a synchronous value, enabling secure retrieval patterns and future compatibility with secret-manager integrations. `Cypress.env()` continues to work in v15 but emits deprecation warnings and can be blocked via the `allowCypressEnv: false` configuration flag. Non-sensitive configuration that should be surfaced in the Cypress App's resolved config panel can instead be published via the new `Cypress.expose()` API.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts
// v15.10+: replace all Cypress.env('API_KEY') with cy.env('API_KEY')

Cypress.Commands.add('seedApiCall', (endpoint: string) => {
  cy.env('API_KEY').then((apiKey: string) => {
    cy.request({
      method: 'POST',
      url: `${endpoint}/seed`,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      },
      body: { reset: true },
    }).then((resp) => {
      expect(resp.status).to.eq(200);
    });
  });
});

// In test file — no synchronous env read; value retrieved asynchronously
it('seeds the database before assertions', () => {
  cy.seedApiCall('/api/admin');
  cy.visit('/dashboard');
  cy.get('[data-cy="user-count"]').should('not.be.empty');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.env()` for all new code in projects running Cypress 15.10+. The async API future-proofs secret retrieval and avoids the synchronous global-state footgun where `Cypress.env()` was accidentally read before config was fully resolved in some plugin setups. When NOT to use: do not mix `cy.env()` and `Cypress.env()` in the same helper — pick one path per codebase and enforce it via an ESLint rule (`no-restricted-syntax` targeting `Cypress.env(`). Named alternative: `Cypress.expose()` for non-sensitive values that are not secrets — it surfaces them in the App's Resolved Configuration view, making debugging configuration drift much easier in CI.

---

### 262. `justInTimeCompile` for Large Component Test Suites (v14.0+)  [official]

`justInTimeCompile` (JIT) graduated from `experimentalJustInTimeCompile` in Cypress 14.0 and is now enabled by default (`justInTimeCompile: true`). JIT compiles only the resources directly needed by each spec file immediately before that spec runs, rather than eagerly compiling the entire project upfront. For large component test suites with hundreds of specs, this can reduce initial startup time from minutes to seconds and eliminates the "full rebuild on every run" overhead that made component testing feel slow in CI. JIT is currently webpack-only; Vite-based component test setups already benefit from on-demand module resolution and do not require JIT.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — explicitly confirm JIT is on (it is by default in v14+)
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  component: {
    devServer: {
      framework: 'react',
      bundler: 'webpack',
    },
    // JIT is true by default; set false only for debugging bundler cold-start issues
    justInTimeCompile: true,
    specPattern: 'src/**/*.cy.{ts,tsx}',
    // Pair with indexHtmlFile for monorepo setups with custom HTML shells
    indexHtmlFile: 'cypress/support/component-index.html',
  },
});

// cypress/support/component.tsx — React 19 mount with ErrorBoundary wrapper
import React from 'react';
import { mount } from 'cypress/react';
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { ErrorBoundary } from 'react-error-boundary';

Cypress.Commands.add('mount', (component, options = {}) => {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient({
    defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false } },
  });
  const wrapped = (
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <ErrorBoundary fallback={<div data-cy="error-boundary">Error</div>}>
        {component}
      </ErrorBoundary>
    </QueryClientProvider>
  );
  return mount(wrapped, options);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use JIT for webpack-based component test suites with >50 specs where cold-start compilation time is noticeable. JIT is safe to leave enabled globally. When NOT to use: if you encounter a bundler-level error that is hard to trace (e.g., an import resolve failure that disappears and reappears intermittently), temporarily set `justInTimeCompile: false` to force full upfront compilation and expose the real error. Named alternative: migrating to Vite (`bundler: 'vite'`) naturally achieves on-demand compilation and additionally benefits from HMR during `cypress open` interactive sessions.

---

### 263. `cy.origin()` + `cy.session()` for SSO / Third-Party OAuth Flows  [official]

Cypress 14.0 made `cy.origin()` mandatory for any cross-origin navigation, including subdomain hops. Combining `cy.session()` (for credential caching) with `cy.origin()` (for executing commands on the identity-provider domain) produces a highly efficient SSO login command. The session is set up once, cached across tests in the same run, and only re-established when the `validate()` callback detects an expired session. Data passed into `cy.origin()` callbacks must use the `args` option because the callback runs in an isolated JS context with no closure access to outer variables.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts
declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      loginSSO(username: string, password: string): Chainable<void>;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.add('loginSSO', (username: string, password: string) => {
  cy.session(
    [username, password],
    () => {
      cy.visit('/app');
      // App redirects to identity provider on a different subdomain
      cy.origin(
        'https://auth.example.com',
        { args: { username, password } },
        ({ username, password }) => {
          cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(username);
          cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type(password);
          cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
          // Wait for redirect back to the app origin
          cy.url().should('include', 'app.example.com');
        }
      );
    },
    {
      validate() {
        // Session is valid as long as the /api/me endpoint returns 200
        cy.request({ url: '/api/me', failOnStatusCode: false })
          .its('status')
          .should('eq', 200);
      },
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true, // reuse across all spec files in one run
    }
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use this pattern for any real SSO or OAuth flow where mocking the identity provider is impractical (e.g., staging environments with a live IdP). `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` means the login is performed once per CI run, not once per spec. When NOT to use: do not use this pattern when the identity provider is unreliable or rate-limits test logins — use `cy.intercept()` to mock the OAuth token exchange instead. Named alternative: `cy.task('getOAuthToken')` + setting `document.cookie` in `onBeforeLoad` for fully mocked auth flows that never touch the real IdP.

---

### 264. `before:response` Interceptor Phase for Response Header Mutation  [official]

`cy.intercept()` supports three lifecycle phases: `before:response` (fires before response handlers and before the browser receives data), `response` (fires after `before:response`), and `after:response` (fires after the browser has received all data). The `before:response` phase is the only phase where mutating `res.headers` is guaranteed to take effect before the browser parses the response. This is essential for injecting or removing security headers (e.g., removing `Content-Security-Policy` to allow test scripts, or injecting `Cache-Control: no-store` to prevent caching in tests).

```typescript
// Remove CSP header globally so injected test scripts are never blocked
// Place in cypress/support/e2e.ts
beforeEach(() => {
  cy.intercept({ middleware: true }, (req) => {
    req.on('before:response', (res) => {
      // Strip CSP so Cypress's own script injection is never blocked
      delete res.headers['content-security-policy'];
      delete res.headers['content-security-policy-report-only'];
      // Force no-cache so stale responses don't mask test state
      res.headers['cache-control'] = 'no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate';
    });
  });
});

// Per-test: inject a correlation header into ALL responses for distributed tracing
it('all responses carry the test run correlation ID', () => {
  const correlationId = Cypress.currentTest.title.replace(/\s+/g, '-');
  cy.intercept({ middleware: true }, (req) => {
    req.on('before:response', (res) => {
      res.headers['x-test-correlation-id'] = correlationId;
    });
  });

  cy.visit('/');
  cy.get('[data-cy="app-shell"]').should('exist');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `before:response` when you need to mutate response headers before the browser processes them — CSP removal, CORS header injection, cache-busting. The `middleware: true` flag ensures this handler runs before any per-route handlers regardless of definition order. When NOT to use: do not use `before:response` to read final response state for assertions — use `after:response` instead, which fires when the browser has finished receiving the response. Named alternative: `cy.intercept(url, { headers: { 'Cache-Control': 'no-store' } })` as a StaticResponse — simpler but replaces the entire response rather than mutating headers on a proxied real response.

---

### 265. `cy.clock()` with `setSystemTime()` for Date-Relative UI Testing  [official]

`cy.clock()` returns a clock object that exposes `setSystemTime()` (added in Cypress 10.7), allowing the controlled system time to be changed mid-test without resetting the fake timers. This enables testing relative-time UI elements ("2 days ago", "expires tomorrow") by pinning the clock to a known date rather than computing expected strings from `new Date()`. The key pattern is calling `cy.clock(new Date('2026-01-15T12:00:00'))` before `cy.visit()` so the page's JavaScript initializes with the fake clock already installed.

```typescript
describe('Relative timestamp rendering', () => {
  it('shows "2 days ago" for items created 2 days before current time', () => {
    // Pin the clock BEFORE visiting so all JS initialization uses the fake time
    const now = new Date('2026-03-10T10:00:00.000Z');
    cy.clock(now);

    cy.visit('/feed');
    cy.get('[data-cy="feed-item-1"]')
      .find('[data-cy="timestamp"]')
      .should('have.text', '2 days ago'); // item created 2026-03-08

    // Advance time by 24 hours to test the "3 days ago" transition
    cy.tick(24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
    // After tick, relative-time components should re-render
    cy.get('[data-cy="feed-item-1"]')
      .find('[data-cy="timestamp"]')
      .should('have.text', '3 days ago');
  });

  it('shows "expires today" badge for items expiring on the current date', () => {
    const expiryDate = new Date('2026-06-01T00:00:00.000Z');
    cy.clock(expiryDate);
    cy.visit('/offers');
    cy.get('[data-cy="offer-badge"]').should('contain.text', 'Expires Today');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.clock()` + `setSystemTime()` / `cy.tick()` whenever UI renders date-relative strings so tests don't become flaky as calendar time advances. Pin the clock to a static date in fixtures. When NOT to use: do not combine `cy.clock()` with `cy.intercept()` `delay` options exceeding `cy.tick()` increments — the real timer still tracks wall-clock time for the Cypress proxy layer; only browser JS timers are faked. Named alternative: inject a `testCurrentDate` URL query parameter that the app reads to override its clock — no Cypress-specific clock needed, but requires a production code branch guarded by `process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test'`.

---

### 266. `Cypress.require()` for Cross-Origin Callback Dependencies  [official]

Inside `cy.origin()` callbacks, standard `import()` and CommonJS `require()` do not work because the callback is serialized, transmitted to the secondary origin's browser context, and executed there. `Cypress.require()` is the sanctioned mechanism for loading shared utilities (e.g., a `loginHelpers.ts` module) within `cy.origin()` callbacks. It requires `experimentalOriginDependencies: true` in `cypress.config.ts`. Without this, sharing logic across origins requires inlining code directly into the callback — a maintenance burden when the shared logic evolves.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    experimentalOriginDependencies: true,
  },
});

// cypress/support/origin-helpers.ts — shared utility used across origins
export function fillLoginForm(username: string, password: string): void {
  cy.get('[name="username"]').clear().type(username);
  cy.get('[name="password"]').clear().type(password);
  cy.get('[type="submit"]').click();
}

// In a test: use Cypress.require() to load the helper inside cy.origin()
it('completes OAuth login via identity provider', () => {
  cy.visit('/start-oauth');

  cy.origin(
    'https://idp.example.com',
    { args: { user: 'alice@example.com', pass: 'secret' } },
    ({ user, pass }) => {
      // Cypress.require() loads the module in the secondary origin's JS context
      const { fillLoginForm } = Cypress.require(
        '../../support/origin-helpers'
      ) as typeof import('../../support/origin-helpers');

      fillLoginForm(user, pass);
      cy.url().should('include', 'app.example.com/callback');
    }
  );

  cy.get('[data-cy="logged-in-banner"]').should('be.visible');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `Cypress.require()` when multiple tests share login or interaction logic that must execute inside `cy.origin()` callbacks — it eliminates copy-paste duplication across callbacks. When NOT to use: do not use `Cypress.require()` for large utility files with deep dependency trees; the serialization and transfer overhead can slow down tests. Inline small one-off helpers directly in the callback. Named alternative: `cy.task()` for side-effects that can be handled entirely in Node (e.g., generating a magic-link token via a DB call) — avoids needing cross-origin JS execution altogether.

---

### 267. `cy.intercept()` `times` Counter + Overflow Guard Pattern  [official]

`cy.intercept()` accepts a `times` property in the `RouteMatcher` options to restrict the number of requests matched by a rule. Once exhausted, the rule is automatically removed and subsequent requests pass through to the real server unrecorded. The overflow guard pattern installs a second catch-all intercept after the primary `times`-limited one — if any overflow request hits the catch-all, the test fails with a descriptive error rather than silently sending traffic to a real API.

```typescript
it('submits the form exactly once and does not double-post on retry click', () => {
  // Primary rule: match only 1 POST, then exhaust the rule
  cy.intercept(
    { method: 'POST', url: '/api/orders', times: 1 },
    { statusCode: 201, body: { id: 'ord-001' } }
  ).as('firstOrder');

  // Overflow guard: catches any request past the exhausted rule
  cy.intercept('POST', '/api/orders', (req) => {
    req.reply({
      statusCode: 500,
      body: { error: 'Test guard: unexpected duplicate POST to /api/orders' },
    });
    throw new Error('Overflow: duplicate POST /api/orders was NOT expected');
  }).as('overflowGuard');

  cy.visit('/checkout');
  cy.get('[data-cy="place-order"]').click();
  cy.wait('@firstOrder').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 201);
  cy.get('[data-cy="order-confirmation"]').should('be.visible');

  // Button should be disabled after first submit — overflow guard catches regressions
  cy.get('[data-cy="place-order"]').should('be.disabled');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the overflow guard pattern when testing idempotency-sensitive endpoints (payment submissions, form posts, webhook triggers) where a duplicate request is a bug, not a test artifact. The guard converts a silent false-pass into a loud immediate failure. When NOT to use: do not add overflow guards for polling endpoints or endpoints that legitimately receive multiple requests per user action. Named alternative: `cy.get('@alias.all').should('have.length', 1)` — simpler but only works if the `times`-limited rule remains active; the overflow guard is more reliable across navigation.

---

### 268. Custom `cy.mount()` with Angular 19 `TestBed` Providers  [official]

Angular's Cypress component testing integration uses `TestBed` under the hood. Customizing `cy.mount()` to inject `provideHttpClient()`, `provideRouter([])`, and application-level providers eliminates the need to redeclare them in every spec. Angular 19 introduced standalone components as the default; `cy.mount()` accepts them directly without a `declarations` array. The `MountConfig` type from `cypress/angular` gives full TypeScript coverage over mount options.

```typescript
// cypress/support/component.ts — Angular 19 custom mount
import { Type } from '@angular/core';
import {
  provideHttpClient,
  withInterceptorsFromDi,
} from '@angular/common/http';
import { provideRouter } from '@angular/router';
import { provideStore } from '@ngrx/store';
import { MountConfig, mount } from 'cypress/angular';
import { reducers } from '../../src/app/store';

type CyMountOptions<T> = MountConfig<T> & {
  initialState?: Record<string, unknown>;
};

Cypress.Commands.add(
  'mount',
  <T>(component: Type<T>, options: CyMountOptions<T> = {}) => {
    const { initialState = {}, ...mountConfig } = options;
    return mount(component, {
      ...mountConfig,
      providers: [
        provideHttpClient(withInterceptorsFromDi()),
        provideRouter([]),
        provideStore(reducers, { initialState }),
        ...(mountConfig.providers ?? []),
      ],
    });
  }
);

// In spec file — Angular 19 standalone component test
import { UserCardComponent } from './user-card.component';

it('renders the user display name and role badge', () => {
  cy.mount(UserCardComponent, {
    componentProperties: { user: { id: '1', name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' } },
  });
  cy.get('[data-cy="user-name"]').should('have.text', 'Alice');
  cy.get('[data-cy="role-badge"]').should('have.text', 'admin');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use a customized `cy.mount()` for Angular apps with shared providers (HTTP client, Router, Store) so individual specs stay clean. The `initialState` pattern allows specs to seed NgRx store state without dispatching actions, making tests faster and more isolated. When NOT to use: do not add every provider globally in `cy.mount()` — lazy-loaded feature providers should remain in the spec that needs them to keep the test boundary tight. Named alternative: Angular `TestBed.configureTestingModule()` configured in a `beforeEach` — equivalent power but more verbose and not reusable across specs without a helper factory.

---

### 269. `cy.task()` for Database Seeding and Teardown in Node  [official]

`cy.task()` executes arbitrary Node code in the `setupNodeEvents` callback, making it the canonical way to seed databases, purge test records, and read secrets from environment without reaching into the browser context. Tasks must return a non-`undefined` value (or a Promise resolving to non-`undefined`) — returning `null` is the convention when a task has no meaningful return value. Pair tasks with `before` / `after` hooks (not `beforeEach` / `afterEach`) for expensive seeding operations that can be shared across all tests in a suite.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — task registration
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import { seedDatabase, teardownDatabase, queryUser } from './cypress/plugins/db';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    setupNodeEvents(on) {
      on('task', {
        async 'db:seed'(scenario: string) {
          await seedDatabase(scenario);
          return null; // explicit null — task must not return undefined
        },
        async 'db:teardown'() {
          await teardownDatabase();
          return null;
        },
        async 'db:getUser'(email: string) {
          const user = await queryUser(email);
          return user ?? null; // null if not found — never return undefined
        },
      });
    },
  },
});

// In spec file
describe('User profile page', () => {
  before(() => {
    cy.task('db:seed', 'user-profile-suite'); // seed once for the whole describe
  });

  after(() => {
    cy.task('db:teardown');
  });

  it('displays the seeded user email', () => {
    cy.task('db:getUser', 'alice@example.com').then((user) => {
      expect(user).to.have.property('email', 'alice@example.com');
    });
    cy.visit('/profile/alice');
    cy.get('[data-cy="profile-email"]').should('have.text', 'alice@example.com');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.task()` for all database and filesystem interactions that must run in a Node environment — it is more reliable than `cy.exec()` (which spawns a separate shell process with its own PATH and environment limitations). When NOT to use: do not register long-running or non-terminating processes as tasks (e.g., a dev server); tasks must resolve or the test hangs indefinitely. Named alternative: HTTP API seed endpoints (e.g., `cy.request('POST', '/api/test/seed', { scenario })`) — simpler to debug but requires a test-only route in the server that must be blocked in production.

---

### 270. Svelte 5 Component Testing with `cy.mount()` and Runes  [official]

Cypress added Svelte 5 Alpha support in v14.0 and stabilized it across v15.x. Svelte 5 introduced "runes" — reactive primitives (`$state`, `$derived`, `$effect`) — which replace the implicit reactivity from Svelte 4 stores. When mounting Svelte 5 components in Cypress, props are passed via the `props` option as plain values; rune-based reactivity is driven by the component's own internal state. `cy.mount()` returns a wrapper object containing the mounted component instance, usable for controlled state transitions in tests.

```typescript
// cypress/support/component.ts — Svelte 5 setup
import { mount } from 'cypress/svelte';

Cypress.Commands.add('mount', mount);

// In spec file — Svelte 5 component with $state rune
// Component source (Counter.svelte):
//   let count = $state(0);
//   function increment() { count++; }

import Counter from '../../src/lib/Counter.svelte';

describe('Counter component (Svelte 5 runes)', () => {
  it('starts at the provided initial count', () => {
    cy.mount(Counter, { props: { initialCount: 5 } });
    cy.get('[data-cy="count"]').should('have.text', '5');
  });

  it('increments on button click', () => {
    cy.mount(Counter, { props: { initialCount: 0 } });
    cy.get('[data-cy="increment"]').click().click().click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="count"]').should('have.text', '3');
  });

  it('emits the updated count via a callback prop', () => {
    const onChangeSpy = cy.spy().as('onChange');
    cy.mount(Counter, { props: { initialCount: 0, onChange: onChangeSpy } });
    cy.get('[data-cy="increment"]').click();
    cy.get('@onChange').should('have.been.calledOnceWith', 1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use Svelte 5 component testing in Cypress when the component has complex reactive logic (derived state, effects) that is easier to assert against through the real DOM than through unit tests of the rune values in isolation. Cypress component tests verify the rendered output; Vitest unit tests verify the rune logic. When NOT to use: do not write Cypress component tests for Svelte 5 components that are purely presentational with no interactivity — a simple snapshot-style Vitest test is faster and CI-cheaper. Named alternative: `@testing-library/svelte` with Vitest — full rune support, no browser overhead, but loses the real DOM environment that Cypress provides.

---

### 271. Cypress Cloud Test Replay + Smart Orchestration Setup  [official]

Cypress Cloud Test Replay records the exact sequence of DOM states, network requests, and console output during every test run, enabling post-run replay of failures without re-running them. The new **Cloud MCP** (Model Context Protocol) tool exposes real-time test run data to AI assistants, enabling natural-language questions about failures grounded in actual run data. Cloud Smart Orchestration combines Spec Prioritization (failed specs run first), Parallelization, and Auto Cancellation (stops the run when a configurable failure threshold is hit) to minimize CI cost and feedback loop time.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — Cloud integration setup
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    // Cypress Cloud project ID (set CYPRESS_PROJECT_ID in CI env)
    projectId: process.env.CYPRESS_PROJECT_ID,

    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      on('task', {
        'log:cloudRunUrl'(runId: string) {
          const projectId = config.projectId;
          console.log(
            `Cypress Cloud: https://cloud.cypress.io/projects/${projectId}/runs/${runId}`
          );
          return null;
        },
      });
      return config;
    },
  },
});

// In CI (GitHub Actions) — record + parallel + Smart Orchestration
// cypress run \
//   --record \
//   --key ${{ secrets.CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY }} \
//   --parallel \
//   --ci-build-id ${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
// Auto Cancellation threshold is configured in Cypress Cloud UI:
// Cloud > Project Settings > Smart Orchestration > Auto Cancellation
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use Cypress Cloud with Test Replay for any project where CI failures are intermittent or hard to reproduce locally — the replay eliminates the "works on my machine" debugging cycle. Auto Cancellation saves real money on parallel CI machines when a suite-wide regression is introduced. When NOT to use: do not enable `--record` for local development runs or PR preview branches where you don't need Cloud analytics — it adds network overhead and consumes Cloud usage minutes. Named alternative: `cypress run --headed --no-exit` locally for interactive debugging; `DEBUG=cypress:*` env variable for low-level proxy and runner diagnostics.

---

### 272. `cy.prompt()` AI-Powered Test Generation (v15.13 Beta)  [official]

`cy.prompt()` is a beta command (graduated from experimental in v15.13.0 — no configuration flag required) that accepts a plain-English instruction and uses an AI model to generate and execute the corresponding Cypress commands. It includes a self-healing mechanism that retries with adjusted selectors when elements are not found in cache. A "Convert to Code" modal in the Cypress App allows developers to inspect the generated command sequence and commit it as permanent test code, closing the loop between AI-generated exploration and durable test logic.

```typescript
// cy.prompt() basic usage — plain-English action description
it('fills and submits the registration form using AI-generated steps', () => {
  cy.visit('/register');

  // cy.prompt() generates and executes the Cypress commands internally
  cy.prompt(
    'Fill in the registration form with name "Bob Smith", ' +
    'email "bob@test.com", and password "Secr3t!"'
  );
  cy.prompt('Click the "Create Account" button');

  // Always assert with standard Cypress commands after AI-driven interaction
  cy.url().should('include', '/welcome');
  cy.get('[data-cy="welcome-message"]').should('contain.text', 'Bob Smith');
});

// Pairing cy.prompt() with explicit selectors for verifiable coverage
it('navigates to settings and updates notification preferences', () => {
  cy.loginSSO('user@example.com', 'pass');
  cy.visit('/dashboard');

  cy.prompt('Open the user settings menu and navigate to Notifications');
  cy.url().should('include', '/settings/notifications');

  // Use explicit selectors for assertions — do not delegate assertions to cy.prompt()
  cy.get('[data-cy="email-notifications-toggle"]').should('be.visible').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="save-settings"]').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="success-toast"]').should('be.visible');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.prompt()` for rapid exploratory test drafting and for translating acceptance criteria written in plain English into runnable Cypress steps. It is especially useful for onboarding contributors unfamiliar with Cypress selectors. When NOT to use: do not commit tests that rely exclusively on `cy.prompt()` steps — the AI-generated commands are non-deterministic and may change behavior across Cypress or app updates. Always use the "Convert to Code" flow to produce stable, selector-explicit test code before merging. Named alternative: Cypress Studio (available by default since v15.4) — click-to-record generates explicit `cy.get().click()` / `.type()` steps; lower AI unpredictability but requires manual browser interaction.

---

### 273. Firefox WebDriver BiDi for Network Interception (v14.1+)  [official]

Cypress 14.1 migrated Firefox 135+ from the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) to the WebDriver BiDi protocol. BiDi brings Firefox's network interception capabilities much closer to parity with Chromium, enabling `cy.intercept()`, `cy.stub()` on browser APIs, and response modification to work reliably in Firefox tests for the first time. Teams running cross-browser suites can now run the full `cy.intercept()`-heavy test suite on Firefox without special guards. WebDriver BiDi is a W3C standard, so this also improves long-term portability across browser engines.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — cross-browser config, BiDi auto-enabled for Firefox 135+
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    setupNodeEvents(on) {
      on('before:browser:launch', (browser, launchOptions) => {
        if (browser.name === 'firefox' && browser.majorVersion >= 135) {
          // BiDi is active automatically — log for CI audit trail
          console.log(
            'Firefox BiDi active — full cy.intercept() support enabled'
          );
        }
        return launchOptions;
      });
    },
  },
});

// This cy.intercept() call now works identically in Chrome AND Firefox 135+
it('intercepts API in Firefox with full BiDi support', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products', { fixture: 'products.json' }).as(
    'products'
  );
  cy.visit('/shop');
  cy.wait('@products');
  cy.get('[data-cy="product-list"]').children().should('have.length.gt', 0);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use Firefox in your cross-browser matrix for any app where Firefox user share is meaningful — BiDi removes the last major blocker for full Cypress support on Firefox. Run Chrome (primary), Firefox (BiDi), and optionally WebKit for broad coverage. When NOT to use: do not run the full suite on all three browsers in every PR — gate multi-browser runs to nightly/release pipelines to keep PR feedback loops fast. Named alternative: Playwright for cross-browser E2E — native BiDi support and broader browser coverage, but requires a separate test codebase; prefer Cypress Firefox for teams already invested in Cypress.

---

### 274. `Cypress.ElementSelector` API — Selector Priority Customization (v15.0)  [official]

Cypress 15.0 renamed `Cypress.SelectorPlayground` to `Cypress.ElementSelector` as part of an API cleanup. The underlying capabilities are identical: `defaults()` sets attribute priority, and `override()` installs a custom generator callback that receives the DOM element and returns a CSS selector string. Projects customizing selector generation must update the reference before upgrading to v15 or the customization silently stops working. v15 also added `name` attribute to the default selector priority list.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts — v15.0+ selector customization
// BEFORE (v14 and earlier — now fails silently in v15):
// Cypress.SelectorPlayground.defaults({ selectorPriority: ['data-cy', 'id'] });

// AFTER (v15.0+):
Cypress.ElementSelector.defaults({
  selectorPriority: [
    'data-cy',
    'data-testid',
    'data-test',
    'aria-label',
    'name',     // new in v15: added to default priority list
    'id',
    'class',
    'tag',
    'nth-child',
  ],
});

// Custom override: prefer aria-label for interactive elements, fall back to data-cy
Cypress.ElementSelector.override((element: HTMLElement) => {
  const ariaLabel = element.getAttribute('aria-label');
  if (ariaLabel) {
    return `[aria-label="${CSS.escape(ariaLabel)}"]`;
  }
  const dataCy = element.getAttribute('data-cy');
  if (dataCy) {
    return `[data-cy="${dataCy}"]`;
  }
  const dataTestId = element.getAttribute('data-testid');
  if (dataTestId) {
    return `[data-testid="${dataTestId}"]`;
  }
  return null; // fall back to Cypress default
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `Cypress.ElementSelector.override()` when your design system uses `aria-label` or `name` attributes as the primary accessible identifier — Studio and the Selector Playground will then generate selectors that align with your accessibility strategy. When NOT to use: do not customize the selector strategy to produce brittle positional selectors (`.nth-child()`) — this makes auto-generated tests fragile to markup changes. Named alternative: enforcing `data-testid` or `data-cy` on all interactive elements via an ESLint rule (`eslint-plugin-testing-library`) is more reliable than custom selector overrides.

---

### 275. Conditional GraphQL Operation Aliasing for Batching-Safe Intercepts  [official]

GraphQL APIs send all operations to a single endpoint (typically `POST /graphql`). `cy.intercept()` can alias individual operations by reading `req.body.operationName` in the route handler and setting `req.alias` dynamically — but only when the body is a single operation object (not an array, which happens when Apollo Client or urql batching is enabled). The conditional alias pattern handles both batched and non-batched requests safely without requiring a test-environment feature flag to disable batching.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts — reusable GQL intercept helper
function interceptGql(
  operationName: string,
  response?: Record<string, unknown>
): Cypress.Chainable {
  return cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql', (req) => {
    // Guard: Apollo/urql batch mode sends an array body
    if (Array.isArray(req.body)) {
      const matched = req.body.some(
        (op: { operationName?: string }) => op.operationName === operationName
      );
      if (!matched) return;
      req.alias = `gql_${operationName}_batched`;
      if (response) req.reply({ data: response });
      return;
    }
    if (req.body?.operationName !== operationName) return;
    req.alias = `gql_${operationName}`;
    if (response) req.reply({ data: response });
  });
}

// In spec file
it('displays user profile after GetUser resolves', () => {
  interceptGql('GetUser', {
    user: { id: '1', name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' },
  });
  cy.visit('/users/1');
  cy.wait('@gql_GetUser');
  cy.get('[data-cy="profile-name"]').should('have.text', 'Alice');
});

it('optimistically updates name after UpdateUser mutation', () => {
  interceptGql('UpdateUser', { user: { id: '1', name: 'Alice Updated' } });
  cy.get('[data-cy="edit-name"]').clear().type('Alice Updated');
  cy.get('[data-cy="save"]').click();
  cy.wait('@gql_UpdateUser');
  cy.get('[data-cy="profile-name"]').should('have.text', 'Alice Updated');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the conditional alias pattern for any GraphQL endpoint where batching might be enabled — it handles both modes without requiring a test-environment feature flag. When NOT to use: do not use per-operation `req.alias` for performance-monitoring assertions where you need to time every single GraphQL request including batched ones — use a blanket `cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql').as('gql_all')` and inspect `req.body` in `cy.wait('@gql_all.all')`. Named alternative: `msw` (Mock Service Worker) with `graphql.query('GetUser', ...)` — cleaner GQL-aware API, but requires a service worker setup and is harder to correlate with Cypress timing assertions.

---

## Additional Community Gotchas (Cycle 33) [community]

234. **`cy.origin()` callbacks cannot contain `cy.intercept()` — network mocking set up inside a `cy.origin()` block is silently ignored and requests reach the real server** [community] — `cy.intercept()` is implemented at the Cypress proxy level, which operates on the primary origin's network traffic. The secondary origin's network traffic routes through a different proxy instance that does not have access to intercept rules defined in the primary context. WHY: The two origins run in isolated browsing contexts with separate network stacks; Cypress's proxy cannot inject intercept handlers across this boundary at runtime. Fix: register all `cy.intercept()` rules before entering `cy.origin()` at the primary-context level — the proxy intercepts cross-origin requests if they are registered before navigation begins.

235. **`justInTimeCompile: true` (webpack only) can produce a stale-cache error when two specs share a re-exported barrel `index.ts` — changing a component imported via the barrel causes only the changed component's spec to recompile, leaving barrel-importing specs running against a stale bundle** [community] — JIT compiles each spec's dependency graph independently. When Component A exports through `components/index.ts` and Spec B only imports from `index.ts`, JIT may not trace the invalidation chain through the barrel re-export in watch mode (`cypress open`). WHY: Webpack's module invalidation graph follows explicit `import` edges; barrel re-exports add indirection that some versions of Cypress's JIT asset graph tracker do not resolve. Fix: configure `resolve.alias` to avoid barrel re-exports in test code, or set `justInTimeCompile: false` in watch mode only via `CYPRESS_justInTimeCompile=false`.

236. **`cy.session()` `validate()` calling `cy.request()` triggers global `Cypress.Commands.overwrite('request', ...)` wrappers — debug wrappers calling `cy.task()` emit unexpected task calls on every test that restores a cached session** [community] — `cy.session()` internally calls `cy.request()` in its validation step. If the team has a global request wrapper (for logging or auth header injection), that wrapper fires during every session validation including silent restore-checks that should be zero-overhead. WHY: `Commands.overwrite()` is global with no "internal only" call path. Fix: guard the overwrite with a path check: `if (options.url?.includes('/api/me')) return originalFn(options);` — or use `{ log: false }` in the validate `cy.request()` call to suppress log output without unwrapping.

237. **`cy.clock()` does NOT freeze `performance.now()` by default — debounce utilities and animation-frame schedulers using `performance.now()` instead of `Date.now()` are unaffected by `cy.tick()`** [community] — `cy.clock()` wraps `sinon.useFakeTimers()` with a default `toFake` list that includes `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearInterval`, and `Date`. `performance.now()` is NOT in the default list. WHY: `performance` is a separate Web API object; sinon requires explicit opt-in to fake it. Fix: `cy.clock(Date.now(), ['setTimeout', 'clearTimeout', 'setInterval', 'clearInterval', 'Date', 'performance'])`. Warning: faking `performance` can break browser-internal timing APIs like `requestAnimationFrame` scheduling — test carefully after enabling it.

238. **Svelte 5 `$effect()` runes run asynchronously after DOM updates — asserting on `$effect()`-driven output immediately after a user action fails intermittently because the effect has not yet executed** [community] — In Svelte 5, `$effect()` runs after the next microtask following a reactive update, similar to React's `useEffect()`. A `cy.get('[data-cy="btn"]').click()` followed immediately by asserting on an element rendered by an async `$effect()` can race. WHY: Cypress retry-ability does handle eventual DOM changes up to `defaultCommandTimeout`, but effects gated on `fetch()` inside `$effect()` may exceed the default timeout if the mock is not set up correctly. Fix: always wait for a network alias before asserting on `$effect()`-driven output: `cy.wait('@effectData')` then assert, or set a selective timeout: `.should('exist', { timeout: 10000 })`.

239. **`cy.env()` (v15.10 async command) cannot be called inside `cy.intercept()` request handlers — the intercept handler is a synchronous proxy callback and `cy.env()` enqueues a command onto the test queue that never executes inside the handler** [community] — `cy.intercept()` handlers are synchronous event callbacks processed by Cypress's proxy layer, not the Cypress command queue. Calling `cy.env('SECRET')` inside a handler enqueues a new command onto the test's command queue, but the proxy callback has already returned — the command never runs and the value is always `undefined`. WHY: The Cypress command queue and the proxy event loop are separate execution contexts; commands queued from inside a proxy callback are detached orphans. Fix: retrieve the env value before registering the intercept and close over it: `cy.env('API_KEY').then(key => { cy.intercept('/api/...', req => { req.headers['Authorization'] = \`Bearer ${key}\`; }); });`

### 276. Angular 21 Zoneless Component Testing with `cypress/angular-zoneless`  [official]

Angular 21 defaults to zoneless change detection using the `provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()` provider, removing the dependency on `zone.js`. Cypress 15.8.0 introduced the `cypress/angular-zoneless` harness to test zoneless components natively — without importing `zone.js` into the test environment. Using the standard `cypress/angular` harness with a zoneless component causes incorrect test behavior because Cypress will not trigger change detection at the right moments. The zoneless harness uses Angular's `ApplicationRef.tick()` and signal-driven change detection to synchronise the test with the component's rendering cycle.

```typescript
// cypress/component/user-card.cy.ts — zoneless Angular 21 component test
import { mount } from 'cypress/angular-zoneless';   // ← not 'cypress/angular'
import { UserCardComponent } from './user-card.component';
import { signal } from '@angular/core';

describe('UserCardComponent (zoneless)', () => {
  it('updates the displayed name when the name signal changes', () => {
    const name = signal('Alice');

    mount(UserCardComponent, {
      componentProperties: { name },   // pass signal as prop
    });

    cy.get('[data-cy="user-name"]').should('have.text', 'Alice');

    // Mutate the signal and verify the DOM reacts
    cy.then(() => name.set('Bob'));
    cy.get('[data-cy="user-name"]').should('have.text', 'Bob');
  });

  it('emits the correct event when the delete button is clicked', () => {
    const deleteSpy = cy.spy().as('deleteSpy');
    mount(UserCardComponent, {
      componentProperties: { name: signal('Carol'), onDelete: deleteSpy },
    });

    cy.get('[data-cy="delete-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('@deleteSpy').should('have.been.calledOnceWith', 'Carol');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cypress/angular-zoneless` for any Angular 21+ component that was bootstrapped without `zone.js` (i.e., uses `provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()`). When NOT to use: do not mix `cypress/angular` and `cypress/angular-zoneless` in the same test suite — the harnesses use different change-detection strategies and mixing them causes subtle false-positives. Named alternative: Angular Testing Library (`@testing-library/angular`) with `renderHook` for purely logic-focused unit tests where DOM rendering is not the focus.

### 277. `cy.intercept()` Bandwidth Throttling and Network Error Circuit-Breaker  [official]

`cy.intercept()` supports `throttleKbps` to simulate slow connections and `forceNetworkError: true` combined with `times` to reproduce circuit-breaker behavior in the UI. Throttling is applied after the response body is received — it slows the browser's consumption of the response stream rather than adding server latency. The `times` option limits how many requests a route matches, enabling a "fail once then recover" pattern that validates retry logic without permanently degrading the test environment. Pairing both techniques in a single test validates both degraded-network UX and resilience recovery in one spec.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/network-resilience.cy.ts
describe('Network resilience patterns', () => {
  it('shows a loading skeleton under a 56 Kbps throttled connection', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products', (req) => {
      req.reply({
        statusCode: 200,
        fixture: 'products.json',
        throttleKbps: 56,   // simulate dial-up for large payload test
      });
    }).as('slowProducts');

    cy.visit('/shop');
    // Assert skeleton is visible BEFORE the throttled response arrives
    cy.get('[data-cy="skeleton-loader"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.wait('@slowProducts');
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-list"]').children().should('have.length.gt', 0);
    cy.get('[data-cy="skeleton-loader"]').should('not.exist');
  });

  it('retries once after a network error and then succeeds (circuit-breaker)', () => {
    // First request → network error; second request → real fixture
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/orders', { forceNetworkError: true, times: 1 }).as(
      'firstAttempt'
    );
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/orders', { fixture: 'orders.json' }).as(
      'retryAttempt'
    );

    cy.visit('/orders');
    cy.wait('@firstAttempt');
    cy.get('[data-cy="retry-banner"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="retry-btn"]').click();
    cy.wait('@retryAttempt');
    cy.get('[data-cy="order-list"]').should('exist');
    cy.get('[data-cy="retry-banner"]').should('not.exist');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `throttleKbps` to gate loading-state and progressive-enhancement tests in your critical E2E suite; use `forceNetworkError + times` to validate retry UI logic. When NOT to use: do not use `throttleKbps` in the majority of tests — it significantly increases suite runtime. Reserve bandwidth simulation for a dedicated "slow network" CI job. Named alternative: Chrome DevTools Protocol network conditions via `cy.task('setNetworkConditions', ...)` using the CDP plugin — more granular (round-trip latency + download + upload), but requires a custom plugin and is Chromium-only.

### 278. `cy.session()` Timestamp-Sentinel Idle-Timeout Validation  [official]

`cy.session()` has no built-in `idleTimeout` option, but applications commonly expire sessions after a period of inactivity tracked via a `localStorage` or `cookie` sentinel. The recommended pattern encodes an expiry timestamp during setup and checks it in `validate()` — if the stored value is absent or the timestamp is in the past, the validate callback fails (triggering a re-login) rather than making an expensive `/api/me` round-trip on every restore. This approach is pure-browser, requires no network call, and avoids triggering `Commands.overwrite('request')` wrappers accidentally.

```typescript
// cypress/support/auth.ts — timestamp sentinel session validation
const SESSION_EXPIRY_KEY = 'session_expires_at';
const SESSION_TTL_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000; // 30 minutes to match app idle timeout

export function loginWithSentinel(email: string, password: string): void {
  cy.session(
    ['sentinel', email],
    () => {
      cy.visit('/login');
      cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(email);
      cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type(password, { log: false });
      cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
      cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
      // Write an expiry sentinel after successful login
      cy.window().then((win) => {
        win.localStorage.setItem(
          SESSION_EXPIRY_KEY,
          String(Date.now() + SESSION_TTL_MS)
        );
      });
    },
    {
      validate() {
        // Cheap localStorage read — no network call needed
        cy.window()
          .its(`localStorage.${SESSION_EXPIRY_KEY}`)
          .should('exist')
          .then((expiry) => {
            expect(Number(expiry)).to.be.greaterThan(Date.now());
          });
      },
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
    }
  );
}
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the sentinel pattern when the application stores session expiry metadata client-side and your `/api/me` endpoint is slow or triggers auth-wrapper side effects. When NOT to use: do not use this pattern if session expiry is server-controlled only (e.g., a sliding-window cookie without client-side metadata) — the sentinel would never expire and `validate()` would never re-trigger login. Named alternative: validate with a `cy.request('/api/me')` call guarded by `{ log: false, failOnStatusCode: false }` — simpler but makes a network round-trip on every session restore.
