### 279. `Cypress.Commands.addQuery()` — Typed Retry-Able Query (Double-Function Pattern)  [official]

`Cypress.Commands.addQuery()` creates retry-able queries that return a function yielding a subject — fundamentally different from `Commands.add()` which enqueues a command. The outer function runs once (setup), and the inner function runs on every retry until the assertion passes or the timeout is reached. This makes `addQuery()` suitable for wrapping synchronous DOM lookups that must retry. TypeScript declaration merging via `Cypress.Chainable<Subject>` augmentation provides full intellisense. The inner function must be synchronous — returning a Promise from the inner function causes retry-ability to break silently.

```typescript
// cypress/support/queries.ts — typed addQuery with declaration merging
declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      getByRole(
        role: string,
        options?: { name?: string | RegExp }
      ): Chainable<JQuery<HTMLElement>>;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.addQuery(
  'getByRole',
  function getByRole(role: string, options?: { name?: string | RegExp }) {
    // Outer function: validate args, set timeout (runs once)
    this.set('timeout', Cypress.config('defaultCommandTimeout'));

    // Inner function: runs on every retry — MUST be synchronous
    return () => {
      const selector = options?.name
        ? `[role="${role}"][aria-label="${options.name}"]`
        : `[role="${role}"]`;
      const elements = Cypress.$(selector);

      if (elements.length === 0) {
        throw new Error(`No element with role "${role}" found`);
      }
      return elements;
    };
  }
);

// Usage in spec:
it('finds a button by ARIA role and label', () => {
  cy.visit('/dashboard');
  cy.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).should('be.visible').click();
  cy.getByRole('alert').should('contain.text', 'Saved successfully');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `addQuery()` when building custom selectors that need Cypress's built-in retry-ability (e.g., ARIA role lookups, shadow DOM traversal). When NOT to use: do not use `addQuery()` for commands that trigger side effects (clicking, typing, network requests) — use `Commands.add()` for those. Named alternative: `cy.get('[role="button"][aria-label="Save"]')` — simpler for one-off selectors; `addQuery()` is only worth the setup cost for project-wide reuse.

### 280. `cy.prompt()` Placeholders for Cache-Stable Dynamic Values  [official]

`cy.prompt()` caches AI-generated command sequences keyed on the exact prompt string and the DOM snapshot. If dynamic values (user IDs, timestamps, auth tokens) are embedded directly in the step string, every test run with different data triggers a fresh AI call — burning rate-limit quota and slowing CI. The `placeholders` option replaces dynamic tokens with stable named keys before the prompt is sent to the AI; the actual value is injected at runtime without invalidating the cache. This pattern is essential for maintaining CI efficiency on paid Cypress Cloud plans and is required for keeping secrets out of AI-sent data.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/checkout.cy.ts — using placeholders to stabilise prompt cache
describe('Checkout flow', () => {
  it('completes a purchase with a dynamic order ID', () => {
    const orderId = `ORD-${Date.now()}`;    // dynamic every run
    const cardNumber = Cypress.env('TEST_CARD_NUMBER'); // sensitive value

    cy.visit('/cart');

    cy.prompt(
      [
        'Add the first product to the cart',
        'Proceed to checkout',
        // Use placeholder tokens — actual values never sent to AI
        'Enter card number {{cardNumber}} in the payment field',
        'Confirm the order and note order ID {{orderId}}',
      ],
      {
        placeholders: {
          cardNumber,     // injected at runtime, not in cached key
          orderId,        // dynamic — cache remains valid across runs
        },
      }
    );

    cy.url().should('include', '/confirmation');
    cy.get('[data-cy="order-id"]').should('contain.text', orderId);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `placeholders` for any `cy.prompt()` step that includes run-specific or user-specific data, and always for sensitive values (passwords, tokens, card numbers). When NOT to use: do not use `cy.prompt()` steps (with or without placeholders) as the primary test coverage strategy in CI — `cy.prompt()` is E2E-only, Chromium-only, and requires Cypress Cloud; prefer converting generated code to explicit Cypress commands via the "Code" modal before merging. Named alternative: `cy.type(Cypress.env('TEST_CARD_NUMBER'))` — explicit, offline, no AI quota usage.

### 281. `cy.origin()` with `Cypress.require()` for Shared Utilities (experimentalOriginDependencies)  [official]

By default, the `cy.origin()` callback cannot import modules — it serializes only the function body, not its closure. The `experimentalOriginDependencies` flag enables `Cypress.require()` inside `cy.origin()` callbacks, allowing shared utilities, helpers, and constants to be loaded from the secondary origin's context. Unlike `require()`, `Cypress.require()` is resolved relative to the spec file rather than the secondary-origin page, enabling cross-cutting test utilities to be shared. The argument to `Cypress.require()` must be a string literal — it cannot be a variable, because the static path is evaluated at parse time to build the dependency bundle.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/sso-login.cy.ts
// cypress.config.ts must have: experimentalOriginDependencies: true

it('logs in via the SSO provider and returns to the app', () => {
  cy.session('sso-session', () => {
    cy.visit('/login');
    cy.get('[data-cy="sso-login-btn"]').click();

    cy.origin(
      'https://sso.example.com',
      () => {
        // Cypress.require() — string MUST be a literal, not a variable
        const { fillSsoForm } = Cypress.require(
          '../../support/sso-helpers'
        );

        fillSsoForm({
          username: Cypress.env('SSO_USER'),
          password: Cypress.env('SSO_PASS'),
        });
      }
    );

    // Back on the primary origin after SSO redirect
    cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
    cy.get('[data-cy="user-avatar"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `Cypress.require()` inside `cy.origin()` when helper functions must be shared across multiple cross-origin tests without copy-pasting callback bodies. When NOT to use: do not use `Cypress.require()` for importing modules with side effects (e.g., modules that call `cy.intercept()` at module level) — such modules would execute outside the primary command queue. Named alternative: pass pre-computed values through the `args` option — simpler for data, but cannot share functions or class methods.

### 282. `cy.intercept()` `req.reply()` vs `req.continue()` vs `before:response` Decision Matrix  [official]

`cy.intercept()` handlers have three distinct response strategies that are frequently confused. `req.reply()` immediately stubs a response and stops further handler matching — the server is never called. `req.continue()` forwards the modified request to the real server (or the next matching handler) and optionally inspects or mutates the real response via a callback — incurs real network latency. `req.on('before:response', ...)` is the non-blocking middleware option: it intercepts the real response and allows header/body mutation without forking the request path. Choosing the wrong strategy produces subtly wrong tests.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/intercept-strategies.cy.ts
describe('req.reply() vs req.continue() vs before:response', () => {
  it('[stub] uses req.reply() for fully-stubbed responses (no server call)', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/config', (req) => {
      req.reply({ featureFlags: { newUI: true } }); // server never called
    }).as('stubConfig');
    cy.visit('/');
    cy.wait('@stubConfig');
    cy.get('[data-cy="new-ui-banner"]').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('[passthrough] uses req.continue() to modify request then inspect real response', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/user', (req) => {
      req.headers['x-test-mode'] = 'true'; // add header before forwarding
      req.continue((res) => {
        // Real response received — assert or mutate it
        expect(res.statusCode).to.eq(200);
        res.body.displayName = res.body.displayName.toUpperCase();
      });
    }).as('user');
    cy.visit('/profile');
    cy.wait('@user');
    cy.get('[data-cy="user-display-name"]').should('match', /^[A-Z\s]+$/);
  });

  it('[middleware] uses req.on("before:response") for non-blocking header injection', () => {
    cy.intercept({ url: '/api/**', middleware: true }, (req) => {
      req.on('before:response', (res) => {
        res.headers['x-test-injected'] = 'true';
        // Does NOT block — control returns to next handler immediately
      });
    });
    cy.request('/api/health').its('headers.x-test-injected').should('eq', 'true');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `req.reply()` when test isolation requires deterministic, network-free responses. Use `req.continue((res) => ...)` when you need to assert on real server responses or partially override response fields. Use `req.on('before:response', ...)` for cross-cutting middleware (CORS header injection, auth header logging) that should not change control flow. When NOT to use: do not use `req.continue()` in unit-style E2E tests — real network calls add latency and non-determinism. Named alternative: `cy.request()` for pure API contract tests where no browser interaction is needed.

---

### 283. TypeScript Module Augmentation for Custom Cypress Commands  [official]

TypeScript requires explicit declaration merging to make custom commands visible to the compiler — without it, `cy.myCommand()` produces a type error. The canonical pattern augments `Cypress.Chainable` in the `Cypress` namespace inside `cypress/support/commands.ts`. Since Cypress 15.x and TypeScript 6, using `interface` merging (not `type` alias) is required: type aliases cannot be merged. The declaration must live inside a `.ts` file included in the `tsconfig.json` types path — placing it in a `.d.ts` file that is not referenced causes the augmentation to be silently ignored.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts — canonical TS module augmentation

declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      /**
       * Log in via the API and cache the session with cy.session().
       * @param email - User email
       * @param password - User password (not logged)
       */
      loginApi(email: string, password: string): Chainable<void>;

      /**
       * Assert that a toast notification with the given text is visible.
       * @param text - Expected toast message (partial match)
       */
      assertToast(text: string): Chainable<JQuery<HTMLElement>>;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.add('loginApi', (email: string, password: string) => {
  cy.session([email, 'api'], () => {
    cy.request({
      method: 'POST',
      url: '/api/auth/login',
      body: { email, password },
      log: false,
    }).then(({ body }) => {
      window.localStorage.setItem('authToken', body.token);
    });
  });
});

Cypress.Commands.add('assertToast', (text: string) => {
  return cy
    .get('[data-cy="toast"]', { timeout: 8000 })
    .should('be.visible')
    .and('contain.text', text);
});

export {}; // ensure file is treated as a module (not a script)
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use module augmentation for any command shared across more than 2 spec files — it provides compile-time safety and IDE autocompletion. When NOT to use: do not add commands for one-off test helpers that are used only once — an inline helper function inside the spec is simpler and does not pollute the global command namespace. Named alternative: `cy.wrap(myHelper())` — keeps logic local to the spec and avoids the augmentation overhead.

---

### 284. `cy.clock()` with Explicit `toFake` List for `performance.now()` Control  [official]

`cy.clock()` wraps `sinon.useFakeTimers()` but only fakes a default subset of time APIs: `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearInterval`, and `Date`. Animations, debounce utilities, and performance-sensitive libraries using `performance.now()` are unaffected by `cy.tick()` unless `performance` is added to the `toFake` array explicitly. Faking `performance` can break `requestAnimationFrame` scheduling in some browsers — always test the full animation cycle after enabling it. The safest approach is to add `performance` only when the test proves it is necessary.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/debounce-search.cy.ts — controlling performance.now()-aware debounce
describe('Search debounce (250ms, uses performance.now())', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Explicitly include 'performance' so performance.now()-based debounce is frozen
    cy.clock(Date.now(), [
      'setTimeout',
      'clearTimeout',
      'setInterval',
      'clearInterval',
      'Date',
      'performance',   // ← opt-in: controls performance.now() and hrtime
    ]);
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    cy.clock().invoke('restore');
  });

  it('does not fire the search API until 250ms have elapsed', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/search*').as('search');
    cy.visit('/');

    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('cypress');
    // Advance by 100ms — debounce should NOT have fired yet
    cy.tick(100);
    cy.get('@search.all').should('have.length', 0);

    // Advance to 250ms — debounce fires
    cy.tick(150);
    cy.wait('@search')
      .its('request.url')
      .should('include', 'query=cypress');
  });

  it('resets the debounce timer on each keystroke', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/search*').as('search');
    cy.visit('/');

    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('c');
    cy.tick(200);
    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('y'); // resets debounce
    cy.tick(200);
    // Still below 250ms since last keystroke — should NOT have fired
    cy.get('@search.all').should('have.length', 0);
    cy.tick(50);
    cy.wait('@search');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Add `'performance'` to `toFake` only when testing code that explicitly uses `performance.now()` for timing (custom debounce, animation schedulers, Web Audio). When NOT to use: do not add `'performance'` by default — it can break browser-internal `requestAnimationFrame` and `IntersectionObserver` scheduling. Named alternative: mock the `debounce` function itself at the module level using `cy.stub()` on the imported module — avoids all `performance.now()` complexity.

---

### 285. `--posix-exit-codes` Flag for Consistent CI Pipeline Integration (v15.4+)  [official]

Cypress 15.4.0 introduced the `--posix-exit-codes` CLI flag, which forces Cypress to use POSIX-standard exit codes. Without the flag, Cypress uses custom exit codes (e.g., `1` for test failures, `3` for config errors) that some CI systems misinterpret. With `--posix-exit-codes`, all failures map to exit code `1`, which is universally recognised by Bash `&&`/`||` chains, GitHub Actions `if: failure()` conditions, and Jenkins pipeline `sh` steps. Teams integrating Cypress into polyglot CI pipelines benefit most — custom exit codes often cause silent swallowing of Cypress failures in Jenkins or Bitbucket Pipelines.

```typescript
// package.json scripts — recommended CI invocations
// {
//   "scripts": {
//     "cy:run:ci": "cypress run --posix-exit-codes --record --key $CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY",
//     "cy:run:smoke": "cypress run --posix-exit-codes --spec 'cypress/e2e/smoke/**'"
//   }
// }

// .github/workflows/e2e.yml — GitHub Actions integration
// - name: Run Cypress E2E tests
//   run: npx cypress run --posix-exit-codes --record --key ${{ secrets.CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY }}
//   env:
//     CYPRESS_BASE_URL: ${{ env.APP_URL }}
// - name: Upload artifacts on failure
//   if: failure()   # Works correctly with exit code 1 from --posix-exit-codes
//   uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
//   with:
//     name: cypress-screenshots
//     path: cypress/screenshots
//     if-no-files-found: ignore   # v6 schema change: was 'require-files-found'

// cypress.config.ts — document the expectation for new team members
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    env: {
      CI_EXIT_CODE_MODE: 'posix',  // documentation only — flag is CLI-only
    },
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      // Note: --posix-exit-codes is a CLI flag only, not configurable here.
      // Add to npm scripts and CI YAML files.
      return config;
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `--posix-exit-codes` on all CI invocations, especially in pipelines that chain commands with `&&` or use POSIX-based error trapping. When NOT to use: do not use it when calling Cypress via the Module API (`cypress.run()`) — the Module API returns a `results` object with a `status` field; exit codes do not apply. Named alternative: check `result.status === 'failed'` from the Module API return value — gives programmatic access to failure status without relying on process exit codes.

---

### 286. `cy.task()` Database Reset: `before`/`after` vs `beforeEach`/`afterEach` Strategy  [official]

`cy.task()` bridges Cypress and Node.js to perform database operations. The correct placement of `cy.task('db:seed')` and `cy.task('db:reset')` calls affects both test isolation and suite speed. A `beforeEach` seed guarantees a clean state before every test but is expensive for large seed datasets. A `before` seed with `afterEach` targeted cleanup is faster but risks state leakage if a test is interrupted before `afterEach` runs. The recommended hybrid: use `before` for read-only reference data and `beforeEach` for mutable state. `cy.task()` must return a value (not `undefined`) — return `null` for void operations.

```typescript
// cypress/support/db.ts — typed task map pattern
export interface DbTaskMap {
  'db:seed:users': { count: number } | null;
  'db:reset:orders': null;
  'db:create:order': { orderId: string; total: number };
  'db:delete:order': { orderId: string } | null;
}

declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      dbTask<K extends keyof DbTaskMap>(
        event: K,
        arg?: unknown
      ): Chainable<DbTaskMap[K]>;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.add('dbTask', (event, arg?) =>
  cy.task(event, arg ?? null)
);

// cypress/e2e/orders.cy.ts — hybrid seed strategy
describe('Order management', () => {
  before(() => {
    // Seed read-only reference data once (users, products)
    cy.dbTask('db:seed:users', { count: 5 });
  });

  beforeEach(() => {
    // Reset only the mutable state (orders) before each test
    cy.dbTask('db:reset:orders');
  });

  it('creates a new order and persists it', () => {
    cy.dbTask('db:create:order', { orderId: 'test-001', total: 99.99 });
    cy.visit('/orders');
    cy.get('[data-cy="order-row"]').should('have.length', 1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `beforeEach` database resets for tests where mutation order matters and cleanup-on-failure is critical. Use `before` + `afterEach` for expensive seed operations where test independence can be guaranteed by only deleting test-created records. When NOT to use: do not use `afterEach` for `db:reset` in isolation-first test suites — if Cypress crashes mid-test, `afterEach` does not run, and the next test sees dirty state. Named alternative: `cy.request()` to call a test-only `DELETE /api/test/reset` endpoint — avoids task setup overhead but requires a test-only endpoint in the server.

---

### 287. `cy.intercept()` Global Auth Header Middleware with `middleware: true`  [official]

When every API call in the app requires an `Authorization` header, registering a single middleware intercept with `{ middleware: true }` is cleaner than adding header injection to every individual intercept or using `cy.request()` wrappers. Middleware routes always run first regardless of definition order, and they do not consume the route's match slot — subsequent specific intercepts still match. The middleware pattern also prevents test token leakage: by centralising auth header injection, individual test specs cannot accidentally omit it.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts — global auth header middleware
beforeEach(() => {
  cy.window().then((win) => {
    const token = win.localStorage.getItem('authToken');
    if (!token) return;

    // Register middleware BEFORE any test-specific intercepts
    cy.intercept(
      { url: '/api/**', middleware: true },
      (req) => {
        req.headers['Authorization'] = `Bearer ${token}`;
        // Middleware continues without replying — subsequent handlers still fire
      }
    );
  });
});

// cypress/e2e/dashboard.cy.ts — no auth header boilerplate in test specs
describe('Dashboard', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.loginApi('user@example.com', Cypress.env('USER_PASSWORD'));
    cy.visit('/dashboard');
  });

  it('loads the dashboard widgets', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/dashboard/widgets', {
      fixture: 'widgets.json',
    }).as('widgets');
    cy.reload();
    cy.wait('@widgets');
    cy.get('[data-cy="widget"]').should('have.length.gt', 0);
  });

  it('shows an error banner when the widgets API returns 500', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/dashboard/widgets', {
      statusCode: 500,
      body: { error: 'Internal Server Error' },
    }).as('widgetsFail');
    cy.reload();
    cy.wait('@widgetsFail');
    cy.get('[data-cy="error-banner"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use global middleware auth injection for applications with a consistent authentication model across all API endpoints. When NOT to use: do not use this pattern when different tests need different auth roles — middleware registered in `beforeEach` applies to all calls in that test; use per-test `cy.intercept()` overrides for role-specific scenarios instead. Named alternative: `cy.request()` with a shared `headers` object — fine for API-only tests, but does not inject headers into browser-initiated fetch/XHR calls.

### 288. Cypress Cloud MCP Integration for AI-Assisted Test Triage  [official]

Cypress Cloud's Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration exposes live test run data, flake statistics, and failure details to AI assistants (Claude, Copilot, Cursor). Once installed, the MCP server answers questions like "which tests are flakiest this sprint?" or "what are the most common failure patterns in the last 10 runs?" directly in the AI assistant's context. The integration requires configuring the MCP server with a Cypress Cloud API key and is read-only — it cannot trigger runs or modify tests. For teams using AI-assisted code review, this reduces the context-switching cost of correlating CI failures with source changes.

```typescript
// .mcp.json — Cypress Cloud MCP server configuration
// Place in project root or ~/.config/mcp/config.json for global access
// {
//   "mcpServers": {
//     "cypress-cloud": {
//       "command": "npx",
//       "args": ["@cypress/mcp-server"],
//       "env": {
//         "CYPRESS_CLOUD_API_KEY": "${CYPRESS_CLOUD_API_KEY}"
//       }
//     }
//   }
// }

// cypress/e2e/flake-tagged.cy.ts — companion pattern: tag tests for MCP triage analytics
// Using @cypress/grep to mark known-flaky tests for Cloud flake analytics
describe('Payment flow', { tags: ['@smoke', '@payment'] }, () => {
  it(
    'completes a card payment',
    { tags: ['@flaky'] },   // surfaces in MCP flake query results
    () => {
      cy.visit('/checkout');
      cy.get('[data-cy="card-number"]').type('4111111111111111');
      cy.get('[data-cy="expiry"]').type('12/29');
      cy.get('[data-cy="cvv"]').type('123');
      cy.get('[data-cy="pay-btn"]').click();
      cy.get('[data-cy="success-message"]').should('be.visible');
    }
  );
});

// Example AI assistant queries enabled by MCP (no code changes required):
// "Show me the 5 flakiest tests in the @payment tag from the last 7 days"
// "What error messages appear most in the @smoke failures this week?"
// "Which specs have > 10% failure rate in the main branch CI runs?"
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the Cloud MCP integration for teams with 50+ tests in CI where failure triage is a regular time sink. When NOT to use: do not use the MCP integration as a substitute for fixing flaky tests — it surfaces patterns, but the fix still requires code changes. Named alternative: Cypress Cloud's built-in Flaky Test Management dashboard — visual, no AI setup required, but requires manual investigation vs. conversational AI triage.

### 289. `experimentalFastVisibility` Opt-In with Shadow DOM Guard  [official]

`experimentalFastVisibility` (introduced in v15.8.0) replaces Cypress's legacy visibility detection algorithm with a point-sampling approach that is constant-time in the common case. The critical limitation: Shadow DOM elements are not yet supported — visibility checks on elements inside shadow roots may incorrectly report `false` (invisible) or `true` (visible) depending on the shadow boundary. Teams using Web Components or design systems built on Shadow DOM must add a per-spec opt-out until the limitation is resolved. The flag is overridable per-spec via `Cypress.config()`, enabling a gradual rollout strategy.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — enable experimentalFastVisibility globally
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    experimentalFastVisibility: true,
  },
  component: {
    experimentalFastVisibility: true,
    devServer: {
      framework: 'react',
      bundler: 'vite',
    },
  },
});

// cypress/e2e/web-components.cy.ts — per-spec opt-out for shadow DOM tests
// Disable fast algorithm for this spec which uses shadow DOM components
Cypress.config('experimentalFastVisibility', false);

describe('Web Components with shadow DOM', () => {
  it('checks visibility of a slot element inside a shadow root', () => {
    cy.visit('/wc-demo');
    // Without the opt-out, this assertion may fail incorrectly (shadow DOM bug)
    cy.get('my-card').shadow().find('[data-cy="card-title"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('my-button').shadow().find('button').should('not.be.disabled');
  });
});

// cypress/e2e/standard-dom.cy.ts — uses fast visibility (inherits from config)
describe('Standard DOM tests (no shadow DOM)', () => {
  it('detects modal visibility efficiently with the fast algorithm', () => {
    cy.visit('/');
    cy.get('[data-cy="open-modal-btn"]').click();
    // Point-sampling algorithm — ~10x speedup on large DOM trees
    cy.get('[data-cy="modal-overlay"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="modal-close"]').should('be.visible').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="modal-overlay"]').should('not.exist');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Enable `experimentalFastVisibility` globally and add per-spec opt-outs only for specs that interact with shadow DOM. When NOT to use: do not enable it in projects where the majority of components are Web Components until the shadow DOM limitation is patched. Named alternative: wait for the Cypress changelog to announce shadow DOM support in the fast algorithm — the fix will be a point release update.

---

### 290. `cy.request()` Typed API Contract Test with Response Shape Assertion  [official]

`cy.request()` accepts a TypeScript generic type parameter that types the `body` of the `Response` object, enabling compile-time-checked API contract tests. Combined with a custom response-shape assertion helper, this pattern produces readable, self-documenting API contract tests without spinning up a browser. The key advantage over `fetch`-based contract tests is that `cy.request()` runs inside Cypress's command queue and integrates with `cy.intercept()`, `cy.task()`, and `cy.session()` for auth setup and database seeding.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/api-contracts.cy.ts — typed API contract tests

interface UserResponse {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  displayName: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'user' | 'viewer';
  createdAt: string; // ISO 8601
}

interface ErrorResponse {
  code: string;
  message: string;
  details?: Record<string, string[]>;
}

describe('User API contract tests', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.loginApi('admin@example.com', Cypress.env('ADMIN_PASSWORD'));
  });

  it('GET /api/users/:id returns a well-typed user shape', () => {
    cy.request<UserResponse>({
      method: 'GET',
      url: '/api/users/user-1',
    }).then(({ status, body }) => {
      expect(status).to.eq(200);
      expect(body).to.have.all.keys([
        'id', 'email', 'displayName', 'role', 'createdAt',
      ]);
      expect(body.role).to.be.oneOf(['admin', 'user', 'viewer']);
      expect(body.createdAt).to.match(/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T/); // ISO 8601
      expect(body.email).to.include('@');
    });
  });

  it('POST /api/users returns 422 with validation errors for missing fields', () => {
    cy.request<ErrorResponse>({
      method: 'POST',
      url: '/api/users',
      body: {},
      failOnStatusCode: false,
    }).then(({ status, body }) => {
      expect(status).to.eq(422);
      expect(body.code).to.eq('VALIDATION_ERROR');
      expect(body.details).to.have.property('email');
      expect(body.details).to.have.property('password');
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.request()` API contract tests for the API layer of your test pyramid — they run faster than full E2E tests and do not require a rendered UI. When NOT to use: do not use `cy.request()` for testing complex request sequences that depend on browser state (cookies, service workers, WebSockets) — use E2E tests with `cy.intercept()` for those. Named alternative: dedicated HTTP testing tools like `supertest` (Node.js) or `pact` (contract testing) — better for pure API testing outside a browser context, but separate from your Cypress suite.

## Additional Community Gotchas (Cycle 34) [community]

240. **`cy.origin()` throws a hard error when `cy.intercept()` is called inside the callback — it does NOT silently ignore it in Cypress 14+** [community] — Contrary to older community documentation describing silent ignoring, Cypress 14.0+ throws a synchronous error: "cy.intercept() is not supported within cy.origin() callbacks." WHY: `cy.intercept()` must be registered with the primary origin's proxy server at the Cypress command queue level; the secondary origin context has no access to the proxy configuration API, and the error is now surfaced explicitly rather than silently dropped. Fix: hoist all `cy.intercept()` registrations to before the `cy.origin()` call — the proxy intercepts cross-origin traffic registered at the primary level without needing to be inside the callback.

241. **`cy.prompt()` re-calls the AI and burns rate-limit quota even when the prompt string is unchanged if the DOM snapshot differs — any dynamic content (timestamps, live counters, A/B variants) in the DOM invalidates the cache on every run** [community] — `cy.prompt()` keys its cache on both the prompt string AND a hash of the DOM snapshot at the time of first execution. If the page contains live-updating elements (a clock, unread notification count, A/B test variant injected by a script), the DOM hash changes on every run. WHY: The AI needs the current DOM to pick stable selectors; caching without a DOM hash would produce incorrect selectors when the app changes, but this design choice means any dynamic content kills cache hits. Fix: use `cy.intercept()` to return static fixtures before the prompt call, use `cy.clock()` to freeze timestamps, and set A/B variant deterministically via a query parameter in `cy.visit()`.

242. **`cy.session()` `validate()` calling `cy.request()` fires all `Cypress.Commands.overwrite('request')` wrappers — debug logging wrappers that call `cy.task('log', ...)` trigger unexpected task calls on every test that restores a cached session** [community] — `cy.session()` internally invokes `cy.request()` during the `validate()` step to check authentication state. If a global `Commands.overwrite('request', ...)` wrapper has been registered for logging or auth header injection, that wrapper runs during every silent session restoration check, not just during explicit test requests. WHY: `Commands.overwrite()` is a global hook with no "internal only" call path; Cypress has no mechanism to distinguish validate-triggered requests from spec-triggered ones. Fix: add a guard option to the overwrite — check `if (options._internal) return originalFn(options)` and pass `{ _internal: true }` in the validate `cy.request()` call; or use `{ log: false }` to suppress at minimum the log output.

243. **`experimentalFastVisibility` silently misreports visibility for elements inside shadow roots — `should('be.visible')` may pass when the element is hidden by the shadow host's CSS overflow or clip** [community] — The point-sampling algorithm used by `experimentalFastVisibility` samples bounding-rectangle corners and center to detect occlusion. Shadow DOM boundaries are opaque to this algorithm — it cannot cross the shadow boundary to evaluate whether a shadow host's `overflow: hidden` or `clip-path` is hiding its shadow content. WHY: The `checkVisibility()` Web API used in the fast algorithm's first pass does not fully account for shadow host CSS in all browser implementations. Fix: add `Cypress.config('experimentalFastVisibility', false)` at the top of any spec file that tests Web Components with shadow DOM until the bug is patched in a future Cypress release.

244. **`cy.intercept()` with `delay` set to a value ≥ 2,147,483,647ms (2^31 − 1) throws a synchronous `RangeError` since Cypress 15.13.1 — tests with very large delay values crash immediately rather than sending the response after a delay** [community] — Cypress 15.13.1 added explicit validation capping the `delay` option at the 32-bit signed integer maximum (`2^31 − 1` ms ≈ 24.8 days). Any value at or above this limit throws: `RangeError: delay value must be less than 2^31`. Prior to this version, the value silently wrapped to a negative number, causing the response to be sent immediately — a subtle false-positive that made timeout tests appear to pass. WHY: JavaScript's `setTimeout()` uses a 32-bit signed integer for the delay; Cypress previously passed the value to `setTimeout` unchecked. Fix: cap delay values to a sensible test-oriented maximum (e.g., `30_000` for a 30-second simulated timeout).

245. **Angular zoneless components tested with `cypress/angular` (not `cypress/angular-zoneless`) silently pass all assertions even when component state is incorrect — `zone.js` change detection fires at the wrong moment in zoneless mode, producing false-positive test results** [community] — When an Angular 21+ zoneless component is mounted using the standard `cypress/angular` harness, the test harness imports `zone.js` and wraps the component's change detection cycle in `NgZone`. In a zoneless component, there is no `NgZone` subscription — `zone.js` does not trigger `ApplicationRef.tick()` for signal-driven reactive updates. As a result, DOM updates driven by `@signal()` or `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush` may not be reflected during the test, and assertions can pass against stale DOM content. WHY: `zone.js` and zoneless change detection are architecturally incompatible; the standard harness cannot bridge the gap. Fix: replace `import { mount } from 'cypress/angular'` with `import { mount } from 'cypress/angular-zoneless'` for all zoneless components (requires Cypress 15.8.0+).

### 291. `Cypress.stop()` Conditional Halt on First Failure  [official]

`Cypress.stop()` (introduced in Cypress 14.2.0) halts test execution on the current machine when called. In `cypress run` mode it skips remaining specs but still uploads results to Cypress Cloud; in `cypress open` mode it stops execution while leaving the interactive UI open for inspection. The most common pattern is an `afterEach` guard that stops the run when the suite has reached an actionable failure state, avoiding noise from cascading downstream failures that are all caused by the same root issue. Unlike `autoCancelAfterFailures` (a Cloud-side setting), `Cypress.stop()` executes client-side and works in offline / non-recorded runs too.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts

// Stop on first failure in CI — avoids cascading noise when setup breaks
afterEach(function () {
  if (Cypress.env('CI') && this.currentTest?.state === 'failed') {
    // Log the failure context before stopping
    cy.task('log', `[STOP] halting run after failure: ${this.currentTest.fullTitle()}`);
    // Return immediately so subsequent hooks don't run
    Cypress.stop();
    return;
  }
});

// Alternatively, stop only when a critical smoke test fails
// so regression suites do not run against a broken environment
Cypress.Commands.add('smokeGate', (endpoint: string) => {
  cy.request({ url: endpoint, failOnStatusCode: false }).then((res) => {
    if (res.status !== 200) {
      cy.log(`[smokeGate] ${endpoint} returned ${res.status} — stopping run`);
      Cypress.stop();
    }
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `Cypress.stop()` when a single upstream failure (e.g., broken auth, missing seed data) would cause every downstream test to fail for the same reason. Avoid it in development mode — stopping on first failure destroys the ability to see the full picture of what's broken across the suite.

---

### 292. `cy.env()` Selective Secret Fetching vs `Cypress.env()` Deprecation  [official]

`cy.env()` (introduced in Cypress 15.10.0) is the successor to the now-deprecated `Cypress.env()`. The new command accepts an **array** of key names and returns an object containing only the requested keys, preventing accidental serialisation of the entire environment config into the browser context. It integrates naturally into Cypress command chains because it is asynchronous — unlike the synchronous `Cypress.env()` getter. Setting `allowCypressEnv: false` in `cypress.config` enforces the migration by making `Cypress.env()` throw at runtime, which is useful for enforcing the new pattern across a team.

```typescript
// cypress/support/auth.ts

// BEFORE (deprecated — exposes all env vars to browser state):
// const token = Cypress.env('API_TOKEN');

// AFTER — request only what this command needs
Cypress.Commands.add('loginWithToken', () => {
  cy.env(['API_TOKEN', 'API_BASE_URL']).then(({ API_TOKEN, API_BASE_URL }) => {
    cy.request({
      method: 'POST',
      url: `${API_BASE_URL}/auth/token`,
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${API_TOKEN}` },
      log: false,           // never log sensitive auth requests
      failOnStatusCode: true,
    }).then((res) => {
      window.localStorage.setItem('auth_token', res.body.access_token);
    });
  });
});

// cypress.config.ts — enforce migration across the team
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    allowCypressEnv: false,   // Cypress.env() now throws a runtime error
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Migrate to `cy.env()` as soon as the team upgrades to Cypress 15.10+. The asynchronous nature requires wrapping all secret access in `.then()` chains, which is slightly more verbose — but the reduced attack surface for env-variable leakage in recorded runs justifies the change. For non-sensitive public config (feature flags, API version strings), use the synchronous `Cypress.expose()` instead.

---

### 293. `Cypress.expose()` for Public Configuration — Synchronous Access Pattern  [official]

`Cypress.expose()` (introduced Cypress 15.10.0) provides **synchronous** access to public, non-sensitive configuration values defined in the `expose` block of `cypress.config`. Values are available without a command chain, making them safe to use in `beforeEach` setup logic, `describe` block titles, and TypeScript type guards. The key distinction from `cy.env()` is intentional: `Cypress.expose()` is for feature flags, API version strings, and environment labels — never for credentials.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    expose: {
      apiVersion: 'v3',
      featureFlags: {
        newCheckout: true,
        legacyCart: false,
      },
      environment: process.env.DEPLOY_ENV ?? 'local',
    },
  },
});

// cypress/support/e2e.ts — synchronous access, no .then() needed
const config = Cypress.expose();

// Skip legacy tests when the new checkout is active
const featureFlags = Cypress.expose('featureFlags') as { newCheckout: boolean; legacyCart: boolean };

Cypress.Commands.add('skipIfLegacyDisabled', () => {
  if (!featureFlags.legacyCart) {
    cy.log('Legacy cart disabled — skipping test');
    return;
  }
});

// Use in describe titles for readable CI output
describe(`Checkout flow [${Cypress.expose('apiVersion')}]`, () => {
  it('completes a purchase', () => {
    cy.visit(`/checkout?api=${Cypress.expose('apiVersion')}`);
    cy.get('[data-cy="place-order"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="confirmation"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `Cypress.expose()` is a clean replacement for reading `Cypress.env()` for public values. Its synchronous nature makes it usable in places where `cy.env()` cannot work (e.g., module-level code, `describe` titles). Never store secrets here — all values set via `expose` are visible in the Command Log and recorded video.

---

### 294. `Cypress.ElementSelector` Custom Selector Priority for AI-Generated and Studio Selectors  [official]

`Cypress.ElementSelector` (renamed from `Cypress.SelectorPlayground` in Cypress 15.0.0) controls which attributes Cypress prioritises when generating selectors in Cypress Studio, `cy.prompt()`, and the interactive Selector Playground. Configuring it in `cypress/support/e2e.ts` ensures that AI-generated selectors from `cy.prompt()` use your team's `data-*` testing attributes rather than unstable auto-generated `id` or `class` values. The API extends to custom attribute patterns, ARIA roles, and composite selectors when single attributes are not unique enough.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts

// Define team-wide selector priority — applied to Studio, cy.prompt(), and Playground
Cypress.ElementSelector.defaults({
  selectorPriority: [
    'data-cy',        // team standard: highest priority
    'data-testid',    // fallback for third-party component libs
    'data-test',      // legacy attribute still present in older pages
    'aria-label',     // accessibility-first fallback
    'name',           // form field fallback
    'id',             // last resort — often auto-generated
    // 'class' intentionally omitted — too fragile
  ],
});

// Custom selector function for nth-child fallback when no data-* exists
Cypress.ElementSelector.getSelector((el: HTMLElement) => {
  const dataCy = el.getAttribute('data-cy');
  if (dataCy) return `[data-cy="${dataCy}"]`;

  const ariaLabel = el.getAttribute('aria-label');
  if (ariaLabel) return `[aria-label="${CSS.escape(ariaLabel)}"]`;

  // Return null to fall through to Cypress's built-in logic
  return null;
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Configure `Cypress.ElementSelector` during initial project setup so that every selector generated by Studio and `cy.prompt()` is stable from day one. If added retroactively after a team has already used Studio/`cy.prompt()`, existing generated selectors are not automatically updated — only new selectors use the new priority. Named alternative: annotate every interactive element with `data-cy` attributes manually, bypassing the need for selector priority customisation entirely.

---

### 295. Cypress Module API — Programmatic Run with `exitCode` (v15 Breaking Change)  [official]

The Cypress Module API allows `cypress.run()` to be called from a Node.js script, returning a Promise that resolves with a detailed results object. In Cypress 15.0.0, the property name changed from `result.code` to `result.exitCode` — a breaking change for any CI orchestration script that parsed the exit code programmatically. The Module API is useful for post-run hooks: sending Slack notifications on failure, re-running only the failed spec files, or triggering downstream deployment pipelines only when all tests pass.

```typescript
// scripts/run-tests.ts — programmatic Cypress run with post-run handling
import cypress from 'cypress';
import { IncomingWebhook } from '@slack/webhook';

const SLACK_URL = process.env.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL ?? '';

async function runTests(): Promise<void> {
  const results = await cypress.run({
    browser: 'chrome',
    spec: 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts',
    record: true,
    key: process.env.CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY,
  });

  // v15+ uses exitCode; v14 and earlier used code
  const exitCode = (results as any).exitCode ?? (results as any).code ?? 1;

  if (exitCode !== 0 && results.totalFailed > 0) {
    const webhook = new IncomingWebhook(SLACK_URL);
    await webhook.send({
      text: `Cypress: ${results.totalFailed} test(s) failed in ${results.totalDuration}ms`,
      attachments: results.runs.flatMap((run) =>
        run.tests
          .filter((t) => t.state === 'failed')
          .map((t) => ({ text: t.title.join(' > '), color: 'danger' }))
      ),
    });
  }

  process.exit(exitCode);
}

runTests().catch((err) => {
  console.error('cypress.run() threw:', err);
  process.exit(1);
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use the Module API when you need post-run logic that goes beyond what `--reporter` and `--reporter-options` can express (e.g., conditional retries, Slack notifications, deployment gates). When NOT to use: avoid it for simple CI pipelines — the standard `cypress run` CLI with a Mocha reporter is simpler and less brittle. The `exitCode` rename in v15 is the most common migration footgun; guard against it with the `?? (results as any).code` fallback shown above.

---

### 296. `--posix-exit-codes` Flag and Exit Code 112 for Cloud-Required Runs  [official]

By default, `cypress run` returns the number of failed tests as the process exit code. When failures exceed 255, this wraps around to a misleading value due to modulo-256 arithmetic. The `--posix-exit-codes` flag (added in Cypress 15.4.0) switches to POSIX-standard codes: `0` for all tests passing, `1` for any failure, and `112` for network-connectivity errors when `--record` or `--parallel` are used and Cypress Cloud is unreachable. Using this flag is now the recommended approach for any CI pipeline that parses exit codes.

```typescript
// .github/workflows/cypress.yml (excerpt)
// jobs:
//   test:
//     steps:
//       - uses: cypress-io/github-action@v7
//         with:
//           browser: chrome
//           record: true
//           parallel: true
//           command: npx cypress run --posix-exit-codes --record --parallel

// scripts/ci-gate.sh — interpret POSIX exit codes
// EXIT=$?
// if [ $EXIT -eq 0 ]; then echo "All tests passed"; fi
// if [ $EXIT -eq 1 ]; then echo "Tests failed"; fi
// if [ $EXIT -eq 112 ]; then echo "Network error — Cypress Cloud unreachable"; fi

// cypress.config.ts — enable posixExitCodes via config (alternative to CLI flag)
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    posixExitCodes: true,
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      on('after:run', (results) => {
        if ('exitCode' in results) {
          console.log(`[CI] Cypress exit code: ${results.exitCode}`);
        }
      });
      return config;
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Always use `--posix-exit-codes` in CI when your pipeline or orchestration script distinguishes between "test failures" and "infrastructure/network failures" — exit code 112 enables automatic retry logic for transient Cloud connectivity issues rather than treating them as genuine test failures. When NOT to use: if your CI system post-processes the number of failures (e.g., creates a graph of failures over time), `--posix-exit-codes` loses that granularity — keep the default if you need the raw count.

---

### 297. `justInTimeCompile` for Large Webpack Component Test Suites  [official]

`justInTimeCompile` (promoted from experimental to default in Cypress 14.0.0) compiles only the resources directly referenced by the current component spec, rather than building the entire project graph before the first spec runs. For large Angular or React webpack monorepos, this can reduce the time to first test from minutes to seconds. The feature is **webpack-only** — it has no effect when using Vite as the dev server. Teams upgrading from Cypress 13.x with `experimentalJustInTimeCompile: true` can remove the explicit flag since it is now the default.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — explicit configuration for webpack CT
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import webpackConfig from './webpack.config';

export default defineConfig({
  component: {
    devServer: {
      framework: 'react',
      bundler: 'webpack',
      webpackConfig,
    },
    // justInTimeCompile is ON by default for webpack — explicit only to document intent
    // Set false ONLY if you have a custom plugin that requires the full bundle upfront
    // justInTimeCompile: false,
    specPattern: 'src/**/*.cy.{ts,tsx}',
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      on('before:run', () => {
        console.log('[CT] justInTimeCompile active — only referenced modules compiled');
      });
      return config;
    },
  },
});

// cypress/support/component.tsx — mount helper for React 18+
import React from 'react';
import { mount } from 'cypress/react18';
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';

// Wrap all components in standard providers
Cypress.Commands.add('mountWithProviders', (component, options = {}) => {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient({
    defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false, staleTime: 0 } },
  });
  mount(
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>{component}</QueryClientProvider>,
    options
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** `justInTimeCompile` is transparent for most projects — leave it at the default. The only reason to disable it is if a custom webpack plugin (e.g., a code-generation plugin that processes all modules at startup) requires the full build graph before any spec runs. Vite-based projects do not benefit and the flag is silently ignored.

---

### 298. `cy.press()` for Keyboard Navigation and Focus-Trap Testing (v14.3+)  [official]

`cy.press()` (introduced Cypress 14.3.0) dispatches native `keydown` and `keyup` events to the browser window rather than to a specific element, making it ideal for testing application-level keyboard shortcuts, focus traps, and modal dismissal via `Escape`. Unlike `cy.type('{key}')` which targets a focused element, `cy.press()` operates at the `window` level and triggers the browser's transient activation state. It accepts a single key string — multi-key combinations are not supported; use `cy.type()` with modifier syntax for chord shortcuts.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/keyboard-nav.cy.ts

describe('Keyboard navigation and focus trap', () => {
  beforeEach(() => cy.visit('/'));

  it('closes modal with Escape key', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="open-modal-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="modal"]').should('be.visible');

    // cy.press() dispatches to window — no element focus needed for Escape
    cy.press('Escape');
    cy.get('[data-cy="modal"]').should('not.exist');
  });

  it('traps focus inside dialog with Tab cycling', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="open-dialog-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="dialog"]').should('be.visible');

    // Tab through focusable elements inside the dialog
    cy.get('[data-cy="dialog-first-input"]').focus();
    cy.press('Tab');
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'dialog-second-input');

    cy.press('Tab');
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'dialog-close-btn');

    // Tab from last element should wrap back to first (focus trap)
    cy.press('Tab');
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'dialog-first-input');
  });

  it('navigates menu items with arrow keys', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="menu-trigger"]').click().focus();
    cy.press('ArrowDown');
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'menu-item-1');
    cy.press('ArrowDown');
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'menu-item-2');
    cy.press('Enter');
    cy.get('[data-cy="menu-trigger"]').should('not.have.class', 'open');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cy.press()` for window-level keyboard events (modal close, global shortcuts) and focus-trap cycle testing. Use `cy.type()` for element-scoped text input and modifier chord shortcuts (`{ctrl+a}`, `{shift+Tab}`). Note that `cy.press()` yields `null` — you cannot chain element queries directly off it; start a new `cy.get()` chain after each `cy.press()` call.

---

### 299. `cy.prompt()` Placeholders for Cache-Stable Dynamic Values (Beta, v15.13+)  [official]

`cy.prompt()` (graduated to beta in Cypress 15.13.0) generates test code from natural-language step descriptions using AI. Its cache keys on both the prompt string AND the DOM snapshot at call time. The `placeholders` option replaces volatile runtime values in the prompt with stable tokens, preventing cache invalidation when test data changes between runs. Placeholders also protect sensitive values from appearing in the Cypress Cloud prompt log. Without placeholders, any change to a user name, date, or ID in the step text triggers a full AI re-generation call, burning rate-limit quota.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/order-flow.cy.ts
describe('Order placement flow', () => {
  it('places an order for a dynamic SKU', () => {
    const skuId = Cypress.env('TEST_SKU_ID') as string;
    const userName = 'Alice';

    cy.visit('/shop');

    // WITHOUT placeholders — cache-busted every time skuId or userName changes:
    // cy.prompt([`Search for product ${skuId}`, `Add to cart as ${userName}`]);

    // WITH placeholders — prompt text is stable; values are substituted at runtime:
    cy.prompt(
      [
        'Search for product {{sku}} and open the detail page',
        'Add the product to the cart',
        'Proceed to checkout as user {{user}} and confirm the order summary',
      ],
      {
        placeholders: {
          sku: skuId,    // substituted at runtime, NOT visible in Cloud prompt log
          user: userName,
        },
      }
    );

    // Verify the AI-generated steps landed the user on confirmation
    cy.get('[data-cy="order-confirmation"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="order-number"]').should('match', /^ORD-\d+$/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Always use `placeholders` for any value that changes between test runs (IDs, dates, usernames, amounts). The performance gain from cache hits is significant — a cached prompt completes in milliseconds; an AI round-trip takes 2-10 seconds and consumes quota. `cy.prompt()` is E2E-only (not supported in component testing) and Chromium-only; it requires Cypress Cloud authentication or a valid `--key` flag even in local development.

---

### 300. `cy.intercept()` TypeScript Generic Typing for Request and Response Bodies  [official]

`cy.intercept()` accepts two TypeScript generic type parameters — `<RequestBody, ResponseBody>` — that type the `req.body` and `res.body` properties inside handler callbacks. This pattern catches shape mismatches at compile time, making intercept handlers self-documenting and reducing the chance of silently passing `undefined` to mock response builders. The generics are particularly valuable in GraphQL stubs where the operation body and response shape are both well-defined interfaces.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/products.cy.ts

interface ProductSearchRequest {
  query: string;
  filters: {
    category?: string;
    minPrice?: number;
    maxPrice?: number;
  };
}

interface ProductSearchResponse {
  items: Array<{
    id: string;
    name: string;
    price: number;
    inStock: boolean;
  }>;
  total: number;
  page: number;
}

describe('Product search with typed intercepts', () => {
  it('stubs search results and asserts request shape', () => {
    cy.intercept<ProductSearchRequest, ProductSearchResponse>(
      'POST',
      '/api/products/search',
      (req) => {
        // req.body is typed as ProductSearchRequest at compile time
        expect(req.body.query).to.be.a('string');
        expect(req.body.filters).to.exist;

        req.reply({
          statusCode: 200,
          body: {
            items: [
              { id: 'p-1', name: 'Widget A', price: 29.99, inStock: true },
              { id: 'p-2', name: 'Widget B', price: 49.99, inStock: false },
            ],
            total: 2,
            page: 1,
          } satisfies ProductSearchResponse,
        });
      }
    ).as('productSearch');

    cy.visit('/products');
    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('Widget');
    cy.wait('@productSearch').its('request.body.query').should('eq', 'Widget');
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-card"]').should('have.length', 2);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Add generic types to `cy.intercept()` whenever you have well-defined request/response interfaces (REST API contracts, GraphQL schemas). The compile-time safety is zero-cost at runtime and pays dividends when the API schema changes — TypeScript surfaces the breaking mismatch before the test even runs. When NOT to use: for quick ad-hoc stubs with inline fixture objects, the generic annotation adds ceremony without much benefit — use untyped intercepts for throwaway stubs and typed ones for long-lived canonical stubs.

---

### 301. `cy.intercept()` `middleware: true` for Global Request Header Injection  [official]

Setting `middleware: true` on a `cy.intercept()` route makes it execute **first** (in defined order) even when other more-specific routes match the same URL. Standard routes match in reverse registration order (last registered wins); middleware routes always run before non-middleware routes. This makes `middleware: true` the correct tool for cross-cutting concerns: injecting authentication headers on every outbound request, logging all network traffic, or throttling bandwidth globally without interfering with per-test stubs.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts

// Register a global auth header middleware before every test
beforeEach(() => {
  // This intercept runs first for ALL requests — even those also matched by test-level stubs
  cy.intercept(
    { url: '/api/**', middleware: true },
    (req) => {
      const token = window.localStorage.getItem('auth_token');
      if (token) {
        req.headers['Authorization'] = `Bearer ${token}`;
      }
      // Pass to next handler — do NOT call req.reply() here
      req.continue();
    }
  ).as('authMiddleware');

  // Global bandwidth throttle for all media requests (simulates slow 3G)
  cy.intercept(
    { resourceType: 'image', middleware: true },
    (req) => {
      req.on('response', (res) => {
        res.setThrottle(50); // 50 kbps
      });
      req.continue();
    }
  );
});

// In a specific test, a non-middleware intercept for the same URL runs AFTER the middleware:
it('loads products with auth header and slow images', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products', { fixture: 'products.json' }).as('products');
  cy.visit('/products');
  cy.wait('@products')
    .its('request.headers')
    .should('have.property', 'Authorization');
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `middleware: true` for cross-cutting network concerns that should apply universally — auth injection, logging, global throttling. Avoid applying `middleware: true` to URL patterns that are too broad (e.g., `'**'`) without carefully calling `req.continue()` on every branch; a middleware that calls `req.reply()` unconditionally will intercept and block all requests it matches.

---

### 302. `injectDocumentDomain` Deprecation — Migrating Cross-Subdomain Tests to `cy.origin()`  [official]

`injectDocumentDomain` was introduced in Cypress 14.0.0 as a transitional config option for teams that previously relied on setting `document.domain` to enable same-origin DOM access across subdomains. It was deprecated immediately upon introduction because Chrome is removing the `document.domain` setter. The correct migration is to replace all cross-subdomain interactions with `cy.origin()` blocks, which proxy-level rather than DOM-level cross-origin access — no reliance on `document.domain` required.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — MIGRATION: remove injectDocumentDomain
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    // BEFORE (deprecated — will break when Chrome removes document.domain):
    // injectDocumentDomain: true,

    // AFTER: remove the option entirely and use cy.origin() in tests
    baseUrl: 'https://app.example.com',
  },
});

// cypress/e2e/cross-subdomain.cy.ts — BEFORE migration
// cy.visit('https://auth.example.com/login');
// cy.get('#email').type('user@example.com'); // broke without injectDocumentDomain

// AFTER migration — wrap cross-subdomain interactions in cy.origin()
describe('Cross-subdomain auth flow', () => {
  it('logs in via auth subdomain and lands on app', () => {
    cy.visit('https://app.example.com');

    // Navigate to auth subdomain
    cy.origin('https://auth.example.com', () => {
      cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type('user@example.com');
      cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type('secret');
      cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
    });

    // Back on app subdomain — cy.origin() block ends, primary origin resumes
    cy.url().should('include', 'app.example.com/dashboard');
    cy.get('[data-cy="welcome-banner"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Migrate away from `injectDocumentDomain` before Chrome removes `document.domain` support entirely — there is no fixed date but the removal has been in progress since 2022. `cy.origin()` is more verbose but architecturally sound and compatible with Chrome, Firefox, WebDriver BiDi, and Electron.

---

### 303. `cy.session()` Unique ID Design — Preventing Silent Cache Collisions  [official]

`cy.session()` caches session state keyed on the first argument (the session ID). If two different user types share a partially overlapping ID array, Cypress will silently serve the wrong cached session — a subtle false-positive that makes tests pass with incorrect user permissions. The session ID must include **every** parameter that distinguishes one session from another: user role, email, tenant ID, feature flag variant, and API environment. A helper factory function enforces this discipline across the test suite.

```typescript
// cypress/support/session.ts

type UserRole = 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer' | 'guest';
type Tenant = 'tenant-a' | 'tenant-b';

interface SessionParams {
  role: UserRole;
  email: string;
  tenant: Tenant;
  env: string; // 'staging' | 'production'
}

export function createUserSession(params: SessionParams): void {
  const { role, email, tenant, env } = params;

  // Session ID includes ALL discriminating dimensions — no silent collisions
  cy.session(
    [role, email, tenant, env],     // array serialises to a stable cache key
    () => {
      cy.visit(`https://${tenant}.example.com/login`);
      cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(email);
      cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type(Cypress.env(`${role.toUpperCase()}_PASSWORD`));
      cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
      cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
    },
    {
      validate() {
        // Validate role — not just authentication status
        cy.request({ url: '/api/me', failOnStatusCode: false, log: false })
          .then((res) => {
            expect(res.status).to.eq(200);
            expect(res.body.role).to.eq(role);
            expect(res.body.tenant).to.eq(tenant);
          });
      },
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
    }
  );
}

// Usage in spec:
// createUserSession({ role: 'admin', email: 'admin@tenant-a.com', tenant: 'tenant-a', env: 'staging' });
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** The session factory pattern pays off immediately in any multi-role or multi-tenant test suite. The cost is a slightly more verbose setup, but the benefit is deterministic cache isolation — the wrong cached session is one of the hardest Cypress bugs to diagnose because assertions may pass while testing the wrong user's view. Always include the API environment in the session ID when tests run against multiple environments in the same Cypress run.

---

### 304. GitHub Actions Cypress `v7` Action with `upload-artifact@v6` and `ubuntu-24.04`  [official]

The recommended GitHub Actions setup for Cypress runs changed significantly in 2025-2026: the `cypress-io/github-action` now pins to `@v7`, Ubuntu runners default to `ubuntu-24.04`, and artifact upload/download actions moved to `v6`/`v7` respectively. The `v6` upload-artifact action changed the `require-files-found` boolean to `if-no-files-found: error|warn|ignore`, breaking workflows that used the old option. Cypress Docker images now require the non-root user `1001` when running Firefox to avoid permission errors on the new Ubuntu 24.04 kernel.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/cypress.yml
name: Cypress E2E
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  cypress-run:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    container:
      image: cypress/browsers:22.15.0
      options: --user 1001          # required for Firefox on ubuntu-24.04 kernel

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        containers: [1, 2, 3, 4]

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run Cypress tests
        uses: cypress-io/github-action@v7
        with:
          browser: chrome
          record: true
          parallel: true
          group: UI-Chrome-${{ matrix.containers }}
        env:
          CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY: ${{ secrets.CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY }}
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # v6 artifact upload — note if-no-files-found replaces require-files-found
      - name: Upload test artifacts
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: cypress-screenshots-${{ matrix.containers }}
          path: cypress/screenshots
          if-no-files-found: ignore    # was 'require-files-found: false' in v5
          retention-days: 7

  download-artifacts:
    needs: cypress-run
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v7
        with:
          pattern: cypress-screenshots-*
          merge-multiple: true
          path: all-screenshots
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Pin to `cypress-io/github-action@v7` and `actions/upload-artifact@v6` together — mixing major versions (e.g., `@v6` action with `upload-artifact@v5`) introduces schema incompatibilities. Always test the workflow change in a feature branch before merging to main; the `ubuntu-24.04` + Firefox `--user 1001` requirement only applies to containerised runs.

---

### 305. `cy.intercept()` `req.on('before:response')` Non-Blocking Response Modification  [official]

The `req.on('before:response', handler)` lifecycle event fires after the upstream server responds but before the response is forwarded to the browser, enabling response mutation without blocking the request. Unlike `req.continue((res) => { ... })`, which wraps the entire request/response cycle in a single blocking middleware call, `req.on('before:response')` is additive — multiple handlers can be registered on the same request, and each runs independently. This pattern is ideal for injecting analytics headers, stripping CSP headers in testing, or mutating `Set-Cookie` attributes without rewriting the full intercept handler.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/response-mutation.cy.ts

describe('Response header mutation via req.on()', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/**', (req) => {
      // Register a before:response handler — does NOT block the request
      req.on('before:response', (res) => {
        // Strip CSP headers that would block inline scripts in test harness
        delete res.headers['content-security-policy'];
        delete res.headers['x-frame-options'];

        // Inject a test-environment marker header
        res.headers['x-test-env'] = 'cypress';
      });

      // DO NOT call req.reply() here — let the request continue to the real server
      req.continue();
    }).as('apiRequests');
  });

  it('confirms CSP header is stripped and test marker is present', () => {
    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.wait('@apiRequests').then((interception) => {
      expect(interception.response?.headers).not.to.have.property(
        'content-security-policy'
      );
      expect(interception.response?.headers['x-test-env']).to.eq('cypress');
    });
  });

  it('mutates response body for a specific endpoint', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/config', (req) => {
      req.on('before:response', (res) => {
        // Mutate specific fields in the response body without full stub
        res.body = {
          ...res.body,
          featureFlag_newUi: true,   // force-enable feature flag in response
        };
      });
      req.continue();
    });

    cy.visit('/app');
    cy.get('[data-cy="new-ui-banner"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `req.on('before:response')` when you want to mutate a real server response rather than fully replacing it with a fixture. This is superior to `req.continue((res) => { ... })` when multiple independent concerns need to modify the same response (e.g., header stripping AND body mutation from different support files), because each handler is additive rather than replacing the previous one.

---

## Additional Community Gotchas (Cycle 35) [community]

246. **`cy.env()` throws a `TypeError` at runtime if you pass a string instead of an array — the new API accepts ONLY an array of key names, and the error message does not clearly explain the array-only requirement** [community] — `cy.env('MY_KEY')` (a string argument) throws `TypeError: keys must be an array of strings` rather than returning the single value. This trips up developers migrating from `Cypress.env('MY_KEY')` (which accepts a string) because the call signature looks similar. WHY: The array-only design is intentional — it forces explicit enumeration of requested keys to prevent accidental mass-exposure of the environment config; a string form would make the "selective fetch" guarantee ambiguous. Fix: always pass an array even for a single key: `cy.env(['MY_KEY']).then(({ MY_KEY }) => ...)`.

247. **`Cypress.stop()` does NOT skip the current test — it only prevents subsequent tests from running; assertions in the same test after `Cypress.stop()` still execute unless you `return` immediately** [community] — Developers expect `Cypress.stop()` to behave like `cy.skip()` and abort the current test mid-execution. In reality, `Cypress.stop()` enqueues a "stop after this test" signal in the runner; the current test completes fully, including all remaining `cy.*` commands and assertions. WHY: Cypress's command queue is already running when `Cypress.stop()` is called; there is no mechanism to abort mid-queue without corrupting the runner state. Fix: always pair `Cypress.stop()` with a synchronous `return` in the calling function to prevent downstream commands from being queued.

248. **`cy.intercept()` `middleware: true` routes that call `req.reply()` instead of `req.continue()` silently swallow all subsequent test-level intercepts for the matched URL — the test-level stubs never run** [community] — A middleware intercept that calls `req.reply()` terminates the request at the proxy layer, returning a mock response immediately. Any non-middleware `cy.intercept()` registered in the test for the same URL is never reached because the request was already resolved. WHY: `req.reply()` in a middleware handler is a short-circuit; the intent of `middleware: true` is to mutate and pass through (`req.continue()`), not to terminate. Fix: audit all middleware intercepts for `req.reply()` calls — replace with `req.continue()` and use a non-middleware intercept for the stub response.

249. **`cy.prompt()` does not support canvas elements, iframes, or multi-element assertions — using natural language that references these elements causes the AI to generate invalid selectors that silently select nothing** [community] — When a `cy.prompt()` step references a chart drawn on a `<canvas>` or content inside a cross-origin `<iframe>`, the AI cannot introspect those elements from the DOM snapshot and generates a CSS selector that matches the container element rather than the intended interactive target. The generated code does not throw; it simply interacts with the wrong element or times out silently. WHY: The DOM snapshot used for selector generation is the serialised accessible DOM — `<canvas>` pixel content and cross-origin `<iframe>` documents are opaque to this serialisation. Fix: use explicit `cy.get('[data-cy="canvas-wrapper"]')` + `cy.trigger()` commands for canvas interactions; avoid `cy.prompt()` for any step that requires iframe traversal.

250. **The `Cypress.ElementSelector` priority change does NOT retroactively update selectors already generated by Cypress Studio or `cy.prompt()` — existing generated code in spec files continues to use the old priority after `Cypress.ElementSelector.defaults()` is reconfigured** [community] — Developers assume that updating `Cypress.ElementSelector.defaults()` in `support/e2e.ts` will cause Studio and `cy.prompt()` to regenerate more stable selectors for previously generated code. In fact, generated selectors are output as static strings in spec files at generation time; no runtime re-evaluation occurs. WHY: Cypress Studio and `cy.prompt()` write selector strings directly into spec source code; the ElementSelector API only affects the generation process, not already-written strings. Fix: re-run Studio or `cy.prompt()` generation after updating `ElementSelector.defaults()` to regenerate affected specs — there is no automatic migration.

251. **`cy.session()` `validate()` returning a rejected promise does NOT re-trigger the session setup function when `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` is set and the session was cached on a different machine in a parallel Cypress Cloud run — the test fails with "session validation failed" rather than re-establishing the session** [community] — When `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` is used in a parallel Cloud run, Cypress serialises the session cache and distributes it to other machines. If `validate()` fails on the receiving machine (e.g., because the auth token expired during distribution), Cypress does not re-run the setup function on that machine; instead it fails the test with a non-descriptive validation error. WHY: The re-run-on-validation-failure guarantee applies only to the machine that originally created the session; cross-machine cache restoration is best-effort with no automatic fallback. Fix: use short-lived tokens with an expiry well within the expected run duration, or set `cacheAcrossSpecs: false` and accept the additional login overhead per machine.

252. **`justInTimeCompile` is silently ignored for Vite-based component testing — there is no warning in the console, so developers believe the performance optimisation is active when it is not** [community] — `justInTimeCompile` is documented as a webpack-only feature, but Cypress does not emit any warning when the option is set in a Vite CT project. The option is parsed and silently discarded. Developers who migrated from webpack to Vite while keeping the config key believe they are getting optimised compilation but are actually running Vite's standard cold-start behaviour. WHY: Vite's module graph is fundamentally different from webpack's; the optimisation technique does not apply. Fix: remove `justInTimeCompile` from Vite CT config files to avoid confusion; rely on Vite's native ESM hot-module replacement for fast spec start-up instead.

### 306. Angular 21 Zoneless Component Testing with `cypress/angular-zoneless`  [official]

Cypress 15.8.0 introduced `cypress/angular-zoneless` as a dedicated testing harness for Angular projects that use Angular's zoneless change detection. Prior to this, Angular CT projects always required `zone.js` even in zoneless applications, which masked timing bugs specific to `provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()`. The new harness eliminates that dependency mismatch. Note that `autoDetectChanges` and `autoSpyOutputs` are deprecated and removed in the zoneless harness, since signal-based change detection makes them unnecessary. Use `createOutputSpy()` for output spying instead. [official]

```typescript
// cypress/support/component.ts  — zoneless project setup
import { mount } from 'cypress/angular-zoneless';
import { createOutputSpy } from 'cypress/angular-zoneless';

Cypress.Commands.add('mount', mount);

// cypress/component/counter.cy.ts
import { CounterComponent } from './counter.component';
import { createOutputSpy } from 'cypress/angular-zoneless';

describe('CounterComponent (zoneless)', () => {
  it('emits countChange when incremented', () => {
    const countSpy = createOutputSpy<number>('countChange');

    cy.mount(CounterComponent, {
      componentProperties: {
        countChange: countSpy,
      },
    });

    cy.get('[data-cy="increment"]').click();
    cy.get('@countChange').should('have.been.calledOnceWith', 1);
  });

  it('reads signal-based title from input', () => {
    cy.mount(CounterComponent, {
      componentProperties: { title: 'My Counter' },
    });
    cy.get('[data-cy="title"]').should('have.text', 'My Counter');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff / When to use:** Use `cypress/angular-zoneless` whenever your Angular project is configured with `provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()` or Angular 20+ default zoneless projects. Mixing `cypress/angular` (zone-based harness) with a zoneless app will silently import `zone.js`, polluting the test environment and hiding zone-related timing bugs. The limitation is that `autoSpyOutputs: true` (which generates spies for all outputs automatically) is gone; you must create each spy explicitly with `createOutputSpy()`.
