### 456. `cy.end()` Deprecation — Migrating Chain-Break Idioms to Explicit Statements  [official]

Cypress 15.15.0 deprecated `cy.end()`, marking it for removal in a future major release. The command existed to reset the subject of a command chain back to `null`, enabling developers to write long chains that pivoted to a fresh subject mid-way — a pattern that sacrificed readability for compactness. The recommended replacement is to simply start a new `cy` chain on the next line: each `cy.*` call is already an implicit chain root when it appears as a statement. Automated migration is straightforward because `.end()` always appears at a chain boundary.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/user-list.cy.ts

// BEFORE — .end() resets subject back to null so a new chain can begin
cy.get('[data-cy="user-cheryl"]')
  .click()
  .end()
  .get('[data-cy="user-charles"]')
  .click()
  .end()
  .get('[data-cy="save-button"]')
  .should('be.enabled');

// AFTER — explicit new statements; same semantics, no deprecation warning
cy.get('[data-cy="user-cheryl"]').click();
cy.get('[data-cy="user-charles"]').click();
cy.get('[data-cy="save-button"]').should('be.enabled');

// ESLint codemod: add to .eslintrc.cjs to flag remaining .end() calls
// 'cypress/no-unnecessary-waiting': 'error' (or write a custom rule)
// Quick grep to find all sites before upgrading:
// grep -rn '\.end()' cypress/
```

**Tradeoff.** The migration is mechanical and safe — `cy.end()` and starting a new chain produce identical runtime behaviour because Cypress resets the subject for each top-level `cy.*` call. The only risk is in helper functions that return the chain; if a helper returns `.end()` so callers can chain further, the return type changes from `Cypress.Chainable<null>` to `void`. Audit all helper return types before removing `cy.end()` calls inside them. [official]

---

### 457. `cy.prompt()` — AI Natural-Language Test Generation with Placeholders  [official]

`cy.prompt()` became generally available in Cypress 15.13.0 after exiting beta. It accepts an array of natural-language step strings and converts them into executable Cypress commands at runtime, using AI inference connected to Cypress Cloud. The `placeholders` option lets you pass dynamic values without embedding them in the prompt string — Cypress caches the AI-generated command sequence separately from the placeholder values, so cache hits are achieved even when credentials or IDs change between runs.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/checkout-ai.cy.ts
// Requires: Cypress Cloud authentication + Chromium browser

describe('Checkout flow (AI-generated steps)', () => {
  it('completes a purchase with dynamic order ID', () => {
    const orderId = Cypress.env('TEST_ORDER_ID'); // dynamic per CI run

    cy.visit('/shop');

    // placeholders prevent orderId from busting the AI response cache
    cy.prompt(
      [
        'Click the first product card',
        'Click the "Add to cart" button',
        'Open the shopping cart sidebar',
        'Verify the cart contains 1 item',
        'Click "Proceed to Checkout"',
        'Fill in the discount code field with {{discountCode}}',
        'Submit the order form',
      ],
      {
        placeholders: {
          discountCode: `SAVE-${orderId}`,
        },
      }
    );

    // Traditional assertions after AI steps complete
    cy.get('[data-cy="order-confirmation"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.prompt()` is limited to E2E tests on Chromium browsers and requires an authenticated Cypress Cloud connection — CI pipelines on unauthenticated runners or air-gapped environments will fail at the `cy.prompt()` call. The self-healing mode (keeping `cy.prompt()` in production test files) re-invokes the AI on every run, exhausting the per-user hourly call limit (100-600 depending on account tier) on large suites. Prefer the generate-and-export workflow: run `cy.prompt()` once in `cypress open`, inspect the generated commands, then replace the `cy.prompt()` call with the static generated code in the committed file. [official]

---

### 458. `cy.press()` — Native Keyboard Dispatch for Focus-Order and Trap Testing  [official]

`cy.press()` dispatches real browser keyboard events (not simulated DOM events), making it the authoritative command for testing focus management, focus traps, keyboard navigation order, and ARIA keyboard interaction patterns. Unlike `cy.type()`, `cy.press()` does not require a focused element — it dispatches to the currently focused element in the document, making it composable with `cy.focused()` to build focus-order traversal chains. Named keys are available via `Cypress.Keyboard.Keys`.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/modal-focus-trap.cy.ts
describe('Modal focus trap', () => {
  it('keeps focus inside the modal when Tab is pressed', () => {
    cy.visit('/');
    cy.get('[data-cy="open-modal"]').click();

    // First focus target after modal open
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'modal-close-btn');

    // Tab through all focusable elements — focus should cycle back
    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB);
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'modal-input-name');

    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB);
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'modal-input-email');

    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB);
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'modal-submit-btn');

    // Tab past the last element — focus should wrap to the first
    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB);
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'modal-close-btn');

    // ESC closes the modal
    cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.ESC);
    cy.get('[data-cy="modal"]').should('not.exist');
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'open-modal');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.press()` yields `null`, so you cannot chain `.should()` directly on its result — always follow it with `cy.focused()` or a `cy.get()` to assert post-press state. F1–F12 function keys are blocked by Cypress because browsers intercept them as shortcut keys; use `cy.type('{F5}')` for function key simulation if a legacy application requires it (with the caveat that `cy.type()` produces synthetic events). `cy.press()` also triggers browser transient activation, which can unintentionally dismiss `beforeunload` dialogs if a navigation-guarded page is active. [official]

---

### 459. `cy.session()` `cacheAcrossSpecs` — Cross-Spec Auth Reuse with Validate-on-Restore  [official]

`cy.session()` with `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` shares a single established session across all spec files in a run, eliminating the login overhead that occurs when each spec file independently establishes its own session. The `validate` callback is the safety mechanism: if session restoration silently returns an expired token (a common issue with JWT-based auth), the validate function detects the failure and triggers the `setup` function to re-authenticate before the first test in each spec executes.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts

Cypress.Commands.add('loginAsAdmin', () => {
  cy.session(
    // Session ID includes role — distinct sessions per role in same run
    ['admin', Cypress.env('ADMIN_EMAIL')],
    () => {
      // Setup: log in via UI or API
      cy.request({
        method: 'POST',
        url: '/api/auth/login',
        body: {
          email: Cypress.env('ADMIN_EMAIL'),
          password: Cypress.env('ADMIN_PASSWORD'),
        },
      }).then(({ body }) => {
        // Store token in localStorage so all subsequent requests are authenticated
        window.localStorage.setItem('auth_token', body.token);
        window.localStorage.setItem('auth_expires', String(body.expiresAt));
      });
    },
    {
      // Share session across all spec files — login runs at most once per CI job
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true,

      validate() {
        // Validate: make an authenticated API call that returns 401 on expiry
        cy.request({
          url: '/api/me',
          failOnStatusCode: false,
        }).its('status').should('eq', 200);
      },
    }
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` introduces a shared-state dependency between spec files — if one spec corrupts the session (e.g., logs out, changes the password), all subsequent specs in the run will fail. Guard against this by combining `cacheAcrossSpecs` with a strict `validate` callback that catches corruption, and by ensuring specs that modify auth state create a new session ID rather than reusing the shared one. In `cypress open` mode, sessions persist across spec reruns until "Clear All Sessions" is clicked; CI runs start fresh each time, so `cacheAcrossSpecs` saves the most time in CI pipelines with 20+ spec files. [official]

---

### 460. `cy.intercept()` `forceNetworkError` — Offline and Error-Boundary Testing  [official]

`cy.intercept()` with `forceNetworkError: true` in the `StaticResponse` object simulates a network-level failure — the request never reaches the server and the browser receives a connection-refused error rather than an HTTP error response. This is the correct way to test offline states, fetch error boundaries, and service-worker fallback logic, because a `statusCode: 503` response still has a valid HTTP envelope, which some error handlers treat differently from a true network failure.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/offline-banner.cy.ts
describe('Offline error boundary', () => {
  it('shows the offline banner when the API is unreachable', () => {
    // Simulate complete network failure for all API calls
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/**', { forceNetworkError: true }).as('apiFailure');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');

    // The app should display an offline banner, not a 503 error page
    cy.get('[data-cy="offline-banner"]')
      .should('be.visible')
      .and('contain.text', 'Unable to connect');

    // Confirm the request was indeed intercepted (not cached)
    cy.wait('@apiFailure');
  });

  it('recovers when connectivity is restored', () => {
    // Start offline
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/status', { forceNetworkError: true }).as('offline');
    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.get('[data-cy="offline-banner"]').should('be.visible');

    // Restore — remove the interceptor and re-enable real requests
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/status').as('online');
    cy.get('[data-cy="retry-btn"]').click();
    cy.wait('@online');
    cy.get('[data-cy="offline-banner"]').should('not.exist');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `forceNetworkError: true` is silently ignored when the browser serves the request from its HTTP cache — the interceptor never fires and the application receives a cached 200 response, making the "offline" test a false positive. Always inject `Cache-Control: no-store` via a global `middleware: true` interceptor before tests that rely on `forceNetworkError`, or set `cy.visit({ headers: { 'Cache-Control': 'no-cache' } })` for the initial navigation. Additionally, `forceNetworkError` triggers the browser's built-in `net::ERR_FAILED` error, which causes Cypress to log an "Uncaught exception" warning — suppress it with `cy.on('uncaught:exception', () => false)` if the application does not catch fetch errors globally. [official]

---

### 461. `cy.intercept()` GraphQL Operation-Name Matching with `req.alias` Body Inspection  [official]

REST URL matching is insufficient for GraphQL APIs because all operations share a single `/graphql` endpoint. The correct pattern is to inspect the POST body's `operationName` field inside the `routeHandler` callback and conditionally set `req.alias` so that `cy.wait('@aliasName')` can target a specific operation. A utility function wraps this pattern to keep test files DRY.

```typescript
// cypress/support/graphql-helpers.ts

/**
 * Intercepts all GraphQL POST requests.
 * Inside the handler, assigns an alias equal to the operation name
 * so tests can wait for specific queries/mutations with cy.wait('@QueryName').
 */
export function interceptGraphQL(): void {
  cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql', (req) => {
    // Body is already parsed by Cypress — access operationName directly
    const opName: string | undefined = req.body?.operationName;
    if (opName) {
      req.alias = opName;
    }
  });
}

// cypress/e2e/product-page.cy.ts
import { interceptGraphQL } from '../support/graphql-helpers';

describe('Product detail page', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    interceptGraphQL();
    cy.visit('/products/42');
  });

  it('displays product details after GetProduct resolves', () => {
    cy.wait('@GetProduct').its('request.body.variables.id').should('eq', '42');
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-title"]').should('not.be.empty');
  });

  it('shows related products after GetRelated resolves', () => {
    cy.wait('@GetRelated');
    cy.get('[data-cy="related-list"]').children().should('have.length.gte', 3);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Setting `req.alias` inside a handler rather than using the `.as()` chainer means the alias is registered lazily — if a request fires before the `cy.intercept()` registration completes (a race condition in `cy.visit()` pages that issue GraphQL requests before JS hydration), the alias is never set and `cy.wait('@GetProduct')` times out. Call `interceptGraphQL()` in a `beforeEach` before any `cy.visit()` or navigation to guarantee the handler is registered before the page fires its first request. [official]

---

### 462. Angular 20 Component Testing Setup with Cypress 15  [official]

Cypress 15.0.0 added official Angular 20 component testing support. The setup follows the standard `@cypress/angular` scaffolding path but requires `zone.js` to be explicitly imported in `cypress/component/support/component.ts` to prevent `ChangeDetectorRef`-related test flakes — Angular 20 no longer imports `zone.js` automatically when standalone components are used. The Cypress Angular harness wraps `TestBed.configureTestingModule()` internally and exposes a `MountConfig` type for providers and declarations.

```typescript
// cypress/component/support/component.ts
import './commands';
import 'zone.js'; // Required: Angular 20 standalone components omit this import

// cypress/component/button.cy.ts
import { MountConfig } from 'cypress/angular';
import { ButtonComponent } from '../../src/app/shared/button/button.component';
import { HttpClientTestingModule } from '@angular/common/http/testing';

const mountConfig: MountConfig<ButtonComponent> = {
  imports: [HttpClientTestingModule],
  componentProperties: {
    label: 'Submit',
    disabled: false,
  },
};

describe('ButtonComponent', () => {
  it('renders with the provided label', () => {
    cy.mount(ButtonComponent, mountConfig);
    cy.get('button').should('contain.text', 'Submit').and('not.be.disabled');
  });

  it('emits clicked event on interaction', () => {
    const clickedSpy = cy.spy().as('clickedSpy');
    cy.mount(ButtonComponent, {
      ...mountConfig,
      componentProperties: { label: 'Send', disabled: false, clicked: clickedSpy },
    });
    cy.get('button').click();
    cy.get('@clickedSpy').should('have.been.calledOnce');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Angular 20 standalone components do not need `TestBed` module declarations — passing `declarations: [ButtonComponent]` in `mountConfig` causes a warning and will throw in Angular 21. Use `imports: [ButtonComponent]` instead for standalone components and `declarations: [ButtonComponent]` only for NgModule-based components. The Cypress Angular harness does not support `TestBed.inject()` for accessing injected services after mount; use `cy.spy()` on the service's methods via `componentProperties` or `providers: [{ provide: MyService, useValue: { method: cy.stub() } }]` instead. [official]

---

### 463. `experimentalRunAllSpecs` — Sequential Multi-Spec Review Mode in `cypress open`  [official]

`experimentalRunAllSpecs`, added in Cypress 15.9.0 and extended to component testing in the same release, adds a "Run All Specs" button to the Cypress Test Runner UI. Clicking it runs all visible spec files sequentially in the current open-mode tab without switching to headless mode. This is valuable during development sessions where a developer wants to verify that a refactor has not broken any spec — without the overhead of exiting `cypress open` and re-running `cypress run`.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    // Enable the "Run All Specs" button in cypress open
    experimentalRunAllSpecs: true,

    // Optional: exclude slow integration specs from the "run all" set
    // by placing them in a separate directory not matched by specPattern
    specPattern: 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts',
    excludeSpecPattern: 'cypress/e2e/slow-integration/**/*.cy.ts',

    baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
  component: {
    // Also available for component testing as of 15.9.0
    experimentalRunAllSpecs: true,
    devServer: { framework: 'react', bundler: 'vite' },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `experimentalRunAllSpecs` in `cypress open` runs specs sequentially in a single browser tab, which means each spec shares the browser tab's history and `localStorage` state unless your `beforeEach` explicitly clears them. In normal `cypress run` mode, each spec gets a fresh tab (or fresh session with `experimentalSingleTabRunMode`); in `experimentalRunAllSpecs` open mode, state bleed between specs is more likely than in CI. Always add a `beforeEach(() => { cy.clearLocalStorage(); cy.clearCookies(); })` in your global support file when using this feature to prevent ordering-dependent failures. [official]

---

### 464. `cypress-axe` Retry Option for Dynamic-Content Accessibility Checks  [community]

Modern SPAs load content asynchronously after the initial render; running `cy.checkA11y()` immediately after `cy.visit()` can produce false positives (violations on skeleton screens that are replaced milliseconds later) or miss violations in content that loads after the initial accessibility check. The `cypress-axe` library's `retries` and `interval` options address this by re-running the axe scan until no violations are found or the retry limit is exhausted.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/dashboard-a11y.cy.ts
import 'cypress-axe';

describe('Dashboard accessibility', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.injectAxe();
  });

  it('has no critical or serious violations after data loads', () => {
    // Wait for the loading skeleton to be replaced by real content
    cy.get('[data-cy="stats-panel"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="loading-skeleton"]').should('not.exist');

    cy.checkA11y(
      '[data-cy="main-content"]', // scope to main content area
      {
        includedImpacts: ['critical', 'serious'],
        // Retry up to 5 times with 500ms interval for late-loading widgets
        retries: 5,
        interval: 500,
      },
      (violations) => {
        // Custom violation callback: log to terminal via cy.task
        cy.task(
          'logA11yViolations',
          violations.map((v) => ({
            id: v.id,
            impact: v.impact,
            description: v.description,
            nodes: v.nodes.length,
          }))
        );
      }
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Setting `retries: 5` with `interval: 500` adds up to 2.5 seconds to a test that has zero violations — the retry loop exits immediately on a clean pass, but the overhead of re-running axe five times on a large DOM is non-trivial. Scope the check to the relevant container selector rather than the full `document` to minimise axe scan time; on a 2 000-node DOM, a scoped scan is typically 3-5× faster than a full-page scan. Pin the `axe-core` version in `package.json` (`"axe-core": "4.10.x"`) to avoid WCAG rule changes between runs from silently adding new violations to a previously-passing test. [community]

---

### 465. `cy.intercept()` `times` — One-Shot Stubs Without Alias Pollution  [official]

The `times` option in the `routeMatcher` object limits how many requests a `cy.intercept()` handler matches. Setting `times: 1` creates a one-shot stub that returns the mock response only for the first matching request and then passes subsequent requests to the real server. This is the canonical pattern for testing "first-load cold-cache" vs "subsequent-load warm-cache" behaviour without registering two separate intercepts that would require two aliases and two `cy.wait()` calls.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/search-cache.cy.ts
describe('Search result caching', () => {
  it('fetches from API on first search then uses client cache on repeat', () => {
    // First request: intercepted with stub (cold cache)
    cy.intercept(
      { method: 'GET', url: '/api/search?q=cypress', times: 1 },
      { fixture: 'search-results.json', delay: 200 }
    ).as('firstSearch');

    // Subsequent requests pass through to real server (warm cache)
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/search?q=cypress').as('subsequentSearch');

    cy.visit('/');
    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('cypress');
    cy.wait('@firstSearch');
    cy.get('[data-cy="results-list"]').should('have.length', 10);

    // Repeat search — should NOT make another network request
    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').clear().type('cypress');
    // @subsequentSearch should NOT be called — the client should use its cache
    cy.get('@subsequentSearch.all').should('have.length', 0);
    cy.get('[data-cy="results-list"]').should('have.length', 10);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** When `times: 1` is combined with `.as()`, the alias resolves only once — a second `cy.wait('@firstSearch')` in the same test will time out because the interceptor has already been consumed. If you need to assert on the request details of a one-shot intercept, capture everything you need from the first `cy.wait()` response object; do not call `cy.wait()` on the alias again. The `times` option is also silently ignored when the request is served from browser HTTP cache — pair it with the global `Cache-Control: no-store` middleware pattern to guarantee the stub fires. [official]

---

### 466. Cypress 15 Memory Optimization — Command Log Trimming in Long Open-Mode Runs  [official]

Cypress 15.14.0 introduced automatic command log memory optimization for long-running `cypress open` sessions. The runner now periodically clears aged command log entries from completed tests to prevent unbounded memory growth — prior to this fix, running 200+ component tests sequentially in open mode would accumulate all command log DOM nodes, causing browser memory to balloon past 2 GB and eventually crash the tab. The optimization is automatic and requires no configuration.

```typescript
// cypress/component/support/component.ts

// No config needed — memory optimization is automatic in Cypress 15.14.0+.
// However, if your CI pipeline runs cypress in --headed mode (e.g. for video
// recording) and you observe OOM crashes on long suites, verify that you are
// on 15.14.0+ before investigating other causes:
//
//   npx cypress --version
//
// If pinned to an older version, force-enable the optimization via env var
// (available as a back-port toggle in 15.12.x):
//
//   CYPRESS_EXPERIMENTAL_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT=true npx cypress run

// Practical safeguard: if your suite exceeds 150 component tests, split
// it into two separate component test projects with distinct devServer ports
// so each run is capped at a manageable log size even on older Cypress versions.

// cypress.config.ts — separate component test projects (Cypress 15.x multi-project)
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  component: {
    specPattern: 'src/components/**/*.cy.tsx',
    devServer: { framework: 'react', bundler: 'vite' },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Command log trimming removes visual history for already-completed tests in `cypress open` — if you scroll back to investigate a passing test that ran 100 tests ago, its command log entries are gone. This is a deliberate trade-off: memory stability takes priority over unlimited scrollback in long runs. For post-hoc debugging, rely on Cypress Cloud's test replay feature (which captures the full timeline before trimming) or add `cy.log()` calls that emit to the terminal via `cy.task('log', message)` for structured records that survive beyond the command log. [official]

---

### 467. `cy.origin()` Spec-Bridge Persistence Fix — Cypress 15.15.0 Multi-Origin Stability  [official]

Cypress 15.15.0 resolved a long-standing `cy.origin()` regression where the spec-bridge iframe that mediates cross-origin communication persisted between tests instead of being torn down and rebuilt at the end of each test. The symptom was that the second test in a spec that used `cy.origin()` would silently re-use the stale spec-bridge from the first test, causing commands inside the `cy.origin()` callback to execute against the wrong origin context or throw `CypressError: cy.origin() requires the callback to be a static, synchronous function`.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/cross-origin-checkout.cy.ts
// Requires: Cypress 15.15.0+ for stable spec-bridge teardown

describe('Cross-origin checkout flow', () => {
  it('logs in on auth subdomain then lands on main app', () => {
    cy.visit('https://app.example.com/checkout');

    // Redirects to auth.example.com for SSO
    cy.origin('https://auth.example.com', () => {
      cy.get('[data-cy="sso-email"]').type('user@example.com');
      cy.get('[data-cy="sso-submit"]').click();
    });

    // Back on main domain after auth redirect
    cy.url().should('include', 'app.example.com/checkout');
    cy.get('[data-cy="checkout-form"]').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('shows error on invalid SSO token', () => {
    // In Cypress < 15.15.0 this test would inherit the stale spec-bridge
    // from the previous test and throw; in 15.15.0+ the bridge is rebuilt
    cy.visit('https://app.example.com/checkout');

    cy.intercept('POST', 'https://auth.example.com/token', {
      statusCode: 401,
      body: { error: 'invalid_token' },
    });

    cy.origin('https://auth.example.com', () => {
      cy.get('[data-cy="sso-email"]').type('bad@example.com');
      cy.get('[data-cy="sso-submit"]').click();
      cy.get('[data-cy="auth-error"]').should('be.visible');
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The spec-bridge rebuild on each test adds a small fixed overhead (approximately 80-120 ms per test that uses `cy.origin()`) compared to the stale-bridge behaviour. For suites with many cross-origin tests, this is a worthwhile correctness trade-off. Note that `cy.intercept()` registered on the primary origin is NOT forwarded into the `cy.origin()` callback — intercepts targeting the secondary origin must be registered inside the callback using the `args` pass-through pattern; functions (including spy references) cannot be passed as `args` due to structured-clone limitations. [official]

---

### 468. `cy.wait()` Rejection Handling During Retry Teardown — Guard Against Flaky Timeout Errors  [official]

Cypress 15.14.2 fixed a bug where `cy.wait()` would emit an unhandled rejection during the retry teardown phase — specifically, when a test was failing due to a command timeout while a `cy.wait('@alias')` was still pending, the internal rejection of the wait was surfaced as an additional unhandled error that masked the original test failure with a confusing `cy.wait()` timed out` message. The fix ensures that pending waits are cleanly aborted during teardown without surfacing secondary rejections.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/api-timeout.cy.ts
// Pattern: guard against aliased wait timeouts masking the real assertion failure

describe('API timeout graceful degradation', () => {
  it('shows a timeout message if the API takes more than 5 s', () => {
    // Intercept and delay — this WILL time out (intentional)
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/data', (req) => {
      req.reply({ delay: 10_000, body: {} });
    }).as('slowData');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');

    // Test the UI's timeout handling — do NOT cy.wait('@slowData') here,
    // because the delay exceeds the assertion timeout and would cause the
    // secondary rejection fixed in 15.14.2. Instead, assert on the UI state.
    cy.get('[data-cy="loading-timeout-msg"]', { timeout: 8_000 })
      .should('be.visible')
      .and('contain.text', 'This is taking longer than expected');

    // If you must wait for the slow request to verify it was made,
    // override the timeout explicitly to match the stub delay
    cy.wait('@slowData', { timeout: 12_000 });
    cy.get('@slowData').its('request.url').should('include', '/api/data');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The Cypress 15.14.2 fix is transparent — no code changes are required. However, the underlying pattern is still important: when testing timeout-handling UI, do not use `cy.wait('@alias')` with the default timeout if the intercept delay exceeds that timeout; always pass an explicit `{ timeout: N }` option to `cy.wait()` that exceeds the stub delay, or assert on the UI state rather than waiting for the request. Using `cy.wait()` with an undersized timeout in a timeout-testing scenario was always semantically incorrect; the fix merely prevents the secondary rejection from hiding the original error. [official]

---

### 469. Vite 8 + Cypress 15.14.0 — Full TypeScript 6 and Vite 8 Component Testing Setup  [official]

Cypress 15.14.0 introduced simultaneous official support for TypeScript 6 and Vite 8 in component testing. The upgrade is mostly transparent, but two configuration changes are required: (1) `@vitejs/plugin-react` version must be `≥ 5.0.0` for Vite 8 compatibility (it no longer accepts Vite 7 peer dependency); (2) TypeScript 6's new strict defaults (`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`) must be addressed in test helpers before enabling `strict: true` in `tsconfig.json`.

```typescript
// package.json — verify these peer dependency versions
// "cypress": ">=15.14.0",
// "vite": ">=8.0.0",
// "@vitejs/plugin-react": ">=5.0.0",
// "typescript": ">=6.0.0"

// cypress.config.ts — Vite 8 + TypeScript 6 component testing config
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'; // must be ^5.0.0 for Vite 8
import tsconfigPaths from 'vite-tsconfig-paths'; // resolves TS path aliases in Vite

export default defineConfig({
  component: {
    devServer: {
      framework: 'react',
      bundler: 'vite',
      viteConfig: {
        plugins: [
          react(),
          tsconfigPaths(), // honours "paths" in tsconfig.json under Vite 8
        ],
        // Vite 8: explicit esbuild target for TypeScript 6 class field syntax
        esbuild: {
          target: 'es2022',
        },
      },
    },
    specPattern: 'src/**/*.cy.{ts,tsx}',
    supportFile: 'cypress/component/support/component.ts',
  },
});

// tsconfig.json — TypeScript 6 strict defaults (address before enabling strict:true)
// {
//   "compilerOptions": {
//     "strict": true,
//     "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,   // new default in TS6 under strict
//     "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,  // new default in TS6 under strict
//     "moduleResolution": "bundler"        // required for tsx + path aliases
//   }
// }
```

**Tradeoff.** `vite-tsconfig-paths` is a third-party plugin and is not maintained by the Vite or Cypress teams; if it lags behind Vite 8 API changes, path alias resolution breaks without an obvious error message. Validate path alias resolution in CI by adding a test that imports a helper via its alias path (`import { setup } from '@test-helpers/setup'`) — if the alias is broken, the test file will fail to load with a module-not-found error rather than a test assertion failure, which is easy to overlook in CI output. [official]

---

### 470. `cy.intercept()` Partial Fixture Merge with `req.continue()` Response Mutation  [official]

A common need in integration tests is to return a mostly-realistic API response (loaded from a fixture) but override one or two fields to exercise a specific code path — for example, returning the production user fixture but setting `plan: 'free'` to test the free-tier upgrade banner. The `req.continue(res => { ... })` pattern achieves this by proxying the request to the real server and then mutating the response body before it reaches the browser, or by using a fixture as the base and spreading the override fields.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/upgrade-banner.cy.ts
import freeTierUser from '../fixtures/users/free-tier-user.json';

describe('Upgrade banner', () => {
  it('shows upgrade banner for free-tier users', () => {
    // Return the fixture but override the plan field to simulate free tier
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/me', (req) => {
      req.reply((res) => {
        // Merge override into the response body (keep all other fixture fields)
        res.body = { ...freeTierUser, plan: 'free', trialDaysLeft: 0 };
        res.statusCode = 200;
      });
    }).as('getUser');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.wait('@getUser');

    cy.get('[data-cy="upgrade-banner"]')
      .should('be.visible')
      .and('contain.text', 'Upgrade to Pro');
  });

  it('hides upgrade banner for pro-tier users', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/me', (req) => {
      req.reply((res) => {
        res.body = { ...freeTierUser, plan: 'pro', trialDaysLeft: null };
      });
    }).as('getUser');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.wait('@getUser');
    cy.get('[data-cy="upgrade-banner"]').should('not.exist');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `req.continue(res => { res.body = ... })` sends the request to the real server and then mutates the response — this requires the real server to be running and reachable, which is not always true in isolated unit-test environments. If the real server is unavailable, the request will fail with a network error before the response mutation callback is invoked, causing a confusing error message. For environments without a real server, use `req.reply({ body: { ...freeTierUser, plan: 'free' } })` instead (static stub with no server round-trip). Reserve the `req.continue()` mutation pattern for integration test environments where a real server is available and the response fixture approach would require maintaining large duplicated fixture files. [official]

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 47

320. **`cy.end()` removal timeline is not communicated via deprecation warnings in test output — teams discover the removal only when upgrading to the next major version and their entire test suite fails on startup with `cy.end is not a function`** [community] — A developer upgrades from Cypress 15 to Cypress 16 (which removes `cy.end()`) and discovers that 47 spec files each throw `TypeError: cy.end is not a function` on load, blocking the entire test run from executing. The team was unaware that `cy.end()` was deprecated in 15.15.0 because the deprecation only produces a browser console warning (not a failing test or CI-visible log line), and the developer's CI pipeline suppresses the browser console output. WHY: Cypress deprecation warnings are emitted to the browser DevTools console, not to the Cypress terminal output or the test result JSON — they are invisible in headless CI unless the team explicitly captures browser console logs via `cy.on('window:console', ...)` or the Cypress Cloud console log capture. Fix: add a `cy.on('window:console', (type, ...args) => { if (type === 'warn') console.warn(...args); })` listener in `cypress/support/e2e.ts` to surface browser-level deprecation warnings to the terminal; run `grep -rn '\.end()' cypress/` as a pre-upgrade audit step; add a CI job that runs `npx cypress run --version` and compares against the semver range specified in `package.json` to catch unplanned upgrades.

321. **`cy.prompt()` throws `CypressError: cy.prompt() requires a Cypress Cloud connection` in CI pipelines where `CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY` is not set, causing the entire test run to fail — the error is not a soft skip but a hard failure that aborts the spec** [community] — A developer commits a test file that uses `cy.prompt()` to generate test steps and merges it to the main branch. CI runs without `CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY` (set only in the Cypress Cloud-connected pipeline, not in the developer preview pipeline). The `cy.prompt()` call throws a hard error that aborts the spec file and marks the entire CI check as failed. WHY: `cy.prompt()` requires an authenticated Cypress Cloud session to call the AI backend; when `CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY` is absent, Cypress throws immediately rather than failing gracefully, because an unauthenticated `cy.prompt()` call has no fallback — there is no offline mode and no way to queue the request for later. Fix: gate all `cy.prompt()` calls with an environment check — `if (Cypress.env('CYPRESS_RECORD_KEY')) { cy.prompt([...]) }` — or, better, adopt the generate-and-export workflow: run `cy.prompt()` once in `cypress open`, export the generated commands to static test code, and delete the `cy.prompt()` call from the committed file; this avoids the runtime Cypress Cloud dependency entirely.

322. **`cy.press()` with `Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB` triggers browser transient activation, which causes a `beforeunload` confirmation dialog to appear on navigation-guarded pages — the unexpected dialog blocks subsequent Cypress commands and causes a test timeout** [community] — A developer tests keyboard navigation on a form page that uses `window.addEventListener('beforeunload', (e) => { e.preventDefault(); e.returnValue = ''; })` to warn users about unsaved changes. After adding a `cy.press(Cypress.Keyboard.Keys.TAB)` call to test focus order, subsequent navigation commands (`cy.visit()` or `cy.go('back')`) hang because the `beforeunload` dialog is blocking the browser's navigation. WHY: `cy.press()` dispatches a real browser keyboard event, which triggers the browser's transient user activation state (unlike `cy.type()`, which uses synthetic events that do not set transient activation); once transient activation is set, the `beforeunload` handler's `e.preventDefault()` call is honoured by the browser, showing a native confirmation dialog that Cypress cannot dismiss programmatically. Fix: suppress the `beforeunload` dialog in tests that use `cy.press()` by injecting `cy.window().then(win => win.removeEventListener('beforeunload', ...))` before the navigation, or by setting `cy.on('window:before:unload', () => false)`; add a comment explaining why the suppression is necessary so future maintainers do not remove it.

323. **`cy.session()` IDs that include `Cypress.env()` values cause cross-worker session contamination in Cypress Cloud parallel runs when two workers happen to generate the same session ID from different spec files — one worker restores the other worker's session and inherits its authentication state** [community] — A developer uses `cy.session(['user', Cypress.env('ADMIN_EMAIL')])` as the session ID in multiple spec files, intending each spec to have its own admin session. In Cypress Cloud parallel mode, two workers run concurrently and each calls `cy.session(['user', adminEmail])` in `beforeEach`. Worker B's `cy.session()` call finds a cached session ID that matches the one created by Worker A (because the session cache is shared across the run when `cacheAcrossSpecs: true`), and restores Worker A's session cookies — which may have been mutated by Worker A's tests running concurrently. WHY: `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` shares a single session cache file across all parallel workers via Cypress Cloud; session IDs that encode only role and email (not spec-file or worker identity) collide across workers that should have independent sessions. Fix: include the spec filename in the session ID when `cacheAcrossSpecs: false` is needed for isolation — `cy.session(['user', adminEmail, Cypress.spec.name])` — and reserve `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` only for truly shared read-only sessions (e.g., a session that does not mutate server state) where cross-worker sharing is intentional.

324. **`cy.intercept()` `forceNetworkError: true` is silently ignored when the matching request URL is in the browser's HTTP disk cache — the interceptor registers successfully and the alias is set, but the request never hits the Cypress proxy and is served from cache, causing `cy.wait('@alias')` to time out** [community] — A developer adds `cy.intercept('/api/config', { forceNetworkError: true })` to simulate an offline state and calls `cy.visit('/')`. The application loads normally because `/api/config` was cached by the browser from a previous test or from a prior `cy.visit()` in the same spec file with `cacheAcrossSpecs: true`. The `cy.wait('@alias')` times out with "No request ever made to route" because the browser served the response from its disk cache without making a network request. WHY: `cy.intercept()` operates at the Cypress proxy level — it can only intercept requests that actually traverse the network layer; browser disk cache hits bypass the proxy entirely, so the interceptor never fires regardless of whether `forceNetworkError`, `times`, or `delay` are set. Fix: inject a global `cy.intercept('**', { middleware: true }, (req) => { req.headers['Cache-Control'] = 'no-cache'; req.headers['Pragma'] = 'no-cache'; })` interceptor in a `beforeEach` to force all requests through the network layer; alternatively, call `cy.clearCookies()` and `cy.clearLocalStorage()` plus set `Cypress.config('pageLoadTimeout', 0)` to prevent disk cache use during the test.

325. **Angular 20 standalone component `cy.mount()` fails with `NullInjectorError: No provider for ChangeDetectorRef` when the component uses `inject(ChangeDetectorRef)` at the field level — Cypress Angular harness does not provide `ChangeDetectorRef` in the TestBed injector when `standalone: true` is set implicitly** [community] — A developer migrates an Angular component from constructor injection (`constructor(private cdr: ChangeDetectorRef)`) to Angular 20 field injection (`private cdr = inject(ChangeDetectorRef)`) and finds that the component's Cypress tests begin throwing `NullInjectorError` on `cy.mount()`. The error does not occur in the live application or in the component's Karma unit tests. WHY: the Cypress Angular harness creates a minimal TestBed environment that provides `ChangeDetectorRef` automatically for components mounted via the `NgModule` path; when `standalone: true` is inferred (Angular 20 default for components without `@NgModule`), the harness does not add `ChangeDetectorRef` to the TestBed injector automatically — it must be declared explicitly in the `providers` array of `MountConfig`. Fix: add `providers: [{ provide: ChangeDetectorRef, useExisting: ChangeDetectorRef }]` to the `MountConfig` passed to `cy.mount()`; alternatively, add `import 'zone.js'` to `cypress/component/support/component.ts` (which causes the Angular zone-aware `ChangeDetectorRef` to be registered globally) — this is also required for `zone.js`-dependent lifecycle hooks in Angular 20 standalone components.
