### 501. `cy.env()` Async Secure Variable Access with `{log:false}` Guard  [official]

Introduced in Cypress 15.10.0, `cy.env()` replaces the deprecated synchronous `Cypress.env()` for reading sensitive environment variables inside tests. Unlike `Cypress.env()`, which hydrated all environment variables into the browser window object, `cy.env()` fetches only the variables you explicitly name, reducing accidental exposure in Command Log output. The `{log:false}` option suppresses the value from appearing in the Cypress App Command Log — essential for tokens and passwords.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/login-with-cy-env.cy.ts
// Requires Cypress >= 15.10.0
// cypress.config.ts: define { env: { ADMIN_EMAIL: '...', ADMIN_PASSWORD: '...' } }
// or CYPRESS_ADMIN_EMAIL / CYPRESS_ADMIN_PASSWORD OS env vars

describe('Admin login (cy.env secure access)', () => {
  it('logs in with credentials sourced from cy.env()', () => {
    // Fetch only the variables needed — values never serialised into window
    cy.env('ADMIN_EMAIL', { log: false }).then((email: string) => {
      cy.env('ADMIN_PASSWORD', { log: false }).then((password: string) => {
        cy.visit('/admin/login');

        cy.get('[data-cy="email-input"]').type(email, { log: false });
        cy.get('[data-cy="password-input"]').type(password, { log: false });
        cy.get('[data-cy="login-btn"]').click();

        cy.get('[data-cy="admin-dashboard"]').should('be.visible');
      });
    });
  });

  it('destructures multiple env vars in one chain using cy.wrap()', () => {
    // Fetch two variables in parallel using Promise.all inside cy.wrap()
    cy.wrap(
      Cypress.Promise.all([
        cy.env('ADMIN_EMAIL', { log: false }),
        cy.env('ADMIN_PASSWORD', { log: false }),
      ] as unknown as Promise<string>[]),
    ).then(([email, password]) => {
      cy.session([email], () => {
        cy.visit('/admin/login');
        cy.get('[data-cy="email-input"]').type(email as string, { log: false });
        cy.get('[data-cy="password-input"]').type(password as string, { log: false });
        cy.get('[data-cy="login-btn"]').click();
        cy.get('[data-cy="admin-dashboard"]').should('be.visible');
      });
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.env()` is asynchronous — it returns a Cypress chainable and must be consumed inside `.then()` callbacks or chained commands. Calling `cy.env()` at the top-level synchronous scope of a describe block (i.e., not inside a `before()`/`beforeEach()`) will enqueue the command but the resolved value will not be available to synchronous code that follows. Migrate incrementally: enable `allowCypressEnv: false` in a dedicated lint CI job before enabling it globally, so failures surface per-package rather than across the whole monorepo. [official]

---

### 502. `Cypress.expose()` Public Config Binding for Non-Sensitive Values  [official]

`Cypress.expose()` (introduced in Cypress 15.10.0) provides a synchronous mechanism for surfacing non-sensitive configuration values to tests without routing through the deprecated `Cypress.env()` path. Values registered via the `expose` block in `cypress.config.ts` are synchronously accessible via `Cypress.expose('key')` anywhere in test code. This is the recommended pattern for feature flags, environment names, API base URLs, and other public runtime configuration that must be read synchronously inside `before()` hooks or conditional `describe()` blocks.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    baseUrl: 'https://staging.example.com',
    expose: {
      // Non-sensitive values only — these are serialised into the browser context
      APP_ENV: 'staging',
      API_BASE_URL: 'https://api.staging.example.com',
      FEATURE_FLAGS: {
        NEW_CHECKOUT: true,
        DARK_MODE: false,
      },
    },
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      return config;
    },
  },
});

// cypress/e2e/feature-flag-aware.cy.ts
describe('Checkout flow', () => {
  const flags = Cypress.expose('FEATURE_FLAGS') as { NEW_CHECKOUT: boolean; DARK_MODE: boolean };

  // Conditionally run the new checkout suite only if the flag is on
  if (flags.NEW_CHECKOUT) {
    it('renders new checkout wizard', () => {
      cy.visit('/checkout');
      cy.get('[data-cy="checkout-wizard"]').should('be.visible');
    });
  } else {
    it('renders legacy checkout form', () => {
      cy.visit('/checkout');
      cy.get('[data-cy="checkout-form-legacy"]').should('be.visible');
    });
  }

  it('reads API base URL for explicit request assertions', () => {
    const apiBase = Cypress.expose('API_BASE_URL') as string;
    cy.request(`${apiBase}/health`).its('status').should('eq', 200);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `Cypress.expose()` is designed for public, non-sensitive values — everything registered under `expose` is serialised into the browser runtime and is visible in the Cypress App's configuration panel and in browser developer tools. Never place secrets, tokens, or passwords under `expose`; use `cy.env()` with `{log:false}` for those. Unlike `cy.env()`, `Cypress.expose()` is synchronous and can be safely called at describe-block scope for conditional test registration. [official]

---

### 503. `allowCypressEnv: false` Migration Lint Gate for Monorepos  [official]

The `allowCypressEnv` configuration option (introduced in Cypress 15.10.0 alongside `cy.env()`) throws a hard error at test startup whenever any code calls the deprecated `Cypress.env()` API. Setting `allowCypressEnv: false` in `cypress.config.ts` acts as a compile-time-equivalent lint gate: any spec that has not yet been migrated to `cy.env()` or `Cypress.expose()` will fail immediately with a descriptive error, preventing silent use of the old insecure path.

```typescript
// packages/billing/cypress.config.ts — per-package config in a monorepo
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    baseUrl: 'https://billing.staging.example.com',
    // Enforce migration: any Cypress.env() call throws immediately
    allowCypressEnv: false,
    expose: {
      APP_PACKAGE: 'billing',
      BILLING_VERSION: '3.2.0',
    },
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      return config;
    },
  },
});

// cypress/support/e2e.ts — migration helper to ease incremental adoption
// Centralise all env reads to avoid scattering cy.env() calls across specs
export function getAuthCreds(): Cypress.Chainable<{ email: string; password: string }> {
  return cy.env('BILLING_ADMIN_EMAIL', { log: false }).then((email: string) => {
    return cy.env('BILLING_ADMIN_PASSWORD', { log: false }).then((password: string) => {
      return cy.wrap({ email, password });
    });
  });
}

// cypress/e2e/invoice-access.cy.ts
import { getAuthCreds } from '../support/e2e';

describe('Invoice access (migrated to cy.env)', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    getAuthCreds().then(({ email, password }) => {
      cy.session([email], () => {
        cy.visit('/billing/login');
        cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(email, { log: false });
        cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type(password, { log: false });
        cy.get('[data-cy="login-btn"]').click();
      });
    });
  });

  it('lists invoices', () => {
    cy.visit('/billing/invoices');
    cy.get('[data-cy="invoice-row"]').should('have.length.gte', 1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Roll out `allowCypressEnv: false` per-package in a monorepo rather than globally — enabling it globally in a large repo will break all packages simultaneously. Migrate one package at a time by adding `allowCypressEnv: false` to that package's `cypress.config.ts`, running the test suite to surface remaining `Cypress.env()` call sites, and replacing them with `cy.env()` or `Cypress.expose()` before merging. A codemoded search for `Cypress\.env\(` with `jscodeshift` or `ast-grep` accelerates bulk replacement. [official]

---

### 504. `--pass-with-no-tests` CLI Flag for Conditional Spec Discovery  [official]

Cypress 15.11.0 added the `--pass-with-no-tests` CLI flag to handle runs where zero spec files are discovered. Without this flag, Cypress exits with a non-zero code when no specs match the `--spec` glob, which causes CI pipelines that conditionally run a subset of specs (e.g., only specs tagged `@billing` when the billing module changed) to fail when no tagged specs exist in the changeset. The flag exits `0` silently when no specs are found, allowing conditional spec-tagging pipelines to succeed without special-casing.

```typescript
// .github/workflows/affected-tests.yml (excerpt — shows CLI usage context)
// Run only specs tagged @billing when billing files changed
// If no @billing specs exist, --pass-with-no-tests prevents pipeline failure

// cypress/e2e/invoice-list.cy.ts
// @tags: ['@billing', '@smoke']
describe('Invoice list @billing', { tags: ['@billing', '@smoke'] }, () => {
  it('renders invoice table', () => {
    cy.visit('/billing/invoices');
    cy.get('[data-cy="invoice-table"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});

// cypress/plugins/tag-filter.ts — custom tag-filter plugin for --env grepTags
// Used alongside cypress-grep to run only specs matching a tag pattern
// CLI: npx cypress run --env grepTags=@billing --spec 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts' --pass-with-no-tests
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    env: {
      // cypress-grep: only run tests matching the tag
      grepTags: '',
      grepFilterSpecs: true,  // skip spec files with no matching tags entirely
      grepOmitFiltered: true,
    },
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      // eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-require-imports
      require('@bahmutov/cy-grep/src/plugin')(config);
      return config;
    },
  },
});

// CI shell (illustrative — not TypeScript):
// affected=$(node scripts/detect-affected-tags.mjs) # e.g. '@billing'
// npx cypress run \
//   --env grepTags="${affected}" \
//   --spec 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts' \
//   --pass-with-no-tests
// exit $?   # always 0 if no matching specs; non-zero only on actual test failures
```

**Tradeoff.** `--pass-with-no-tests` masks mis-configured spec globs — if the glob accidentally matches nothing due to a path typo, the run will silently succeed instead of alerting that expected specs were not found. Pair it with an upstream step that logs the number of discovered spec files so the CI log makes it clear whether the empty run was intentional. Do not use `--pass-with-no-tests` in full-suite smoke runs where the absence of specs would indicate a build or configuration error. [official]

---

### 505. Brotli-Compressed Response Passthrough via `cy.intercept()`  [official]

Cypress 15.11.0 added Brotli decompression support to the proxy layer, meaning responses compressed with `Content-Encoding: br` are now transparently decoded before `cy.intercept()` route handlers receive the response body. Prior to 15.11.0, intercepting a Brotli-compressed API response would yield a raw binary `body` that could not be JSON-parsed, causing assertions on `response.body` to fail silently. The fix is transparent for most teams, but requires awareness when working with proxied Brotli endpoints in older versions or when explicitly testing compression headers.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/brotli-api.cy.ts
// Requires Cypress >= 15.11.0 for transparent Brotli decode in cy.intercept()
describe('Product catalog (Brotli-compressed API)', () => {
  it('intercepts and asserts decoded response body from Brotli endpoint', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/v2/products', (req) => {
      req.on('response', (res) => {
        // In 15.11.0+ the body is decoded — safe to assert as JSON
        expect(res.headers['content-encoding']).to.eq('br');
        // Body is already decoded by the proxy — no manual decompress needed
        expect(res.body).to.have.property('data').that.is.an('array');
      });
      req.continue();
    }).as('getProducts');

    cy.visit('/products');
    cy.wait('@getProducts').then((interception) => {
      // Assert decoded body — would have been binary Buffer in < 15.11.0
      expect(interception.response?.body.data).to.have.length.greaterThan(0);
      expect(interception.response?.body.data[0]).to.have.keys(['id', 'name', 'price']);
    });
  });

  it('stubs a Brotli endpoint with plain JSON (Cypress always serves uncompressed stubs)', () => {
    // Stubs are served uncompressed by Cypress proxy regardless of Accept-Encoding
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/v2/products', {
      statusCode: 200,
      body: { data: [{ id: '1', name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 }], meta: { total: 1 } },
    }).as('stubbedProducts');

    cy.visit('/products');
    cy.wait('@stubbedProducts');
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-card"]').should('have.length', 1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Cypress stubs are always served uncompressed (no `Content-Encoding` header) regardless of the client's `Accept-Encoding` request header — if your application code inspects `Content-Encoding` to detect whether it's talking to the real server vs. a Cypress stub, this will produce a false-negative. In such cases, add `headers: { 'Content-Encoding': 'identity' }` to your `StaticResponse` stubs or use `req.on('before:response')` to inject a custom `Content-Encoding` header. [official]

---

### 506. `cy.end()` Deprecation — Migration to `cy.wrap(null)` for Chain Termination  [official]

`cy.end()` was deprecated in Cypress 15.15.0. Its purpose was to terminate a command chain and yield `null` so that subsequent chained commands start from a clean state rather than from the subject of the previous command. The replacement pattern is `cy.wrap(null)` or simply starting a new `cy.get()` chain without chaining off the previous subject. The deprecation notice warns that `cy.end()` will be removed in a future major version.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/chain-termination.cy.ts

// BEFORE: cy.end() pattern (deprecated in 15.15.0)
// cy.get('[data-cy="first-item"]')
//   .click()
//   .end() // <-- deprecated
//   .get('[data-cy="second-item"]')
//   .should('be.visible');

// AFTER: preferred replacement patterns

describe('Chain termination (post-cy.end() migration)', () => {
  it('uses new top-level cy.get() instead of .end()', () => {
    // Pattern 1: Start a new top-level command (recommended for readability)
    cy.get('[data-cy="first-item"]').click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="second-item"]').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('uses cy.wrap(null) when chaining is required by helper function structure', () => {
    // Pattern 2: cy.wrap(null) when the next chain must be the return value
    function clickAndReset(selector: string): Cypress.Chainable<null> {
      return cy.get(selector).click().then(() => cy.wrap(null));
    }

    clickAndReset('[data-cy="first-item"]').then(() => {
      cy.get('[data-cy="second-item"]').should('be.visible');
    });
  });

  it('uses cy.then() to explicitly discard the subject', () => {
    // Pattern 3: .then(() => null) discards subject inline
    cy.get('[data-cy="first-item"]')
      .click()
      .then(() => null)
      .then(() => {
        cy.get('[data-cy="second-item"]').should('be.visible');
      });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.wrap(null)` is semantically equivalent to the old `cy.end()` but is more explicit about intent. In practice, the most readable migration for most `cy.end()` call sites is to simply break the chain into two separate top-level `cy.*` commands — this removes nesting and improves test readability. Automated migration via codemod is straightforward: `cy.get(...).something().end()` → `cy.get(...).something();\ncy.` at the next command. [official]

---

### 507. Bootstrap Script Injection via `<script data-cy-bootstrap>` for SSR Hydration  [official]

Cypress 15.11.0 introduced support for `<script data-cy-bootstrap>` elements, which allow React (and other SSR framework) applications to inject a small script before Cypress's own bootstrap injection. This solves a class of hydration mismatch warnings that appear when `suppressHydrationWarning` is set on the root element — the React server-rendered HTML contains Cypress-specific attributes injected during the previous test, causing React's hydration to detect a mismatch between server HTML and the client tree. The bootstrap script runs before React hydration, allowing the app to strip Cypress-injected attributes before React compares the DOM.

```typescript
// public/cypress-bootstrap.js — loaded via <script data-cy-bootstrap src="/cypress-bootstrap.js">
// This script runs BEFORE React hydration, stripping Cypress-injected attributes
(function () {
  if (typeof window.__cypress !== 'undefined') {
    // Strip data-cy-* attributes injected by the previous Cypress test session
    document.querySelectorAll('[data-cy-root]').forEach(function (el) {
      el.removeAttribute('data-cy-root');
    });
    // Signal to React that the DOM has been cleaned — suppress hydration mismatch
    document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-cy-bootstrap-ran', 'true');
  }
})();

// index.html (Next.js / Vite SSR)
// <head>
//   <!-- Cypress bootstrap: runs before React hydration to clean injected attrs -->
//   <script data-cy-bootstrap src="/cypress-bootstrap.js"></script>
// </head>

// cypress/e2e/ssr-hydration.cy.ts
describe('SSR hydration (no mismatch with bootstrap script)', () => {
  it('visits the page without React hydration mismatch warnings', () => {
    // Spy on console.error to catch any residual hydration warnings
    cy.visit('/', {
      onBeforeLoad(win) {
        cy.stub(win.console, 'error').as('consoleError');
      },
    });

    cy.get('[data-cy="app-root"]').should('be.visible');

    // Assert no hydration mismatch warnings fired during initial render
    cy.get('@consoleError').then((stub) => {
      const calls = (stub as sinon.SinonStub).args;
      const hydrationErrors = calls.filter(([msg]) =>
        typeof msg === 'string' && msg.includes('Hydration failed')
      );
      expect(hydrationErrors).to.have.length(0);
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `<script data-cy-bootstrap>` element is only executed when Cypress is actively running — in production builds the script tag is present but the `window.__cypress` guard prevents any mutations. This is safe for production deployment but adds a non-zero byte penalty to the initial HTML payload. If your team has strict CSP headers that block inline or external scripts not explicitly listed, add the `cypress-bootstrap.js` origin to the `script-src` CSP directive in your test environment configuration. [official]

---

### 508. Vite 8 Component Testing with HMR Module Graph Invalidation Guard  [official]

Cypress 15.14.0 added official support for Vite 8 in component testing. Vite 8 changed how the module graph is invalidated during HMR — specifically, it no longer automatically propagates invalidation through dynamic import boundaries when using the `optimizeDeps.include` list. This affects Cypress component testing when shared utility modules are imported both as direct spec imports and as `optimizeDeps.include` entries: changes to the utility may not trigger spec recompilation in `open` mode, causing stale test behaviour.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — Vite 8 component testing configuration
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { resolve } from 'path';

export default defineConfig({
  component: {
    devServer: {
      framework: 'react',
      bundler: 'vite',
      viteConfig: {
        plugins: [react()],
        optimizeDeps: {
          // Vite 8: do NOT include shared test utilities in optimizeDeps.include
          // They must remain in the module graph for HMR invalidation to propagate
          include: [
            // Only third-party packages, not workspace-local utilities
            'react',
            'react-dom',
            '@tanstack/react-query',
          ],
          // Exclude local test helpers so Vite 8 HMR tracks their dependency graph
          exclude: ['@/test-utils', '@/mocks'],
        },
        resolve: {
          alias: {
            '@': resolve(__dirname, 'src'),
          },
        },
      },
    },
    specPattern: 'src/**/*.cy.{ts,tsx}',
    supportFile: 'cypress/support/component.ts',
  },
});

// cypress/support/component.ts
import { mount } from 'cypress/react18';

declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      mount: typeof mount;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.add('mount', mount);
```

**Tradeoff.** Removing shared utilities from `optimizeDeps.include` means Vite 8 will not pre-bundle them, resulting in slightly slower cold-start times in the Cypress component test runner's first launch (the utilities are compiled on-demand per-spec). The trade-off is correct HMR invalidation: when a shared utility changes, all dependent specs reload properly. For CI runs (which always start cold), the `optimizeDeps` setting has no effect on correctness — only on development-mode HMR. [official]

---

### 509. TypeScript 6 Template-Literal Branded Types on `cy.intercept()` URL Patterns  [community]

Cypress 15.14.0 added TypeScript 6 support. TypeScript 6 stabilised template-literal type inference in generic positions, enabling a community pattern that brands `cy.intercept()` URL pattern strings at the type level to prevent mixing up glob patterns with literal paths. By creating a nominal `GlobPattern` brand type and a `RouteAlias` brand type, you catch common mistakes (e.g., passing a raw literal path where a glob is expected, or aliasing the same route under two different names) at compile time.

```typescript
// cypress/support/types/intercept-brands.ts
declare const __glob: unique symbol;
declare const __alias: unique symbol;

// Branded string types — only assignable via the helper functions below
export type GlobPattern = string & { [__glob]: true };
export type RouteAlias = string & { [__alias]: true };

// Factory helpers — the only way to create branded values
export function glob(pattern: string): GlobPattern {
  return pattern as GlobPattern;
}
export function alias(name: string): RouteAlias {
  return name as RouteAlias;
}

// cypress/support/routes.ts — centralise all route registrations
import { glob, alias, type GlobPattern, type RouteAlias } from './types/intercept-brands';

export const Routes = {
  products: {
    list: glob('/api/products*'),
    create: glob('/api/products'),
    detail: glob('/api/products/*'),
  } satisfies Record<string, GlobPattern>,
  orders: {
    list: glob('/api/orders*'),
  } satisfies Record<string, GlobPattern>,
} as const;

export const Aliases = {
  getProducts:  alias('getProducts'),
  createProduct: alias('createProduct'),
  getOrders:    alias('getOrders'),
} as const satisfies Record<string, RouteAlias>;

// cypress/e2e/product-list.cy.ts
import { Routes, Aliases } from '../support/routes';

describe('Product list', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.intercept('GET', Routes.products.list, { fixture: 'products.json' })
      .as(Aliases.getProducts);
  });

  it('renders product cards', () => {
    cy.visit('/products');
    cy.wait(`@${Aliases.getProducts}`);
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-card"]').should('have.length.gte', 1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** TypeScript 6 template-literal brand inference only works in strict mode (`"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json`). If your `cypress/tsconfig.json` uses `"strict": false` (common in older Cypress setups), the `[__glob]` and `[__alias]` brands will not be enforced and the pattern degrades silently to plain `string`. Run `tsc --noEmit --strict` as part of your CI pre-flight to confirm branded type enforcement is active. This pattern adds a one-time authoring cost (defining Routes and Aliases) but significantly reduces the cognitive overhead of maintaining large intercept suites with many route aliases. [community]

---

### 510. `cy.intercept()` `req.destroy()` Network Error Simulation  [official]

`cy.intercept()` route handlers expose `req.destroy()`, which terminates the proxied connection without sending any response — simulating a network-level error (ECONNRESET) rather than an HTTP error response. This is the correct way to test application error boundaries that specifically handle `ERR_NETWORK` or `fetch()` rejections, which behave differently from a `{ statusCode: 500 }` stub: the browser `fetch()` promise rejects with a `TypeError: Failed to fetch`, and no `Response` object is available.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/network-error-boundary.cy.ts
describe('Product list — network error boundary', () => {
  it('shows error boundary when fetch rejects with network error', () => {
    // req.destroy() simulates ECONNRESET — fetch() rejects, no HTTP status available
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products', (req) => {
      req.destroy();
    }).as('networkError');

    cy.visit('/products');

    // Do NOT cy.wait('@networkError') — the alias resolves immediately on destroy
    // but waiting is optional since the UI will update asynchronously
    cy.get('[data-cy="error-boundary"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="error-message"]')
      .should('contain.text', 'Network error');

    // Confirm no HTTP status was returned (error boundary should not show a status code)
    cy.get('[data-cy="error-status-code"]').should('not.exist');
  });

  it('recovers after retry following network error', () => {
    let callCount = 0;

    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products', (req) => {
      callCount += 1;
      if (callCount === 1) {
        req.destroy(); // First call: network error
      } else {
        req.reply({ statusCode: 200, body: { data: [], meta: { total: 0 } } });
      }
    }).as('productsRequest');

    cy.visit('/products');
    cy.get('[data-cy="retry-btn"]').click();
    cy.wait('@productsRequest');
    cy.get('[data-cy="empty-state"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `req.destroy()` causes the underlying TCP socket to reset — in some browser/OS combinations this surfaces as `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` rather than `net::ERR_FAILED`, and application code that inspects `error.message` for specific network error strings may behave differently than expected. Always combine `req.destroy()` tests with assertions on the visible UI state (error boundary rendered) rather than on the specific error message string, since error message wording varies between Chrome versions and platforms. [official]

---

### 511. `cy.origin()` Dynamic-Key URL Workaround with `cy.wrap()` Preprocessor  [community]

A known limitation in Cypress 15.x is that `cy.origin()` does not natively support cross-origin URLs whose path or query string contains dynamic keys appended after navigation (e.g., OAuth state parameters, nonce values generated server-side). The application navigates to `https://idp.example.com/auth?state=abc123` and then redirects back with additional query parameters; the `cy.origin()` callback URL argument must be an exact string literal or a variable evaluated before entering the callback. The workaround is to pre-resolve the target URL using `cy.wrap()` and pass the resolved origin string explicitly.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/oauth-dynamic-state.cy.ts
describe('OAuth flow with dynamic state parameter', () => {
  it('handles dynamic query-key redirect after IdP authorization', () => {
    const idpOrigin = Cypress.env('IDP_ORIGIN') as string; // e.g. 'https://idp.example.com'

    cy.visit('/dashboard');

    // Intercept the redirect to capture the dynamic state value BEFORE entering cy.origin()
    cy.intercept('GET', `${idpOrigin}/auth*`, (req) => {
      // Extract the state param from the outgoing URL
      const url = new URL(req.url);
      req.headers['x-cy-state'] = url.searchParams.get('state') ?? '';
      req.continue();
    }).as('idpRedirect');

    cy.get('[data-cy="login-with-sso"]').click();

    // Wait for the initial redirect and capture the dynamic state
    cy.wait('@idpRedirect').then((interception) => {
      const state = interception.request.headers['x-cy-state'] as string;

      // Now enter cy.origin() with the pre-resolved origin and state in args
      cy.origin(idpOrigin, { args: { state } }, ({ state: capturedState }) => {
        // Complete IdP form — this is the static part of the IdP page
        cy.get('[data-cy="idp-username"]').type('testuser@example.com');
        cy.get('[data-cy="idp-password"]').type('password123', { log: false });
        cy.get('[data-cy="idp-submit"]').click();

        // Verify the callback URL contains the expected state to confirm no CSRF
        cy.url().should('include', `state=${capturedState}`);
      });
    });

    // After cy.origin() completes, back in primary origin
    cy.get('[data-cy="dashboard-header"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `cy.intercept()` to capture request headers mid-flight introduces a timing dependency: if the application issues the IdP redirect before `cy.intercept()` is registered, the state will not be captured. Register the `cy.intercept()` route in a `beforeEach()` hook (before `cy.visit()`) rather than inline before the click event. Also note that injecting arbitrary headers (`x-cy-state`) into requests to third-party IdPs is safe in a test environment where the real IdP is a stub, but in tests against a real external IdP, header injection may trigger CORS pre-flight failures. [community]

---

### 512. WYSIWYG `contenteditable` Typing with `cy.type()` `force: true` and Focus Pre-check  [community]

Rich text editors built on `contenteditable` elements (Quill, Tiptap, Froala, Lexical) are a persistent source of Cypress gotchas. The root problem is that `contenteditable` elements do not receive input through the DOM `value` property — they rely on `execCommand`, `InputEvent`, or `beforeinput`/`input` events dispatched against the focused element. `cy.type()` with `{ force: true }` bypasses actionability checks but still requires the element to be focused in the browser's active frame. The correct pattern is to explicitly click the editor, wait for the editor's own focus state class, and then type.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/rich-text-editor.cy.ts
describe('Tiptap rich text editor', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.visit('/editor');
    // Wait for the editor JS bundle to hydrate the contenteditable
    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').should('exist').and('have.attr', 'contenteditable', 'true');
  });

  it('types text into the editor and asserts content', () => {
    // Click to focus — do NOT skip this step; cy.type() needs an active focus
    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').click();

    // Wait for focus class to confirm editor has received focus
    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').should('have.class', 'is-focused');

    // Type content — force:true bypasses actionability but focus is already set
    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').type('Hello, {bold}World{/bold}!', { force: true });

    // Assert rendered output in the editor DOM
    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').find('strong').should('contain.text', 'World');
  });

  it('inserts a link via keyboard shortcut', () => {
    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').click().type('Visit our site', { force: true });

    // Select all text
    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').type('{ctrl+a}', { force: true });

    // Open link dialog via Ctrl+K (Tiptap default)
    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').type('{ctrl+k}', { force: true });
    cy.get('[data-cy="link-input"]').type('https://example.com');
    cy.get('[data-cy="link-confirm"]').click();

    cy.get('.tiptap.ProseMirror').find('a[href="https://example.com"]').should('exist');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.type()` with `{ force: true }` does not simulate true browser keyboard events via CDP — it dispatches synthetic DOM events that most editor frameworks accept, but some frameworks (Lexical in particular) partially validate event `isTrusted` flags and may silently discard non-trusted events in certain input paths. For editors that reject synthetic events, use `cy.press()` (Cypress 15.1.0+) which dispatches via the real browser keyboard API and produces trusted events, or use `cy.realType()` from the `cypress-real-events` plugin. [community]

---

### 513. `cy.session()` Global Clear with `Cypress.session.clearAllSavedSessions()`  [official]

`Cypress.session.clearAllSavedSessions()` (available since Cypress 12.x) purges all cached session data for all session IDs in the current spec run. It is useful in `before()` hooks at the describe-block level when you need to ensure no session leaks from previous spec files in a long run, or in CI pipelines that reuse browser profiles between test batches. Unlike `cy.session(id, setup, { cacheAcrossSpecs: false })`, which only prevents caching, `clearAllSavedSessions()` actively evicts sessions that may have been cached by other specs.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/multi-tenant-isolation.cy.ts
describe('Multi-tenant data isolation', () => {
  before(() => {
    // Purge all sessions from any previously-run specs in this browser process
    // Prevents tenant A session leaking into tenant B tests
    Cypress.session.clearAllSavedSessions();
  });

  function loginAs(tenant: 'tenant-a' | 'tenant-b', role: 'admin' | 'viewer'): void {
    cy.session(
      [tenant, role],
      () => {
        cy.visit('/login');
        cy.get('[data-cy="tenant-input"]').type(tenant);
        cy.get('[data-cy="role-select"]').select(role);
        cy.get('[data-cy="login-btn"]').click();
        cy.get('[data-cy="dashboard"]').should('be.visible');
      },
      {
        validate() {
          cy.request('/api/session').its('status').should('eq', 200);
        },
        cacheAcrossSpecs: false, // isolation: do not share sessions between spec files
      },
    );
  }

  it('tenant A admin cannot see tenant B data', () => {
    loginAs('tenant-a', 'admin');
    cy.visit('/data');
    cy.get('[data-cy="data-row"]').each(($row) => {
      cy.wrap($row).should('contain.text', 'tenant-a');
    });
  });

  it('tenant B viewer sees only their own records', () => {
    loginAs('tenant-b', 'viewer');
    cy.visit('/data');
    cy.get('[data-cy="data-row"]').each(($row) => {
      cy.wrap($row).should('contain.text', 'tenant-b');
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `Cypress.session.clearAllSavedSessions()` is a synchronous call but its effect is applied before any test in the current spec runs. Calling it inside a `beforeEach()` hook defeats the purpose of `cy.session()` caching — every test will re-run the session setup function. Place it in a `before()` hook (runs once per describe block) or in `cypress/support/e2e.ts` inside a `before()` hook registered globally. Avoid calling it in `afterEach()` unless you specifically need a clean session for every single test, as the repeated session setup overhead will significantly slow down suite execution. [official]

---

### 514. GitLab CI Hanging Test Detection with `cy.task()` Timeout Guard  [community]

A recurring problem on GitLab CI (and similar shared-runner environments) is that Cypress tests hang indefinitely when the application under test enters a frozen state — for example, a spinner that never resolves due to a missing API stub or an uncaught promise rejection that silently swallows the error. Cypress's default `defaultCommandTimeout` only applies to individual commands, not to the total time a test is allowed to run. A `cy.task()` timeout guard in `cypress.config.ts` combined with a Node.js `AbortController` provides a cross-platform "watchdog" that kills the Cypress process after a configurable deadline.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — timeout watchdog for GitLab CI hanging prevention
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    defaultCommandTimeout: 10_000,
    taskTimeout: 30_000, // cy.task() must resolve within 30s or Cypress fails the test
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      on('task', {
        // Watchdog task: schedules a forced process exit after 'ms' milliseconds
        // Used in beforeEach to restart the guard timer per test
        startWatchdog({ ms, label }: { ms: number; label: string }): null {
          const controller = new AbortController();
          const timer = setTimeout(() => {
            console.error(`[WATCHDOG] Test "${label}" exceeded ${ms}ms — aborting Cypress process`);
            // On GitLab CI, exit 1 causes the job to fail and surfaceable in GitLab UI
            process.exit(1);
          }, ms);

          // Expose a way for the test to cancel the watchdog on success
          (global as Record<string, unknown>).__cypressWatchdog = { controller, timer };
          return null;
        },

        cancelWatchdog(): null {
          const watchdog = (global as Record<string, unknown>).__cypressWatchdog as
            | { timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> }
            | undefined;
          if (watchdog) {
            clearTimeout(watchdog.timer);
            delete (global as Record<string, unknown>).__cypressWatchdog;
          }
          return null;
        },
      });

      return config;
    },
  },
});

// cypress/support/e2e.ts — global watchdog hooks
const WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT_MS = 90_000; // 90s per test max

beforeEach(function () {
  cy.task('startWatchdog', {
    ms: WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT_MS,
    label: this.currentTest?.fullTitle() ?? 'unknown',
  });
});

afterEach(() => {
  cy.task('cancelWatchdog');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The watchdog `process.exit(1)` call terminates the entire Cypress Node.js process, which means all remaining specs in the run are skipped — this is intentional for GitLab CI to surface the hanging test as a job failure rather than silently timing out the entire CI job after 60 minutes. However, the abrupt exit means Cypress does not write its final JSON results file or upload to Cypress Cloud, so you lose the test dashboard report for the run. Mitigate this by writing partial results to a JSON file inside the `startWatchdog` task before the `setTimeout` fires, then uploading that file as a GitLab CI artifact. [community]

---

### 515. `cy.intercept()` Middleware Ordering with `req.on()` Priority Chaining  [official]

When multiple `cy.intercept()` routes match the same request, Cypress applies them in reverse registration order (last registered wins for response stubbing). However, `req.on()` event handlers attached within route handler callbacks are applied in registration order within each interceptor. Understanding this layering is essential when composing a "middleware stack" of intercept handlers — for example, an auth token injector, a latency simulator, and a response logger — so that each layer runs in the correct order without one overwriting another's modifications.

```typescript
// cypress/support/intercept-middleware.ts
// A composable middleware system built on cy.intercept() req.on() ordering

/**
 * Layer 1 (register LAST — innermost, runs first on response):
 * Injects auth token into all API requests
 */
export function withAuthToken(token: string): void {
  cy.intercept('/api/**', (req) => {
    req.headers['Authorization'] = `Bearer ${token}`;
    req.continue();
  });
}

/**
 * Layer 2 (register SECOND — runs after auth injection):
 * Adds artificial latency to simulate slow network in E2E tests
 */
export function withLatency(ms: number): void {
  cy.intercept('/api/**', (req) => {
    req.on('before:response', (res) => {
      res.setDelay(ms);
    });
    req.continue();
  });
}

/**
 * Layer 3 (register FIRST — outermost, runs last on response):
 * Logs all API requests and response status codes to Cypress task for CI audit
 */
export function withRequestLogger(): void {
  cy.intercept('/api/**', (req) => {
    const start = Date.now();
    req.on('after:response', (res) => {
      cy.task(
        'logApiCall',
        { url: req.url, method: req.method, status: res.statusCode, durationMs: Date.now() - start },
        { log: false },
      );
    });
    req.continue();
  });
}

// cypress/e2e/api-middleware-stack.cy.ts
import { withAuthToken, withLatency, withRequestLogger } from '../support/intercept-middleware';

describe('API middleware stack (auth + latency + logging)', () => {
  before(() => {
    cy.env('API_TOKEN', { log: false }).then((token: string) => {
      // Register in REVERSE order of intended execution:
      // withRequestLogger registers FIRST (outermost), withAuthToken LAST (innermost)
      withRequestLogger();   // register first — runs last on response
      withLatency(200);      // register second
      withAuthToken(token);  // register last — runs first (auth header added before request leaves)
    });
  });

  it('requests include auth header and latency is applied', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products').as('getProducts');
    cy.visit('/products');
    cy.wait('@getProducts', { timeout: 15_000 }) // extra timeout for 200ms latency
      .its('request.headers.Authorization')
      .should('match', /^Bearer .+/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The "last registered wins" rule applies only to response stubbing (when a handler calls `req.reply()` instead of `req.continue()`). For pass-through handlers that use `req.continue()`, all matching interceptors run in reverse registration order on the request path and forward registration order on the response path. Drawing the execution order on paper before implementing a multi-layer intercept stack prevents subtle bugs where a later-registered handler overwrites a header set by an earlier one. When in doubt, use a single `cy.intercept()` handler with explicit ordering logic inside the callback rather than multiple overlapping interceptors. [official]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 50

336. **`cy.env()` called at describe-block scope (synchronously, outside a command hook) enqueues the async command but the resolved value is `undefined` in any synchronous code that follows — a developer who writes `const email = cy.env('ADMIN_EMAIL')` at describe scope expecting a string receives a Cypress Chainable object, not the string value, and all subsequent calls that reference `email` as a string silently operate on `[object Object]`** [community] — A developer migrates from `Cypress.env('ADMIN_EMAIL')` to `cy.env('ADMIN_EMAIL')` and replaces the call at the top of a describe block without wrapping it in `before()`. The `const email` variable holds the Chainable object, and `cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(email)` types the literal string `[object Object]` into the field, which fails the login assertion without indicating that `cy.env()` was called incorrectly. WHY: `cy.env()` is an asynchronous Cypress command that returns a Chainable — it is not a synchronous accessor like `Cypress.env()`. Resolved values are only available inside `.then()` callbacks or downstream Cypress commands chained off the `cy.env()` call. Fix: always call `cy.env()` inside `before()`, `beforeEach()`, or a `cy.then()` callback and capture the result in a closure variable that is scoped to the hook, not to the describe block.

337. **`Cypress.expose()` values that contain functions or class instances are silently dropped during serialisation — the `expose` config block uses JSON serialisation to transfer values from the Cypress config (Node.js process) to the browser context, so any non-JSON-serialisable value (function, Date, Map, Set, Uint8Array) is omitted without an error, and `Cypress.expose('myKey')` returns `undefined` for those keys** [community] — A developer adds `expose: { rateLimitFn: (x: number) => x * 2 }` to `cypress.config.ts` to share a helper function with tests, and calls `Cypress.expose('rateLimitFn')` inside a spec expecting a callable function. The returned value is `undefined` because the function was silently dropped during JSON serialisation. The error surfaces only when the spec tries to call `Cypress.expose('rateLimitFn')(5)` and throws `TypeError: Cypress.expose(...) is not a function`. WHY: The `expose` config block is serialised via `JSON.stringify` to transfer values across the Node.js/browser boundary — JSON.stringify silently omits object keys whose values are functions, `undefined`, `Symbol`, or non-serialisable types (Date becomes a string, Map/Set become `{}`). Fix: only place plain JSON-serialisable values (primitives, plain objects, arrays) under `expose`; move helper functions to a shared TypeScript module imported directly by spec files.

338. **`--pass-with-no-tests` masks a mis-typed `--spec` glob that accidentally matches zero files — in a CI pipeline that dynamically generates the spec glob from a changed-files list, a path separator bug (backslash on Windows) can produce a glob that matches nothing, and `--pass-with-no-tests` causes the entire Cypress run to exit 0 and report "All tests passed" with zero tests executed, making the pipeline appear green when the intended test coverage was never applied** [community] — A Windows-based CI runner generates the spec glob `cypress\\e2e\\billing\\*.cy.ts` using backslash separators, which Cypress's glob engine does not match on any platform (globs require forward slashes). With `--pass-with-no-tests`, the run exits 0. The billing suite is never executed. WHY: Cypress uses the `minimatch` library for spec glob matching, which requires forward-slash path separators regardless of the host OS — backslash path separators in glob patterns are interpreted as escape characters, not directory separators, causing all path-containing globs with backslashes to match zero files. Fix: always normalise paths to forward slashes before passing to `--spec`; add an explicit assertion step in CI that checks `cypress run --list-specs` output is non-empty before invoking `--pass-with-no-tests`.

339. **`req.destroy()` inside `cy.intercept()` causes the Cypress proxy to log an `ECONNRESET` warning in the terminal that is not associated with any test failure — when multiple tests call `req.destroy()`, the terminal output fills with `Error [ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED]: Cannot call write after a stream has been destroyed` lines from the proxy, which obscures genuine errors in the CI log and triggers false alerts in log-monitoring tools that scan for the word "Error"** [community] — A QA team adds `req.destroy()` tests for network error boundaries across 30 components. In CI, each `req.destroy()` call prints an `ECONNRESET` proxy warning to stdout. Log-monitoring (e.g., Datadog Log Management, Splunk) triggers an `Error spike` alert because it counts all lines containing "Error" in the CI output, including the expected Cypress proxy warnings. WHY: `req.destroy()` terminates the proxied socket, which causes Node.js's `http.ClientRequest` in the Cypress proxy to attempt to write the response to an already-closed stream, emitting the `ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED` warning. This is expected behaviour but Cypress does not suppress the warning because it is emitted by the Node.js stream machinery, not by Cypress itself. Fix: redirect Cypress terminal output to a file and apply a grep filter to strip known proxy teardown warnings before piping to log-monitoring; or add `{ log: false }` to the `cy.intercept()` call to suppress Cypress-level logging (does not suppress Node.js stream warnings, but reduces noise in the Cypress App).

340. **`Cypress.session.clearAllSavedSessions()` called in a `beforeEach()` hook causes every test to re-run the session setup function, negating the performance benefit of `cy.session()` caching — in a suite of 50 tests that each use `cy.session()` for login, adding `clearAllSavedSessions()` to `beforeEach()` multiplies total run time by 4–8x compared to the same suite with session caching enabled, because every test now performs a full login cycle instead of reusing the cached session** [community] — A developer adds `Cypress.session.clearAllSavedSessions()` to `beforeEach()` after reading that it should be used to prevent session leaks, not realising that `beforeEach()` runs before every test (not once before the suite). The login setup function takes 3–4 seconds per test; with 50 tests, session caching would reduce the total to ~4 seconds (first test) + 49 × 0.1s (cache hit). With `clearAllSavedSessions()` in `beforeEach()`, every test pays the 3–4s setup cost, increasing suite time from ~9 seconds to ~175 seconds. WHY: `beforeEach()` runs before every individual test — `clearAllSavedSessions()` placed here evicts the session cache between every test, so `cy.session()` never gets a cache hit. The correct placement is a top-level `before()` hook (runs once per describe block) to clear stale sessions from prior spec files without disrupting caching within the current spec. Fix: move `Cypress.session.clearAllSavedSessions()` to a `before()` hook; if per-test isolation is genuinely required, pass `cacheAcrossSpecs: false` to `cy.session()` instead, which prevents cross-spec leakage while still caching within the spec.

## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### 516. `cy.wait()` Two-Stage Timeout Tuning for Slow API Endpoints  [official]

`cy.wait('@alias')` uses two independent timeouts: `requestTimeout` (default 5 000 ms) for the request to leave the browser and `responseTimeout` (default 30 000 ms) for the server to reply. Setting the wrong timeout causes misleading failure messages that suggest the server never replied when the request was actually never sent, or vice versa.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/report-generation.cy.ts
describe('PDF report generation (slow endpoint)', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.intercept('POST', '/api/reports/generate').as('generateReport');
  });

  it('generates a PDF report within SLA', () => {
    cy.visit('/reports');
    cy.get('[data-cy="generate-btn"]').click();

    // Override responseTimeout per-wait for this known-slow endpoint
    cy.wait('@generateReport', { responseTimeout: 90_000 })
      .its('response.statusCode')
      .should('eq', 202); // accepted for async processing

    cy.get('[data-cy="report-status"]', { timeout: 120_000 })
      .should('contain', 'Ready');
  });

  it('rejects request when token is missing (fast failure path)', () => {
    // Keep default timeouts — server should reject immediately
    cy.intercept('POST', '/api/reports/generate', { statusCode: 401 }).as('blockedReport');
    cy.visit('/reports');
    cy.get('[data-cy="generate-btn"]').click();
    cy.wait('@blockedReport').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 401);
    cy.get('[data-cy="error-banner"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Per-wait overrides are safer than raising the global `responseTimeout` in `cypress.config.ts`, which silently inflates the timeout for every `cy.wait()` call in the suite, masking genuinely slow tests that should fail faster. Reserve global overrides for CI environments where network latency is consistently higher than local development. [official]

---

### 517. Multiple Request Array Wait with `cy.wait([])` for Coordinated Page Load Assertions  [official]

`cy.wait(['@alias1', '@alias2', '@alias3'])` blocks until all listed requests complete and returns an array of `Interception` objects in the same order as the aliases. This prevents the classic flake pattern where a test asserts on rendered content before a parallel data-fetch request has resolved.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands/waitForDashboard.ts
export function waitForDashboardLoad(): void {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/user/profile').as('userProfile');
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/notifications*').as('notifications');
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/activity-feed*').as('activityFeed');

  cy.visit('/dashboard');

  // Wait for all three in one command — returns array of Interception objects
  cy.wait(['@userProfile', '@notifications', '@activityFeed']).spread(
    (profile, notifs, feed) => {
      expect(profile.response!.statusCode).to.eq(200);
      expect(notifs.response!.statusCode).to.eq(200);
      expect(feed.response!.statusCode).to.eq(200);
    }
  );
}

// cypress/e2e/dashboard.cy.ts
it('renders all dashboard widgets after load', () => {
  waitForDashboardLoad();
  cy.get('[data-cy="profile-card"]').should('be.visible');
  cy.get('[data-cy="notification-badge"]').should('exist');
  cy.get('[data-cy="activity-list"] li').should('have.length.gt', 0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Waiting for every parallel request on page load introduces tight coupling between the test and the implementation's network topology. If the backend later merges three endpoints into one, all tests using `waitForDashboardLoad()` fail until updated. A lighter alternative — `cy.get('[data-cy="dashboard-loaded"]').should('exist')` on an element that only renders after all data is fetched — decouples the test from network structure at the cost of relying on the implementation to set that rendered state correctly. [official]

---

### 518. `cy.intercept()` GraphQL Operation Name Matching for Mutation vs. Query Aliasing  [official]

GraphQL sends all operations to a single endpoint (e.g., `POST /graphql`), making URL-based aliasing insufficient. Matching on `req.body.operationName` inside the interceptor handler enables separate aliases for queries and mutations, allowing selective `cy.wait()` calls that target only the operation under test.

```typescript
// cypress/support/graphql.ts
type GqlAlias = { operationName: string; alias: string };

export function interceptGql(operations: GqlAlias[]): void {
  cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql', (req) => {
    const op = req.body?.operationName as string | undefined;
    const match = operations.find((o) => o.operationName === op);
    if (match) req.alias = match.alias;
  });
}

// cypress/e2e/product-edit.cy.ts
describe('product edit flow', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    interceptGql([
      { operationName: 'GetProduct',    alias: 'getProduct' },
      { operationName: 'UpdateProduct', alias: 'updateProduct' },
    ]);
    cy.visit('/products/42/edit');
    cy.wait('@getProduct');
  });

  it('saves changes and shows success toast', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-name"]').clear().type('Revised Name');
    cy.get('[data-cy="save-btn"]').click();
    cy.wait('@updateProduct')
      .its('request.body.variables.input.name')
      .should('eq', 'Revised Name');
    cy.get('[data-cy="toast"]').should('contain', 'Saved');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Setting `req.alias` inside the interceptor callback is the only way to alias dynamically-matched requests; calling `.as()` on the `cy.intercept()` chain creates a single alias that resolves on the first matching request regardless of operation name. The dynamic approach requires that the backend includes `operationName` in every POST body — persisted query clients that send only a hash do not set `operationName`, so this pattern needs a separate hash-to-name mapping or a different matching strategy. [official]

---

### 519. `cy.request()` Chained Response Extraction with `.its()` for Typed API Assertions  [official]

`cy.request()` returns a Chainable that wraps the response object. Chaining `.its('body')`, `.its('status')`, or `.its('headers')` directly off `cy.request()` avoids `.then()` callback nesting while keeping assertions retry-able and type-safe when combined with TypeScript generics.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/user-api.cy.ts
interface UserApiResponse {
  id: number;
  email: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'user' | 'viewer';
  createdAt: string;
}

describe('User API contract', () => {
  const userId = 42;

  it('returns correct user shape for GET /api/users/:id', () => {
    cy.request<UserApiResponse>('GET', `/api/users/${userId}`)
      .its('status')
      .should('eq', 200);

    cy.request<UserApiResponse>('GET', `/api/users/${userId}`)
      .its('body')
      .should((body) => {
        expect(body.id).to.eq(userId);
        expect(body.email).to.match(/^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$/);
        expect(['admin', 'user', 'viewer']).to.include(body.role);
        expect(body.createdAt).to.match(/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T/);
      });
  });

  it('returns 404 for non-existent user', () => {
    cy.request({ url: '/api/users/999999', failOnStatusCode: false })
      .its('status')
      .should('eq', 404);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Calling `cy.request()` twice to assert status and body separately is slightly less efficient than one `.then()` with both assertions, but it produces cleaner failure messages — the Cypress command log shows which assertion failed (status vs. body shape) rather than a generic callback error. If minimising HTTP calls is critical (e.g., rate-limited APIs), combine both assertions in a single `.should(callback)` off `.its('body')` after assigning an alias. [official]

---

### 520. `cy.intercept()` `req.continue()` Callback for Real-Response Assertion and Partial Stubbing  [official]

`req.continue((res) => { … })` sends the request to the real server and intercepts the response before it reaches the browser. This enables asserting on real API responses or selectively overriding only part of the response (e.g., injecting a specific field) without fully stubbing the endpoint.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/feature-flags.cy.ts
describe('Feature flag injection via partial response override', () => {
  it('renders beta UI when feature flag is forced on', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/feature-flags', (req) => {
      req.continue((res) => {
        // Modify only the flags field; keep the rest of the real response
        res.body = {
          ...res.body,
          flags: { ...res.body.flags, betaDashboard: true },
        };
      });
    }).as('featureFlags');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.wait('@featureFlags');
    cy.get('[data-cy="beta-banner"]').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('confirms API returns valid flag schema in production', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/feature-flags', (req) => {
      req.continue((res) => {
        // Assert on real response — no modification
        expect(res.statusCode).to.eq(200);
        expect(res.body).to.have.property('flags');
        expect(res.body.flags).to.be.an('object');
      });
    }).as('realFlags');

    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.wait('@realFlags');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Partial stubbing via `req.continue()` requires a live backend, meaning these tests are hybrid integration tests rather than pure unit tests. They are slower and more fragile in offline environments than full stubs, but they catch server-side schema changes that a full stub would never reveal. Use a tagging strategy (e.g., `@needs-backend`) to segregate these tests from pure unit suites in CI. [official]

---

### 521. `Cypress.Commands.overwrite()` for Logging-Aware `cy.visit()` Wrapper  [official]

`Cypress.Commands.overwrite()` replaces a built-in Cypress command while keeping the original available via the `originalFn` argument. Wrapping `cy.visit()` enables injecting cross-cutting concerns — such as performance timing, accessibility checks, or auth token injection — on every navigation without modifying individual tests.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands/visit-override.ts
declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface Chainable {
      visit(url: string, options?: Partial<Cypress.VisitOptions>): Chainable<Window>;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.overwrite(
  'visit',
  (originalFn, url: string, options?: Partial<Cypress.VisitOptions>) => {
    const startTime = Date.now();

    return originalFn(url, options).then((win) => {
      const navDuration = Date.now() - startTime;

      // Log navigation performance to Cypress task for CI dashboards
      cy.task('logNavigation', { url, durationMs: navDuration }, { log: false });

      // Assert performance budget on every navigation
      if (navDuration > 10_000) {
        Cypress.log({
          name: 'PERF WARNING',
          message: `Navigation to ${url} took ${navDuration}ms (budget: 10s)`,
          consoleProps: () => ({ url, navDuration }),
        });
      }
      return cy.wrap(win);
    });
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Overwriting built-in commands makes the test suite behaviour opaque — a developer unfamiliar with the project will not know that `cy.visit()` does extra work unless the override is prominently documented. Prefer explicit helper functions (e.g., `cy.visitWithPerf()`) for optional cross-cutting concerns, and reserve `overwrite()` for concerns that must apply universally (e.g., auth token injection that should never be accidentally omitted). [official]

---

### 522. `cy.session()` `idleTimeout` with localStorage Sentinel for Long-Running Tests  [official]

`cy.session()` validates the cached session before restoring it. A `localStorage` sentinel key — written at login and checked in `validate()` — avoids a full `cy.request()` network round-trip for session validation while still detecting expired tokens. Combining this with `idleTimeout` evicts stale sessions after a configurable period.

```typescript
// cypress/support/auth.ts
const SESSION_SENTINEL_KEY = '__cypress_session_valid__';

export function loginWithSentinel(email: string): void {
  cy.session(
    ['sentinel', email],
    () => {
      cy.visit('/login');
      cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(email);
      cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type(Cypress.env('TEST_PASSWORD'));
      cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
      cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
      // Write sentinel with expiry timestamp
      cy.window().then((win) => {
        win.localStorage.setItem(
          SESSION_SENTINEL_KEY,
          String(Date.now() + 30 * 60 * 1000) // 30-minute TTL
        );
      });
    },
    {
      validate() {
        // Check sentinel expiry without a network call
        cy.window().then((win) => {
          const expiry = Number(win.localStorage.getItem(SESSION_SENTINEL_KEY) ?? '0');
          expect(Date.now()).to.be.lessThan(expiry);
        });
      },
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
    }
  );
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The localStorage sentinel is cheaper than a `/api/me` network check but is less authoritative — the server may have invalidated the session (e.g., forced logout) while the sentinel still appears valid. Use the sentinel approach when CI test suites run in under 30 minutes and server-side revocation between tests is not a concern; use the `cy.request()` validate pattern when testing security-critical flows where server-side session state must be verified. [official]

---

### 523. `cy.get()` with `.filter()` and `.not()` for Complex List Subset Assertions  [official]

`.filter(selector)` and `.not(selector)` are query commands that preserve retry-ability when applied to `cy.get()` results. Chaining them lets tests assert on a specific subset of a dynamic list without introducing `.then()` callbacks that break the retry chain.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/task-list.cy.ts
describe('task list filtering', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/tasks*').as('getTasks');
    cy.visit('/tasks');
    cy.wait('@getTasks');
  });

  it('shows only incomplete tasks in the active view', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="task-item"]')
      .filter(':not([data-completed="true"])')
      .should('have.length.gt', 0)
      .each(($el) => {
        expect($el).not.to.have.attr('data-completed', 'true');
      });
  });

  it('overdue tasks have the correct visual indicator', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="task-item"]')
      .filter('[data-overdue="true"]')
      .should('have.length.gt', 0)
      .each(($el) => {
        cy.wrap($el)
          .find('[data-cy="overdue-badge"]')
          .should('be.visible');
      });
  });

  it('completed tasks are excluded from the default view', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy="task-item"]')
      .not('[data-completed="true"]')
      .should('have.length.gt', 0);
    cy.get('[data-cy="task-item"][data-completed="true"]').should('not.exist');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `.filter()` and `.not()` are synchronous DOM queries — if the items re-render after the filter runs (e.g., a list sort triggered by a React state update), the filtered set may be stale. Wrap the entire assertion chain in `.should(callback)` if re-render races are observed. Also note that `.each()` is not retry-able; if an item inside the loop fails assertion, the test does not retry the whole chain — use a `.should('have.length', N)` assertion before `.each()` to ensure the list is stable. [official]

---

### 524. React 18 `Suspense` Boundary Handling in Component Testing with `cy.mount()`  [official]

React 18's concurrent mode and `Suspense` cause components to render a fallback during data loading, which Cypress sees as the DOM being populated immediately. Without a wrapper that provides the data context (mock QueryClient, etc.), `cy.mount()` may assert on the fallback UI rather than the loaded state.

```typescript
// cypress/support/component-mounts/suspense-mount.tsx
import React, { Suspense } from 'react';
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { mount } from 'cypress/react';

const testQueryClient = new QueryClient({
  defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false, gcTime: 0 } },
});

export function mountWithSuspense(component: React.ReactNode): ReturnType<typeof mount> {
  return mount(
    <QueryClientProvider client={testQueryClient}>
      <Suspense fallback={<div data-cy="loading-spinner">Loading…</div>}>
        {component}
      </Suspense>
    </QueryClientProvider>
  );
}

// cypress/component/ProductCard.cy.tsx
import { mountWithSuspense } from '../support/component-mounts/suspense-mount';
import { ProductCard } from '../../src/components/ProductCard';

it('renders product details after suspend resolves', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products/1', { fixture: 'product.json' }).as('product');
  mountWithSuspense(<ProductCard productId={1} />);

  // Wait for fallback to disappear — confirms Suspense resolved
  cy.get('[data-cy="loading-spinner"]').should('not.exist');
  cy.get('[data-cy="product-title"]').should('be.visible');
  cy.get('[data-cy="product-price"]').should('match', /^\$[\d,.]+$/);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `testQueryClient` must have `gcTime: 0` to prevent cached results from one test leaking into the next; without this, the second test may receive stale data and skip the Suspense loading phase entirely, masking bugs in the loading state UI. Also note that React 19 Server Components cannot be mounted in Cypress Component Testing — they require an E2E test against a real server. [official]

---

### 525. `cy.clock()` Deterministic Date Testing with `new Date()` Constructor Stub  [official]

`cy.clock()` freezes `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `requestAnimationFrame` to a fixed timestamp. Passing a Unix timestamp to `cy.clock()` controls the initial "now" value, enabling tests that exercise date-relative UI (e.g., "expires in 3 days") without manipulating real system time.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/subscription-expiry.cy.ts
describe('subscription expiry display', () => {
  const FIXED_NOW = new Date('2026-06-01T12:00:00.000Z').getTime();
  const THREE_DAYS_LATER = new Date('2026-06-04T12:00:00.000Z').toISOString();

  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.clock(FIXED_NOW); // freeze time at 2026-06-01T12:00:00Z
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    cy.clock().invoke('restore'); // always restore — prevents leaking frozen clock into next test
  });

  it('shows "3 days remaining" when subscription expires in 72h', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/subscription', {
      body: { expiresAt: THREE_DAYS_LATER, plan: 'pro' },
    }).as('sub');

    cy.visit('/account/subscription');
    cy.wait('@sub');
    cy.get('[data-cy="expiry-badge"]').should('contain', '3 days remaining');
  });

  it('shows urgent banner when subscription expires in under 24h', () => {
    const soonExpiry = new Date('2026-06-02T00:00:00.000Z').toISOString(); // ~12h later
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/subscription', {
      body: { expiresAt: soonExpiry, plan: 'pro' },
    }).as('sub');

    cy.visit('/account/subscription');
    cy.wait('@sub');
    cy.get('[data-cy="urgent-expiry-banner"]').should('be.visible');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.clock()` does not stub `performance.now()` — frameworks that use `performance.now()` for animation timers or throttling (e.g., React's scheduler in development mode) will continue to advance on real time. This can cause subtle timing differences between clocked tests and production. Additionally, `cy.clock().invoke('restore')` in `afterEach()` is required even if the test passes — an unrestored clock from one spec leaks into subsequent specs in the same browser session. [official]

---

### 526. `data-cy` Attribute Selector Strategy with Custom `selectors.ts` Registry  [official]

Centralising `data-cy` selectors in a typed TypeScript registry file eliminates typo-induced test failures, enables IDE autocomplete, and provides a single location for selector updates when the DOM changes. This is an extension of the Cypress best practice of using `data-*` attributes over CSS class or ID selectors.

```typescript
// cypress/support/selectors.ts
export const Sel = {
  // Auth
  loginEmail:     '[data-cy="email-input"]',
  loginPassword:  '[data-cy="password-input"]',
  loginSubmit:    '[data-cy="login-submit"]',
  // Dashboard
  dashboardTitle: '[data-cy="dashboard-title"]',
  notifBadge:     '[data-cy="notification-badge"]',
  // Products
  productList:    '[data-cy="product-list"]',
  productItem:    '[data-cy="product-item"]',
  productPrice:   '[data-cy="product-price"]',
  // Forms
  formError:      '[data-cy="field-error"]',
  formSuccess:    '[data-cy="form-success-banner"]',
} as const;

type SelKey = keyof typeof Sel;
export const sel = (key: SelKey): string => Sel[key];

// cypress/e2e/login.cy.ts
import { Sel } from '../support/selectors';

it('logs in successfully', () => {
  cy.visit('/login');
  cy.get(Sel.loginEmail).type('user@example.com');
  cy.get(Sel.loginPassword).type('password');
  cy.get(Sel.loginSubmit).click();
  cy.get(Sel.dashboardTitle).should('be.visible');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** A `selectors.ts` registry requires discipline from both test authors and developers — whenever a `data-cy` attribute is renamed in the application source, it must also be updated in the registry. Without a CI lint rule that cross-references `data-cy` values in source HTML/JSX against the registry, the registry can drift out of sync silently. Consider adding a simple Node.js script to `package.json` scripts that greps all `data-cy` values from `src/` and asserts they exist in `selectors.ts`. [community]

---

### 527. `cy.intercept()` Route Matching Priority with `middleware: true` for Global Header Injection  [official]

Routes registered with `{ middleware: true }` run before all other matching interceptors regardless of registration order. This is the correct mechanism for injecting global request headers (e.g., a tracing correlation ID) that must appear on every outbound request, without fighting the reverse-registration-order rule that governs non-middleware interceptors.

```typescript
// cypress/support/intercept-headers.ts
export function injectCorrelationId(testId: string): void {
  cy.intercept(
    { url: '/api/**', middleware: true },
    (req) => {
      req.headers['x-test-correlation-id'] = testId;
      req.headers['x-cypress-run'] = 'true';
      // Do NOT call req.continue() from middleware handlers —
      // control flows to the next handler automatically
    }
  );
}

// cypress/e2e/tracing.cy.ts
describe('API request tracing', () => {
  const testId = `cy-${Cypress.currentTest.titlePath.join('-').replace(/\s+/g, '-')}`;

  beforeEach(() => {
    injectCorrelationId(testId);
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/users').as('getUsers');
  });

  it('sends correlation ID on every API call', () => {
    cy.visit('/users');
    cy.wait('@getUsers')
      .its('request.headers.x-test-correlation-id')
      .should('eq', testId);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Middleware interceptors cannot call `req.reply()` to stub responses — they are designed purely for request modification and must not terminate the request chain. Attempting to stub from a middleware handler causes `req.reply()` to be silently ignored. If you need both global header injection and conditional response stubbing, register one `middleware: true` interceptor for headers and a separate standard interceptor (without middleware) for stubbing. [official]

### 528. `Cypress.config()` Runtime Override for Per-Test Viewport Breakpoint Testing  [official]

`Cypress.config('viewportWidth', N)` and `Cypress.config('viewportHeight', N)` change the active viewport dimensions synchronously at any point inside a test. This enables testing responsive breakpoints within a single spec file without `cy.viewport()` command overhead or per-suite `cypress.config.ts` changes.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/responsive-nav.cy.ts
const BREAKPOINTS = [
  { label: 'mobile',  width: 375,  height: 812 },
  { label: 'tablet',  width: 768,  height: 1024 },
  { label: 'desktop', width: 1440, height: 900  },
] as const;

describe('Responsive navigation', () => {
  BREAKPOINTS.forEach(({ label, width, height }) => {
    describe(`${label} (${width}×${height})`, () => {
      beforeEach(() => {
        cy.viewport(width, height); // preferred — queued as a Cypress command
        cy.visit('/');
      });

      if (width < 768) {
        it('shows hamburger menu on mobile', () => {
          cy.get('[data-cy="hamburger-btn"]').should('be.visible');
          cy.get('[data-cy="desktop-nav"]').should('not.be.visible');
        });
      } else {
        it('shows full navigation bar on wider viewports', () => {
          cy.get('[data-cy="desktop-nav"]').should('be.visible');
          cy.get('[data-cy="hamburger-btn"]').should('not.exist');
        });
      }
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.viewport()` is the preferred approach over `Cypress.config('viewportWidth')` — `cy.viewport()` is queued in the command chain, ensuring the browser resizes before the next command executes, whereas `Cypress.config()` applied synchronously outside the command queue can race with the browser layout engine. Use `cy.viewport()` inside tests and `Cypress.config()` only for non-visual configuration changes (e.g., adjusting `defaultCommandTimeout` for a known-slow step). [official]

---

### 529. `cy.task()` with AbortController for Timeout-Guarded Node.js Operations  [official]

`cy.task()` runs in the Node.js process and blocks the test until the task resolves or rejects. Without a timeout guard inside the task handler, a hung database query or external API call will cause the test to wait until `taskTimeout` (default 60 s) and then fail with a generic timeout error rather than the actual underlying cause.

```typescript
// cypress/plugins/tasks/db-seed.ts
import { Pool } from 'pg';

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL });

export async function seedUserTask(
  userData: { email: string; role: string },
  timeoutMs = 10_000
): Promise<{ userId: number }> {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs);

  try {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
      const result = await client.query<{ id: number }>(
        'INSERT INTO users (email, role) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id',
        [userData.email, userData.role]
      );
      return { userId: result.rows[0].id };
    } finally {
      client.release();
    }
  } catch (err) {
    if ((err as Error).name === 'AbortError') {
      throw new Error(`seedUserTask timed out after ${timeoutMs}ms`);
    }
    throw err;
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

// cypress.config.ts (inside setupNodeEvents)
// on('task', { seedUser: (data) => seedUserTask(data) });

// cypress/e2e/user-management.cy.ts
it('admin can see newly seeded user', () => {
  cy.task('seedUser', { email: 'seed@example.com', role: 'user' })
    .then(({ userId }: { userId: number }) => {
      cy.visit(`/admin/users/${userId}`);
      cy.get('[data-cy="user-email"]').should('contain', 'seed@example.com');
    });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.task()` must return a JSON-serialisable value — Promises that resolve with class instances, functions, or circular references will throw a serialisation error. The `AbortController` pattern provides internal timeout control within the task, but Cypress's `taskTimeout` config is still the outer guard. Set `taskTimeout` to a value slightly higher than the internal timeout (e.g., `taskTimeout: 15_000` if the internal timeout is `10_000`) so the more descriptive internal error message surfaces rather than the generic Cypress timeout message. [official]

---

### 530. `cypress.config.ts` `specPattern` Array for Tiered Test Execution  [official]

The `specPattern` option accepts an array of glob strings as well as a single glob. This enables CI pipelines to select a named subset of tests by overriding `specPattern` via `--config` without maintaining separate config files for smoke, regression, and full-suite tiers.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
    // Default: run all E2E specs
    specPattern: 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.{ts,tsx}',

    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      // CI tier override — passed as CYPRESS_TEST_TIER env variable
      const tier = config.env['TEST_TIER'] as string | undefined;

      if (tier === 'smoke') {
        config.specPattern = 'cypress/e2e/**/*.smoke.cy.{ts,tsx}';
      } else if (tier === 'regression') {
        config.specPattern = [
          'cypress/e2e/**/*.smoke.cy.{ts,tsx}',
          'cypress/e2e/**/*.regression.cy.{ts,tsx}',
        ];
      }
      // 'full' or undefined → use the default pattern above

      return config;
    },
  },
});

// CI usage:
// Smoke: cypress run --env TEST_TIER=smoke
// Regression: cypress run --env TEST_TIER=regression
// Full suite: cypress run
```

**Tradeoff.** Encoding tier logic in `setupNodeEvents` keeps all config in one file but makes the tier selection invisible to developers who only look at `cypress.config.ts` without reading `setupNodeEvents`. A self-documenting alternative is maintaining three config files (`cypress.smoke.config.ts`, `cypress.regression.config.ts`) and selecting via `--config-file`. The single-file approach is better for teams that actively manage `specPattern` arrays; the multi-file approach is better for teams that want each CI job's config to be independently auditable without following conditional logic. [official]
