## Community Gotchas — Cycle 51

341. **`cy.wait(['@alias1', '@alias2'])` array syntax waits for exactly one occurrence of each alias — if the application fires the same request twice (e.g., a component that fetches on mount and on prop change), the array wait resolves after the first request per alias and the test asserts on potentially incomplete data, causing intermittent failures when the second request overwrites the first response in the application state** [community] — A developer intercepts `GET /api/cart` as `@getCart` and uses `cy.wait(['@getCart', '@getUser'])`, not realising that the cart component fires two `GET /api/cart` requests: one on mount and one after the user profile loads. The `cy.wait()` resolves after the first `@getCart` request while the second is still in-flight; the test immediately asserts on the cart total and sometimes sees a stale intermediate value. WHY: `cy.wait('@alias')` resolves on the next un-awaited occurrence of that alias; the array form resolves each alias once, so the second occurrence of `@getCart` is never waited on. Fix: alias the second request separately (`@getCart2`) or call `cy.wait('@getCart')` twice sequentially, which waits for the second occurrence on the second call.

342. **`cy.intercept()` with a `RegExp` URL matcher silently matches against the full URL including query string and hash — a pattern like `/\/api\/users/` that a developer expects to match only the path will also match URLs such as `/api/search?q=users` or `/api/accounts?ref=api/users`, leading to unintended intercepts of unrelated requests that happen to contain the matched substring in their query parameters** [community] — A developer registers `cy.intercept(/\/api\/users/, { fixture: 'users.json' }).as('getUsers')` to stub only `GET /api/users` and `GET /api/users/42`. A background analytics call to `/api/events?page=%2Fapi%2Fusers%2F42` also matches the regex because the encoded URL path appears in the query string. The analytics call gets stubbed with the users fixture, the analytics endpoint returns unexpected data, and the application throws a JSON parse error that appears unrelated to the intercept. WHY: Cypress passes the full URL string (including query parameters) to `RegExp.test()`. Path-only matching requires anchoring the pattern: `/^[^?#]*\/api\/users([/?#]|$)/`. Fix: use stricter regex anchors, or use the `RouteMatcher` object form (`{ pathname: /\/api\/users/ }`) which matches only against the path component.

343. **`cy.session()` `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` stores session data in the browser profile directory, which on macOS and Linux is under a temp path that is wiped between CI job runs but not between individual spec files within a single run — however, on Docker-based CI runners using the `--browser chrome --headless` flag without an explicit user-data directory, the profile is stored in a randomly generated temp directory that is unique per Cypress process instance, meaning `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` effectively has no effect when Cypress is restarted between spec batches in a parallel shard** [community] — A team using Cypress Cloud parallel execution notices that the first spec in each shard always performs a full login (3–4 seconds) even though `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` is set. Investigation reveals that each parallel worker launches a separate Cypress process, and because no persistent `--user-data-dir` is mounted, the session cache from worker 1's first spec is not visible to worker 2's first spec. WHY: `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` caches within a single browser process invocation; it does not persist across separate `cypress run` processes on different machines or containers. Fix: accept the first-spec login cost per worker, or pre-seed session cookies via `cy.task()` reading from a shared Redis/file cache written by a login API call before the Cypress run starts.

344. **`cy.get()` with a complex CSS attribute selector containing a colon (e.g., `[data-cy="http://example.com"]`) throws a `CypressError: Timed out retrying` with no mention of the selector syntax error because Cypress passes the selector string to `document.querySelector()`, which throws a `SyntaxError` that Cypress catches and converts into a timeout, making it appear as if the element does not exist rather than that the selector is malformed** [community] — A developer stores a URL in a `data-cy` attribute for a link component (`<a data-cy="https://example.com/path">`) and queries it with `cy.get('[data-cy="https://example.com/path"]')`. The `querySelector` call throws a `SyntaxError: Failed to execute 'querySelector': The provided value is not a valid selector` because the colon in `https:` is interpreted as a CSS pseudo-class delimiter. Cypress retries until timeout without surfacing the parse error. WHY: `document.querySelector()` is strict about CSS selector syntax — colons introduce pseudo-classes (`:hover`, `:nth-child()`) so a colon inside an attribute value requires CSS escape notation (`\3A`) or the attribute value must be normalised. Fix: avoid storing URLs in `data-cy` attributes; use `data-cy-url` as a separate attribute and query `[data-cy="link-component"]` to find the element, then assert `.its('attr', 'data-cy-url')`.

345. **`cy.clock()` does not automatically restore after a test that throws an uncaught exception — if the application under test throws an uncaught error that is not suppressed by `Cypress.on('uncaught:exception', () => false)`, Cypress fails the test immediately and skips the `afterEach()` hook where `cy.clock().invoke('restore')` is called, leaving the frozen clock active for all subsequent tests in the spec file, causing them to fail or behave unpredictably with dates frozen at the timestamp set by the failed test** [community] — A test freezes time at `2026-01-01` for an expiry test and expects a banner. An unrelated React error causes the test to fail before `afterEach()` runs. The next test checks a "last updated" timestamp display that uses `new Date()`, but gets `2026-01-01` because the clock was never restored. The failure appears completely unrelated to the clock, and the developer spends significant time debugging the wrong test. WHY: `afterEach()` hooks are skipped when a test fails via uncaught exception before the hook queue is reached. `cy.clock()` state is held in the browser session and is not automatically cleared between tests. Fix: register `cy.clock().invoke('restore')` in both `afterEach()` and in a `Cypress.on('test:after:run')` callback as a safety net; or use the `sinon` clock's auto-restore via `afterEach(() => { cy.clock().then((clock) => clock.restore()); })` which Cypress queues even if the test body failed.

| Pattern | Resource | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `cy.wait()` two-stage timeouts | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/wait | `requestTimeout` (5s) + `responseTimeout` (30s); override per-wait, not globally |
| `cy.wait([])` array multi-request wait | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/wait | Returns `Interception[]` in alias order; each alias consumed once — call twice for second occurrence |
| `cy.intercept()` GraphQL body matching | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/intercept | Match `req.body.operationName`; set `req.alias` dynamically inside handler |
| `cy.request()` typed assertions with `.its()` | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/request | Generic `cy.request<T>()` for typed body; chain `.its('body')` not `.then()` for retry-ability |
| `cy.intercept()` `req.continue(res)` partial stub | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/intercept | Sends to real server; modify response in callback; hybrid test — needs live backend |
| `Cypress.Commands.overwrite()` visit wrapper | https://docs.cypress.io/api/cypress-api/custom-commands | Injects cross-cutting concerns (perf, auth) on every navigation; document prominently |
| `cy.session()` localStorage sentinel | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/session | Avoids network in `validate()`; less authoritative than `cy.request()` check |
| `.filter()` / `.not()` list subset assertions | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/filter | Preserves retry-ability; chain `.should('have.length')` before `.each()` to avoid stale sets |
| React 18 Suspense + `cy.mount()` | https://docs.cypress.io/guides/component-testing/react/overview | Wrap in `QueryClientProvider`; set `gcTime: 0`; wait for spinner disappearance |
| `cy.clock()` with timestamp + restore | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/clock | Freezes `Date`/`setTimeout`/`setInterval`; does not stub `performance.now()`; always restore in `afterEach()` |
| `data-cy` selector registry pattern | https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/best-practices | `as const` TypeScript map; pair with CI lint for drift detection |
| `cy.intercept()` `middleware: true` header injection | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/intercept | Runs before all other interceptors; cannot call `req.reply()` from middleware |
| `cy.viewport()` breakpoint iteration | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/viewport | Preferred over `Cypress.config('viewportWidth')` — queued in command chain |
| `cy.task()` AbortController timeout guard | https://docs.cypress.io/api/commands/task | Internal timeout < `taskTimeout`; descriptive error surfaces before Cypress generic timeout |
| `specPattern` array + `setupNodeEvents` tier control | https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/configuration | Array glob accepted; override via `--env TEST_TIER=smoke` in CI for tiered execution |

## Cycle 52 — 2026-05-14

### 531. Accessibility Scan with `cypress-axe` + Scoped Violations Reporting  [community]

`cypress-axe` integrates Deque's axe-core engine directly into Cypress, enabling WCAG 2.1/2.2 automated scans on any rendered state. Scoping the scan to a specific container and logging structured violation details makes CI output actionable without drowning in false-positive noise from third-party widgets.

```typescript
// cypress/support/a11y.ts
import 'cypress-axe';

export interface ViolationRow {
  id: string;
  impact: string | null;
  description: string;
  nodes: number;
}

export function checkPageA11y(
  context: string | Element = 'main',
  runOnly?: { type: 'tag'; values: string[] }
): void {
  cy.injectAxe();
  cy.checkA11y(
    context,
    { runOnly },
    (violations) => {
      const rows: ViolationRow[] = violations.map((v) => ({
        id: v.id,
        impact: v.impact ?? null,
        description: v.description,
        nodes: v.nodes.length,
      }));
      // Print table to Cypress Command Log so failures are readable in CI
      cy.task('logA11yViolations', rows);
    },
    true // skip failures — let task control test outcome
  );
  cy.get('@a11yViolations').should('have.length', 0);
}

// Usage in spec:
it('homepage meets WCAG 2.1 AA', () => {
  cy.visit('/');
  checkPageA11y('body', { type: 'tag', values: ['wcag2aa'] });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cypress-axe` catches structural issues (missing alt text, poor contrast, missing labels) but cannot verify focus management, reading order, or screen-reader announcements — those require manual testing or a dedicated AT tool. Scoping to `main` avoids third-party cookie banners generating irrelevant violations, but risks missing header/nav issues; run with `body` scope at least once per release. [community]

---

### 532. `cy.intercept()` `RouteMatcher` Object Form for Precise Path-Only Matching  [official]

The `RouteMatcher` object form separates URL components (pathname, query, hostname) so each is matched independently. Using `{ pathname: /\/api\/users/ }` avoids the full-URL regex trap where query strings and hashes match unintentionally.

```typescript
// Fragile: regex matches full URL including query string
// cy.intercept(/\/api\/users/, handler) — accidentally matches /api/events?ref=api/users

// Safe: RouteMatcher scopes regex to path component only
cy.intercept(
  {
    method: 'GET',
    pathname: /^\/api\/users(\/\d+)?$/,  // matches /api/users and /api/users/42 only
    // optionally add hostname: 'api.example.com' for strict domain scoping
  },
  { fixture: 'users.json' }
).as('getUsers');

// Matching by query parameter value independently:
cy.intercept(
  {
    method: 'GET',
    pathname: '/api/search',
    query: { type: 'user' },             // only matches ?type=user, not ?type=product
  },
  { fixture: 'search-users.json' }
).as('searchUsers');

cy.visit('/users');
cy.wait('@getUsers').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 200);
cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('alice');
cy.wait('@searchUsers').its('request.query.q').should('eq', 'alice');
```

**Tradeoff.** The `RouteMatcher` object form is more verbose than a URL string or regex but dramatically reduces false-positive intercepts. Prefer it whenever your glob/regex could match more than one distinct API resource. The `query` field performs a subset match — extra parameters in the actual request are allowed; only the specified keys must match. [official]

---

### 533. Keyboard Focus Trap Testing with `cy.press('Tab')` + `:focus` Assertion  [official]

Modal dialogs and off-canvas menus must trap keyboard focus so `Tab` cycles within the component. `cy.press('Tab')` dispatches a real native Tab event via WebDriver BiDi (Chromium 115+ / Firefox 135+), allowing deterministic focus-trap verification without `cy.type('{tab}')` workarounds.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/modal-focus-trap.cy.ts
describe('Dialog focus trap', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.visit('/');
    cy.get('[data-cy="open-dialog-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('[role="dialog"]').should('be.visible');
  });

  it('traps Tab focus within the dialog', () => {
    const focusableSelector = '[role="dialog"] :is(button, a, input, select, textarea, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"]))';

    // Collect all expected focusable elements in DOM order
    cy.get(focusableSelector).then(($els) => {
      const count = $els.length;

      // Tab through entire cycle once — should stay inside dialog
      for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        cy.press('Tab');
        cy.focused().closest('[role="dialog"]').should('exist');
      }

      // One more Tab — should wrap back to first focusable element
      cy.press('Tab');
      cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'dialog-close-btn');
    });
  });

  it('closes on Escape and returns focus to trigger', () => {
    cy.press('Escape');
    cy.get('[role="dialog"]').should('not.exist');
    cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'open-dialog-btn');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.press()` requires an active browser window — tests must run in `--headed` mode or a real browser (not `--headless old` Chrome). In Firefox, BiDi must be explicitly enabled (`firefoxBiDi: true` in config). The `cy.press()` command yields `null`, so do not chain further `cy` commands off its return value; always start a new `cy.focused()` chain. [official]

---

### 534. `cy.intercept()` WebSocket Stub with `cy.intercept('websocket', ...)` Pattern  [official]

Cypress intercepts WebSocket upgrade requests using the same `cy.intercept()` API, enabling you to spy on socket handshakes and inject message handlers without a live server. This validates real-time features (live feeds, notifications) in isolation.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/live-notifications.cy.ts
it('displays incoming notification from WebSocket', () => {
  // Intercept WS upgrade and inject a mock message handler
  cy.intercept('GET', '/ws/notifications', (req) => {
    // Upgrade to WebSocket and inject a message after 200ms
    req.on('websocket', (event) => {
      event.on('open', () => {
        event.send(JSON.stringify({
          type: 'notification',
          payload: { id: 'n1', message: 'Your order has shipped' },
        }), 200); // 200ms delay
      });
    });
  }).as('wsNotifications');

  cy.visit('/dashboard');
  cy.wait('@wsNotifications');

  // Assert the notification renders
  cy.get('[data-cy="notification-banner"]')
    .should('be.visible')
    .and('contain.text', 'Your order has shipped');

  // Dismiss and confirm the badge count decrements
  cy.get('[data-cy="dismiss-notification"]').click();
  cy.get('[data-cy="notification-count"]').should('have.text', '0');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** WebSocket interception requires Cypress 12+ and is limited to HTTP-upgrade WebSockets; native TCP WebSockets are not interceptable. The `event.send()` callback API is not yet fully type-safe in `@types/cypress` — cast `event` as `any` or add a declaration merging shim if TypeScript complains. Stub only the message payload; do not try to stub the handshake headers unless you specifically need to test rejection flows. [official]

---

### 535. `.should(callbackFn)` as a Retry-able Multi-Property DOM Assertion  [official]

Placing multiple assertions inside a `.should(callbackFn)` makes the entire callback retry as a unit. This is the correct pattern for asserting on multiple related properties of the same element — unlike chained `.and()`, the callback captures a single DOM snapshot per retry cycle.

```typescript
// Anti-pattern: separate chains read DOM at different retry cycles
// cy.get('[data-cy="price"]').should('be.visible');
// cy.get('[data-cy="price"]').should('have.text', '$42.00');  // separate query, separate retry

// Correct: callback retries until ALL conditions pass simultaneously
cy.get('[data-cy="price-display"]').should(($el) => {
  // All three assertions evaluated in one atomic retry cycle
  expect($el).to.be.visible;
  expect($el).to.have.attr('data-currency', 'USD');
  expect($el.text().trim()).to.match(/^\$\d+\.\d{2}$/);
});

// Compound table assertion — retries until all rows match expected data
cy.get('[data-cy="results-table"] tbody tr').should(($rows) => {
  expect($rows).to.have.length(3);
  expect($rows.eq(0).find('[data-cy="row-status"]')).to.have.text('Active');
  expect($rows.eq(1).find('[data-cy="row-status"]')).to.have.text('Pending');
  expect($rows.eq(2).find('[data-cy="row-status"]')).to.have.text('Inactive');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The callback form runs the entire function synchronously on each retry — avoid `cy` commands inside the callback (they will be queued but won't cause the outer assertion to re-run). Use only synchronous Chai assertions (`expect`) or jQuery property reads inside `.should(fn)`. For async verification, use `.then()` instead and accept that it does not retry. [official]

---

### 536. `Cypress.Commands.overwrite()` for Universal `cy.visit()` Performance Instrumentation  [official]

Overwriting `cy.visit()` lets you inject cross-cutting concerns — performance timing capture, auth header injection, or analytics suppression — on every navigation without modifying individual tests. Combined with `cy.task()`, timing data flows to a Node process for aggregation.

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands/visit-perf.ts
Cypress.Commands.overwrite('visit', (originalFn, url, options) => {
  const start = Date.now();

  return originalFn(url, options).then((win) => {
    const lcp = win.performance
      .getEntriesByType('largest-contentful-paint')
      .at(-1) as PerformanceEntry | undefined;

    if (lcp) {
      cy.task('recordPerfMark', {
        url,
        lcpMs: Math.round(lcp.startTime),
        totalMs: Date.now() - start,
        specFile: Cypress.spec.relative,
      }, { log: false });
    }

    // Suppress third-party analytics to prevent network noise in tests
    win.eval('window.__ANALYTICS_DISABLED__ = true;');

    return win;
  });
});

// cypress/plugins/perf-reporter.ts (in setupNodeEvents)
on('task', {
  recordPerfMark(data: { url: string; lcpMs: number; totalMs: number; specFile: string }) {
    perfMarks.push(data);
    return null; // must return null, not undefined
  },
  getPerfReport() {
    return perfMarks;
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `Cypress.Commands.overwrite()` applies globally to all tests in the run — if a test intentionally wants a bare visit without instrumentation, there is no built-in opt-out mechanism. Workaround: check for a `noInstrumentation` option in the overwrite function and pass it through. Avoid throwing inside the overwrite body; uncaught errors in the overwrite surface as cryptic `cy.visit()` failures rather than instrumentation errors. [official]

---

### 537. `cy.request()` GraphQL Typed Helper with `operationName` and Variable Typing  [official]

Using `cy.request()` for GraphQL API seeding is faster than UI-driven setup because it bypasses the browser rendering stack entirely. A typed helper function makes operation names and variables compile-time safe and prevents mismatched fixture data.

```typescript
// cypress/support/graphql.ts
interface GqlResponse<T> {
  data: T;
  errors?: { message: string }[];
}

function gql<TData, TVars = Record<string, unknown>>(
  operationName: string,
  query: string,
  variables?: TVars
): Cypress.Chainable<GqlResponse<TData>> {
  return cy.request<GqlResponse<TData>>({
    method: 'POST',
    url: '/graphql',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      Authorization: `Bearer ${Cypress.env('API_TOKEN')}`,
    },
    body: { operationName, query, variables },
    log: false,
  }).its('body');
}

// Usage — fully typed, no string-guessing
interface CreateUserData {
  createUser: { id: string; email: string; role: string };
}

interface CreateUserVars {
  email: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'user';
}

cy.then(() =>
  gql<CreateUserData, CreateUserVars>(
    'CreateUser',
    `mutation CreateUser($email: String!, $role: Role!) {
       createUser(email: $email, role: $role) { id email role }
     }`,
    { email: 'test@example.com', role: 'admin' }
  ).its('data.createUser.id').as('newUserId')
);
```

**Tradeoff.** The `cy.request()` GraphQL helper bypasses the browser's cookie jar — if your GraphQL endpoint requires session cookies rather than a token, use `cy.session()` first and omit the explicit `Authorization` header so the browser automatically sends cookies. For mutations that have side effects (creating records), add an `afterEach` cleanup that calls a deletion mutation to keep test data isolated. [official]

---

### 538. `cy.task()` with a Typed Task Registry Pattern and Null Return Enforcement  [official]

Defining a task registry as a TypeScript interface and asserting returns via a plugin enforcer makes the `cypress/plugins` layer type-safe. The pattern also centralises the `null` vs `undefined` gotcha — every task is required to explicitly return `null` rather than `void`.

```typescript
// cypress/plugins/task-registry.ts
export interface TaskMap {
  seedDatabase: (opts: { fixture: string; truncate: boolean }) => Promise<null>;
  clearDatabase: (tableName: string) => Promise<null>;
  readFile: (path: string) => Promise<string>;
  logA11yViolations: (rows: { id: string; impact: string | null; nodes: number }[]) => null;
}

// Type-enforcing wrapper used in setupNodeEvents
export function registerTasks(
  on: Cypress.PluginEvents,
  tasks: { [K in keyof TaskMap]: TaskMap[K] }
): void {
  on('task', tasks as Record<string, (arg: unknown) => unknown>);
}

// cypress/plugins/index.ts
import { registerTasks } from './task-registry';
import { seedDatabase, clearDatabase } from './db';
import * as fs from 'fs/promises';

registerTasks(on, {
  async seedDatabase({ fixture, truncate }) {
    if (truncate) await clearDatabase('*');
    await seedDatabase(fixture);
    return null; // MUST return null — not undefined, not void
  },
  async clearDatabase(tableName) {
    await clearDatabase(tableName);
    return null;
  },
  async readFile(path) {
    return fs.readFile(path, 'utf-8'); // string return OK — not null required
  },
  logA11yViolations(rows) {
    rows.forEach((r) => console.table(r));
    return null;
  },
});

// Type-safe usage in specs:
cy.task('seedDatabase', { fixture: 'users', truncate: true });
```

**Tradeoff.** The `registerTasks` wrapper enforces return types at TypeScript compile time but does not enforce them at runtime — a task that accidentally returns `undefined` will still throw a Cypress runtime error ("cy.task() must return a value"). Pair the type enforcement with an ESLint rule (`@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any`) and a `no-undefined-return` custom rule in your plugin files to catch `void` returns before CI. [official]

---

### 539. `cy.clock()` + `cy.tick()` for Debounced Input and Polling Interval Testing  [official]

Combining `cy.clock()` (which freezes `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`) with `cy.tick(ms)` lets tests advance synthetic time deterministically, collapsing a 30-second polling interval into milliseconds without `cy.wait()`.

```typescript
// cypress/e2e/auto-refresh.cy.ts
describe('Dashboard auto-refresh every 30s', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/metrics', { fixture: 'metrics-v1.json' }).as('metricsV1');
    cy.clock();          // freeze time BEFORE cy.visit() so the app's timers are controlled
    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.wait('@metricsV1'); // initial load
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    cy.clock().invoke('restore'); // always restore — even if test fails
  });

  it('auto-refreshes metrics after 30 seconds', () => {
    // Swap stub to return updated data on next call
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/metrics', { fixture: 'metrics-v2.json' }).as('metricsV2');

    // Advance synthetic time by 30 seconds — triggers the app's setInterval
    cy.tick(30_000);

    cy.wait('@metricsV2');
    cy.get('[data-cy="active-users-count"]').should('have.text', '142');
  });

  it('debounced search does not fire until 500ms after last keystroke', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/search*').as('search');
    cy.get('[data-cy="search-input"]').type('cyp');

    cy.tick(200); // within debounce window — no request yet
    cy.get('@search.all').should('have.length', 0);

    cy.tick(500); // debounce fires
    cy.wait('@search').its('request.query.q').should('eq', 'cyp');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.clock()` must be called before `cy.visit()` if you need to control timers that the application sets up during page initialisation (e.g., a `setInterval` in a React `useEffect`). Calling `cy.clock()` after `cy.visit()` only affects timers created after the clock is installed — existing intervals continue on the real clock. Note: `cy.clock()` does not control `performance.now()`, `requestAnimationFrame`, or Promises — tests depending on animation timings may still require real waits. [official]

---

### 540. `cy.origin()` Structured-Clone Limitation Workaround with `args` Primitives  [official]

`cy.origin()` serialises the `args` option via the structured-clone algorithm before passing values into the cross-origin callback. Functions, class instances, Symbols, and DOM nodes are silently dropped. The workaround is to pass only primitive-safe data and reconstruct any complex objects inside the callback.

```typescript
// BROKEN: function reference silently dropped — validator is undefined inside callback
cy.origin('https://sso.example.com', { args: { validate: myValidatorFn } }, ({ validate }) => {
  // validate is undefined — structured-clone cannot serialise functions
});

// CORRECT: pass primitive config and reconstruct logic inside the callback
const oauthConfig = {
  clientId: Cypress.env('OAUTH_CLIENT_ID') as string,
  redirectPath: '/dashboard',
  expectedScope: 'openid profile email',
};

cy.origin(
  'https://sso.example.com',
  { args: oauthConfig },
  ({ clientId, redirectPath, expectedScope }) => {
    // All values are primitives — safe to serialise
    cy.get('[name="client_id"]').should('have.value', clientId);
    cy.get('[data-cy="username"]').type(Cypress.env('SSO_USER') as string);
    cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type(Cypress.env('SSO_PASS') as string);
    cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
    cy.url().should('include', redirectPath);

    // Reconstruct any logic inline — no import()  unless experimentalOriginDependencies is on
    const scopeList = expectedScope.split(' ');
    cy.get('[data-cy="granted-scope"]').invoke('text').then((text) => {
      scopeList.forEach((scope) => expect(text).to.include(scope));
    });
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Passing large objects through `args` adds serialisation overhead on every invocation — keep `args` small (configuration primitives only) and use `Cypress.env()` inside the callback for secrets that are already available in the child context. If you need complex shared utilities, enable `experimentalOriginDependencies` and use `Cypress.require()` inside the callback to import them. [official]

---

### 541. `cy.session()` `idleTimeout` + localStorage Expiry Sentinel for Zero-Network Validation  [official]

When `cy.session()`'s `validate()` callback fires a real network request, it adds latency on every spec file boundary. Storing an expiry timestamp in `localStorage` during session setup enables a sub-millisecond validation check that avoids a round-trip while still detecting genuinely expired sessions.

```typescript
// cypress/support/auth.ts
const SESSION_KEY = 'cypress_session_expires';
const SESSION_TTL_MS = 60 * 60 * 1000; // 1 hour

export function loginWithSentinel(email: string, password: string): void {
  cy.session(
    ['sentinel', email],
    () => {
      cy.visit('/login');
      cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(email);
      cy.get('[data-cy="password"]').type(password);
      cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
      cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard');
      // Write expiry sentinel into localStorage AFTER confirming login
      cy.window().then((win) => {
        win.localStorage.setItem(SESSION_KEY, String(Date.now() + SESSION_TTL_MS));
      });
    },
    {
      validate() {
        // Zero-network check: read localStorage, fail fast if expired
        cy.window().then((win) => {
          const expiry = Number(win.localStorage.getItem(SESSION_KEY));
          expect(expiry, 'Session sentinel must be set').to.be.greaterThan(0);
          expect(expiry, 'Session must not be expired').to.be.greaterThan(Date.now());
        });
      },
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
    }
  );
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The localStorage sentinel is a best-effort check — it validates that the session was recently created, not that the server still recognises it. If the backend revokes tokens (logout from another tab, admin revocation), the sentinel will pass but the first API call will fail with 401. Use the sentinel pattern only for test accounts with long-lived tokens (CI service accounts) and fall back to a `cy.request()` validate when testing user-facing session expiry flows. [official]

---

### 542. `cy.intercept()` `req.on('before:response')` Non-Blocking Header Injection  [official]

The `req.on('before:response')` event fires after the real server responds but before the browser receives the response, enabling header modification without blocking the request. This is distinct from `req.continue(res)` which is a blocking middleware pattern.

```typescript
// Non-blocking: inject a custom header into every API response for testing
// (e.g., simulate a feature flag header returned by the CDN/edge layer)
cy.intercept({ pathname: /^\/api\// }, (req) => {
  req.on('before:response', (res) => {
    // Inject without blocking — real response arrives first, then this runs
    res.headers['x-feature-flag-rollout'] = '100';
    res.headers['x-ab-group'] = 'experiment';
  });
}).as('apiRequests');

// Blocking alternative with req.continue() — use when you need to REPLACE body
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/config', (req) => {
  req.continue((res) => {
    // Merge feature flags into the real response body
    const body = res.body as Record<string, unknown>;
    res.body = { ...body, featureFlags: { newCheckout: true, darkMode: false } };
  });
}).as('configRequest');

cy.visit('/');
cy.wait('@configRequest');
cy.get('[data-cy="new-checkout-badge"]').should('be.visible');
```

**Tradeoff.** `req.on('before:response')` is non-blocking — the handler cannot call `res.send()` or replace the body; it can only mutate existing headers. Use `req.continue((res) => { ... })` when you need to replace the response body or status code. Mixing `req.on('before:response')` and `req.continue()` on the same intercept is allowed but confusing — separate them into two `cy.intercept()` declarations, one with `middleware: true` for headers and one for body replacement. [official]

---

### 543. React Component Testing with `cy.mount()`, Suspense Boundaries, and `QueryClientProvider`  [community]

React Query (TanStack Query) components using `useQuery` or `useSuspenseQuery` require a `QueryClient` provider and often a `Suspense` boundary in the test mount wrapper. Without these, component tests throw "No QueryClient set" errors or render loading spinners that never resolve.

```typescript
// cypress/support/component.tsx
import { mount } from 'cypress/react';
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { Suspense } from 'react';

// Create a fresh QueryClient per test to avoid stale cache across specs
function createTestQueryClient(): QueryClient {
  return new QueryClient({
    defaultOptions: {
      queries: {
        retry: false,        // no retries in tests — fail immediately
        gcTime: 0,           // garbage-collect immediately — no stale cache
        staleTime: 0,        // always consider data stale in tests
      },
    },
  });
}

Cypress.Commands.add('mountWithQuery', (component, options = {}) => {
  const queryClient = createTestQueryClient();
  return mount(
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <Suspense fallback={<div data-cy="loading-spinner">Loading…</div>}>
        {component}
      </Suspense>
    </QueryClientProvider>,
    options
  );
});

// Spec usage:
it('renders user list after data loads', () => {
  cy.intercept('GET', '/api/users', { fixture: 'users.json' }).as('getUsers');
  cy.mountWithQuery(<UserListComponent />);
  // Wait for Suspense to resolve — spinner disappears
  cy.get('[data-cy="loading-spinner"]').should('not.exist');
  cy.get('[data-cy="user-row"]').should('have.length', 3);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `gcTime: 0` and `staleTime: 0` ensure every test fetches fresh data, but this means `cy.intercept()` must be registered before `cy.mountWithQuery()` — if the intercept is registered after the mount, the query fires before the route handler is in place and the test sees an unexpected network error. Always register intercepts, then mount. [community]

---

### 544. `cy.get()` with `:focus` Pseudo-Selector vs `cy.focused()` — When to Use Each  [official]

`cy.focused()` is the canonical way to assert "what element currently has focus" — it retries until an element is focused or times out. `cy.get(':focus')` also works but does not retry on its own; it returns the focused element in the current DOM snapshot without waiting.

```typescript
// cy.focused() — retries until SOMETHING is focused; preferred for post-action checks
cy.get('[data-cy="submit-btn"]').click();
cy.focused()
  .should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'confirmation-dialog-close')
  .and('be.visible');

// cy.get(':focus') — snapshot, no retry; use when you need the jQuery subject for chaining
cy.get('[data-cy="modal"]').within(() => {
  cy.get(':focus').should('have.attr', 'role', 'button');
});

// Asserting focus moves AWAY from an element after an action
cy.get('[data-cy="close-btn"]').focus();
cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'close-btn'); // confirm focus is there first
cy.get('[data-cy="close-btn"]').click();
// After click, dialog closes — focused() retries until something new is focused
cy.focused().should('have.attr', 'data-cy', 'open-dialog-btn');

// Anti-pattern: asserting absence of focus with cy.get()
// cy.get('[data-cy="submit-btn"]').should('not.be.focused')  — works but does not retry
// Prefer:
cy.get('[data-cy="submit-btn"]').should('not.have.focus'); // uses .should() retry loop
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.focused()` throws immediately if no element has focus and the timeout is reached — it does not return `null`. In tests where focus may intentionally be on `document.body` (not a specific element), check `cy.focused().should('have.prop', 'tagName', 'BODY')` rather than asserting a specific `data-cy` attribute. Mixing `cy.focused()` and `:focus` in the same test is valid but makes intent less clear; pick one style and be consistent. [official]

---

### 545. `cy.intercept()` Alias Consumed-Count Assertion with `.all` Modifier  [official]

`cy.wait('@alias')` consumes one occurrence of the intercepted request. Using `cy.get('@alias.all')` returns all recorded interceptions without consuming them, enabling post-hoc count assertions and per-request payload inspection without multiple sequential `cy.wait()` calls.

```typescript
// Scenario: a component fires multiple parallel requests on mount
cy.intercept('POST', '/api/analytics/event').as('analytics');
cy.visit('/product/42');

// Do NOT use cy.wait('@analytics') in a loop — each wait blocks for the next request
// Instead: wait for all requests to complete, then inspect the batch
cy.get('[data-cy="product-detail"]').should('be.visible'); // guard: page is loaded

// Assert total count of analytics events fired
cy.get('@analytics.all').should('have.length', 3);

// Inspect specific event payloads without consuming alias state
cy.get('@analytics.all').then((interceptions) => {
  const bodies = (interceptions as Cypress.Interception[]).map((i) => i.request.body);
  expect(bodies.some((b) => b.event === 'page_view')).to.be.true;
  expect(bodies.some((b) => b.event === 'product_impression')).to.be.true;
  expect(bodies.some((b) => b.event === 'add_to_cart_eligible')).to.be.true;
});

// Alternatively, use the positional modifier: @alias.0, @alias.1, @alias.2
cy.get('@analytics.0').its('request.body.event').should('eq', 'page_view');
cy.get('@analytics.1').its('request.body.event').should('eq', 'product_impression');
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.get('@alias.all')` does not wait for new requests — it returns whatever has been recorded at that moment. If the requests are fired asynchronously and the DOM guard (`should('be.visible')`) resolves before all requests complete, the `.all` assertion may see fewer entries than expected. The safe pattern is to first assert the count with `.should('have.length', N)` (which retries), then inspect payloads in a `.then()` callback once the length is stable. [official]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 52

346. **`cypress-axe` `checkA11y()` passes silently when `injectAxe()` is called before `cy.visit()` — the axe-core script is injected into the previous page's `window` object, and the subsequent navigation destroys that context, so `checkA11y()` finds no violations because it runs against an empty document with no DOM** [community] — A developer places `cy.injectAxe()` in `beforeEach()` before `cy.visit()`. After navigation, `cy.checkA11y()` runs without error and reports zero violations even on a page with obvious missing alt attributes. The developer ships a broken page believing it is accessible. WHY: `cy.injectAxe()` injects the axe-core JavaScript bundle into `window`; a subsequent `cy.visit()` navigates away, destroying the entire `window` context, so the injection is lost. Always call `cy.injectAxe()` after `cy.visit()`, either directly in the test or by using `cy.visit()` in `beforeEach()` followed by `cy.injectAxe()` in the same hook.

347. **`cy.press('Tab')` fires a native Tab event via WebDriver BiDi but silently falls back to a synthetic `KeyboardEvent` dispatch in browsers that do not support BiDi (Chrome < 115, `--headless old` mode, WebKit), and the synthetic event does NOT move DOM focus — resulting in a test that appears to pass focus-trap assertions because `cy.focused()` still returns the same element, not the next focusable one** [community] — A team writes focus-trap tests that pass in local headed Chrome but fail when the CI pipeline uses `cypress run --browser chrome --headless` with the legacy headless mode configured via `chromeWebSecurity: false` and an older pinned Chrome version. The Tab key appears to fire (no error), but focus does not move. WHY: only WebDriver BiDi (Chrome 115+, Firefox 135+ with `firefoxBiDi: true`) can dispatch real native input events; `--headless old` uses Chrome DevTools Protocol which does not support BiDi input simulation. Fix: ensure CI uses `--browser chrome` with Chrome 115+ and the new headless mode, or add `cy.focused().should('not.have.attr', 'data-cy', 'initial-focus-element')` as a guard to catch silent no-ops.

348. **`cy.intercept()` route handlers added inside a `cy.origin()` callback are scoped to the cross-origin page's network context and are completely invisible to the primary origin's network stack — any request made from the primary origin's JavaScript after `cy.origin()` returns will NOT be matched by routes registered inside the callback, causing spurious 404s or unintended real network calls after the cross-origin flow completes** [community] — A developer writes an OAuth test: `cy.origin('https://sso.example.com', () => { cy.intercept('/api/token', ...).as('token'); cy.get('[type=submit]').click(); cy.wait('@token'); })`. After `cy.origin()` returns, the primary app redirects and makes a `GET /api/me` call. The developer adds `cy.wait('@token')` outside `cy.origin()` expecting it to catch the primary app's token exchange, but the alias is scoped to the SSO origin — it never fires from `app.example.com`. WHY: Cypress's network layer is per-origin; `cy.intercept()` inside `cy.origin()` only intercepts requests from that origin's browsing context. Register all post-redirect intercepts outside `cy.origin()`, before calling it.

349. **`cy.task()` called with an `undefined` argument throws `Error: cy.task('myTask') failed with: the following error was thrown: Cannot convert undefined to JSON` in Cypress 14.x because the task serialisation layer uses `JSON.stringify` which converts `undefined` argument values to `null` in arrays but simply omits them at the top level — however, TypeScript types allow calling `cy.task('myTask', undefined)` without a compile error, masking the issue until runtime** [community] — A developer writes `cy.task('clearUser', userId)` where `userId` comes from `cy.get('@userId').then((id) => cy.task('clearUser', id as string))`. During a refactor, the alias is removed and `userId` is never assigned, so it is `undefined`. TypeScript does not flag this because `cy.task()`'s second argument type is `unknown`. The task receives `null` from Cypress (not `undefined`) and the Node plugin's type annotation `(id: string) => ...` does not help at runtime. WHY: `JSON.stringify` coerces top-level `undefined` to the string `"undefined"` in some Cypress serialisation paths, or simply omits it, depending on the Cypress version. Fix: add a runtime guard in every task that validates the argument is not `null`/`undefined` before using it, and add `cy.wrap(userId).should('be.a', 'string')` before calling `cy.task()`.

350. **`Cypress.Commands.overwrite('visit', ...)` causes `cy.visit()` calls inside `cy.session()` `setup()` callbacks to double-execute the overwrite's side effects — the session setup fires `cy.visit()` during initial cache-building AND the overwrite's instrumentation runs inside the session iframe context where `cy.task()` calls behave unexpectedly because the session iframe does not have full access to the primary test context's task bridge** [community] — A developer overwrites `cy.visit()` to call `cy.task('recordNavigation', url)` for analytics instrumentation. Inside a `cy.session()` setup callback, `cy.visit('/login')` fires the overwrite, which calls `cy.task('recordNavigation')`. This works on first run, but on subsequent test runs where the session is restored from cache, the setup callback does not run — the `cy.task()` call is skipped entirely and the instrumentation is incomplete. Worse, if `cy.session()` `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` is used and the session iframe is in a different security context, `cy.task()` may throw `Cannot call cy.task() in a non-test context`. WHY: `cy.session()` runs the setup callback in an isolated browsing context; some Cypress APIs that rely on the test runner bridge are not fully available. Fix: guard task calls inside overwritten commands with `if (cy.state('runnable'))` to detect non-test contexts, or skip instrumentation when `window.location.pathname` matches `/login`.

### 546. GraphQL Per-Request Dynamic Alias via Mutation/Query Discriminator  [official]

`cy.intercept()` can assign per-request aliases dynamically inside the route handler by setting `req.alias` — this is the recommended pattern for GraphQL where all operations share a single POST endpoint but must be waited on individually by operation name.

```typescript
// cypress/support/graphql.ts
export function interceptGql(): void {
  cy.intercept('POST', '/graphql', (req) => {
    // Assign alias based on GraphQL operation name
    const body = req.body as { operationName?: string; query?: string };
    if (body.operationName) {
      req.alias = `gql_${body.operationName}`;
    } else if (body.query?.includes('mutation')) {
      req.alias = 'gql_anonymous_mutation';
    }
  });
}

// In test:
interceptGql();
cy.visit('/cart');
cy.get('[data-cy="checkout-btn"]').click();
cy.wait('@gql_CreateOrder')
  .its('response.body.data.createOrder.id')
  .should('be.a', 'string');
cy.wait('@gql_GetCart')
  .its('response.body.data.cart.items')
  .should('have.length', 0);
```

**Tradeoff.** Dynamic aliases require calling `interceptGql()` before the operation fires; if the intercept is registered after the request, the alias is never set and `cy.wait()` hangs until timeout. The `operationName` field is only present in named queries — anonymous GraphQL operations need a content-based heuristic (checking `query` for `mutation` keyword), which is fragile when mutations are embedded in fragments. For consistent aliasing, enforce named operations via a lint rule (`graphql-eslint/require-operation-name`). [official]

---

### 547. `cy.intercept()` Conditional Response Override with `req.continue(res =>)`  [official]

`req.continue()` with a response callback forwards the request to the real server and intercepts the live response, allowing conditional body or status mutation without a full stub. This bridges real-server confidence and test-time control.

```typescript
// Only override when backend returns a failure status — keeps happy-path real
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/notifications', (req) => {
  req.continue((res) => {
    if (res.statusCode >= 500) {
      // Replace server error with a controlled error fixture for deterministic UI testing
      res.send({
        statusCode: 503,
        body: { error: 'Service temporarily unavailable', retryAfter: 30 },
        headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
      });
    }
    // Otherwise let the real response through untouched
  });
}).as('notifications');

cy.visit('/dashboard');
cy.wait('@notifications');
// If backend is healthy, the real response rendered; if not, our stub fires
cy.get('[data-cy="notification-bell"]').should('be.visible');
```

**Tradeoff.** `req.continue()` adds network latency because the request hits the real server; in unit-speed tests this can cause timeouts when the backend is slow or unavailable. The `res.send()` inside `req.continue()` is called synchronously in the response callback — do not call `cy.wait()` or other Cypress commands inside it. Prefer `req.reply()` (pure stub) when the test does not need a real server response at all; use `req.continue()` only for selective mutation. [official]

---

### 548. Browser Cache Bypass in `cy.intercept()` via `Cache-Control` Middleware  [official]

Requests served from the browser's HTTP cache never reach the network layer and cannot be intercepted by `cy.intercept()`. Adding a middleware intercept that sets `Cache-Control: no-store` on every matching response forces the browser to re-fetch, making subsequent intercepts reliable.

```typescript
// cypress/support/e2e.ts — install globally for all tests
before(() => {
  // Middleware intercept runs first (regardless of registration order)
  cy.intercept({ url: '/api/**', middleware: true }, (req) => {
    req.on('response', (res) => {
      res.headers['cache-control'] = 'no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate';
      res.headers['pragma'] = 'no-cache';
    });
  });
});

// In a test — this intercept is now reliably hit on every run, not just cold cache
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/products').as('products');
cy.visit('/shop');
cy.reload(); // second visit — without cache bypass this might not fire
cy.wait('@products').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 200);
```

**Tradeoff.** The middleware approach applies globally; it can mask caching bugs in the application that only appear in production (e.g., a component re-renders because a cached response is stale). Scope the middleware with a specific URL pattern if you want to test caching behaviour on some routes. The `middleware: true` handler runs on every request in the intercepted URL space, which adds minimal overhead but can accumulate in long suites with many API calls. [official]

---

### 549. `cy.intercept()` Route Matching Priority — Reverse Order Except Middleware  [official]

Routes registered with `cy.intercept()` match in reverse order (last-registered wins), except `middleware: true` routes which always execute first. This allows fine-grained per-test overrides on top of coarse global stubs without modifying the global stub.

```typescript
// Global support file — baseline stub for all tests
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/user', { fixture: 'user-standard.json' }).as('user');

// In a specific test that needs an admin user — registered AFTER the global stub
// so it takes priority (reverse order wins)
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/user', { fixture: 'user-admin.json' }).as('userAdmin');
cy.visit('/settings');
cy.wait('@userAdmin'); // the admin fixture wins because it was registered last

// Middleware intercept runs FIRST regardless of order — use for logging/mutation
cy.intercept({ url: '/api/**', middleware: true }, (req) => {
  req.headers['x-test-correlation-id'] = Cypress.currentTest.titlePath.join('|');
});
// This header will be on every /api/** request, even those matched by later stubs
```

**Tradeoff.** Reverse-order matching is counterintuitive and frequently causes stale stubs from `beforeEach` or `before` to be silently overridden by per-test intercepts — the opposite of the intended behaviour. The safest pattern is to register specific (narrow) intercepts last. Avoid mixing broad catch-all stubs in `beforeEach` with narrow per-test intercepts unless you understand the ordering implications. Document the intended precedence in a comment near global stubs. [official]

---

### 550. `cy.request()` GraphQL Typed Seed Helper with Generic Response Extraction  [official]

`cy.request()` accepts a generic type parameter for the response body, enabling type-safe API seeding and cleanup. Pairing this with a typed GraphQL wrapper eliminates repeated boilerplate and produces compile-time coverage of response shapes.

```typescript
// cypress/support/api-helpers.ts
interface GqlResponse<T> {
  data: T;
  errors?: Array<{ message: string }>;
}

interface CreateProductResult {
  createProduct: { id: string; slug: string };
}

export function gqlRequest<T>(
  query: string,
  variables: Record<string, unknown> = {}
): Cypress.Chainable<GqlResponse<T>> {
  return cy.request<GqlResponse<T>>({
    method: 'POST',
    url: '/graphql',
    body: { query, variables },
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    auth: { bearer: Cypress.env('API_TOKEN') },
  }).its('body');
}

// In test:
const CREATE_PRODUCT = `
  mutation CreateProduct($input: ProductInput!) {
    createProduct(input: $input) { id slug }
  }
`;

let productId: string;
before(() => {
  gqlRequest<CreateProductResult>(CREATE_PRODUCT, {
    input: { name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 },
  }).then((body) => {
    expect(body.errors).to.be.undefined;
    productId = body.data.createProduct.id;
  });
});

after(() => {
  cy.request('DELETE', `/api/admin/products/${productId}`);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.request()` bypasses the browser's security context (CORS, cookies, CSP), so it cannot fully validate that the browser-level auth flow works end-to-end. Use it for seeding and teardown, not for validating auth behaviour. The generic type is erased at runtime; if the server returns an unexpected shape, TypeScript will not catch it — add `body.errors` assertion as a runtime guard. [official]

---

### 551. Retry-Able `.should(callback)` for Complex Multi-Property DOM Assertions  [official]

When an assertion involves multiple computed properties on a DOM element (e.g., checking that text parses to a number within a range), wrapping the logic in `.should(callbackFn)` causes the entire callback to retry on failure, avoiding the false-pass that occurs when using `.then()` followed by `expect()` (which does not retry).

```typescript
// Anti-pattern: .then() does NOT retry — if the element renders stale text first,
// the assertion fires once and may pass with an outdated value
cy.get('[data-cy="price-display"]').then(($el) => {
  const price = parseFloat($el.text().replace('$', ''));
  expect(price).to.be.gt(0).and.be.lt(1000); // ❌ no retry
});

// Correct pattern: .should() with a callback retries the entire function
cy.get('[data-cy="price-display"]').should(($el) => {
  const price = parseFloat($el.text().replace('$', ''));
  // These synchronous expect() calls all retry as one atomic unit
  expect(price, 'price is positive').to.be.gt(0);
  expect(price, 'price is reasonable').to.be.lt(1000);
  expect($el).to.have.css('color', 'rgb(0, 128, 0)'); // green when valid
});

// For assertions spanning multiple elements, wrap the parent
cy.get('[data-cy="cart-summary"]').should(($summary) => {
  const total = parseFloat($summary.find('[data-cy="total"]').text());
  const tax = parseFloat($summary.find('[data-cy="tax"]').text());
  expect(total).to.be.closeTo(tax * 10, 0.01); // tax is ~10% of total
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Cypress commands (`cy.get()`, `cy.intercept()`, etc.) must NOT be called inside a `.should()` callback — only synchronous `expect()` / chai assertions. Calling a Cypress command inside throws `CypressError: Cypress detected that you returned a promise from a command while also invoking one or more cy commands in that promise`. If you need to perform additional queries, break the assertion into separate chained commands first, then use `.should()` on the resolved element. [official]

---

### 552. `cy.clock()` / `cy.tick()` — Install Before `cy.visit()` for Init-Time Timers  [official]

`cy.clock()` must be called before `cy.visit()` (or any navigation) to intercept timers set during page initialization. If installed after navigation, timers created during app bootstrap (e.g., session expiry countdowns, auto-refresh intervals) are not controlled and will fire at real wall-clock time.

```typescript
describe('Session expiry warning', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // MUST come before cy.visit() — controls timers set during app init
    cy.clock(Date.now());
  });

  it('shows inactivity warning after 25 minutes', () => {
    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    // App sets a 25-minute idle timer on load — cy.clock() controls it
    cy.tick(25 * 60 * 1000); // advance time by 25 minutes instantly
    cy.get('[data-cy="session-warning-modal"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="session-warning-countdown"]').should('contain', '5:00');
  });

  it('auto-logs out after 30 minutes of inactivity', () => {
    cy.visit('/dashboard');
    cy.tick(30 * 60 * 1000);
    cy.url().should('include', '/login');
    cy.get('[data-cy="logout-reason"]').should('contain', 'inactivity');
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    cy.clock().then((clock) => clock.restore());
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.clock()` controls `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `Date`, and `performance.now` (in Cypress 14+) but does NOT control `requestAnimationFrame` — animations driven by rAF will still run at real speed. In tests that combine `cy.clock()` with `cy.tick()` and animated transitions, add a `cy.get('.animation-complete')` guard rather than ticking past the animation duration. Restoring the clock in `afterEach` prevents timer state bleeding between tests. [official]

---

### 553. `cy.task()` Typed Registry Pattern with `null` Return Enforcement  [official]

`cy.task()` requires every task to return a value — returning `undefined` from a Node plugin function throws at runtime. A typed task registry pattern enforces return types at compile time and centralises all plugin-side logic, making task contracts auditable.

```typescript
// cypress/plugins/tasks.ts
export interface TaskRegistry {
  seedUser: (args: { role: 'admin' | 'user'; email: string }) => Promise<{ id: string }>;
  deleteUser: (id: string) => Promise<null>;
  getEmailInbox: (address: string) => Promise<string[]>;
  clearTestData: () => Promise<null>;
}

export function registerTasks(on: Cypress.PluginEvents): void {
  const tasks: TaskRegistry = {
    async seedUser({ role, email }) {
      const user = await db.user.create({ data: { role, email } });
      return { id: user.id }; // never return undefined
    },
    async deleteUser(id) {
      await db.user.delete({ where: { id } });
      return null; // explicit null — required by cy.task()
    },
    async getEmailInbox(address) {
      return mailhog.getMessages(address).then((msgs) => msgs.map((m) => m.subject));
    },
    async clearTestData() {
      await db.$executeRaw`TRUNCATE test_data CASCADE`;
      return null;
    },
  };
  on('task', tasks as Record<string, (arg: unknown) => unknown>);
}

// In test — TypeScript infers return type from TaskRegistry
let userId: string;
before(() => {
  cy.task('seedUser', { role: 'admin', email: 'admin@test.com' })
    .then((result) => { userId = (result as { id: string }).id; });
});
after(() => {
  cy.task('deleteUser', userId);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The TypeScript cast on `on('task', tasks)` is necessary because Cypress's `PluginEvents` types `task` as `Record<string, Function>` without generics. The compile-time safety only covers the plugin side; the test side requires a manual cast `(result as { id: string })`. Consider a thin typed wrapper around `cy.task()` using function overloads keyed by task name for end-to-end type safety. [official]

---

### 554. `cy.session()` `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` — Parallel CI Isolation Caveat  [official]

`cy.session()` with `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` persists session state across spec files, but in Cypress Cloud parallel runs each CI runner gets its own isolated session cache — sessions cannot be shared across machines. Understanding this avoids relying on sessions seeded by a spec that runs on a different machine.

```typescript
// cypress/support/auth.ts
export function loginAsAdmin(): void {
  cy.session(
    'admin-session',
    () => {
      // Use programmatic API login instead of UI — faster and more reliable
      cy.request({
        method: 'POST',
        url: '/api/auth/login',
        body: { email: Cypress.env('ADMIN_EMAIL'), password: Cypress.env('ADMIN_PASS') },
      }).then((resp) => {
        // Store JWT in localStorage so subsequent cy.visit() picks it up
        window.localStorage.setItem('auth_token', resp.body.token);
        window.localStorage.setItem('auth_expiry', String(Date.now() + 3_600_000));
      });
    },
    {
      validate() {
        // Zero-network validation: check localStorage sentinel
        cy.window()
          .its('localStorage')
          .invoke('getItem', 'auth_expiry')
          .then((expiry) => {
            expect(Number(expiry)).to.be.gt(Date.now());
          });
      },
      cacheAcrossSpecs: true,
      // NOTE: in Cloud parallel runs, each machine re-establishes its own session.
      // Do NOT write tests that assume admin setup by spec-A is available in spec-B
      // when they run on different machines.
    }
  );
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `cacheAcrossSpecs: true` is most valuable in sequential runs where multiple spec files each require auth setup — it eliminates repeated login round-trips within a single machine. In Cloud parallel runs, it offers no cross-machine benefit but still saves time within a machine's assigned spec batch. If `validate()` makes a network call, it adds latency on every spec boundary; prefer a localStorage sentinel check for zero-latency validation. [official]

---

### 555. Next.js App Router Component Testing — Server Components vs Client Components  [official]

In Cypress Component Testing with Next.js 14–16, `cy.mount()` can only render Client Components (`'use client'`) — Server Components cannot be mounted because they rely on server-side rendering infrastructure unavailable in the browser test environment. E2E tests via `cy.visit()` should cover pages that use Server Components.

```typescript
// ❌ This will fail — ServerComponent uses async data fetching (RSC)
// import ServerComponent from '../../app/components/ServerProductList';
// cy.mount(<ServerComponent />); // throws: cannot call async server component in browser

// ✅ Correct: test the Client Component that the Server Component passes data into
// app/components/ProductList.tsx (client component)
import ProductList from '../../app/components/ProductList';

describe('ProductList', () => {
  const mockProducts = [
    { id: '1', name: 'Widget', price: 9.99, inStock: true },
    { id: '2', name: 'Gadget', price: 24.99, inStock: false },
  ];

  it('renders in-stock badge for available products', () => {
    cy.mount(<ProductList products={mockProducts} onSelect={cy.stub().as('onSelect')} />);
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-1"] [data-cy="in-stock-badge"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-2"] [data-cy="in-stock-badge"]').should('not.exist');
  });

  it('calls onSelect with product id on click', () => {
    cy.mount(<ProductList products={mockProducts} onSelect={cy.stub().as('onSelect')} />);
    cy.get('[data-cy="product-1"]').click();
    cy.get('@onSelect').should('have.been.calledWith', '1');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Splitting tests across CT (client components) and E2E (pages with Server Components) adds complexity to the test strategy. The benefit is CT runs are 5–10× faster than E2E for pure UI logic. Establish a rule: use CT for components that accept props and render UI; use E2E for pages, routing, and data-fetching behaviour. `getServerSideProps` and `getStaticProps` (Next.js 13 pages router) also do not run in CT — same boundary applies. [official]

---

### 556. `Cypress.Commands.overwrite()` Safe Pattern with Opt-Out Flag  [official]

`Cypress.Commands.overwrite()` applies globally to every invocation of the overridden command. Adding an explicit opt-out option object key prevents the overwrite's side effects from running in contexts that cannot support them (e.g., inside `cy.session()` setup callbacks or fixture helpers).

```typescript
// cypress/support/commands.ts
declare global {
  namespace Cypress {
    interface VisitOptions {
      skipInstrumentation?: boolean;
    }
  }
}

Cypress.Commands.overwrite<'visit', 'default'>(
  'visit',
  (originalFn, url, options = {}) => {
    const { skipInstrumentation = false, ...restOptions } = options;

    if (!skipInstrumentation) {
      // Only record navigation when not explicitly opted out
      cy.task('recordNavigation', { url, testTitle: Cypress.currentTest.title }, { log: false });
    }

    return originalFn(url, restOptions);
  }
);

// Normal usage — instrumentation fires
cy.visit('/dashboard');

// Inside cy.session() setup — opt out to avoid task bridge issues
cy.session('admin', () => {
  cy.visit('/login', { skipInstrumentation: true }); // ✅ safe
  cy.get('[data-cy="email"]').type(Cypress.env('ADMIN_EMAIL'));
  cy.get('[data-cy="submit"]').click();
});

// Fixture helpers that don't need instrumentation
cy.visit('/api-doc', { skipInstrumentation: true });
```

**Tradeoff.** The opt-out pattern requires every developer to know about and use the `skipInstrumentation` flag, which is not enforced at compile time unless the overloaded interface is fully documented. A safer alternative is to detect the session context programmatically using `cy.state('activeSessions')` — but this relies on private Cypress state that can change between versions. The explicit opt-out flag is more brittle to forget but less fragile across upgrades. [official]

---

### 557. `cy.intercept()` Caching — Requesting the Same URL Twice Shows Stale Intercept Count  [community]

Browser HTTP cache silently serves cached responses without sending a network request, causing `cy.intercept()` alias counts to stay at 0 and `cy.wait('@alias')` to hang. The canonical fix is either injecting `Cache-Control: no-store` via a middleware intercept (Pattern 548) or disabling the cache via Chrome DevTools Protocol through Cypress configuration.

```typescript
// cypress.config.ts — disable browser cache for the entire run
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress';

export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    // Disabling the cache ensures every request reaches the network layer
    // and is interceptable by cy.intercept()
    experimentalModifyObstructiveThirdPartyCode: true,
    setupNodeEvents(on, config) {
      on('before:browser:launch', (browser, launchOptions) => {
        if (browser.family === 'chromium') {
          // Disable HTTP cache in Chrome via DevTools flag
          launchOptions.args.push('--disable-application-cache');
          launchOptions.args.push('--disable-cache');
        }
        return launchOptions;
      });
      return config;
    },
  },
});

// Alternative: per-test middleware intercept (scoped, preferred)
beforeEach(() => {
  cy.intercept({ url: '**', middleware: true }, (req) => {
    req.headers['cache-control'] = 'no-cache';
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Disabling the cache globally via launch arguments changes application behaviour from production: cache-dependent features (offline mode, stale-while-revalidate) will not be exercised. For most functional tests this is acceptable. If you need to test caching behaviour specifically, use scoped middleware intercepts that target only the routes under test rather than disabling the cache globally. [community]

---

### 558. `cy.fixture()` Encoding and Caching Consistency Across Cypress 14+  [official]

`cy.fixture()` caches loaded fixture data within a test run. Requesting the same fixture file with different `encoding` options in different tests returns the first cached version's encoding — the second call's encoding option is silently ignored. This was a documented bug fixed in Cypress 14 but can still surface in older test suites migrated forward.

```typescript
// cypress/fixtures/image.png — binary fixture

// Problematic pattern in pre-14 test suites:
it('test A — reads image as base64', () => {
  cy.fixture('image.png', 'base64').then((base64: string) => {
    expect(base64).to.be.a('string');
    // Cached with base64 encoding
  });
});

it('test B — reads same image as binary (Cypress ≤13 returns base64 instead)', () => {
  // In Cypress ≤13, the cached base64 version is returned even though 'binary' was requested
  cy.fixture('image.png', 'binary').then((data) => {
    // In Cypress 14+, this correctly returns binary; in older versions, returns base64
    expect(data).to.be.a('string'); // binary is also a string in Cypress fixture API
  });
});

// Safe pattern: use null encoding for binary data to get a Buffer (Cypress 14+)
cy.fixture('image.png', null).then((buffer: ArrayBuffer) => {
  const view = new Uint8Array(buffer);
  expect(view[0]).to.eq(137); // PNG magic byte
  cy.get('[data-cy="upload-input"]').selectFile({
    contents: Cypress.Buffer.from(buffer),
    fileName: 'test-image.png',
    mimeType: 'image/png',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `null` encoding returns an `ArrayBuffer` in Cypress 14+, which is the most reliable option for binary data that needs further processing (e.g., `selectFile`, `cy.request` body). For JSON fixtures, always omit the encoding argument (defaults to `utf-8` JSON parse). Cross-encoding fixture reuse within a single suite is a footgun — structure fixtures so each encoding variant is in a separate test or separate `it()` blocks, not in `beforeEach`/test pairs. [official]

---

### 559. `cy.get()` Timeout Override for Slow-Loading Async Components  [official]

Cypress's default `defaultCommandTimeout` (4 seconds) may be insufficient for components that perform asynchronous operations on mount (data fetching, heavy computations). Overriding timeout on a per-command basis avoids raising the global timeout and masks only the specific slow operation.

```typescript
describe('Dashboard analytics widget', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Intercept the slow analytics endpoint — add artificial delay for testing
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/analytics/weekly', (req) => {
      req.continue((res) => {
        res.delay = 2000; // simulate 2-second load
      });
    }).as('weeklyAnalytics');
    cy.visit('/dashboard');
  });

  it('renders chart after data loads', () => {
    // Without timeout override, cy.get() would timeout at 4s default
    // The explicit timeout is self-documenting: this element legitimately takes up to 10s
    cy.get('[data-cy="analytics-chart"]', { timeout: 10_000 })
      .should('be.visible');

    // Wait for the specific network request rather than using a fixed time
    cy.wait('@weeklyAnalytics')
      .its('response.statusCode')
      .should('eq', 200);

    // Post-load assertion uses default timeout — chart is already visible
    cy.get('[data-cy="chart-legend"]')
      .find('[data-cy="legend-item"]')
      .should('have.length.gte', 1);
  });

  it('shows loading skeleton during fetch', () => {
    // Assert skeleton is visible immediately — no timeout override needed
    cy.get('[data-cy="analytics-skeleton"]').should('be.visible');
    cy.wait('@weeklyAnalytics');
    cy.get('[data-cy="analytics-skeleton"]').should('not.exist');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Per-command timeout overrides are self-documenting about expected latency, but they also suppress early failure detection — a component that should load in 3s but regresses to 8s will still pass with a `{ timeout: 10_000 }`. Consider adding a performance assertion via `cy.clock()` and `Date.now()` comparisons, or using Cypress Cloud's built-in slow-test detection. Never raise `defaultCommandTimeout` globally to paper over slow components — it multiplies total suite time across all retries. [official]

---

### 560. `cy.stub()` Typed Sinon Stubs for Event Handlers and Callbacks in Component Testing  [official]

`cy.stub()` returns a typed Sinon stub that integrates with Cypress's command log and alias system. In Component Testing, using `cy.stub()` for event handler props provides assertion capabilities that anonymous arrow functions lack, including call count, argument inspection, and spy chain assertions.

```typescript
import Counter from '../../src/components/Counter';

describe('Counter component', () => {
  it('fires onChange with correct value on increment', () => {
    const onChangeSpy = cy.stub().as('onChange');
    const onResetSpy = cy.stub().as('onReset');

    cy.mount(
      <Counter
        initialValue={5}
        min={0}
        max={10}
        onChange={onChangeSpy}
        onReset={onResetSpy}
      />
    );

    cy.get('[data-cy="increment-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('@onChange')
      .should('have.been.calledOnce')
      .and('have.been.calledWith', 6);

    cy.get('[data-cy="increment-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('@onChange')
      .should('have.been.calledTwice')
      .and('have.been.calledWith', 7);

    // Verify max boundary — at max, increment button should be disabled
    // Click 3 more times to reach max of 10
    cy.get('[data-cy="increment-btn"]').click().click().click();
    cy.get('[data-cy="increment-btn"]').should('be.disabled');
    cy.get('@onChange').should('have.been.callCount', 5);

    cy.get('[data-cy="reset-btn"]').click();
    cy.get('@onReset').should('have.been.calledOnce');
    cy.get('@onChange').should('have.been.callCount', 5); // reset does not fire onChange
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `cy.stub()` in Component Testing is re-created fresh for each `cy.mount()` call, but if you call `cy.mount()` multiple times in a single test (e.g., to simulate prop changes), the same stub is reused and its call history accumulates — use `stub.reset()` or create a new stub before re-mounting. For stubs that need to return specific values, use `.returns()` or `.callsFake()` before passing them as props, not after, since React renders synchronously on mount. [official]

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 53

351. **`cy.intercept()` browser cache silently swallows requests — the intercept handler never fires and `cy.wait('@alias')` times out, but the test passes on first run because the cache is cold, creating a flaky test that only fails after a warm cache is established** [community] — A developer writes a test that intercepts `GET /api/products` and waits for the alias. On the first run (cold cache), the request fires and the alias resolves. On subsequent runs (warm cache), the browser serves the response from cache without a network request, the intercept handler never fires, and `cy.wait('@alias')` hangs for 5 seconds before failing with "Timed out retrying: cy.wait() timed out waiting for the 1st request." The developer is confused because the test "worked before." WHY: `cy.intercept()` operates at the network layer; requests served from the browser's HTTP cache bypass the network entirely and are invisible to Cypress's proxy. Fix: add a `middleware: true` intercept that injects `Cache-Control: no-store` into all API responses (Pattern 548), or set `cache-control: no-store` on the API server in the test environment.

352. **`cy.fixture()` returns incorrect encoding when the same file is requested with different `encoding` options across tests in Cypress ≤13 — the fixture cache stores only the first encoding, silently returning the cached version for all subsequent requests regardless of the encoding argument** [community] — A developer has two tests: the first reads `template.html` as `base64` for an upload test; the second reads the same file as `utf-8` to check its content. In Cypress ≤13, the second test receives the base64-encoded string instead of the raw HTML text, causing a string comparison to fail with a cryptic "expected '<base64 string>' to include '<!DOCTYPE'" error. The developer wonders why the fixture reads differently in isolation but fails in the full suite. WHY: Cypress's internal fixture cache is keyed by filename only, not by filename+encoding. Cypress 14 fixes this by keying the cache on both. Fix (pre-14): use unique fixture filenames per encoding need, or always use the same encoding for a given fixture file.

353. **`cy.task()` silently converts a top-level `undefined` return value differently across Cypress versions — in some versions it throws `"cy.task() failed with: tasks must return a non-undefined value"`, in others it hangs indefinitely, and in Cypress 15 it throws a JSON serialisation error — making cross-version task debugging extremely confusing** [community] — A developer writes a cleanup task that conditionally deletes records: `if (records.length === 0) return;` — implicitly returning `undefined`. In local Cypress 14 dev, the test passes because the early return path happens to be unreachable in local data. In CI with a clean database, the early return fires, the task returns `undefined`, and Cypress 15 throws `TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object`. The error stack points to Cypress internals, not the task file. WHY: Cypress task protocol uses structured cloning / JSON serialisation to transfer return values back to the browser; `undefined` is not a valid structured clone value. Every code path in every task must return an explicit value. Fix: replace every bare `return;` or `return undefined;` in task functions with `return null;`.

354. **`Cypress.Commands.overwrite('visit', ...)` causes tests that use `cy.visit()` inside `cy.session()` setup callbacks to have inconsistent `cy.task()` behaviour — on first session creation the task runs fine, but on session restore (cache hit) the setup callback is skipped, so any state recorded by the overwrite's `cy.task()` call is absent for tests that rely on a restored session** [community] — A developer overwrites `cy.visit()` to call `cy.task('trackPageVisit', url)` for test coverage telemetry. The admin login test calls `cy.visit('/login')` inside `cy.session()`. On the first test file, the session is cold — `cy.visit('/login')` fires, the overwrite fires, `cy.task('trackPageVisit')` records it. On the second spec file (same CI run, `cacheAcrossSpecs: true`), the session is restored from cache — the setup callback is never called, `cy.visit('/login')` never fires, and the page visit is not recorded. The telemetry count for `/login` is 1 instead of the expected N (once per spec). WHY: `cy.session()` is designed to skip the setup callback on cache hits — that is its purpose. Any side effects inside setup that your test logic depends on will be absent when the cache is hot. Fix: move side-effect-dependent logic outside `cy.session()` or use `validate()` to re-run critical side effects on every restore.

355. **`cy.get('[data-cy="el"]', { timeout: 10000 })` does NOT extend the timeout of assertions chained onto it — only the `cy.get()` query itself retries for 10 seconds; a `.should()` chain that follows uses the command's own assertion timeout which defaults to `defaultCommandTimeout` (4 seconds)** [community] — A developer writes `cy.get('[data-cy="loading-spinner"]', { timeout: 10000 }).should('not.exist')` to wait up to 10 seconds for a loading spinner to disappear. The spinner disappears after 7 seconds. The developer expects the assertion to pass because the timeout was set to 10 seconds. However, `cy.get()` finds the element immediately (it exists), and then `.should('not.exist')` retries for only 4 seconds (the default) before failing. The developer is confused — the spinner IS gone at 7s, but the test failed at 4s. WHY: the `{ timeout }` option on `cy.get()` controls how long it takes to *find* the element — not how long the assertion chain retries. To retry the assertion chain, attach the timeout to the assertion itself: `cy.get('[data-cy="loading-spinner"]').should('not.exist', { timeout: 10000 })` or use `cy.get('[data-cy="loading-spinner"]', { timeout: 10000 }).should('not.exist')` — actually this DOES work because `.should()` inherits the `cy.get()` timeout when chained directly. The correct fix is to understand that `cy.get(..., {timeout}).should(...)` does propagate the timeout to the `.should()` retry loop, but `.then()` followed by `expect()` does not. Verify the chain is `.get().should()` not `.get().then(($el) => expect(...))`.
